@@118476786 <h> In My City Is Yours at the Art Gallery of NSW , Beijing artist Cao Fei offers uncanny visions of lost futures and melancholy presents . By Patrick Lau . <h> Cao Fei 's My City Is Yours at the Art Gallery of NSW <p> A few months ago , in the food court at an airport , I met a robot . It was 2am or 4am , my destination was a continent away beyond the date line and I was very tired . Most of the airport was quiet and dark in the way only cavernous , busy spaces -- cathedrals , factories -- can be , but the food court was still chaotic . <p> There was a purported system : diners were meant to leave their trays at one of several collection points and the robots would come and take them to the kitchen to be cleared . Inevitably , it did n't work . <p> Chairs and luggage were left blocking aisles , or the trays were dumped at the wrong angle , or there were just too many people moving around or slumped over tables for the robots to handle . The robots kept bumping into each other and apologising . As I got up to leave , I felt one nudging me from behind . It had a cutesy emoji face painted on its chrome shell and was smeared with coffee and hoisin . " I 'm lost , " it pleaded . " Can you help me ? " <p> Cao Fei 's exhibition , My City Is Yours , is speckled with moments and encounters like this : uncanny , unruly technology ; warped time ; the litter of human culture and industrial activity ; the weird hubs where it all takes place . Currently running at the Art Gallery of NSW , the artist and her team have taken advantage of the space offered by the Naala Badu building to construct a mini city that 's as boisterous as a mall or market . <p> The exhibition forms part of the Sydney International Art Series 2024-25 across the summer , which also encompasses Magritte at AGNSW and Julie Mehretu at the MCA . Like Magritte , Cao is interested in transforming the everyday into something shocking with a change of perspective or position . Like Mehretu , she uses explosive colour to express abstract and even unspeakable truths . Unlike those exhibitions , however , at My City Is Yours I played an arcade game about being a delivery person , while on a video behind me journalist and author Benjamin Law gyrated . <p> It 's the first time Cao Fei has held a major solo exhibition in Sydney , though much has been made of her personal connection . Her home town , Guangzhou , is twinned with Sydney and Cao 's late sister , Cao Xiaoyun ( 1971-2022 ) , was a Sydneysider and herself an artist . Some of her works are presented here . <p> The video and multimedia artworks are each hosted in their own installation , which reproduce or invent spaces relevant to the work . The exhibition concerns itself with cities during periods of transition -- Guangzhou , Sydney , Beijing -- as well as virtual representations and manifestations of urban geography . <p> The earliest work here is Cosplayers ( 2004 ) , a film that encompasses much of the themes and techniques that are refined in the later pieces . The short video presents young Guangzhou inhabitants -- the first generation raised on the internet -- playing fantastical characters amid the churning landscape of a city partly torn down , partly under construction . It 's a surrealist piece mixed with an unglamorous examination of how fantasy is built . <p> The exhibition space is folded , so the exhibits run up against one another and overlap . Exit the demolished Hongxia cinema ( Nova , 2019 ) and find yourself in a much-missed Cantonese restaurant in Sydney ( Goodbye , Marigold , 2024 ) . Tour a factory floor and through the next door be slung into space , or the multiverse , or the metaverse . Visit the quiet domesticity of a small living room and travel through time . Sit in a foam pit . <p> My City Is Yours is about the experience of being there , as much as the works themselves . It explores digital geography and virtual reality but reminds the viewer that they 're piloting a body in meatspace , not a ghost in a machine . <p> In this , the exhibition deliberately both rewards and challenges your attention span . Some of the video works are lengthy , and the collective run time is more than 10 hours . Nova , a fantastical romance about Sino-Soviet cooperation , transhumanism and lost timelines , is a full-length feature film at 97 minutes . Asia One ( 2018 ) , at 63 minutes , does n't rush the unfolding of its narrative about China 's transition to a high-technology industrial society , via the surveilled lives of workers in an automated warehouse . <p> They 're worth slowing down and spending time with , and repeat visits are warranted . It 's possible to spend hours with the hypertextual Hongxia suite alone , for instance : you 've seen the film about the building , now try the VR experience . <p> But around each corner , the alluring stimulus of hyperpop music and garish bubble-gum neon are constantly drawing and repelling the viewer onwards , battering them through the exhibit like a pinball through a machine . It 's loud , it 's bustling . It 's dim but lights blare , as in a dark arcade or casino , and the soundtracks of various works intrude on one another and compete for your attention . My City Is Yours calls attention to the experience of multi-multi-media consumption -- scrolling TikTok while streaming Netflix -- and how unnatural and quotidian our cyborg existences are . <p> The works are both playful and melancholy , sometimes simultaneously . La Town ( 2014 ) presents a surrealist apocalypse of a cityscape , inspired by Resnais ' 1959 Hiroshima mon amour and constructed using rail scale miniature models . Narrators muse on decadence , doom and decay over footage of plastic figurines that are frozen in time . <p> A section devoted to RMB City ( 2007-2012 ) , Cao 's virtual metropolis , celebrates the freedom and potential that digital mediation can produce . Built using the faddish Second Life , an early attempt at a metaverse platform , RMB City boasted " a running economy , manifesto , and mayor " , and hosted artists and architects , elections and auctions , dance parties and digital love affairs . The city and its inhabitants were all watched over with loving grace by Cao 's avatar , China Tracy . During much of the pre-Olympics Beijing boom , Cao spent up to 12 hours a day fiddling in cyberspace while the city remade itself outside her window . One of the works here , i.Mirror ( 2007 ) , documents a flirtation and relationship developed during that time . It explores the freedom to represent oneself as whoever you 'd like to be in an internet relationship . <p> China Tracy later had a digital baby , which is as innocent or sinister as you 'd like it to be . Technology in these works can produce community or atomisation , connection or alienation : none is inevitable . <p> Cao is obsessed with the hauntologies of forgotten digital and physical futures , of suburbs built and bulldozed and technologies that promised a better hereafter . The retro-futurist nostalgia that runs throughout the exhibition ties in to Cao 's interest both in bending time and space , and in the material causes and consequences of techno-industrial culture . If you want an image of the future , picture a man moving boxes around a logistics fulfilment centre , forever . <p> Whose Utopia ( 2006 ) poses questions to migrant workers at a light-bulb factory in the Pearl River Delta : " What do you hope for the future ? How do you feel about the factory ? " The 20-minute film juxtaposes hypnotising footage of humans and robots assembling light bulbs with dreamlike performances of factory-floor dance routines , followed by lingering portraiture . <p> Goodbye , Marigold re-creates the Chinatown yum cha restaurant using original furnishings , while Golden Wattle ( 2024 ) memorialises Cao Xiaoyun in an intimate living-room setting , with a series of interviews running on the television . Both are deeply affecting visitations from the past . Duotopia Vol 1 ( 2022 ) , on the other hand , puts a video about a kind of floating octopus skyscraper on the ceiling and calls it Italian Futurism . <p> The works revel in lost possibilities , invented tenses , the consolations and consequences of Hello Kitty kitsch . What Philip K. Dick called " kipple " -- the self-reproducing detritus of material cultures -- is sprinkled throughout . Old posters , packaging and broken components , the stuff that accumulates and propagates itself in the corners of cities and glitchy software and memories , are sometimes around the fringes of the frame , sometimes in focus . <p> Here are the futures that got away : the grand narratives of linear time and progress , the dreams of flying cars and robot servants . Or the prosaic belief that an invisible hand or command economy will guide us inexorably to a utopian destination . What we have instead , Cao says , is a playground ; a collection of clutter that the artist and the viewer can choose to make horrifying or joyous . <p> Cao Fei : My City Is Yours is showing at AGNSW , Sydney , until April 13 . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 4 , 2024 as " Unruly utopias " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take time , to doggedly hold to account politicians and the political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . In a country with a concentration of media ownership unlike anything else in the world , it is vitally important . Your subscription helps make it possible . 
@@118479412 <h> Students were unfazed at a $40,000 HECS debt . Years on , the reality has sunk in <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> When the Morrison government hiked arts degree fees in 2021 , it was labelled by critics as an ideological attack on the humanities . If the aim was to discourage young people from studying arts , it did not seem to work -- immediately at least . <p> Students flocked to arts degrees during the pandemic , seemingly unfazed by the idea of a $40,000 HECS debt . But almost four years on , alarm bells are ringing . Enrolments have fallen dramatically to a 10-year low , humanities departments have faced brutal cuts and scholars harbour deep concerns for the future of once-thriving faculties . <p> Whether the humanities in Australia are the victim of an anti- " woke " culture war -- or , as conservative critics contend , suffering from self-inflicted irrelevance -- remains contested . <p> Arts students Layla Wang and Tanisha Kurlekar at the University of Sydney.Credit : Janie Barrett <p> In common with many of her fellow arts students , 20-year-old Layla Wang has been on the receiving end of more than a few diminishing remarks about her choice of degree . " You see so many jokes on TikTok like , ' Oh , you do an arts degree , have fun being a barista ' , " she says . " That sort of stigma has been around for decades . " <p> But Wang , president of Sydney University 's Arts Students ' Society , has no regrets about her choice , saying her studies so far have sharpened her critical thinking and allowed her to see and understand the world in a more nuanced way . And the study body is diverse with a range of political views and perspectives , despite stereotypes that suggest otherwise . <p> " I think it 's really important to be respectful , but saying that arts degrees are merely a form of ' woke indoctrination ' is an extremely poor perspective , " Wang says . <p> Advertisement <p> Professor Simon Marginson , a former Melbourne University academic and now higher education expert at Oxford University , says the anti-humanities line is getting tougher and more critical . He says there is a clear student flight away from the humanities in Britain and Australia , a trend that is also emerging in the US . <p> In the face of falling demand and as universities face funding pressures , humanities and some social sciences faculties have been first in the firing line . " But the evidence that comes through is there are a bunch of students who are really passionate and committed to humanities , " he says . " And they defy their families and their friends and do it anyway . And they actually do OK in the labour market . " <p> In practice , the legislation meant students wanting to study classical subjects such as history , politics and philosophy as well as communications faced fee increases of 113 per cent . It immediately increased the price of standard three-year arts degrees to above $40,000 ; next year , the cost will exceed $50,000 . But not all humanities subjects were penalised . English and languages subjects , for example , moved to the cheapest category because they were seen as areas of skills shortages . <p> Despite the fee hikes ' intent of diverting students into STEM and more " vocational " degrees such as engineering , teaching and nursing , there was no immediate drop in demand . In fact , demand for society and culture courses -- which include arts and communication degrees but also law -- peaked during the pandemic , with 121,293 new domestic enrolments in society and culture courses in 2020 and 116,823 in 2021 . <p> Advertisement <p> The most recent federal Education Department data tells a different story , revealing a dramatic decline in society and culture subjects since the pandemic . Just 97,313 new students started the courses in 2023 , the lowest number in 10 years and a 20 per cent decrease on 2020 . Overall demand for university has softened since 2020 , but at a slower rate than the decline of society and culture enrolments . <p> The reasons for the decline in humanities students , Marginson suspects , are many . On the one hand , tabloids and governments are pushing an ever more vicious anti-humanities narrative . <p> " It 's part of the culture wars , the perception that humanities students are more left wing and critical and so on , " he says . " Those who are bearing down on the universities are saying they are too liberal , which is very much the Republican line in the US and coming through in the UK now on the critical right . " <p> He says there is also a broader cultural shift towards more utilitarian and vocationally focused degrees . As the world emerged from the pandemic and cost of living pressures began to bite , people became more focused on immediate employability and cost-of-living pressures . Marginson believes larger and established universities -- among them Sydney and Melbourne universities and , in Britain , Oxford and Cambridge -- will retain strong humanities programs . He says the big cuts have begun at mid-tier universities and will continue . <p> Australian National University higher education academic Professor Andrew Norton says humanities ' enrolments were declining before Job-ready Graduates . " I think it 's probably partly to do with the fact that students just do n't read as much any more , " he says . He says any rise in arts enrolments that occurred during the pandemic was likely linked to the job market and the countercyclical nature of the university sector . " If there are fewer jobs , people study , " Norton says . <p> And , if anything , the recent decline in arts may be more precipitous than the data suggests . Norton says law subjects , which are included in society and culture cluster , are more resilient due to their more clearly vocational nature and may to some extent be masking the downward trend in the arts . " Law has had some volatility but has never entered a major decline like humanities subjects . " <p> Advertisement <h> Faculties cut <p> Last month , staff at Wollongong University were shocked by the scope of proposed cuts : 90 full-time academic roles in 25 disciplines were being made redundant as part of a major overhaul of degrees . History , foreign languages , geography and mathematics are among departments facing major cuts . For foreign languages , the proposal was brutal . The university wants to wipe out its foreign language and linguistics department altogether . <p> Languages and linguistics discipline leader at the university , Dr Rowena Ward , says the university regards the department as unviable because of declining enrolment trends -- a claim she rejects . Ward says the study of languages in Australia is generally not valued as it should be , and some people even believe apps like Duolingo are interchangeable with a university-level course . <p> Loading <p> Languages are labour-intensive and require a lot more face-to-face learning time than other subjects , she says . They are funded at a high rate by the federal government , which makes them among the cheapest subjects for students to take . " Recent upper management is so focused on dollar signs they 're not really looking at things in a broader sense , " she says . <p> University of Wollongong interim vice chancellor and president John Dewar says the draft proposal is necessary for the long-term viability of the university and to address a $35 million drop in revenue this year . <p> A spokesman said the proposed closure of the languages department came despite significant efforts to improve viability , for example through a compulsory language minor in the bachelor of international studies . <p> Advertisement <p> The National Tertiary Education Union says the degree overhauls will massively reduce subject choices and flexibility , with students forced to take eight generic subjects and to limit choices within majors . <p> Wollongong University humanities academic and branch president Fiona Probyn-Rapsey cites " cutting Languages , cutting the only subject at the university that focuses on feminism , cutting history and areas of environmental humanities , climate change and sustainability " . <p> " These are all the areas that empower students and enact the social licence that university managements so desperately seek , " the professor says . " The outcomes are perverse , but they reflect a general hollowing out of education as a political good and community right . " <p> Australian Catholic University , under former vice chancellor Greg Craven , embarked on a bold plan to strengthen its humanities research . Between 2016 and 2020 , it set up Melbourne-based specialised research institutions and programs in philosophy , theology and history . <p> Australian Historical Association president Professor Michelle Arrow , a Macquarie University academic , says the ACU cuts were a turning point for humanities in Australia . She says the current mood among history academics is bleak , with a general feeling that the sector is in decline . <p> " It 's pretty tragic , " she says . " There 's long been a sense among university management that humanities research does n't bring in as much money as science research does . And we do n't frame humanities discoveries in the same way as we would STEM . " <p> Advertisement <p> Arrow believes the publicity about the high cost of arts degrees is starting to affect student choice . The cost , she says , is especially worrying parents , who are concerned children will carry a large debt without viable job prospects . " What Job-ready Graduates did was pick up on an insidious stereotype that arts and humanities are not job-ready , which does n't actually correlate with the data , " she says . <p> Professor Michelle Arrow . <p> Arrow believes sandstone universities will continue with humanities degrees . But cuts will be acutely felt in the regions . " We will really end up with a two-tier system ... if you can afford to , and you are in a city , you 'll get access to a good arts and humanities education , but if you 're in the regions you wo n't , " she says . " That 's something that we should be concerned about . " <h> A war within <p> But not everyone thinks politics or broader social forces have caused a decline in the once thriving world of the humanities . <p> John Carroll , retired academic sociologist and Emeritus Professor at La Trobe University in Melbourne , blames the decline on the politicisation of humanities and advocates for a return to a pure study of the classics . <p> " The culture wars came out of this steady loss of nerve among the majority of academics teaching in the humanities , " he says . " The basic task is to take up the best works of the culture and introduce students to them , including ways of thinking and analysing and writing . <p> Loading <p> " Since the 1960s , I think the humanities have steadily become politicised and have lost ... touch with their basic mission . They 've turned to political action . It 's trying to change the world , which is not the job of humanities : it is to train students to understand themselves and the world they live in . " <p> Carroll says the content taught at universities has become too boring for students , who want to study the classics but are forced to analyse them through the " imagined political bias " of the authors . <p> " If a student is doing an arts degree studying English , they 'll find it very difficult to find courses on say , Shakespeare and Jane Austen , and they 'll find that most are politicised on feminism or colonialism or whatever the political fad of the moment is , " he says . <p> " I do n't think there 's anything wrong with those studies , but that 's not the fundament of what humanities should be doing . <p> " As a result , it 's hard for students going into university to find things that interest them . " <p> Carroll is an advocate for the controversial Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation , funded by a multimillion-dollar bequest from late healthcare magnate Paul Ramsay . <p> It funds degrees , with generous scholarships , in the great works of Western Civilisation , featuring generous scholarships and small class sizes conducive to in depth and dogged discussions . <p> But the bequest led to a culture war , with failed negotiations to take the program to the Australian National University and Sydney University , amid concerns about academic autonomy and accusations that it was a training centre for the next generation of right-wing ideologues . <p> Eventually , the centre reached agreements to roll out the degrees at Australian Catholic University , Wollongong University and Queensland University . <p> Loading <p> Carroll thinks that if there is a future for humanities in Australia , it 's through the Ramsay Centre 's approach of going back to the basics of teaching the classics . <p> " I think it 's a grim period in the short to medium term of humanities . Faculties in Australia are withering away , almost disappearing , " he said . <p> " But history goes through cycles ... people want to understand themselves and the societies in which they live . And if they 're going to do that , they need the humanities . <p> " It 's a basic need that will come back . " <p> Arrow does not agree that Australian universities have rejected the conventional core of humanities scholarship , with topics such as the foundations of Australian democracy still fundamental to curriculums . <p> " But , of course , you ca n't understand that story without understanding the people it historically excluded as well , " she says . " I do n't think we can return it to just studying 10 Great Books , and that 's all we do , but there is definitely room for that kind of thing . A pluralism of approaches is always really important . " <p> She thinks the humanities have been squeezed at both ends of the political spectrum . The Liberals " were very anti humanities even though a lot of them have arts degrees " , she says . On the Labor side , " there 's a really instrumentalist view of higher education , which is very much about training people for jobs in the workplace not helping people expand their understanding of arts and culture and humanities " . <h> The $50,000 arts degree <p> From next year , the cost of the average arts degree is set to exceed $50,000 -- a direct result of the Morrison government increases . The impact of these on student choice is still up for debate . Most agree that broader societal views about humanities , as well as a post-COVID-19 focus on vocational pathways , have played into the decline in enrolments . <p> First-year arts student Tanisha Kurleka , 19 , does n't think that the high cost of the degree is much of a demotivating factor -- especially at a university with prestige value . " I do n't think the fee discourages people , especially when you start straight from high school , " the Sydney University international relations student says . " But how other people view arts and look down on it does , that might discourage them . " <p> She said her studies had changed her view of the world -- but not necessarily how people might think . " I know I was super ' woke ' when I came to uni , but it helped me see other sides to debates and the spectrum , " she says . <p> Kurleka and Wang want to study law eventually , a key factor being the clearer professional pathways from that degree . <p> Western Sydney University vice chancellor George Williams believes the Morrison-era reforms are now having an impact on student choice , but not in the way it was intended . " What we are seeing is students who are deciding not to study at all , they 're not coming to university , " he says . " We 've seen a very significant decline in undergraduate enrolments . " <p> Loading <p> Williams says he is concerned about the decline in humanities education and the cuts universities had made as a result . In a world full of misinformation , he believes the critical thinkers humanities create and nurture are more important than ever . <p> " This is the type of education we really need at the moment , " he says . " Humanities is one of the most important building blocks of a prosperous , fair inclusive country . <p> " I think in the world in which we live things like history and philosophy are vital skills . We need to understand where we 've come from to understand where we are today . " <p> Williams says the messaging of the Job-ready Graduates scheme was clear and damaging . " It says , as a community we do n't believe students should be studying this in the same way , we do n't value it , and we 're actively asking students to do something else , " he says . " That 's a powerful political symbol . It 's wrong , and needs to be called out , but it 's undeniable . "

@@118479986 <p> More struggling West Australian families than ever are having to make the choice between paying their electricity bill and putting food on the table . <p> Labor , in its first Budget after coming to office in 2017 , doubled the fixed daily supply charge for electricity users from 48.6 cents to 94.9 cents , increasing an average electricity bill by 10 per cent . <p> The increase has cost the average household $1352 and was an unfair and punitive change which disproportionately impacted working families , pensioners , and vulnerable West Australians , who could not mitigate it even with reduced usage . <p> Last week , I committed a WA Liberal Government to reversing this unfair increase because only a change to the fundamentals of how we charge people for electricity will provide meaningful , long-term , sustainable relief . <p> It 's a structural reform that gives families control over their energy costs into the future . <p> On the broader energy stage , Labor 's reckless plan to rip both coal and then gas from the State 's energy mix , without renewable generation and storage to replace it , will lead to electricity shortages and rampant price increases . <p> The inevitable cost rises associated with this already faltering energy plan will only serve to push more families to the financial brink . <p> The Liberal Opposition knows we need a feasible , long-term energy policy that will deliver transition to carbon neutral power generation while keeping the lights on and air conditioners running at a price families can afford . <p> While the Cook Labor Government will close almost 1000MW of baseload generation over the next six years , a WA Liberal Government would build 300MW of new gas generation capacity , and boost gas supply in the Dampier to Bunbury Natural Gas Pipeline so there is enough affordable energy to keep WA families from sitting in the dark . <p> The whizzing wind-powered pinwheels and twinkling solar-powered lights have been falling off the Cook Labor Government 's fantasy energy policy for some time . <p> While it was always a cobbled-together set of vote-saving intentions driven by Labor 's vested union and green interests , recent developments have left the policy both rudderless and toothless . <p> Rudderless since energy experts and analysts began earlier this year warning of both gas shortages and electricity blackouts under the policy . <p> The Australian Energy Market Operator foreshadowed WA could be facing blackouts as early as 2025 if the Cook Government continues to rush headlong into mothballing all coal generation by 2030 without operating viable alternative sources . <p> EnergyQuest chief executive Rick Wilkinson also predicted the conditions that led to Sydney gas prices jumping by 43 per cent in June this year could be repeated in WA by 2028 . <p> Mr Wilkinson said a shortage of gas would be especially damaging because WA is more reliant on the fuel to cut carbon emissions than other parts of the country . <p> And toothless since the Cook Government decided to walk away from its own Climate Change Act , which would have enshrined a commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2050 and a 2030 target for State government emissions . <p> Even Cook Government Minister Reece Whitby admitted his Government would need the impetus of the legislation to reach its target . <p> " This Government recognises that legislated targets . . . are the best way to mobilise the capital required for the net zero transition , " Mr Whitby said . <p> Both the Cook Government and WA Liberal energy policies commit to carbon-neutral electricity for WA by 2050 , however , the pathways to and the likelihood of success for the two policies could not be more divergent . <p> Labor is also using its sugar hits , like the latest $350 electricity rebate , to gloss over the behind-the-scenes shambles -- at least until after the March election next year . <p> West Australians should be in no doubt there will be no such largess once the State election is behind us . <p> A WA Liberal Government will continue with the current plan for 4400MW of lithium battery storage and 810MW of wind generation but we will also extend the lifespan of Collie A and Muja Units 7 and 8 coal-fired power stations , until new gas generation is built . <p> We will maintain coal use where necessary , until gas generation is ready to replace it , and then use gas to take WA to a high-technology , low-emissions future . <p> The WA Liberals are committed to meeting our target of being carbon neutral by 2050 -- but it will not come at a cost of reliability or affordability for WA families .

@@118480983 <p> Andrew van der Westhuyzen , one of Australia 's pre-eminent creatives , has announced the launch of his debut book Cabal , the first in a series of illustrated science-fiction short story works . <p> Marking the culmination of two decades of illustrative and writing exploration of cli-fi survivalism , technological advancement and a uniquely visualised world , Cabal documents a thought-provoking series that pays homage to Van der Westhuyzen 's passion for nature and the environment . <p> Less of a traditional graphic novel and more illustrated short story , Cabal is a meandering journey , both a provocation and celebration of technology and human invention and its relationship to the living world . <p> The story was born through Van der Westhuyzen 's childhood spent in nature in New Zealand 's countryside and a move to the city , a transition that sparked conflict between a love for fast moving innovation and the remoteness of being in the environment . It was this feeling that spawned bringing both ideas together through a survival story , one where technology and invention helps and hinders in a natural setting . Through the Sci-fi genre , he has communicated the tale through the bending of typical narrative rules . <p> On a desperate mission to establish a habitable future for civilization , sabotage strands a group of scientists on their would-be new home world . There , they find themselves at the mercy of L1V , the AI sent to ready the planet for human presence . <p> " I am incredibly proud to bring the Cabal world into the real world and breathe life into this 20-year odyssey . Collider has provided me with a platform to experiment with a visual journey and this is only the first chapter in a much more extensive series . The issues of the day make this the ultimate time to launch Cabal , and I hope it will serve as a stimulus to provoke readers to consider new ideas at a time where climate change and nature are colliding with the rapid pace of technology , part bettering and part marring our world , " said Van der Westhuyzen . <p> With a background of over two decades in design and animation , Van der Westhuyzen 's passion for exploring the interconnected mediums culminates in the creation of the Cabal world . Over the past two decades , he has won a number of major awards for a variety of projects on environmental issues such as One Show Award and a Clio Award for The Plastic Forecast with Minderoo Foundation , and a D&amp;AD wooden pencil for carbon neutral book design for Belong . Van der Westhuyen has been involved in many large scale international projects , notably a two minute animated take-over of Times Square in New York City for the Nelson Mandela Foundation . <p> He has also advised on concept and production design on a number of award-winning short-film projects including Daniel Askill 's We Have Decided Not To Die and his recent short film , Universal Machine where Andrew consulted extensively for the design of the android character . <p> Cabal is Van der Westhuyzen 's first book , drawing on years of creative direction , campaign and design sensibilities . @@118481031 <p> Former UK cabinet secretary Lord Gus O'Donnell has called on elected officials to engage in sensible debate about what effective government represents . <p> The self-described former ' chief blob ' of the UK civil service ( poking fun at a derogatory term , ' blob ' , that the ruling class used to refer to top officials of Whitehall ) told an audience at the Blavatnik School of Government this week that , as the demand on bureaucrats increased , it was becoming more difficult to monitor how well they were performing . <p> " I was able to spend the last year interviewing current cabinet secretaries around the world for the Global Government Forum ... and it was quite apparent we 're all facing the same sorts of problems -- climate change , ageing -- basically , people demand better and better public services and want to pay less , " O'Donnell said . <p> " On top of that , there are issues like fake news and trust . Of course , as we kind of grapple with all of that , what civil services are really looking for is ' Can we have some data and evidence on who 's doing well and who 's not ? ' , and ' Can we compare each other ? ' <p> O'Donnell made his remarks at the launch of the inaugural Index of Public Administration , benchmarking the performance of 120 civil services around the world . <p> The index relied on comparing available data from 17 various sources to rank the civil services using 82 metrics across key areas : strategy and leadership , public policy , national delivery , and processes and people . <p> Singapore ranked in overall first place with an index score of 0.85 , followed by Norway ( 0.84 ) , Canada ( 0.83 ) , Denmark ( 0.83 ) , Finland ( 0.82 ) , the UK ( 0.80 ) , New Zealand ( 0.80 ) , Australia ( 0.79 ) , Spain ( 0.78 ) , Estonia ( 0.78 ) , France ( 0.78 ) and the US ( 0.78 ) . <p> Of the index 's overall top five civil services , Denmark ranks in the top 10 for 12 of the 16 themes measured , Norway for 10 themes , Canada and Singapore for 9 themes each and Finland in the top 10 for 8 of the 16 themes . <p> UK mandarin and economist Lord O'Donnell said the index allowed other civil services to look at what their peers were doing well and , where appropriate , " steal ideas with pride " . <p> In a context where the demand for bureaucracies to do more with less was ever increasing , efforts to improve faster and in more ways that one were vital , he said . <p> " Think about the way the world 's changing -- just in the UK , we 've had COVID where the state has suddenly taken over , telling us when we can go out , what we wear , furlough schemes , a massive injection of money -- the state is doing a lot more and intervening a lot more , " O'Donnell said . <p> " And take climate change for example -- we have a global market failure without a global carbon tax . Markets are n't going to solve this on their own , so we need the state to do stuff , and the state needs to get better at providing better public services . Part of that is digitisation , part of that is being better at understanding the behavioural stuff , but we desperately need evidence to achieve it . " <p> While the topic was worthy of debate , Davis said comparative data to show how public services compared to similar nations would help demonstrate what worked best and how to improve government performance using evidence . <p> " With an index like this -- then you can drill down to the proof , " Davis said . <p> " If public trust in the public sector is high , what are they doing there that 's built that ? If we can show that a particular country is very good at a type of service , at procurement , or one of the things that we would like to do well , what can we learn to improve ? <p> " It 's actually going to play into , potentially , what is a very consequential debate going on right now about the role of the public sector , " he said . <p> Shortly after the Blavatnik index was released , Australia 's Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher delivered her 2024 APS reform update in Canberra . The speech has become an annual event to address the government workforce and remain accountable to the Albanese government 's reform agenda , which Labor took to the 2022 election . <p> Ahead of a looming federal election next year , the exact date of which remains unknown , Gallagher said she felt moved to use the platform of her annual address to the APS to defend the work done to rebuild a decade of cuts to the public service . <p> " The opposition has been clear about their plans . I 'll give you a quote : ' There will be 36,000 public servants that will go . ' The shadow treasurer Angus Taylor describes the recent investments in the APS as ' unnecessary spending ' , " Gallagher said . <p> " History has shown with job cuts of the size that are being talked about , we know that it will be the Australian people who pay the price in the end , one way or another . " <p> Gallagher described the Opposition 's demonisation of the public service and attacks on workforce size ( which has grown by 16.2% since June 20 , 2022 , from 159,469 to 185,343 public servants overall ) as part of what she said was a lazy , arrogant and reckless anti-APS campaign . <p> " When the Albanese government commissioned the audit of employment , the results were shocking . For every $4 spent by agencies on departmental purposes , $1 was going to external labour , " Gallagher said . <p> " Australia was n't just losing money under the Coalition government 's arrangements , we were losing the skills and the knowledge that Australians count on . " <p> " The Albanese government knew that to deliver better services , we needed to fundamentally change how we employ people by starting to create secure jobs with 8,800 public servants now doing the work that was previously outsourced , because you ca n't build capability when your workforce is constantly changing , " she added . <p> One of the four pillars of Labor 's APS reform agenda was to " rebuild capability " by rebalancing the mix of public servants and external labour , with $4 billion in savings from reduced consultant spending made since 2022 . <p> Another $500 million in prospective consultant spend has been identified by agencies as work that can be brought back in-house via the strategic commissioning framework . <p> AGC 's work has included projects in strategic policy and organisational transformation across major departments like the Department of Health and Aged Care , the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations , as well as with smaller agencies like the Mint and the Net Zero Economy Agency . <p> " In just a little over 12 months , the AGC has displaced over an estimated $3.6 million in external consulting spend -- and it is growing quickly , starting with 20 staff in its first year , " Gallagher said . <p> " Demand has exceeded supply and they are now on track to have 40 staff by the end of their second year . Picture : Shutterstock <p> As founder of the Mediterranean Conservation Society , Kizilkaya fostered an innovative plan , training local fishers as marine rangers to recover the waterways . He challenged some of Turkey 's Michelin-starred chefs to come to the party by expanding their menus with the tropical fish that have invaded the Mediterranean , via the Suez Canal , as water has warmed through climate change . Eating the problem has helped reduce the threat to the ecosystem posed by fish that prey on native species and overgraze vegetation with few predators . <p> One of these invaders is swimming past us now . On a plate . It is a lion fish ( Asian baligi ) reimagined as a lemony ceviche . The waiter bows , offers deliciously dripping morsels , then Kizilkaya continues his story . <p> Street view in Bodrum . Picture : Shutterstock <p> That pot " created 2000 years before Jesus was born " was found at a sea depth of less than 50 metres but the world remains oblivious to the discovery . Hoisted from a sandy grave , it is now undergoing conservation , at Bodrum Museum of Archaeology . " The shallow waters of the Aegean Sea in front of us are not protected , " Kizilkaya whispers . " We must keep this secret until there is more excavation because people anchor their boats and dance above the waves in this bay . " <p> They 're dancing on the terrace now , decorous people swaying to the ebb and flow of the tide , falling in love with the tiny village of Turkbuku at the northern end of Bodrum peninsula that , until recently , had changed so little . The area slipped into obscurity through much of the 20th century but emerged with fresh , post-pandemic energy to become one of the most glamorous spots in Turkey called , rather dubiously , " the next St Tropez " . The luxury hotels and private villas built on steep hillsides have become a magnet for the jet-setting super-rich . <p> A feast is laid at Macakizi Hotel . <p> I expected this Turkish Riviera to have been squandered by rapacious tourism but instead find only seduction . Sleepy neighbours Bozburun and Datca are only accessible from the sea while at Macakizi , and further along the Turkbuku foreshore , you can still eat fish at a table with your feet in the water . <p> Home-cooking is a way of life in Turkey . The wisdom of good hospitality was encapsulated by Ayla Emiroglu , a kind of celebrity in her own right , who opened the first incarnation of Macakizi in Bodrum town centre in the mid-1970s . @@118525130 <h> 11 artists you must see in the 11th Asia Pacific Triennial <h> Save articles for later <p> The Asia Pacific Triennial is Brisbane 's -- some would say Australia 's -- biggest contribution to contemporary world art . Now in its fourth decade , there is nothing else quite like it . <p> As some indication as to how big a deal it is , the show will be travelling to London 's Victoria and Albert Museum in 2026 , a somewhat ironic achievement given how loudly colonialism is decried in many of the artworks . <p> This year 's APT explores themes of history , crisis , war , empathy , social action and Indigenous peoples , as well as the healing of culture and of the environment . Works range from hand-woven traditional textiles to high-tech video installations . <p> More than 500 pieces by more than 200 artists are on display at the Queensland Art Gallery and Gallery of Modern Art . Nations across Asia and the Pacific are represented , including , for the first time , Saudi Arabia , Timor-Leste and Uzbekistan . <p> The family-friendly exhibition is entirely free , but potentially daunting . With that in mind , this masthead went along to pick out 11 artists whose work is the most evocative , eye-catching , impactful , and , to our eyes at least , fun . <p> These artists are in no way the only ones worth checking out , but they offer a window into what is a large and imposing show . <h> 1 . Kawita Vatanajyankur , Thailand <p> Vatanajyankur 's video works are hilarious and chilling . They are filmed performance pieces in which her body becomes a tool , or part of a machine : rubbing her face on a plate like a dish brush , rotating like a loom , or measuring rice as a set of scales . The metaphor of the exploitation of workers in the consumer economy could not be plainer . <p> Advertisement <p> Her 2024 work The Machine Ghost in the Human Shell , made in collaboration with MIT scientist Pat Pataranutaporn , pairs her body with an AI ' ghost ' figure to explore the endgame of AI in turning people into mere automatons. <h> 2 . Brett Graham , Aotearoa ( New Zealand ) <p> Graham 's nine-metre black tower Cease Tide of Wrong-Doing looms in the entranceway to the APT inside the GOMA . It 's based on the sacred niu poles that existed during the New Zealand wars over sovereignty ( 1845-1872 ) . His work looks back at colonisation using monumental sculptural forms . <p> O'Pioneer is a three-metre high white turret decorated like a wedding cake . It 's in reference to the wedding of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert in 1840 -- the same year as the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi -- implying the colonial violence upholding traditions of Empire . <h> 3 . Haus Yuriyal , Papua New Guinea <p> Greeting you at the back entrance of the QAG is a vibrant pavilion decorated with shield ( kuman ) designs and 27 dangling string bags ( including one in tribute to the Brisbane Broncos ) . Haus Yuriyal is a large collective of artists in the Jiwaka and Simbu provinces of Papua New Guinea , and this ' haus ' represents their meeting place . <h> 4 . Zac Langdon-Pole , Aotearoa ( New Zealand ) <p> Zac Langdon-Pole 's Another World Inside This One , 2024 -- an axe with a sapling carved from the handle.Credit : Nick Dent <p> Our modern life is a confluence of historical accidents , a confusing puzzle , and so are the large-scale works of Langdon-Pole . They combine different jigsaw puzzles into massive and disorienting wholes . Using more than 64,000 pieces in total , the works mash up different 19-century paintings and space images from the Hubble telescope . <p> The Kiwi artist is also exhibiting a sculpture titled Another World Inside This One . It 's an axe with the wooden handle carved into the shape of a small tree . Inspired by the notion of ' Captain Cook 's axe ' , it 's a surreal object that evokes ideas of conquest -- both of the natural world and of Indigenous peoples . <h> 5 . Nomin Bold and Ochirbold Ayurzana , Mongolia <p> More than 1500 cast-metal skulls form a startling ' curtain ' at GOMA . Some of the skulls have two eye sockets , some have three , and some have just one . The work is both a reminder of mortality ( or memento mori ) and a gesture towards Buddhist ideas of the human , the godly ( with three eyes ) and the monstrous ( with one ) . <p> The artists are from Mongolia , and their work , titled Life Cup , represents " the loss of unity with nature in the process of the country 's urbanisation " , according to co-curator Reuben Keenan. <h> 6 . Dawn Ng , Singapore <p> This video piece in a darkened room shows time-lapse footage of a 60-kilogram block of ice melting . The artist , Dawn Ng , has infused the ice with pigments , making the melting process very beautiful to watch . <p> Ng took inspiration from images of the earth from space . You can read a warning about climate change into it if you like ( the title , The Earth Is an Hourglass , would suggest that ) , but the overwhelming effect is otherworldly and sublime . <p> Piguras Davao , The Silent Witness ( detail ) , 2019 . Piguras Davao , Philippines <p> Ten artists worked on a monumental oil on canvas , 12 metres long , that combines creation myths , history , references to western art , and the Star Wars saga . In making them she deliberately left out the ingredient of hay , which means the bricks are cracking . <p> Awartani 's parents are Palestinian , and her intention is to make us think of war and violence in the Middle East , while also reflecting on the region 's architectural traditions . <h> 10 . Accelerated by Australia 's continued supply of fossil fuels , climate change poses a serious , direct and immediate threat to human and environmental security . In the Pacific and the Torres Strait , rising sea levels caused by climate change threaten to inundate entire islands . <p> Australia has a long and shared history with Pacific island countries and has co-signed legally binding international treaties and agreements , such as the Paris Agreement and the Boe Declaration , pledging action on climate change . <p> Just four days into her new role as Foreign Minister Penny Wong spoke to the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat in Fiji : " Whether it manifests in rising sea levels in Pacific Island countries , or in disastrous bushfires and catastrophic flooding back at home in Australia , we can see that climate change is happening across the Pacific family . " <p> But it is difficult to see how the Albanese Labor Government has succeeded in restoring Australia 's climate leadership , or how it has listened to or acted on Pacific climate priorities . In its first term , the Albanese government has announced the Future Gas Strategy , which locks Australia in for new gas to 2050 and beyond , and has approved seven new coal mines . <p> Australia 's failure to adequately respond to climate concerns is not new or limited to Pacific Island nations . Australia has also failed to address domestic climate concerns . <p> Australia 's climate inaction is having ramifications at home and abroad . Picture Shutterstock <p> At the 2024 Climate Integrity Summit , Torres Strait Island elder Dr Aunty McRose Elu , argued : " Australia 's response to climate change is one of the weakest in the world . Our leaders say they care , but they ignore the scientific evidence and do things that will ensure our communities will go under the water . We are running out of time . " <p> In 2022 , the United Nations Human Rights Committee found that Australia violated Torres Strait Islanders ' rights by failing to protect them from climate change . Attorney-General Mark Dreyfus committed to consider and respond to the UNHRC report " in due course " - as of December 2024 , there has been no formal response . <p> For decades , Pacific Island and Torres Strait Island leaders have articulated their key priorities for climate action with clarity . The previous government 's 2022 Strengthening Australia 's relationships in the Pacific Inquiry acknowledged Pacific Island nations ' deep concern about climate change , and recommended that support for climate change mitigation and adaptation should be a high priority in Australia 's immediate regional assistance program . <p> Despite clear messages from the Pacific , in 2024 , Australia has chosen to conduct another long and resource intensive inquiry into Australia 's response to the priorities of Pacific Island countries and the Pacific region , rather than engage in genuine climate action . <p> Pacific leaders and civil society organisations have consistently advocated for Australia to uphold and fulfil its commitments to listen to and act on warnings of the existential threat of climate change . <p> The Boe Declaration , adopted by the Pacific Islands Forum and Australia in 2018 , is a regional security agreement that acknowledges that " climate change remains the single greatest threat to the livelihoods , security and wellbeing of the peoples of the Pacific " . <p> The Loss and Damage Fund was established at COP28 in 2023 , following decades of Pacific advocacy , to compensate developing states for the climate harms caused by wealthy countries and help them respond to climate impacts . Pacific Island leaders and civil society organisations have called for a significant increase in contributions to the loss and damage fund . At COP29 in Azerbaijan , the Australian government committed just $50 million to the fund - less than 1 per cent of what it allocates to fossil fuel subsidies . <p> In addition , Pacific leaders have advocated for Australia to commit to : The Port Vila Call for a Just Transition to a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific was issued by the governments of Vanuatu , Tuvalu , Tonga , Fiji , Niue and Solomon Islands following a Pacific Islands Forum Economic Ministers Meeting in Suva in 2023 . The Port Vila Call proposes : <p> A fossil fuel-free Pacific and a global , just and equitable phase-out of coal , oil and gas ; <p> New Pacific-tailored development pathways based on 100 per cent renewable energy ; <p> Expanded public and private finance for the just transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy ; <p> Redoubled efforts to reaffirm , strengthen and codify legal obligations with respect to the global phase-out of fossil fuels . <p> The Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty , established in 2019 , aims to " accelerate a transition to renewable energy for everyone , end the expansion of coal , oil and gas , and equitably phase out existing production in keeping with what science shows is needed to address the climate crisis " . The treaty has been signed by Vanuatu , Tuvalu , Fiji , Solomon Islands , Tonga , Niue , Timor-Leste , Antigua and Barbuda , Palau , Colombia , Samoa , Nauru and the Republic of Marshall Islands , and is endorsed by the World Health Organisation and the European Parliament . <p> Despite clear and consistent calls from Pacific neighbours and allies , Australia is showing no signs of a climate course correction : <p> Australia is yet to respond to the UNHRC finding that Australia violated Torres Strait Islanders ' rights by failing to protect them from climate change . <p> Australia has signed the Falepili Union , a security pact which in recognition of " the importance of collective sovereignty , whereby a country 's actions can impact on its neighbours " , will assist people from Tuvalu to migrate to Australia because " we believe the people of Tuvalu deserve the choice to live , study and work elsewhere , as climate change impacts worsen " . Is n't it funny that we are getting that assistance but at the same time , you 're Australia is doing the very thing that is destroying our homes . " 
@@118526143 <p> An independent review of the Department of Veterans ' Affairs ( DVA ) identifying and diagnosing pain points has warned that more veterans are likely to need support with the onset of more challenging social and economic conditions in Australia . <p> An 89% jump in claims made to DVA between the 2017-18 and 2018-19 financial years has been described by a capability review as a " sudden and prolonged spike " . <p> The growth had the effect of overwhelming the department 's processing capacity and building a sizeable backlog of unallocated claims numbering as many as 41,799 at its peak in May 2022 . <p> Driven by a range of factors , DVA 's growth in claims was projected to go in the opposite direction by June 2021 . But the number of clients grew 58% higher than expected to 240,231 . <p> Now a capability review has predicted the volume and demand of claim workloads will reach further record levels because of easier ways to lodge claims online , awareness-raising programs to inform eligible clients about available payments and services , and legislative reform . <p> " Veterans ' needs are evolving , and DVA will need to engage closely with its clients to support their wellbeing in an effective and contemporary way , " the report read . <p> " The transition from ADF to civilian life is a critical period for veterans ... DVA and Defence will need to work together seamlessly to support veterans through this sometimes difficult period . <p> " DVA will also have to navigate changes among the many groups and associations that represent and advocate for veterans . " <p> It is not just the volume of claims that is increasing , they are also becoming more complex . The report noted that the average number of conditions per claim had risen by 63% from 2.6 conditions in 2023 to 4.3 conditions in 2024 . <p> " Each condition requires a separate decision by a DVA delegate , " the report read . <p> DVA 's capability review was published on Friday , two months after the report was endorsed by the APSC on October 1 , 2024 . <p> The review team recognised the " heightened scrutiny " DVA had been subject to , underscoring the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide , with a particular focus on serious issues that had put pressure on leaders and staff . <p> But while DVA staff were committed and dedicated to serving veterans and their families with compassion and empathy , the team acknowledged the organisation was only at the start of a " multi-year change journey " . <p> " The department moved quickly to initiate cultural and workforce reforms in response to the interim report of the royal commission into Defence and veteran suicide which will , alongside increased government investment , enable the department to better support the veteran community , " they said . <p> " We commend these efforts . They will set the department on the right path to embed sustainable change with persistent and continued effort . " <p> Work already underway by DVA to respond to interim recommendations by the royal commission from 2021 was highlighted in the report as having " significant implications for core business " . <p> The review team said that in order for DVA to make the most of the reform opportunity presented by the royal commission , " sophisticated strategic long-term thinking , courage and influence " was required . <p> " DVA will need to focus on the cumulative intent of the royal commission in addition to the government 's response to each specific recommendation , " the report read . <p> " It is an opportunity to envisage a new long-term plan for the department that delivers a modern , seamless experience for veterans and their families . " <p> This is the sixth review of departmental capability completed as part of a pilot for the federal government 's APS reform agenda and designed to assess how well-placed an agency is to meet future objectives and challenges . <p> The report consists of a so-called ' excellence horizon ' outlining what capabilities DVA requires today and within the next four years , and an analysis of organisational capability across the domains of leadership and culture , collaboration , delivery , workforce and enabling functions . <p> " Several interim royal commission recommendations specific to the department ... included the need to eliminate the unallocated claims backlog , improve claims processing , move to a new funding model , and change to a single legislative act to govern veterans ' rehabilitation and compensation claims , " the excellence horizon read . <p> " Following the government 's acceptance of these recommendations , DVA has begun making significant changes to better support veterans and their families . <p> " DVA will continue to deal with a changing client cohort and the increasing complexity of veteran needs . This has already materialised in the form of increased claims . <p> " However , DVA will also need to take the time to deeply consider major veteran issues like how to improve veteran transitions from the Australian Defence Force ( ADF ) and proactively focus on wellbeing ( where needed , noting that just over half of veterans have not sought ongoing DVA support ) . " <p> The capability review explained that future planning for DVA would occur against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty , growing cost-of-living , and policy shifts affecting interdependent systems like health , aged care and disability . These factors all had the potential to affect veterans and change the needs DVA had to respond to , it suggested . <p> Nine " trends and developments " were also identified for DVA to align its organisational capability needs with . Rethinking and redesigning existing policy and service delivery ; strategic communications ; a closer relationship with Defence to support people 's status transition from service ADF members to veterans ; stronger ICT , data and modelling capability ; workforce planning ; modernising business processes ; and enhanced engagement approaches were all raised in this section . <p> Effective partnerships across government , private and non-government sectors , and the efficient use of department resources were also called out in the capability list . <p> " DVA has received budget supplementation since 2018 to help overcome the claims processing backlog . The department 's future financial baseline may not match these levels of funding , " the report read . <p> The Australian government will also face increasingly complex policy problems that require a whole-of-government response , such as the impacts of climate change , geopolitical instability and increases to the cost of living . " <p> DVA 's estimated total department expenses for 2024-25 is $579.7 million , which is an average increase of about $400 million per annum in the last decade . This includes a boost to frontline services injecting additional funding over four years from 2022-23 . <p> DVA 's vision is to respect , empower and support veterans and their families , with the purpose of supporting the wellbeing of those who have defended the nation and commemorating their service and sacrifice . However , its clients comprise only 47.1% of current living veterans . <p> The department collaborates with other government agencies , the ex-service organisation ( ESO ) community , and community groups to administer integrated services including : income support , compensation , healthcare ( both physical and mental ) , a specialist counselling service , rehabilitation , aged care support , transport for treatment , employment and education support , home insurance and subsidised home loans , commemorative events and the maintenance of war graves . <p> In his report foreword , APS commissioner Dr Gordon de Brouwer thanked DVA staff for their willingness and collaboration in participating in the exercise . The process was a " seamless " one , he said . <p> " It has been a challenging time for the department , and I commend Secretary Alison Frame and DVA 's senior executive group for their leadership and commitment to purpose and staff , " de Brouwer said . <p> " The APSC coordinates and supports the delivery of capability reviews of all Commonwealth departments and large agencies . <h> About the author <p> Melissa Coade is The Mandarin 's news editor based in Canberra 's parliamentary press gallery . @@118526155 <p> Australia has long tried to be two things at once -- a trusted friend to Pacific nations in a bid to reduce China 's influence , and a giant exporter of fossil fuels . This diplomatic tightrope has become increasingly hard to walk , as Pacific nations see climate change as an existential threat . <p> This week , Australia 's government was forced to make a choice in a very public forum . It chose fossil fuels . <p> Disappointed by the slow pace of United Nations climate talks , Vanuatu and other Pacific nations launched a case at the International Court of Justice in the Netherlands to clarify the obligations countries have to prevent harm to the Earth 's climate system for current and future generations . <p> While international climate negotiations are often conducted behind closed doors , this case is being broadcast in public . We can clearly see the arguments Australia has laid out and the countries it has aligned itself with . <p> In the courtroom on Monday , Australia sided with major emitters and fossil fuel exporters such as Saudi Arabia , the United States and China to try and minimise their legal liability in contributing to climate change . <h> What 's at stake in this case ? <p> This week marks a milestone in a five-year legal campaign , travelling from a university tutorial in Vanuatu 's capital , Port Vila , through the halls of the United Nations in New York and now to the world 's court in the Hague . The International Court of Justice is the only international court able to settle disputes between United Nations member states . <p> In 2019 , 27 law students at the University of the South Pacific were given a challenge : find the most ambitious legal pathways towards climate justice . They decided filing a case with the world court fitted the bill . <p> In 2023 , Vanuatu and other nations succeeded in passing a resolution at the UN General Assembly requiring the world court to give an advisory opinion on two questions -- what obligations do states have under international law to protect the climate from greenhouse gas emissions , and what are the legal consequences for states causing " significant harm " to the earth 's climate ? <p> Ahead of the hearing , the world court has received a record number of written submissions . Justices will hear two weeks of oral submissions . They will then produce an advisory opinion , expected to set a new benchmark in international law , by clarifying the legal obligations countries have to tackle emissions . <p> While an advisory opinion is not binding , the court 's findings will feed into national court cases and UN climate talks . <p> For Australia , this case presents a direct challenge . It has no plans to phase down fossil fuel exports . In fact , it plans to expand them . <p> If the court 's opinion draws clear lines between fossil fuel exporters and climate damage , it could have severe implications for Australia . It could , for instance , pave the way to compensation lawsuits for climate damage . <p> Since 2000 , Australia has approved more than 700 oil , gas and coal projects . Dozens more are in the approvals pipeline . Just this week the federal government cleared the way for three new coal mines . <p> Australia is now one of the world 's largest exporters of coal and gas . This is relatively new . While coal has been exported since 1801 , large-scale exports of liquefied natural gas only began a decade ago . <p> When burned overseas , emissions from Australia 's fossil fuel exports are now more than double those of its entire domestic economy . These emissions damage our global climate , increasing risk of harm to people in Australia and worldwide . <h> What did Australia argue at the Hague ? <p> In bringing the case , Vanuatu has argued actions causing climate change are unlawful under a range of international obligations including the law of the sea , human rights law and environmental law . <p> Australian delegates commended Vanuatu 's leadership in bringing this case and reiterated Australia 's commitment to working with the Pacific on climate . <p> But after the diplomatic niceties , Australian Solicitor-General Stephen Donaghue got down to business . He told the court only the Paris Agreement -- which requires countries to set targets to cut domestic emissions -- should apply when it comes to mitigating climate change . <p> Donaghue also argued greenhouse gas emissions are different to , say , one country 's toxic waste damaging the environment of another . This , he argued , was because emissions have many sources . <p> Donaghue and the Australian delegation argued the court should take a narrow view of obligations to cut emissions and suggested responsibility for harms caused by climate change could not be pinned on individual states . <p> Australia has also argued protecting human rights does not extend to obligations to tackle climate change . <p> In 2022 , Torres Strait islanders told a UN Human Rights Committee that a failure to address climate change violated their human rights . In response , the Australian government used very similar arguments , claiming climate change was best addressed through UN climate negotiations . <h> What does this mean ? <p> Despite Australia 's arguments , recent rulings by other courts and tribunals suggest the court may not decide in our favour . <p> For example in May , the International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea found greenhouse gas emissions were a form of marine pollution ( because they acidify and heat the ocean ) , which countries have obligations to prevent . The tribunal rejected arguments that state obligations were limited to implementing the Paris Agreement . <p> Relationships with Pacific states are likely to come under strain as the proceedings in the Hague roll on . <p> Matters could come to a head next year , when the court will release its advisory opinion . <p> A decision is still pending on whether Australia will host COP31 , the 2026 UN climate talks , alongside Pacific island countries . <p> If our COP bid succeeds , it could give Canberra a chance to signal a shift away from fossil fuel exports in favour of green exports such as critical minerals and green iron . Doing so would align Australia 's interests with the Pacific -- and present it much more clearly as a partner of choice .

In doing so , the WA Government and manufacturers will develop a broader , and more capable manufacturing base while serving domestic renewable energy needs . " <p> Applications will be " open , continuous , and competitive " until all available funding has been exhausted , the government says . <p> All manufacturers interested in applying for funds under either of the two streams can register to attend in-person information sessions as well as access written guidelines and a pre-recorded webinar here . <p> Joshua S. @@118526177 <h> Chinese EV makers report record October <p> A slew of Chinese electric vehicle ( EV ) makers have announced record sales for the month October , led by BYD , one of the world 's leading best-selling car brands , which saw sales exceed 500,000 for the first time . <p> BYD saw sales reach 502,657 for the month of October . Having ceased production and sale of all internal combustion engine ( ICE ) only vehicles in 2022 , that means all BYD car sales are either plug-in hybrid EV ( PHEV ) or battery EV ( BEV ) models . <p> BYD 's sales are dominated by passenger vehicles , with only 2,131 commercial BEV or PHEVs sold during October . <p> Passenger electrified model sales hit 500,526 for October , up 66.24 per cent year-on-year , and up 19.86 per cent on September . Of that number , BYD sold 189,614 BEVs , up 14.57 percent year-on-year , and 310,912 PHEVs , up 129.30 percent year-on-year . <p> As is becoming increasingly common around the globe , the growth in PHEV sales is strong than that of BEVs , with PHEV growing 129.3 per cent year-on-year and 23.06 per cent over September , and BEV sales managing just a 2.2 per cent gain year-on-year and down 5.51 per cent from September . <p> BYD was n't the only Chinese EV maker to report a record October , with carmaker 's Xpeng , Zeekr , and Leapmotor all reporting record months . <p> Xpeng delivered 23,917 vehicles in October , marking its second consecutive record month , up 19.57 per cent year-on-year and 12.01 per cent on September . <p> Zeekr delivered 25,049 vehicles in October , a 91.55 percent increase year-on-year and a 17.42 percent increase on September , marking its own second consecutive record month . <p> All figures were published at the beginning of November by the respective companies . Reported in English by CnEVPost . <p> Two other Chinese EV manufacturers published steady October sales , with Li Auto delivering 51,443 vehicles for the month , down 4.2 per cent on September 's numbers , while Nio delivered 20,976 vehicles , down only 1 per cent . <p> Joshua S.
