@@118565503 <h> Great power rivalry <p> Syria : Sunni militants and Turkish-backed rebels advanced across Syria this week and reignited the country 's civil war , as a ceasefire held in Lebanon despite Israel and Hezbollah trading fire . <p> In the past 13 years , Syria has experienced a brutal conflict that has fractured the country and left about 600,000 people dead and displaced 12 million people , or about half the population . <p> Until last weekend , the war had settled into a stalemate , in which Syria 's leader Bashar al-Assad , backed by Iran and Russia , retained control of Damascus and 70 per cent of the country . Various slivers were controlled by groups including Kurds , Turkish-backed militants , Sunni Islamists and ISIS . <p> In a surprise move last week , however , an Islamist militia , Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ( HTS ) , launched an offensive and eventually captured the city of Aleppo , extending the territory they already held in the north-west . HTS , which had close ties with al-Qaeda until 2016 , has been designated as a terrorist group by the United States and the United Nations . <p> The HTS offensive was backed by the Syrian National Army , a rebel force supported by T ? rkiye , prompting speculation the country may have approved the campaign . Assad 's backers , Iran and Hezbollah , have been preoccupied with the conflicts in Lebanon and Gaza , and Russia has been focused on the war in Ukraine . <p> On Tuesday , the anti-Assad forces pushed further south , attempting to take the city of Hama . Elsewhere , a US-backed Kurdish group , the Syrian Democratic Forces , battled Assad 's forces . Iran 's foreign affairs minister , Abbas Araghchi , denounced the advance of the " terrorist groups " , saying Tehran would consider sending troops to support Assad . Russia 's air force has reportedly been assisting him . <p> The UN estimated the fighting had killed hundreds of people and displaced about 50,000 . <p> The renewed violence in Syria erupted as an uneasy 60-day truce began between Israel and Hezbollah , an Iran-backed group in Lebanon . Israel last weekend accused Hezbollah of violating the ceasefire and bombed the group 's facilities . Hezbollah then fired at Israel , prompting Israeli air strikes . <p> Hezbollah began firing at Israel on October 8 last year , a day after Hamas , an Iran-backed Palestinian group , crossed from Gaza and launched attacks in southern Israel , leaving 1200 people dead and seizing about 250 hostages . Israel then invaded Gaza as part of a campaign that has left more than 44,000 people dead , according to local officials . <p> As the war in Gaza has continued , Israel has come under growing diplomatic pressure to withdraw from Gaza and the West Bank . <p> Australia this week changed its position and backed a UN resolution that called for an " irreversible " pathway to a two-state solution and demanded Israel " end its unlawful presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as rapidly as possible " . The resolution was backed by 157 countries , with seven abstaining and eight , including the United States , opposed . Australia has shifted position on several recent resolutions . <p> A spokesperson for Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said : " If , on balance , we believe the resolution will contribute to peace and a two-state solution , we will vote for it . " <h> The neighbourhood <p> The Hague : The International Court of Justice this week began hearing a landmark climate change case initiated by Vanuatu that could set out legal obligations on countries to reduce carbon emissions . <p> During the opening session of the two-week hearing Ralph Regenvanu , Vanuatu 's climate envoy , told the court that countries should be required to urgently respond to climate change and to support vulnerable states . <p> " A handful of readily identifiable states have produced the vast majority of historic and current greenhouse gas emissions , " he said . " Yet other countries , including my own , are suffering the brunt of the consequences . " <p> Ninety-nine countries are due to give testimony in what will be the largest hearing in the court 's 80-year history . The court 's advisory opinion will not be legally binding but could be used as a basis for domestic lawsuits around the world . <p> The idea to launch a case in The Hague originated with a group of students at the University of the South Pacific . Their proposal was taken up by Vanuatu and other small island states , which pushed the UN General Assembly to adopt a resolution that asked the court to issue an opinion . <p> The court will be required to answer two questions : what obligations do countries have to protect the environment from greenhouse gas emissions ? And what should the consequences be for countries that harm the environment ? <p> During the hearings on Monday , Australia endorsed Vanuatu 's efforts to tackle climate change but urged the court to adopt a relatively restricted view of the law that would be based on existing treaties such as the Paris Agreement . <p> The court 's opinion is expected to be delivered late next year . <h> Democracy in retreat <p> South Korea : Yoon Suk Yeol , the president of South Korea , faced calls to resign this week after stunning the nation by declaring martial law on Tuesday night . <p> Yoon , who has faced several corruption allegations and is deeply unpopular , imposed martial law in an unscheduled television address at 10.30pm , accusing the opposition of colluding with North Korea and plotting an " insurgency " to try to " overthrow the free democracy " . Following his declaration , troops stormed the National Assembly . <p> But the 300-member assembly convened early on Wednesday and voted 190-0 to rescind martial law . At 4.30am , Yoon gave another televised address to confirm he accepted the assembly 's demand . <p> On Wednesday , protesters in Seoul called for Yoon to resign , as did the country 's umbrella union group . South Korea regularly experienced periods of martial law during its decades as a military dictatorship but none has been imposed since it became a democracy in 1987 . <p> Yoon was elected with a narrow majority in 2022 but has struggled to pass bills , including the budget , since the opposition Democratic Party won a significant majority in parliamentary elections in April . <p> The imposition of martial law appeared to be an attempt by Yoon to force his way through the political impasse . But the move backfired , with several colleagues openly saying it was a mistake . <p> The opposition said Yoon must resign or he will be impeached . Before the martial law declaration , opinion polls showed Yoon 's approval rating was at 25 per cent . @@118565505 <h> Mostafa Azimitabar Migration bills spread fear <p> I work at the Art Gallery of New South Wales , and on this day I was supposed to talk about Magritte -- the exhibition that 's on at the moment . I had a half-hour break time and was getting ready for my talk when I looked at my phone . I saw a message from a friend that parliament was going to pass the new migration laws . <p> I was shocked when I saw the news . <p> It is heartbreaking . How can I explain it ? I am like a broken glass . I am healing myself when I work at the art gallery , when I get connected to people in the community . When I talk about connection , what I mean is that I have received kindness and respect from people here . I love Australia . No matter that this system is cruel , I still feel that Australia is my home . <p> I am Kurdish , and Kurdistan has been occupied for decades , even before the ayatollahs . I was a human rights activist . I could n't bear what the terrorist regime of Iran was doing to innocent people , especially women . <p> I was in danger . I had to flee . I did n't come to Australia for a holiday . It was devastating , the journey so difficult . Then for eight years I was tortured in detention . I could n't get back to my homeland because they would kill me . So I got my refugee status in 2017 . According to international human rights law , people with refugee status can not be deported , because they are in danger . So this bill is against international law . <p> There is also something tricky in these laws . They allow all devices to be confiscated . Politicians have given the reason as stopping drugs -- to prevent crime . <p> But they want to block this connection because when refugees get access to lawyers and activists , then there is a way to get out of detention . The reason I got free , the reason the refugees on Manus got out of detention , was only because we were connected to people . <p> If the authorities had confiscated our phones , I could n't have talked to anyone . It 's as if they would have buried us alive . No one would know what happened to us and no one would have known the punishment that was going on . <p> In the hotel where we were detained in Australia , there was a lot of noise , a lot of harassment , the noise of radios , handcuffs . The guards did a pat search of my body sometimes eight times a day . They would come into my room sometimes 10 times a day . Every morning , without exception , at 6am they would come into my room with a torch . The guards warned me not to talk with media . <p> But we got in touch with amazing Australians , mothers and grandmothers for refugees . These people are our families . I got in touch with many journalists . I went on national television , and the news went everywhere in Australia . <p> If the authorities had confiscated our phones , I could n't have talked to anyone . It 's as if they would have buried us alive . No one would know what happened to us and no one would have known the punishment that was going on . <p> When the Labor Party was in opposition and the Coalition was in government , Labor supported the Medevac legislation . Australians changed the government for different reasons -- one was for refugees . Now this legislation is going to be against refugees , by the party that was supporting them . <p> I remember when the Labor Party supported Medevac , they said some people on Manus Island could come to Australia for medical treatment . We had a choice -- some of my fellow detainees went to the United States , some to Canada or to New Zealand -- they were settled there and I am happy for them . A small number came along with me to Australia . We were transferred here legally , each individual case was signed by the minister . <p> One of the medical conditions I had was asthma . They locked me inside a room , there was a window that I could n't open , all I could see beyond it was a cement wall . It was like a cement coffin . I never received proper medication -- we never got treatment . <p> I had a meeting with Andrew Giles , the former minister for immigration . I went with my lawyer . We talked and I said , " You supported the Medevac refugees . May I ask you to help me to get my medical treatment ? " The minister told me , " If you want medical treatment , go to a third country . If you want to study , go to a third country . " He got angry . <p> When I said I want to live in Australia he said the policy will never change . He said , " Look at my eyes . I am very serious with you . You will never , ever be resettled in Australia . Leave . " <p> Scott Morrison came to the Manus detention centre as minister of immigration in 2013 , a few months before they killed my friend Reza Barati . Morrison came inside with a lot of security guards , and he was yelling . He pointed at us . " You will never , ever come to Australia . Go back to your countries . Do n't play with your life . " <p> The two major parties are against refugees . It 's very obvious that the two major parties are competitive on immigration , they are racing to the bottom . When the topic is about refugees , each of them is trying to do more damage . <p> In this situation , I am very nervous because the election is coming . In this election , they do n't care about anything , they just want to win . And refugees are vulnerable people . <p> The type of bridging visa that I have is temporary and every time I must renew it , every six months , it 's intense . <p> The case workers who call me to tell me I ca n't resettle here , who ask me which country I would like to go to , do n't understand anything about what it is to lead a life of uncertainty after detention . They work for the system , for the bureaucracy . This bill has given them a tool to deport refugees . When they ask questions , they make me uncomfortable every time . Have you committed any crimes ? Have you been in police custody ? Have you moved to another place ? <p> Any refugee who has this temporary visa must tell everything about where they are living . They must give 48 hours ' notice before moving to a new place . Officers are monitoring us . They want to check everything about us . They are looking for a mistake . <p> Politicians are trying to drive fear , to tell society that refugees are dangerous . And only refugees can understand this much suffering . Still we continue , we do n't want to give up -- for different reasons . Many of us have been away from families for over a decade now , and we are forbidden to study or get a qualification . This means we ca n't get a better situation or a better job . <p> Now we are in a very delicate , very fragile situation -- who is on our side ? <p> I do n't know how much support we have , I do n't know how many independent senators or other politicians would fight for us . But I believe people in Australia do n't agree with these laws . I have lived in Australia outside detention nearly three-and-a-half years now , and I have seen people with respect for refugees . I can see that these people are completely different from the ones who locked us up in detention . <p> Now I am living in Australia and I can not live anywhere else . How can I explain it ? The connection I have is based on humanity , a I can not leave this family . I love my job . And this job means I have space . I love my colleagues -- I feel they are protecting me . They are so welcoming . It 's completely different to the message from the government . <p> I came to Australia for safety . I do n't want to go to any other country . It 's like the government is dealing in a kind of human trafficking . That 's a crime . I still have a choice . My choice is to live with the Australian family that has come into my life through my story , through the suffering . Through the eight years in detention . This connection is all my life . <p> I am just sticking all the broken glass together . I am proudly saying I am a refugee , I am a son , I am a brother , I am a worker , I am a friend , I am an artist . I am a human being . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " I can not leave this family " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118565506 <h> Paul Bongiorno Election fight starts to get serious <p> These days Arthur Sinodinos , a former Liberal cabinet minister and ambassador , heads a high-powered consultancy in Washington , DC . As part of that work , he regularly comes back to Australia to keep up with contacts and clients . <p> On his latest trip , he has been telling people the Liberals have conducted research that says the looming election will result in a hung parliament , with the Coalition winning 69 seats to Labor 's 68 . The magic number for a majority government is 75 seats . <p> The prospect of the Dutton-led Coalition finishing a nose ahead of Labor raises fascinating possibilities on how it would get enough of the cross bench to support it in minority . <p> Midweek , Dutton warned " a vote for the teal independents is a vote for Anthony Albanese " . More likely it would be a vote against Dutton and his policies , particularly on climate action . So far he has made no discernible effort to win back those voters who deserted the Liberals for the socially progressive independents . <p> Labor hardheads admit the published opinion polls , which have the government and opposition neck and neck , suggest Labor will lose seats . In their view , however , the prospect of a minority government led by Peter Dutton should work in their favour . This is n't because Dutton is not electable , but precisely because he is . <p> According to one cabinet minister , it means Dutton will not be able to slide into government merely on a protest vote . He will have to come up with policies that are seen to be credibly different from what is on offer from the incumbents . <p> Voting profiler John Black agrees . On ABC TV 's 7.30 , Black said the passing of the bulk of the government 's agenda last week " makes life a bit more challenging for Dutton " . He ca n't " sit back and drift into government like Labor did last time " . <p> Black says the opposition leader " has actually to get out there and present some policies that are going to make a difference to the living standards of ordinary Australians " . <p> On that , both Albanese and Dutton face considerable headwinds . Voters , according to the opinion polls , are unimpressed by or have n't noticed what the Albanese government has done to attempt to alleviate their cost-of-living pain . For his part , Dutton has n't come up with a compelling alternative to replace a government that he is fond of describing as the " most incompetent " the nation has seen for a long time . <p> The stance Dutton has taken in opposing relief measures , such as energy bill discounts , rental assistance , the supermarket code of conduct and , initially , the revamped stage three tax cuts , raises more questions than it provides answers . The one solution the opposition emphasises is to slash government spending . <p> No one understands better than Albanese that in such a hard-fought election , with both the major parties under threat from community independents and the Greens , it is a seat-by-seat battle . <p> The national accounts demonstrate that without this " public demand " at the state and federal levels the anaemic economy would have slid into recession . Government-funded jobs are still real jobs for millions of Australians . Economist Stephen Koukoulas points out that consumers and the private sector are particularly sensitive to interest rates , and he says the accounts show the Reserve Bank is " smashing the economy " with its refusal to cut rates . The bank 's forecasts for economic growth are wildly out of whack , he says . <p> It 's a view shared by other economists , who believe the reforms to the way the RBA sets monetary policy are long overdue . These economists are looking to their implementation early next year , when the treasurer appoints a new board of experts to do the job . <p> Jim Chalmers ' response to the national accounts gives some hope for optimism . He explained the barely growing economy was " being weighed down by interest rates " . <p> Few , if any , are expecting the current board to abandon its orthodoxy on inflation busting at its meeting next week . This , Koukoulas says , is despite the evidence in the latest data showing prices are moderating . <p> The Treasury Laws Amendment ( Reserve Bank Reforms ) bill was one of the 30 or so measures that had been stalled in the Senate for more than six months , only to be passed in the blitz in parliament 's last sitting fortnight for the year . <p> In what one veteran politician describes as the most intense " barnacle removing " he 's seen since the Howard government prepared for an election , Albanese is getting ready to set sail much sooner than he wants us to expect . <p> The opposition certainly sees Australia 's reversal of three key votes in the United Nations dealing with Palestine as part of that " barnacle removing " . Dutton slammed it as a vote-buying exercise " for Green votes in Western Sydney and places like Marrickville " . <p> Australia abandoned its previous position of abstaining , and supported resolutions demanding that Israel end its " unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory as rapidly as possible and to immediately cease all new settlement activities " . <p> Australia 's ambassador to the UN , James Larsen , welcomed the resolution 's confirmation of a high-level international conference next year aimed at implementing a two-state solution . He said , " It remains the only hope of breaking the endless cycle of violence , the only hope to see a secure and prosperous future for both peoples . " <p> Dutton accused the Albanese government of sacrificing the wellbeing of the Jewish community in Australia in the process . The government rejects this characterisation . One insider said , " On the contrary , peace would see a demise in anti-Semitism and a return to the social cohesion before the October 7 attacks sparked Israel 's response . " <p> The Greens see Dutton 's uncompromising support for Israel as his own attempt at vote-buying in seats with a significant Jewish presence , some of which are held by teal independents . <p> The prime minister 's office says the votes in the UN were on their merits but at this stage of the electoral cycle every move is seen through the prism of politics . Labor MPs in seats with high numbers of Arab and Muslim voters will no doubt make sure those voters notice what the government has done . <p> No one understands better than Albanese that in such a hard-fought election , with both the major parties under threat from community independents and the Greens , it is a seat-by-seat battle . Unlike in elections past -- when a majority government had a double-figure buffer , provided by seats in Sydney and Melbourne -- the prime minister ca n't afford to risk seats in Western Australia or target seats in Tasmania . <p> This is the hardball reckoning behind Albanese 's overriding of Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek 's deal with the Greens over Labor 's Nature Positive law reforms , which put on ice the setting up of a promised Environmental Protection Agency and appears to be stalling Plibersek 's decision over the fate of the unique Maugean skate in salmon-farmed Macquarie Harbour , on Tasmania 's west coast . The fish farm is in the must-win seat of Braddon . <p> The salmon industry provides 50 per cent of jobs in Strahan , but Plibersek has no option under the legislation other than to insist she will follow " the science and the law " . The industry is destroying the ecosystem and credible research says it will drive the Maugean skate to extinction . <p> Dutton has no such hindrance or scruples . He assured salmon workers in August that a Coalition government would overturn any decision made by Plibersek to limit their operations . <p> Albanese played a personal role in convincing the popular former leader of the Tasmanian Labor Party , Rebecca White , to abandon her state seat and run for the federal seat of Lyons . He also twisted the arm of Senator Anne Urquhart to run for Braddon . <p> She has maintained an office in Devonport and is widely seen as a community activist . The resignation of popular Liberal MP Gavin Pearce gives Labor a golden opportunity . <p> Among the 69 seats the Liberals are counting on is John Howard 's old seat of Bennelong in Sydney . After the redistribution , Labor 's Jerome Laxale is reckoned at 50-50 with the Liberals ' Scott Yung . The Liberal candidate , who was born in Sydney to Chinese parents , is buoyed by the inclusion of Chatswood in the seat -- adding a significant number of Chinese -- Australian voters . <p> Yung says he was part of the national plan to bring back Chinese -- Australian voters who deserted the Liberals after Dutton and Morrison demonised China and even spoke of going to war with the country . <p> Laxale is loath to even mention his opponent 's name but says he has long been a resident in the electorate and is getting a positive reception , especially when he reminds voters of Peter Dutton 's record . <p> Dutton appears to have hamstrung himself with Chinese and Indian Australians through his promise to reduce the number of foreigners allowed into the country and to restrict their right to buy property . <p> Greens leader Adam Bandt is now calling for a pre-election power-sharing model with Labor -- a chance to show voters how minority government would work . That sent shudders through the government . Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said Bandt was getting ahead of himself , and Labor was seeking majority government " to provide certainty , particularly in these difficult economic times " . <p> Ironically , Albanese has a proven skill set when it comes to dealing with minority government . The success of the Gillard minority government in passing significant reforms such as the National Disability Insurance Scheme and the carbon price was in no small part due to Albanese 's backroom negotiating skills . <p> As George Megalogenis observed in his recent Quarterly Essay , however , Albanese lacks " the poetry of his predecessors " . @@118565507 <h> John Hewson We need a real sovereign wealth fund <p> The Future Fund is Australia 's version of a sovereign wealth fund . Established in 2006 from the proceeds of Telstra 's sale and boosted by budget surpluses , it represents our national savings . Why then should Australians be content to see it support the damaging industries of tobacco , pokies and weapons manufacturers , and fossil fuels ? <p> The fund is no pocket change . It started out at $60 billion , has ballooned to about $230 billion under management and is predicted to grow to about $380 billion by 2032/33 . Then treasurer Peter Costello initially established the Future Fund to provide for the unfunded superannuation liabilities of the government sector , to keep them from impacting on the annual budgets as they fell due . <p> As one of the original proposers of the fund , I can confirm that this was indeed its stated and protected purpose . It was always to be a side fund , not a sovereign wealth fund in the traditional sense , along the lines of the world 's largest , such as those of Norway and Saudi Arabia , built on their massive oil resources . However , it is important to ask , why not ? Why should n't the government make Australia 's Future Fund a genuine sovereign wealth fund , to ensure the benefits of our resource developments and budget discipline are realised for all Australians ? <p> The Future Fund 's mandate is to maximise profitable investments in sharemarkets and other financial instruments relative to a modest earnings benchmark of 4-5 per cent above inflation . Needless to say , those investments have been controversial at times -- at odds with other government policies or even our national interests . <p> This laissez-faire stance on the Future Fund 's investments contrasts with that taken in other countries with their sovereign wealth funds . According to a survey cited by the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds , the proportion of respondents saying they had adopted an environmental , social and governance ( ESG ) approach to investments rose from a quarter in 2020 to 71 per cent in 2021 . <p> Recently , Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher have jointly proposed to " modernise " the fund by directing its investments to key priority areas of national significance , sustainable investments in the essential energy transition , housing and other critical challenges and opportunities . The aim , they said , is to build " on its success to ensure it can play an enduring and prominent role in our economy " . The government has committed not to make any drawdowns from the fund until 2032-33 , provided the fund has the certainty to continue to build its portfolio . <p> Why should n't the government make Australia 's Future Fund a genuine sovereign wealth fund , to ensure that the benefits of our resource developments and budget discipline are realised for all Australians ? <p> Not surprisingly , this ruffled the feathers of the opposition , who predicted it would be " raided " to fund its " pet projects " , and used as a " political slush fund " . They bleated that the new guidelines were against a long-term bipartisan position that the fund should be independent of the government of the day and focused on maximising returns . <p> But this approach for the Future Fund assumes an effective taxation system is in place to ensure that a fair share of profits from the development and exploitation of our resources is preserved for the broader benefit of all Australians . This profit sharing is particularly important , because a large proportion of the proceeds from , for example , the development of our oil and gas resources -- which are important national assets -- accrue to foreign-owned companies , which have often been shown to pay less than their fair share of tax . A related consideration is the windfall revenues to our budgets from unexpected increases in commodity prices . Why should n't these be transferred to a sovereign wealth fund , to make them available to help finance a range of important social , infrastructure and environmental projects ? <p> Populist nonsense often spouted on X argues against budget surpluses as acceptable fiscal policy objectives , maintaining that surpluses are unspent taxpayer dollars that should be used , for instance , to offset the cost of living . In this vein , surely it is worth arguing that such balances should at least be transferred to a sovereign wealth fund ? <p> I believe a proper sovereign wealth fund along the lines proposed by Labor would attract widespread electoral support , especially as its distributions help to finance needed reform in key policy areas . Indeed , many voters simply ca n't understand why superannuation funds , with compulsory contributions as a base and some $3-4 trillion under management , can avoid investing in large projects of national significance , especially infrastructure and challenges such as the energy transition and affordable housing . <p> The opposition attacked the Chalmers-Gallagher announcement in the true spirit of their general negativity , without taking the time to assess whether the proposed changes would be in Australia 's national interest . Surely it 's common sense that a more meaningful role for the Future Fund would include focusing on national policy priorities in its investment decisions , as the ministers said , " where possible , appropriate and consistent with strong returns " . These guardrails should not just be overlooked in an attempt to create the impression the Albanese government is raiding the fund for its short-term political purposes , as further grist for the Coalition 's popular refrain that " you ca n't trust Labor with your money " . <p> Importantly , the government 's proposals are also about improved transparency and accountability for the Future Fund . Indeed , the fund has been criticised in the past for failing to reflect national priorities , such as when our governments were committed to a strong national anti-smoking campaign and the Future Fund was found to be investing in British American Tobacco . Another criticism has been that the fund has invested about half a billion dollars in global defence companies -- about 30 companies engaged in weapons manufacture and aerospace . The fund has also been on the defensive for its early investments in fossil fuels , but increased its exposure by about 10 per cent in the last financial year . <p> About a decade ago , I launched and chaired the Asset Owners Disclosure Project , which focused on the issue of climate risk . We surveyed , rated and ranked the top 500 asset owners globally on their recognition and management of climate risks -- these were the significant pension and superannuation funds , sovereign wealth funds , and foundations/endowment funds whose shareholdings dominated international sharemarkets . <p> Initially , we gave out just a few top-shelf AAA ratings but , over time , peer pressure within the industry saw many institutions attempt to raise their rankings by improving their management of climate risks . Several major portfolio shifts were announced . For example , the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund became a leader in divestment from coal-related investments , and the Rockefeller Foundation , having built its capital out of fossil fuels , announced it was quitting such investments . <p> The evidence from our surveys was used as a basis for the work of the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures set up by the Financial Stability Board , which in turn has led to the push for compulsory disclosure of these investment risks . <p> In this context , we approached the Future Fund to complete our survey . The response was to opt out of the survey , as such risks were considered to be largely irrelevant to their investment strategy . It was our publicised practice to nevertheless still rate and rank those who declined to complete our survey , by using their published reports and statements . In our final ratings report for 2017 , we gave the Future Fund a ranking of C. It is noteworthy that the fund now has an emissions reduction plan , and recently appointed Future Fund chairman Greg Combet says the fund is looking " to invest in businesses that will play a vital role in the energy transition " . <p> I expect things will change at the fund now , with former chair Peter Costello , a noted climate change denier , replaced by Combet , a former minister for climate change and also head of the Net Zero Economy Agency in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet . Indeed , in the latest report of the fund for 2023/24 , the new chair reports " the organisation has long recognised the importance of environmental , social and governance ( ESG ) issues . Further developing our ESG capabilities , in particular in relation to climate risks and opportunities is also a focus for the Board . " <p> In these terms , the Chalmers-Gallagher announcement was n't really breaking new ground for the fund , as it was already active in the investment directions they emphasised . The Coalition 's unjustified and opportunistic scaremongering response was simply another attack on bipartisanship . It seems in our national interest that the Future Fund does its job , as described by Combet recently in the following terms : " The Future Fund is an important national asset with a clear purpose -- to invest for the benefit of future generations of Australians . " <p> To my mind , the sooner it becomes accepted as a full-blown sovereign wealth fund the better for our national interests . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " Nation 's nest egg " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118565508 <h> Screenwriter Lucas Taylor has no social media and does n't even own a smartphone , but that has n't stopped him from being the force behind two hit Australian shows , In Limbo and Black Snow . By Anthony Mullins . <h> Screenwriter Lucas Taylor on the workplace accident that changed his life <p> For the past four years , Lucas Taylor has been one of Australia 's busiest screenwriters and television creators . Against the odds , in a highly competitive and volatile industry , he has two hit shows on air at the same time -- Stan 's Black Snow , with its second season released on January 1 , and ABC-TV 's In Limbo . It 's a remarkable achievement rivalled only by Michael Lucas , the acclaimed writer-creator of The Newsreader and co-creator of Five Bedrooms . <p> What 's more remarkable is how different the two shows are . Black Snow , featuring Vikings star Travis Fimmel , is a dark and brooding cold-case procedural , while In Limbo is a comedy-drama exploring male suicide that is as sensitive and moving as it is hilarious . How do these two incredibly different shows come from the same person ? <p> Search online for Taylor 's backstory and you will find nothing . A " brand " he is not . Despite being a Millennial in his early 40s , Taylor has never had a social media account or a smartphone . " I 'm a fairly private person , " he says , shrugging . " I do n't have any social media ... Trent O'Donnell the set-up director of In Limbo nicknamed me ' Grandpa Words ' because of the flip-phone I was rocking on set . It was that and my propensity for wearing cardigans . " <p> Despite his aversion to 24/7 connectivity or any sort of public profile , Taylor is savvy enough to understand that when you 're the creator and executive producer of two multimillion-dollar shows , there are times when you have to put yourself out there for the sake of the work . " Being an EP comes with responsibilities . " <p> Today Taylor is talking to me from Sydney via Zoom ( he spreads his semi-nomadic time between Brisbane , Sydney and Tasmania ) . For the past 15 minutes we 've been catching up on news , checking in on shared friends and discussing a recent hiking trip Taylor and his partner enjoyed in Europe . The trek was a much-needed break following months of production on season two of Black Snow . Taylor looks refreshed and animated as he describes how , after each day 's hike , they would retreat to a roadside chateau for a local beer and the plat du jour . " I find a lot of inspiration and solace amongst the birds and the mountains and the trees . It 's a good place to open your mind . " <p> Taylor attributes his love of the outdoors to his upbringing in the Northern Rivers region of New South Wales . " Back in the ' 80s and ' 90s , the Northern Rivers was a very different place , " he says . " We were pretty free-range and while we did grow up doing it tough and we did n't have a lot , materially speaking , we also had this sort of idyllic childhood in the way we lived in the country , by the beach , surfing , rabble-rousing , falling out of trees . " <p> The second oldest of four siblings raised by his single mother , Jean , an adult education teacher , Taylor showed an early interest in reading and drama , which his mother actively encouraged . " When I was a kid there were n't cheap airfares , so we had a pretty small-town lens on the world , " he remembers . " Books were a way to open our eyes to a wider world . " His mother 's passion for education saw her children become , apart from a high-achieving television creator , an engineer , a barrister and a philosophy academic . <p> After discovering film and television during a communications degree , Taylor , like many budding media graduates , had few professional opportunities to scratch his newly found filmmaking itch . But instead of the typical arts-adjacent jobs most media graduates pursue while studying or waiting for their big break , Taylor was drawn to an industry far from his studies -- construction . <p> " I would have worked hospitality , but construction paid better , " says Taylor , recalling how he laboured for the father of a childhood friend who ran a concreting business . " I liked the work and liked the people , but if I made a mistake it was like , ' Nice one . Write us a poem about the retaining wall you fucked up . ' ? " <p> During his time in construction Taylor had a workplace accident that would prove fateful . " I was barrowing concrete up a hill when my back basically blew out , rupturing a disk at the base of my spine . " Apart from hospitalisation and months of rehabilitation , the injury meant Taylor was given back-to-work retraining that subsidised his wages . <p> " I would have worked hospitality , but construction paid better . I liked the work and the people , but if I made a mistake it was like , ' Nice one . Write us a poem about the retaining wall you fucked up . ' ? " <p> Seeing an opportunity , Taylor applied to work at Hoodlum Entertainment , a busy Brisbane production company where at the time I was creative director . While interviewing Lucas for the job , I asked what films he had enjoyed lately . " I liked Elegy , " was his reply , referring to the 2008 arthouse film based on a Philip Roth novel . It was an intriguing choice from a nuggety young concreter with a busted back . As it turned out , Lucas 's writing samples were outstanding and I liked Elegy too . He got the job . <p> The opportunity was exactly the industry foothold Taylor needed . " I took it very much as a boot camp in working on other people 's stories , really digging into the craft of how to put a show together , " he says . " It was a great opportunity to see how the sausage was made . " <p> After cutting his teeth as an in-house script editor on murder mysteries such as Secrets and Lies , Harrow and the quirky cult comedy The Strange Calls , Taylor was keen to try creating his own shows . In Limbo , one of the first shows he developed , was a buddy comedy-drama that drew on Taylor 's construction background . It told the tale of two builders , best friends Nate and Charlie . In the opening scene Charlie is preparing to deliver a eulogy as wisecracking Nate provides advice on everything from tie selection to pick-up strategies ( " You want to look sad but still bangable ! " ) . As they arrive at the funeral , a picture on the coffin reveals whose service they 're attending -- Nate 's . Having recently killed himself , he 's now a ghost haunting his best mate . <p> " I 'd been working as a freelance writer on a documentary series called Man Up with producer Jennifer Cummins , " Taylor says . " It was looking at men 's mental health and loneliness and I wrote a series of feature articles that had a comic angle to them . It was , I guess , a light-bulb moment that I could explore this difficult topic through a comic lens rather than through a straight drama lens . " <p> Taylor pitched the series to Cummins as a " comedy about masculinity and a drama about suicide " . She remembers marvelling at the sensitivity and clarity of his thinking . " It was so clear what he wanted to do , " she says . " He 's quite a perfectionist , so you never get the first draft . I said , ' I love it . I completely love it and we 're going to make it . ' ? " <p> The six-episode series , starring Bob Morley and Ryan Corr , was commissioned by the ABC and proved a popular and critical success when it aired in 2023 . Describing it as " luminous " , The New York Times admired how its " light and tender approach understands but does not inflict pain " . Taylor and Cummins are developing a second season . <p> Looking back at the show 's development , Cummins believes Taylor 's confidence in handling the difficult material was an important part of its success . " He 's not an extrovert , but he 's a quietly confident introvert , " she says . " There 's a steely confidence that 's born out of the hard work and his belief in himself . " <p> At the same time , Taylor was getting traction on another one of his ideas , Black Snow , a crime procedural with an equally striking premise . Inspired by the sugarcane fields of his youth , the first season kicks off in a small town as a time capsule is opened , revealing new clues to an unsolved murder . " I was struck that the time capsule was offering a window into the past for this small-town crime , " he says . " And how the show could offer a window into Australia 's past and a bigger crime . " <p> That bigger crime was the notorious practice of blackbirding . From the mid 19th to the early 20th century , tens of thousands of South Sea Islanders were deceived , coerced or outright kidnapped to work the cane fields of Queensland and New South Wales . Recognising that this was not his story to tell , Taylor worked with producer Rosemary Blight from Goalpost Pictures to put together a team of South Sea Island artists to guide the project , including series producer Kaylene Butler and screenwriter Boyd Quakawoot . <p> " It was beautiful , " says Blight when I call to discuss the development process . " Lucas is a great listener . So together they figured out how to tell the story truthfully , how to tell it entertainingly , how to tell it within the genre . " This included Butler discussing potential storylines with island chiefs and feeding their responses back into the writers ' room . " The trust built up because you do trust Lucas . He was sincerely there for the right reasons , so the trust was strong . " <p> Apart from shining a light on a little-told chapter in Australian history , Black Snow also gave voice to a typically neglected character in the crime genre -- the victim . " I was intent on telling a story where the victim of the crime that 's being investigated is n't just a body on a slab , " says Taylor . " They 're usually just sort of a catalyst for someone else 's story but I wanted them to be the living , breathing heart of the show , where they were driving the story forward . " <p> To do this , Taylor devised two interweaving timelines . One followed Detective James Cormack ( Travis Fimmel ) working the case in the present , while the second was driven by teenager Isabel Baker ( Talijah Blackman-Corowa ) , as she investigates the town 's secret past -- a secret that will lead to her death . The innovative approach gives the show a richness and depth that is unusual in the crime genre . <p> The critical and commercial response to the first season was overwhelmingly positive , with nine industry award nominations and strong international sales in more than 20 countries . " We 've sold into Germany , France , Spain , Italy , Africa , former Yugoslavia , the UK , and the BBC have come back for season two , " says Blight , delighted that the show lives on at a time when many die on the vine in the fierce competition for global audiences . <p> For Black Snow 's upcoming second season , Taylor has stepped into a senior executive producer role that allows him to be more hands-on in all stages of the show , from first draft to lock-off . " I want to be deeply involved in every aspect of making a show . My personal feeling is that it leads to a really cohesive story , " says Taylor . " But it 's not for the faint-hearted . " <p> If there is an approach that ties his very different shows together it is , perhaps , Taylor 's interest in what he calls " Trojan-horsing " bigger ideas and themes into his stories -- the grim legacy of blackbirding in season one of Black Snow or male depression in In Limbo . " I 've always had a commercial mindset to tell stories a broad audience would find entertaining , " he says . " But since I 'm going to expend the blood , sweat and tears to try and make them , I also want those stories to have something to say . " <p> For all his success and dedication to the craft , Taylor seems grounded enough to recognise there is a lot more to life than spinning a television tale . " One of the challenges with creating these story worlds is that you end up spending a lot of time in them , " he says . " Whether it 's disappearing for three weeks to break open a new story or being on location for five months to bring it to life . But they 're not the real world . <p> " It 's certainly made easier for me by having a supportive partner who understands it , because you end up spending a lot of time away from home , making what 's essentially a piece of entertainment . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " Taylor made " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118565509 <h> Queensland Theatre 's adaptation of Round the Twist winningly reimagines this much-loved classic for a 21st century audience . By Yen-Rong Wong . <h> Queensland Theatre 's Round the Twist the Musical revitalises an Australian classic <p> I do n't remember much of the television show Round the Twist , except that during wet weather lunches during primary school it was shown on a boxy television that was ceremoniously wheeled out on a trolley . The teachers would turn off the lights , and the gloom and the patter of rain accompanied the theme tune as we all settled in to watch the Twists ' latest adventures in Port Niranda . <p> The stage version , Round the Twist the Musical -- based on Paul Jennings ' short stories and adapted with his blessing -- is not as eerie as my childhood memories of the television show , but it is just as delightful and weird . Paul Hodge -- who is responsible for the book , music and lyrics -- has reimagined this classic for a 21st century audience . <p> Director Simon Phillips successfully wrangles a large cast into a show that is a comic delight for all ages . The Twist family consists of Tony ( Matt Hetherington ) , a single father to teenage twins Pete ( Hanlon Innocent ) and Linda ( Charly Oakley ) , and their little brother Bronson ( Edison Ai and Luka and Sebastian Sero ) . They delight in tormenting the younger Twists , albeit with varying amounts of success . Ren ? e Mulder 's costuming choices across the cast -- striped polo shirts , coloured plaid and ankle socks -- hark back to the ' 90s . The highlight for me , however , was the visual metaphor contained within Harold Gribble 's almost-balding , greasy hairpiece . <p> The stage version , Round the Twist the Musical -- based on Paul Jennings ' short stories and adapted with his blessing -- is not as eerie as my childhood memories of the television show , but it is just as delightful and weird . <p> Round the Twist the Musical is comparable to Matilda the Musical , another childhood classic that has made the leap to both screen and stage . The Gribbles and the Wormwoods are similarly vile , and both shows include beautifully choreographed school scenes , complete with clever manipulations of wooden school desks and chairs . Round the Twist , though , has a spookier atmosphere , thanks in part to Ben Hughes 's lighting design . A blue sheen across the stage signals ghostly presences , enough to pique interest without being actually scary . <p> Mulder brings the Twists ' lighthouse to life . Projected against the back of the theatre , the cleverly designed set allows the audience to see into the lighthouse -- both at ground level and at the top -- without losing sight of the structure itself . This involves solving a mystery wrapped in the lyrics of the television show 's original theme song of the same name . <p> Bronson was played by Ai on opening night , and it was heartwarming to see an Asian boy in such an iconic role . This is not to take anything away from Luka and Sebastian Sero -- friends who attended those shows commented on their fantastic performances . Bronson is the heart of Round the Twist the Musical and has many solo moments -- a big ask for such young performers . His room-clearing farts and stinky feet play an important role in the plot . Along with a curse that forces Pete to say " without my pants " at the end of every sentence , Hodge proves that some things , even if they are somewhat " childish " , will always be funny . <p> Round the Twist the Musical leans into the absurdity of musical theatre , with stage exits involving a mermaid ( Laura Raineri ) diving behind cardboard waves , and characters literally rolling off stage and leaping from a wheelchair into the wings . These blatant non-attempts to cover changes between scenes add a little extra to the show 's comic atmosphere . <p> Fiona Richmond ( Taylah Johns ) plays an important role in the television show as Linda 's best friend and Pete 's crush , hence her inclusion in the stage adaptation , but her relationship with Pete on stage is relatively superficial . Their arc carries a message of accepting everyone for who they are , regardless of outward appearances or what other people might think . Tony 's relationship with Fay James ( Liz Buchanan ) -- who happens to be Bronson 's teacher -- also touches on the realities of single parenthood and the complexities of welcoming a new partner into a family . <p> Hodge maintains a fine balance between these tender moments and the overall comic tone of the production . This can be most clearly seen in the repeated motif of " I 'm not scared ... " This starts with the Twist children asserting they are not afraid of the ghost that lives in the outhouse near the lighthouse , with a song that features a significant number of euphemisms for " toilet " . Near the conclusion of the musical , this sentiment is reversed , with the adults admitting to the children that sometimes things can be scary -- but that this is okay , if we can face these difficulties together . <p> This poignant message is the bedrock on which the rest of the production sits , allowing Round the Twist the Musical to be a funny , spooky , musically nostalgic show about the power of family and community -- an Australian classic revitalised for today 's children , as well as for those who are children at heart . <p> Round the Twist the Musical is playing at QPAC , Brisbane , until December 8 . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " Twists and turns " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118565511 <h> HBO 's Dune : Prophecy fodder more chronic than chronicle <p> It takes all of 13 minutes to realise that , artistically speaking , the new HBO Dune series is n't going to match Denis Villeneuve 's epic Dune movies . Thirteen minutes is the length of the exposition dump that begins the first episode of Dune : Prophecy , an IP-mining series that arrives after a long gestation , many delays , a departed showrunner , a name change and , seemingly , a drastic scaling-back to six cluttered episodes . <p> At once underestimating the audience 's intelligence and ignoring the basic storytelling bones of character and emotion , this opening salvo offers no human introduction to its vast sci-fi world , and nothing specific or relatable to anchor an audience . Instead , as if we 're watching a recap of a previous season , we hurtle into a muddled montage of Terminator-style robot apocalypse and deaths of characters we 've just met . Their significance has to be spelt out in a didactic history lesson , where Emily Watson 's narration sounds like AI -- setting : " school marm " -- voicing a Wikipedia entry . <p> Catching us up -- and weighing us down -- with tales of large-scale conflicts and inciting events , spelling out imminent themes in the series and trotting out cod-feminist platitudes about " women unafraid of their power " , it 's an inauspicious beginning for a series that owes its existence to the success of its cinematic predecessors . <p> While the Dune films are famed for their widescreen vistas and IMAX-ready spectacle , what stands out on subsequent viewings is how beautifully they move , elegantly gliding from set piece to set piece and communicating information to a viewer subtly , sometimes almost imperceptibly . It turns out that Villeneuve , a director who confesses he does n't like dialogue , is still a hell of a writer . <p> A Dune television show loosely adapted from a deep-series book written by Frank Herbert 's son , Brian , was never going to look great in comparison with Villeneuve 's mega-budget , star-filled adaptation of one of science fiction 's iconic texts . It ca n't compete visually , with budgetary constraints scaling down the grand desert vistas and stunning cinematography to a backlot-bound , digital eyesore . <p> Despite many evocations of lore , the series does little to deepen Dune mythology and mostly dilutes the brand . <p> The obvious advantage a series has over a film is the ability to take its time and go deeper . But from its opening , and across its very busy subsequent episodes , Dune : Prophecy clearly is n't concerned with breadth or depth . Helmed by showrunner Alison Schapker , previously behind the much-maligned fourth season of Westworld , and filled with a mixture of English character actors and hot young things , Dune : Prophecy is a hectic hodgepodge that never seems to settle on a coherent identity or tone . <p> It 's well-versed in sci-fi and fantasy staples , cribbing from Game of Thrones , Foundation and Andor , to name a few , but struggles to nail down its own worldbuilding and find a raison d ' ? tre beyond " Warner Bros Discovery Content Piece " . Originally called Dune : The Sisterhood , the series is billed as an exploration of the formative beginnings of the Bene Gesserit , the shadowy sect of nuns who , from behind their mysterious veils and statement-making headwear , wield immense power -- soft , political , super -- across the Imperium of Dune 's " known universe " . <p> It 's a great premise , but not one that has truly been brought to screens . Never mind the sandworms : here 's a soap opera . There 's turned-to-11 acting , laughable sex scenes , dramatic revelations , many gruesome deaths and a barrage of twists and turns . Lots of stuff is thrown at the screen , but only some of it sticks . <p> Set with amusing specificity " 10,148 years before the birth " of Paul Atreides , it plays in dual timelines . In the past we see young Valya Harkonnen ( Jessica Barden from The End of the Fucking World ) and her sister Tula ( Emma Canning ) leaving behind their jerk parents and snow-blasted , whale-trading home planet to become members of the Sisterhood 's fledgling sect . In the present , the Harkonnen sisters are now running the show . Valya ( Watson ) wears the mantle of Mother Superior , while Tula ( Olivia Williams ) , her loyal hand , is in charge of the more covert parts of the ambitious operation . <p> In this early era of the Bene Gesserit , they 've made themselves indispensable by fostering mystical powers of truth divination , finding a place at the side of every powerbroker , politician and royal in the Imperium . This includes the Emperor , Javicco Corrino ( Mark Strong ) , whose headstrong club-going daughter Ynez ( Sarah-Sofie Boussnina ) is committed to joining the Sisterhood , much to the dismay of Empress Natalya ( Jodhi May ) , who condemns these " witches " and asserts her own influence . <p> While there 's much immediate drama in Prophecy , Dune fans will know that the Bene Gesserit are long-scale planners , brokering marriages and steering bloodlines as they aim -- by , say , 10,000 years later -- to covertly control the entire empire . <p> A series solely devoted to palace intrigue and political machinations is a strong idea , especially given that Villeneuve reduced or entirely removed these elements from his movies . However , politics takes a back seat to the menace of an ultra-potent villain , Desmond Hart ( Echuca 's own Travis Fimmel , doing the most acting ) , a trenchcoated soldier who , during a tour of duty on Dune 's famed Arrakis , was swallowed by a sandworm . He has not only lived to tell the tale but emerged with ill-defined dramatic superpowers seemingly on loan from a bad comic book -- and , notably , not drawn from any actual Dune novel . <p> These powers largely consist of sending scary dreams to people across the cosmos , splashy symbolic montages that may also cause the dreamer to spontaneously combust . Hart offers his deadly long-range talents to the Emperor -- who is first appalled and then intrigued -- as a tool of vengeance : a way of striking fear into the hearts of enemies , dissidents and those who dare to employ the outlawed " thinking machines " . <p> " Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind , " someone helpfully intones mid series , another explanatory moment in a production that so often ignores the " show , do n't tell " maxim of filmmaking . Despite the ban , the Sisterhood secretly uses thinking machinery in their glittering genetic database , making them doubly villainous as both AI users and eugenicists . The most interesting elements of Dune : Prophecy interrogate Valya , in both the present and past , as a kind of antihero who wields her own tools of suppression and menace to achieve grander goals . <p> This feeds into the classic Dune themes of prophecy , with questions about its employment for political expedience or as a self-fulfilling mechanism . But the series is more beholden to prophecy 's dramatic convenience , using this device to lay the groundwork for what will happen and then moving towards the inevitability of those spooky music-video visions . <p> Despite many evocations of lore , the series does little to deepen Dune mythology and mostly dilutes the brand . If you like repetitive dream sequences , dialled-up dramatic speeches , two-dimensional characters and TV trashiness , it may play as a mildly entertaining , non-threatening time killer . But fans of the movies , waiting for Villeneuve 's upcoming Dune : Messiah , surely were hoping that the first Dune series would amount to more than " kinda watchable streaming service fodder " . <p> Dune : Prophecy is streaming on Binge . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " Sandworm soapie " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118565512 <h> Barbecued calamari with pistachio and celery pesto <p> Andrew McConnell is the executive chef and co-owner of Cutler &amp; Co , Cumulus Inc , Marion , Gimlet and Supernormal . He is a food editor of The Saturday Paper . <p> Credit : Photography by Earl Carter <p> This recipe works best with bottle squid , which are often smaller than arrow squid . I think they 're a little sweeter and easier to work with and it 's nice to be able to serve them more or less whole . <p> When cleaning the squid , I always like to leave some of the skin on the flesh so that it will caramelise and bring out the flavour . This is another reason to pick smaller squid as the skin on larger ones can be too rubbery to break down . <p> As part of the preparation , the squid is scored on one side . This helps cook it more evenly and stop it from buckling . It also looks pretty . Do n't be fooled : unlike octopus , squid does n't become more tender the longer you cook it . Be a little attentive and do n't take it too far . <p> The celery brings a lovely freshness and coolness to this dish . It 's also a great vehicle for bringing out the flavour of the pistachio . Celery does n't get the love it deserves , but I really like to use it . I like to pickle it and serve it with raw fish . With the squid it brings some moisture and refreshment and carries a good amount of olive oil . <p> Whenever I 'm working with celery , I always hold on to the smaller inner leaves , which have a unique flavour . Here I 've scattered some over the dish as a garnish , but they also work as an addition to a salad , usually in place of soft herbs . <p> Ingredients <p> Time : 20 minutes preparation + 5 minutes cooking <p> Serves 4 <p> 200g celery , preferably from the celery heart <p> 120g pistachio nuts <p> 1 clove garlic , roughly chopped <p> ? cup extra virgin olive oil <p> pinch of dried chilli flakes <p> 1 tbsp freshly grated parmesan cheese <p> zest of 1 lemon , plus some juice <p> salt flakes to season <p> 2 medium-sized squid <p> ? cup aioli ( recipe below ) <p> Method <p> Dice the celery into half-centimetre pieces , reserving any light-yellow leaves . Meanwhile , bring a medium-sized pot of salted water to simmer and quickly blanch the celery for one minute . Drain , refresh in iced water and drain again . <p> Meanwhile , preheat your oven to 180 ? C and roast the pistachio nuts for three minutes . Set aside to cool . <p> When the pistachios are cool , place the blanched celery , nuts and garlic in a food processor . Pulse a few times to make a fine meal , taking care not to over-process , as it is important that it not become a paste or puree . <p> Transfer to a bowl and stir the olive oil , dried chilli , parmesan and lemon zest into the mix . Season with salt to taste . If the mixture seems a bit thick , add a tablespoon of cold water to thin it a touch . Set this " pesto " aside and keep at room temperature until ready to serve . <p> To clean the squid , remove the tentacles and innards from the tube . Cut the squid along one edge , " butterflying " it open . Clean the internal side with some paper towel , removing any unwanted bits and pieces . Leave some of the external skin intact , as this will char and caramelise nicely on the grill . <p> Prepare your barbecue . It will need to be quite hot . Brush the prepared squid with a few drops of olive oil . Apply the internal side of the tube to the heat and , using a spatula or fish press , press gently on the tube to keep it flat so the entire piece caramelises without curling . After two minutes turn the calamari over and continue to cook for two more minutes , applying weight all the while . At this stage it is important not to overcook . Use your intuition as to how long it will take to cook , as each barbecue has a different degree of heat -- it is better to undercook than overcook . When ready , set the calamari aside on a serving plate to cool for a minute , reserving any cooking juices . <p> Cut the calamari into smaller pieces or shred into thin fettuccine-like threads . Toss in a bowl with a few drops of olive oil and lemon juice and the cooking juices . Season with a pinch of salt . <p> Arrange the seasoned calamari on serving plate . Spoon the celery and pistachio sauce over it and add a pinch of chilli and a few celery leaves to finish the dish . <p> Slowly pour the oil over the egg yolk mixture , whisking continuously to incorporate the oil . <p> Season with pepper and extra salt to taste . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " Barbecued calamari with pistachio and celery pesto " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118565513 <h> The vast bulk of Australian wool exports are unprocessed , but Tasmania 's restored Waverley Mills points to a future for high-quality , sustainable domestic manufacturing . By Lucianne Tonti . <h> Waverley Mills : a blueprint for Australian wool manufacturing <p> My niece was n't born yet when I visited Tasmania 's Waverley Mills in September this year , but when I touched one of their merino wool baby blankets , I knew what she would be getting for Christmas . My brother and his Norwegian wife live outside Oslo , where the winters reach subzero temperatures and sunlight dwindles to a few hours a day . Giving my niece ( who is now two months old ) a blanket made from Australian wool , spun and woven in the country 's last full processing factory , felt essential . For my brother it would be a small piece of home , and for his daughter a gift from a place she will one day discover is her home , too . <p> Waverley Mills sits on the banks of Distillery Creek , a 20-minute drive from Launceston Airport through Tasmania 's grey-green rolling hills . The mill was built by Scotsman Peter Bulman in 1874 , just as wool was establishing itself as Australia 's biggest export , an industry so vital to the economy that it would come to be described as " riding on the sheep 's back " . <p> The Scottish founders received a ? 1000 grant from the colonial government to establish the mill . During World War II , the Department of Defence placed a commission for 600,000 army blankets . The mill almost did n't survive the free trade agreements of the 1990s and the influx of cheaper goods from cheaper markets , and has cycled through several sales , bankruptcy and receivership . Until 2008 , it had a longstanding contract with Qantas to supply blankets for business- and first-class passengers . Over the years it has produced tweed , flannel and felted cloth . Even though it 's not perfect -- it 's not even native -- wool might be the closest thing we have to a national product . <p> At 150 years old , Waverley Mills is both a relic and the promise of a different future for Australian textile manufacturing . This country still produces 90 per cent of the world 's fine apparel wool , but due to decades of offshoring and a lack of investment in skills , technology and infrastructure , almost all Australian wool is exported before it has even been washed or scoured . <p> Waverley Mills ' red-brick buildings house the carding machines , spinning facilities and state-of-the-art looms of one of the only remaining domestic processors . The majority of the wool it handles is sourced from Tasmanian farms , and the balance is from the mainland . Those fleeces are scoured in Geelong and come to Launceston to be turned into blankets , throws , shawls and scarves . <p> The mill reverted to using locally processed Australian wool only very recently . <p> When Dave Giles-Kaye came on as managing director in December 2022 , Waverley Mills was no longer able to produce its own yarn . The previous owners had n't maintained the machinery and it had stopped working . They were making blankets out of a polyester-wool blend imported from Italy . " When I started , I wanted to go back to the roots of the business and only deal with natural fibres , " Giles-Kaye says . " First principles : we 're trying to add value to Tasmanian wool before it gets exported . " <p> Even though it 's not perfect -- it 's not even native -- wool might be the closest thing we have to a national product . <p> To restore the mill 's full operations , Giles-Kaye , now the executive director , had to secure sizeable investment . He says more than $10 million has been spent to buy new equipment , repair existing machinery and redevelop the site . Of this , $6 million was in grants from the Albanese government ; another $400,000 came from the Tasmanian government . The remainder was from a group of investors . Now the major shareholders include an entrepreneur with local ties who prefers not to be identified in the media , and Southern Cotton , which owns a cotton gin in New South Wales . <p> The partnership with Southern Cotton arose from a shared ambition to bring value-added processing of natural fibres back to Australia . " They 're not pushing cotton on us , " says Giles-Kaye . " But they wanted to invest because all their cotton goes elsewhere and just disappears . They would like to turn it into a textile . " <p> Giles-Kaye headed up the Australian Fashion Council until the end of 2019 and hopes the government will see the economic opportunity in restoring more domestic capacity to process wool . Australia 's wool exports are worth about $3 billion a year , he says , and " we 've just prepared a document which argues the case for how you turn that three billion into a hundred billion " . <p> Although it might seem niche , even processing 5 per cent of Australia 's wool clip onshore would amount to " a big industry " , says Giles-Kaye . But it 's a long-term plan . He is thinking about the industry over a 20- or 30-year timeframe , anticipating an increase in consumer demand for traceable , sustainable products . It 's a hopeful pushback against the growing tide of cheap , mass-produced synthetic products that has made Australians the world 's biggest consumers of fast fashion , according to The Australia Institute . <p> Although the introduction of sheep and cattle to this country has often been lamented as a source of deforestation , desertification and greenhouse gas emissions , Waverley Mills is committed to using natural materials . All its wool is from Responsible Wool Standard -- certified farms , where the sheep are grazed using regenerative farming practices that sequester carbon and improve ecosystem functionality , biodiversity , soil health and water cycles . Similarly , the mill runs on renewable electricity -- except a boiler , which will soon be replaced and run on gas -- and a new system to manage its wastewater is also being implemented . <p> This sustainable outlook extends to the business 's circularity initiatives . At the back of the property , inside the enormous old shearing shed near a large wooden table -- where years ago the wool would have been graded for its staple length and fineness -- stands a large metal machine used to tear garment and textile waste into shreds that can be spun back into yarn . The machine is the soft green colour of vintage tools and running through its cogs and wheels are the bright yellow fibres of jackets that were worn by personnel in the Victorian Country Fire Authority . The uniform is made from a fire-retardant-treated cotton textile . The CFA is reissuing its uniforms over the next year and tens of thousands of old uniforms will be diverted from landfill and sent to Waverley Mills instead . At the mill , the recycled cotton will be mixed with virgin wool and woven into a golden-yellow car blanket that will be launched in January . Already on sale is a collaboration with Nudie Jeans -- soft blue throws made from 70 per cent virgin wool and 30 per cent recycled denim . <p> The mill is processing 35 tonnes of wool a year , which amounts to about 35,000 products . Giles-Kaye says they have the capacity to process 120 tonnes a year -- it 's something to work towards . " We came back from nothing really to get to where we are now , " he says . Since the carding machine was only fixed in August 2023 , a lot of the growth has happened in just over a year . <p> Given wool 's prominence in this country 's colonial history , at least , it should n't be so hard to buy Australian-made wool products . Waverley Mills itself is proof that , despite the decimation of supply chains , it 's possible to revive hyperlocal textile manufacturing . Giles-Kaye is rightly proud he has been able to protect the mill 's legacy . " When we are at markets , we often have old ladies come over and tell us , ' Oh , I was given a Waverley Mills blanket as a wedding present and I still use it . ' ? " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " The miller 's tale " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers .
