@@118565514 <h> The sleazy world of professional wrestling impresario Vince McMahon trades on scandal and brutality -- and has left in its wake a trail of lost lives , broken men and allegations of abuse . By Martin McKenzie-Murray . <h> The dark side of Vince McMahon 's WWE empire <p> For decades , professional wrestlers seemed to be dying in disproportionate numbers and in violent ways . Wrestlers were murdered , they drowned , they rolled their cars . They suffered overdoses , aneurysms and heart attacks . They died in the ring , after smashing their heads , or they killed themselves with guns or rope . The profession , once defined by steroids and unregulated painkillers , seemed morbidly blighted and its participants subject to terrible odds . <p> " Everybody 's dead , " ex-wrestler Roddy Piper said in an interview with HBO in 2003 . " They 're all dying early and nobody cares about it ... They take them and they screw them up so much . " <p> Piper was 49 at the time , and predicted he would n't live to 65 . He was right . In the same segment , Vince McMahon -- the founder of WWF/WWE and professional wrestling 's most influential and infamous promoter -- was asked if he felt any responsibility for the premature deaths of wrestlers who 'd once worked for him . McMahon became furious , denied any responsibility for the " bad habits " wrestlers had acquired before their involvement with him , and then slapped the notes from the reporter 's hands . <p> There are many obituaries , as there are many prophetic testimonies from those about to die . In 2007 , Andrew Martin -- another retired wrestler who had worked for McMahon 's WWF/WWE -- gave an interview . His hero and mentor , Chris Benoit , had just murdered his wife and young son , before hanging himself . A study of Benoit 's brain found evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy . " I just turned 32 years old and went to eight funerals , " Martin said . " As bad as it may sound , it made me open my eyes and take my foot out the grave . I do n't want to join that club . Either you clean up and straighten up or lay down beside them . " <p> Two years later , Martin lay down beside them . <p> Was the long list of violently premature deaths statistically significant ? Or were these deaths subject to selection bias -- that is , given their curious cultural status , were we reporting and remembering these deaths above others ? <p> According to a 2014 study from Eastern Michigan University , they were significant . The researchers examined publicly available data for 557 male wrestlers ( 62 of whom had died , 49 of them before the age of 50 ) who performed between 1985 and 2011 , and found that among " active professional wrestlers over the past quarter of a century ... there is an alarmingly high premature mortality rate " . What 's more , former pro wrestlers were found to be almost 123 times more likely than the general population to die from a drug overdose . <p> Long before the WWE applied for a softer PG rating , and Dwayne " The Rock " Johnson leveraged wrestling fame into Disney films and rom-coms , pro wrestlers were the ultimate hard-living misfits . Existing in a strange twilight between athlete and actor , they performed fake violence by actually breaking their bones , and to continue their weekly slog -- there was no off-season -- they drank and juiced and swallowed opioids like candy . <p> McMahon instinctively wove his real life into wrestling scripts . Everything could be incorporated . Buyouts were announced on live television , and on the show he 'd just bought . Lawsuits were written into the night 's patter . All of it translated into ratings . <p> Vince McMahon , the sleazy , brutal and hyper-successful P. ? T. Barnum of professional wrestling , was the subject of a biography last year and , recently , a six-part series on Netflix . Earlier this year , he was also the subject of yet another lawsuit alleging sexual misconduct , after which he resigned as executive chairman of TKO -- the company made last year after McMahon 's WWE merged with the UFC . <p> Six hours is a long time to spend with McMahon and his cacophonous universe . Born in a trailer park in 1945 , he was 12 when he first met his father -- a wrestling promoter from whom McMahon inherited his carnie ambition and in whose shadow he forged his own distinctive ruthlessness . <p> McMahon speaks of business as others speak of love -- one former colleague says it 's the only thing he 's ever been faithful to . And if he 's a man who has ever experienced doubt , regret or shame , he 's not one to reveal it publicly . In many hours of tape , committed before the allegations this year of sex trafficking and serious sexual assault , he 's both weird and unrevealing . <p> In the 1980s , McMahon inherited his father 's business in the age of " territories " -- a loosely confederated system of local competitions -- and sought to break or swallow them . Abiding " the law of the jungle " , a favourite phrase of McMahon 's , he would eventually succeed in destroying competitors and making his own cartel , and a product that attracted many millions of viewers every week . <p> In the 1980s , the phenomenon of Hulk Hogan depended on a steroidal physique and his cartoonish avatar as an ultra-dude and Reagan patriot . " We do n't always set trends , we follow them , " McMahon says in the series , which is obvious to anyone who watched him reflect the Iran hostage crisis by creating an Iranian heel , or " bad guy " -- " The Iron Sheik " -- to get whipped by the Hulk . During the first Gulf War , McMahon created an Iraqi villain . <p> The scripting of wrestling once relied on good guys and bad , but in the 1990s the vaudevillian nonsense got darker . Again , McMahon was n't steering pop culture -- just amplifying it in a brash and shameless way . He saw the emergence of hyper-sexualised music videos and the lurid circus of Jerry Springer . He clocked the entrance of death metal and Marilyn Manson to the mainstream , and he created a soap opera populated by villains and ritually degraded women . <p> A major refinement of McMahon 's , in what became an arms race of vulgarity in the ' 90s , was the introduction of himself as the chief heel of all wrestling : Mr McMahon , the unhinged , despotic and sexually depraved billionaire . As crowds of dudes booed him and hurled their Pepsi cups onto the stage , Vince McMahon grinned -- their emotion translated into big bucks , and he knew that , among wrestling crowds , there 's precious little difference between booing and cheering . <p> What do you need to know about Vince McMahon ? The following should tell you plenty . He conscripted his two children into the family business and approved one storyline that involved his daughter being drugged , raped and married in Vegas while under the influence . Her next appearance in a stadium was greeted by thousands of frat boys chanting " slut " and waving placards saying much the same . According to a colleague , McMahon watched the reaction , grinned , then rubbed his fingers together . <p> In 1999 , the wrestler Owen Hart was being lowered from stadium rafters in a harness -- which broke when he was still suspended 25 metres above the ring . He died on the mat , his aorta torn by the force of impact . As medics vainly rushed him to hospital , the night 's entertainment continued . " These people came to see a show , " McMahon says of that night in the Netflix series . " They did n't come to see someone die . And for me as a businessman , it 's : ' Okay , let 's move on . Let 's keep the show going . ' ? " <p> The sweet spot for a wrestling storyline was when fans were genuinely unsure if something was authentic or not . Given the drugs , concussions and ritualised rat-fucking of pro wrestling , one could never be sure when histrionic aggression might actually be real . McMahon knew this , knew the best storylines were ones that borrowed from real life and thus smudged the border of fantasy -- which is why he re-employed so many people who had once sued him . It 's also why few people who know him well say there 's much difference between Vince McMahon the entrepreneur and Mr McMahon the wrestling villain . <p> McMahon instinctively wove his real life into wrestling scripts . Everything could be incorporated . Buyouts were announced on live television , and on the show he 'd just bought . Lawsuits were written into the night 's patter . All of it translated into ratings . <p> Scandal was money . Emotion was profitable . One did n't know if he was playing Mr McMahon when doing a real interview about real deaths , or if he was a genuine , amoral narcissist with weak emotional regulation . I incline towards the latter , but Vince McMahon could n't care less -- this ambiguity helped the bottom line . Pro wrestling was born on the old carnie trails and here now was carnie make-believe on literal steroids and fat cable deals . <p> The lawsuits kept coming . Many for sexual harassment . One for rape . All were settled . That was , until this year 's . That lawsuit was paused , upon request from the Department of Justice , which wanted to investigate . Another lawsuit came in October : this one from five men whose lawyers alleged Vince and his then wife and one-time chief executive , Linda McMahon , had knowingly failed to prevent their sexual abuse as boys at the hands of the late ringside announcer Melvin Phillips Jr . <p> A few months ago , McMahon 's wife of almost 60 years announced they 'd separated . Last month , family friend Donald Trump nominated Linda as his next secretary of education . She had already served in his first cabinet and , with Vince , had made substantial donations to Trump 's first run for the presidency . <p> These days , the old carnie trail leads straight to the White House . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 7 , 2024 as " Sideshow ally " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118567985 <h> HSC disability scheme favours the rich <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> The innate unfairness of the HSC disability provisions scheme is something I have been aware of since my early years practising as a GP and which has only escalated since then ( " Surge in HSC help prompts review " , December 1 ) . I first became aware of it many years ago when repeatedly asked for referrals to medical specialists , which resulted in almost every case in the diagnosis of medical conditions which supported eligibility for disability provisions . Awareness of ability to do this was highest in those parents whose children attended private schools and for whom the cost was not a barrier . Today , with the epidemic of increasing diagnoses of ADHD being made and with even higher expense involved to obtain a diagnosis , it is clear which group of students will be able to have their eligibility certified by a medical professional . That 50 per cent of one of the most expensive private schools students have applied makes it clear that the review is essential . @@118568034 <p> The Coalition 's most vociferous nuclear convert has made the most of his position on a Labor-dominated committee investigating Australia 's energy future . <p> On the day the House Select Committee on Nuclear Energy rolled into Melbourne this week , deputy chair Ted O'Brien lined up interviews with five programs on the ABC alone , where he was challenged by presenters about various aspects of the Coalition 's nuclear policy . <p> Two years after first flagging the plan to build seven reactors in five states , and six months after naming where the publicly funded reactors would be built , many questions remain . <p> The public is no closer to learning how much the Coalition 's nuclear plan would cost , when it would have any impact on their ever-increasing power bills or whether they 'd be built in time to replace the coal-fired power stations already exiting the grid . <p> It placed four Labor MPs on the committee alongside two Coalition members , including O'Brien , and one independent . <p> Amid a fierce political debate over energy policy , the inquiry was seen as a tactic to discredit the nuclear push and stir up opposition in the regional communities where the Coalition wants to build reactors on the site of retiring coal-fired power stations , starting from 2035 . <p> After hearings in Queensland , Victoria and Canberra , O'Brien reckons the Labor-led inquiry has given him a platform to ventilate his plans , or in other words , to " normalise " nuclear . <p> " It was a bit of a political stitch-up , " O'Brien said of the inquiry . <p> " There are people who are adamantly opposed , people who are adamantly for it and the vast majority are open-minded . " <p> In each location , as a committee member , the shadow energy minister conducted interviews with local media , and held informal community consultation sessions , slowly bridging the knowledge gap that exists about nuclear -- a technology that 's been banned in Australia for 20 years . <h> Spin and political strategy <p> The public hearings themselves have been variously described as " civil " , " balanced " and " respectful " by three of the regional mayors whose towns hosted the nuclear roadshow . <p> Witnesses have been invited to give evidence , with nuclear proponents arguing an industrialised nation like Australia needs the reliable , base-load , low-emissions power that nuclear can provide , while opponents have labelled the push a ' smokescreen ' to burn coal and gas for longer . <p> Photo shows A graphic of a nuclear power plant with a nuclear symbol and the numbers 2040 and 2045 in the foreground <p> As the shift away from fossil fuels gathers pace , the Coalition has turned to nuclear fission . These are the numbers you should keep in mind when thinking about its place in Australia 's energy transition . <p> In Biloela , near Gladstone in Queensland , where about 100 community members turned up for the hearing , much of the anger being vented was about the massive expansion of wind and solar farms , changing the landscape in the region . <p> Labor committee member Graham Perrett suspected some on the anti-renewables side had been encouraged to attend . <p> He recounted a conversation with one farmer who could see the Callide coal-fired power station from his kitchen window but was flatly opposed to the idea of a solar farm being built on the property next door . <p> Perrett 's not yet convinced that nuclear can be done any cheaper than Labor 's renewables plan and he 's definitely not convinced Australia can settle a 50-year-old debate about where to store the waste that 's produced . <p> Last month , legislation was passed to allow for the storage and disposal of nuclear waste at the Adelaide shipyard in Osborne . Local residents staged a protest against the plan . ( ABC News : Brant Cumming ) <p> But after attending the Queensland hearings , what surprised him most was " the extreme spin coming off the same set of facts and information " . <p> That just about sums up the debate about energy , a highly complex and politicised policy area where voters are being asked to decide between Labor 's " reckless renewables " or the Coalition 's " un-costed nuclear fantasy " . <h> Regional communities aired plenty of concerns <p> The inquiry has so far held public hearings in Biloela , Nanango in Queensland 's South Burnett region , Traralgon in Victoria 's La Trobe Valley , and Port Augusta in South Australia . In regional towns like these , energy literacy is high . <p> The coal-fired power stations in those towns have been employing hundreds of locals and providing cheap , reliable power for decades and so the prospect of a nuclear power station is , to some , quite attractive . <p> La Trobe Valley Mayor Dale Harriman gave evidence at the Traralgon stop last week , summing the hearing up as " really well-balanced -- some were supportive , some were n't , and a lot were very curious about how it would affect the community " . <p> Darren McCubbin from the Gippsland Climate Change Network received applause when he told the meeting there were renewable projects ready to go , while the Coalition 's nuclear plan would take years to become a reality . <p> At the Biloela hearing , farmers also expressed concerns about how a nuclear power plant might affect the value of their land and the impact on water supplies in a region often drought-declared . <p> Banana Shire Mayor Neville Ferrier gave evidence and said some were clearly " dead against " nuclear , but he estimates about 60 per cent of locals were in favour of it . <p> He 's not taking a position just yet , noting the Coalition must win two elections to turn its nuclear dream into a reality . But he can see the rationale for it . <p> " We need base-load power and we 're not going to get that with renewables alone . So , you keep the coal-fired power stations going or you go nuclear , " Ferrier said . <p> South Burnett Shire Mayor Kathy Duff said it was standing room only at the Nanago Services Club hearing last month . <p> She says her community is worried about job losses , with the Tarong coal-fired power station due to close in just over a decade , as well as the rollout of renewables . <p> " We need to look at nuclear as an option , " she said , adding : " We wanted a lot more information . " <h> The nuclear debate is still light on detail <p> This is the challenge for O'Brien and his colleagues : turning a curiosity about nuclear into such full-throated support that voters will back the plan at next year 's election . <p> As the Coalition prepares to release its costings this week , it needs to convince voters that the economics stack up compared to renewables , and that it could reverse state and federal bans on nuclear power , write new laws and regulations , acquire the technology and build the first plant -- all within the space of a decade . <p> That 's a problem when 90 per cent of Australia 's coal-fired power stations -- the backbone of the energy grid -- are due to close in a decade . <p> Clare Savage , the Australian Energy Regulator , said nuclear could " maybe " play a role in decarbonising the energy grid by 2050 but from her professional experience , she estimated drafting the necessary laws and regulations alone would take 10 years . <p> " Coal ca n't last until you have nuclear power available , " Savage told the hearing . <p> The window for nuclear in Australia , as a means of achieving net zero , is arguably closing . The Coalition has just months to convince Australians to take the leap .

Labor has shrunk from conflict with the Coalition , and abandoned plans to clean up the systemic mismanagement of government . <p> I have wondered before if Labor had a secret mission to uphold the two-party system ahead of success with the help of third parties or independents . Doing so had the additional benefit - or so it was argued - that neither the Greens nor the Teals would get any credit , even though they had done more to make the tough policy a major campaign issue than Labor itself . It was also argued , unconvincingly , that making a deal with the Coalition would bind them more to the ( castrated ) commission because they had voted for it . Court , who has supported Teal candidates and other independents for campaigns based on climate change action . <p> Holmes ? " <p> The legislation rushed through the House of Representatives in less than a day worked heavily to the advantage of Labor and the Coalition , and weakened the power of independents to compete with them . It has been shelved in the Senate until next year . In its current form , it would effectively grandfather many of the rights and privileges of the long-established major parties and exempt them from a number of the limits on election spending . It would also continue a number of deliberately constructed loopholes allowing big donors to escape obligations to report party income , and mechanisms to help the big parties to donate eight times the notional donor limits , by allowing them to donate to each of the state and territory branches of the major parties . <p> Put bluntly , many of the proposals are rorts on the taxpayer and the minor parties . But one can be sure that the Coalition will not complain . They have been colluding with Labor to get around the system for decades . And even as ministers have pretended that the various sham " reforms " over these decades have tightened up scrutiny and proscribed misbehaviour , party officials have been briefing big donors on how to avoid them . <p> Australia does operate by Westminster-style conventions , though not by the same rules as in Britain , Ireland , Canada and New Zealand . Each has adapted over the past century or more according to its own needs . It has never embraced , whether in constitutional form or in practical reality , any assumption of a two-party system , or reason politicians or the public should lean to a binary system . Having multiple players in the game magnifies the areas from which a party can attack . <p> There was no binary system in the first 14 years of federation . There were loose gatherings of people , sometimes bound by loose agreements about supply , but often in bitter argument with each other over matters such as protection , free trade , and states ' rights . A party system scarcely existed in the Australian states in the 19th century , and , as in Britain , many MPs may have belonged loosely to the Tories , the Whigs and the Liberals , but many were not bound by party membership . Labor , in Australia as well as Britain , was the first to develop a legal structure . It is simply impossible to identify principles even of collectivism or individualism . That 's because being left- or right-wing does not predict whether you are authoritarian or laissez-faire . <p> Indeed , it was not until very recent times that the Constitution even mentioned political parties at all . The usages of Westminster government have never much figured in constitutional arguments before governors-general or the High Court . Likewise , " Westminster principles " of ministerial resignation have been honoured mostly in the breach . <p> Various Labor splits from 1917 to about 1942 mean that there were usually at least two , sometimes three Labor parties , each bitterly fighting the others . In the mid-1950s , Labor split again for another 20 years . Don Farrell 's party history owes more to the DLP side of that split than the ALP . At its peak , the DLP had five Senate seats , which it used consciously to keep Labor out of power . <h> All candidates must be treated equally <p> Likewise , Coalition parties have long had splits , even leaving aside the role of the Nationals ( once Country Party ) , formed near the end of WWI . There was a rough unity for 20 years under the Bruce Page governments and the United Australia Party , but the split of 1941 caused the break-up of anti-Labor parties until Bob Menzies welded together the Liberal Party . <p> I do not know why Senator Farrell is telling voters about the existence of some general principle of trying to preserve the two-party system . It is easy enough to understand why the Coalition would go along with the idea that there was such a principle , because it could work only to Labor 's disadvantage . The fact that the Coalition did so could not bind it forward or backwards . Nor could it justify the unequal treatment of parliamentary candidates . We need to require fair and free elections with the same rules applying to everyone . It is as fundamental as the implied right of freedom of political speech . The High Court does not have to play politics . It would simply judge whether the legislation treats all candidates similarly . <p> The High Court might recognise the fundamental and deliberate inequality . It is , after all , no different in principle than an executive decision to give funding to one party only , or only to parties that had achieved 25 per cent of the vote , or only to parties arbitrarily selected by the prime minister . <p> There is also the risk that the " reforms " rule could aggravate unequal treatment . Independent candidates may get the same $5 as major parties do for every vote achieved . In theory at least . But in practice they will not have access to the lurks by which they can classify some expenditure as not being devoted to the political campaign . Thus , for example , pamphlets , social media ads , and TV ads that merely say " vote Labor " or " Vote Labor for cheaper energy " do not amount to campaign expenditure marked against the particular candidate . Only advertising that mentions the candidate is marked as being for the campaign . <p> Because Labor ( and the other side ) are running in every seat , they have much more capacity to claim general rather than individual campaign expenditure . What this may mean in practice is that independents effectively get less money than the big parties do . Labor and the Coalition are already getting more than $100 million a year from taxpayers for election funding . If the gap increases between the practical amounts parties can claim , the disadvantage is multiplied . If all candidates were treated equally , Labor and the Coalition would get about a third of the total funds each . And independents getting more than 4 per cent of the vote would get about a third between them , apportioned by their total vote . It is quite easy to imagine that the new system would have independents getting only about 15 per cent of total funding , even if they hold their proportion of the vote , or increase it . <p> Of course there are definite advantages in some of the changes . It is good that all donations , whether to the party or the candidate , be reported online , and simultaneously with its receipt . Likewise with expenditure . It may be that there is some justification for having higher fundraising limits when independents are involved . This is because of the capacity of party candidates to raise more and appear to spend less . Such limits would not permit the limitless spending of a Clive Palmer . But it could allow a crusading candidate , a Teal for example , raising $2 million from donors . That extra $2 million , added to the publicly funded war chest , would be about equal to what was spent in vulnerable seats at the last election . Some defending candidates , Josh Frydenberg and his challenger , spent even more . <h> Propping up the Coalition is a damn-fool idea <p> David Pope 's view . <p> It is interesting that Albanese is trying to make it harder for independents and smaller parties at just the same time that voters are turning away from the major parties . The turnout for independents , the Greens , One Nation , Jacqui Lambie and others will probably be higher next year than in 2022 . This is no evidence that the higher average vote is because voters are stupid or have been conned . Rather , the big parties are trying to make up for lost revenue caused by declining support . <p> But even more puzzling is why Albanese and Farrell have persuaded themselves that sending their preferences to the Liberals rather than the Greens can work to their benefit . Labor and the Greens may be struggling hard against each other so as to differentiate their policies and ideas . But Labor does not have any chance of retaining government if it can not be sure of getting almost all of the preferences of the Greens . As things stand , Labor may get 32 per cent of the first preference vote . The Greens may get 14 per cent , with preferences going to Labor . The 46 per cent , with other preferences , could be the springboard for victory . In some inner-city electorates , Green candidates may secure enough votes that they actually defeat the Labor candidate , once ( if ) the Coalition votes are distributed to the Greens . The Greens ( or Labor ) can win such contests if they come second in total votes , and are put in by the preferences of the third-highest candidate , the Coalition . <p> Labor may be assuming , as it always does these days , that it can automatically get Green preferences because the Greens , as a left-of-Labor team , have nowhere else to go . Even if Green leaders promoted a vote against Labor , most would revolt . But it might well be different if Labor was actively campaigning against the Greens . That could be a matter of retaliation . But it could also be because many Green supporters are disappointed with Labor in government , and with Albanese in particular . Albanese is not so well-stocked with friends that he can afford to spurn 40 per cent of the votes he received at the last election . <p> Labor indeed would be far better off attacking the Liberals as the actual enemy . It would be better putting the heat on its leaders , avoiding weak compromises and showing some guts and enthusiasm . <p> And dropping the damn-fool idea that it has some obligation to prop up the two-party system . It does n't and trying to do so is the sure path to electoral suicide .

@@118568838 <h> Exactly How Much Can You Save By Turning Off the Lights at Home ? <p> One quick flip can lead to considerable savings . Here 's how much . <p> Erin GoblerContributor <p> Erin Gobler is a personal finance writer based in Madison , Wisconsin . She writes about topics including budgeting , student loans , credit , mortgages , investing and insurance . Her work has been published in financial publications and startups such as NextAdvisor , The Simple Dollar , LendingTree , Robinhood and more . <p> Reducing your energy use by turning off your lights is an excellent way to reduce your carbon footprint . <p> Eoneren/Getty Images <p> Even though we 're close to the autumn season , the northern hemisphere is still experiencing humid and sunnier days . With electricity and energy bill prices still elevated , no matter how you cool and light your home it 's likely been costing you more than expected . And you may be looking for ways to save on energy . <p> Once you add in increased rents , higher mortgage rates and pricier groceries , you might already be feeling a strain on your wallet . However , there are ways to extend your monthly budget . <h> Why turn off your lights ? <p> From talking fridges to iPhones , our experts are here to help make the world a little less complicated . <p> By signing up , you will receive newsletters and promotional content and agree to our Terms of Use and acknowledge the data practices in our Privacy Policy . You may unsubscribe at any time . <p> You 've probably been told time and time again the importance of conserving energy , but you might be wondering why it 's so important . <p> First , reducing your energy usage by turning off your lights is an excellent way to reduce your carbon footprint . Electricity generation is one of the biggest sources of carbon emissions that contribute to climate change . By turning off your lights when you are n't using them , you can do your part to reduce carbon emissions and therefore help the environment . <p> And reducing your home 's energy usage does n't just help the environment -- it also helps your wallet . Turning off lights when you do n't need them can help to reduce your electricity bills . You 'll also extend the life of your light bulbs , which will save you money as well . <p> Buying a smart lightbulb can help you conserve energy by setting your lights to go on and off at certain times -- no more falling asleep with all the lights left on overnight . The inexpensive Wyze bulb is CNET 's pick for best smart light . <p> From talking fridges to iPhones , our experts are here to help make the world a little less complicated . <p> By signing up , you will receive newsletters and promotional content and agree to our Terms of Use and acknowledge the data practices in our Privacy Policy . You may unsubscribe at any time . <h> How much money can you save by turning off the lights ? <p> The amount you can save on your electricity bill by turning off your lights depends on the type of light bulb you use . You can figure your potential savings using the light bulb 's wattage . <p> Let 's say you have a light bulb that 's 40 watts , meaning that in one hour , the bulb will use 0.04 kWh . Then , you can use your electricity price -- which you can find on your most recent utility bill -- to figure out how much you 'll save for that hour . In the case of the 40-watt bulb , if you pay an electricity rate of 10 cents per kWh , your savings by turning that bulb off for one hour would be 0.4 cents . <p> Now , it 's easy to see that number and think it 's simply not worth it to turn off your lights more often . After all , what difference does 0.4 cents make ? <p> First , remember that estimate is for a 40-watt bulb . If you have higher-wattage light bulbs , then the savings will be greater . Next , that estimate uses an energy price of 10 cents per kWh , but in many areas , the price of electricity may be higher than that . <p> Finally , our estimate looked at the savings of turning off one bulb for one hour . You likely have many light bulbs in your house , and there are far more than just one hour in a month . So when you calculate the savings of turning off all of your light bulbs for many more hours per month , your savings will increase significantly . <h> A small change can yield big savings in the long run <p> Turning off your lights when you are n't using them is one of the most basic steps you can take to reduce your energy usage and save money on your electricity bill . Just remember that even a small change can add up to big energy savings for you and also help reduce your carbon footprint.

@@118589747 <h> Heatwave-tolerant potatoes the latest climate ready crops <p> Katherine Meacham-Hensold led research that showed engineering improvements in the photorespiratory bypass of potato led to increased tuber mass in heatwave conditions . Credit : RIPE Project/Katherine Meacham-Hensold <p> Engineering plants to thrive in warmer and drier conditions associated with climate change is an exploding field of scientific study , as researchers all over the world work to stave off the threat of food insecurity . <p> Two new studies have shown how enzymes contribute to plant resilience , with one showing great value in potato crops . <p> The genetic modifications targeted the process known as photorespiration , which has been shown to reduce the yield of soybean , rice , and vegetable crops by up to 40% and happens more often under high temperature conditions . <p> " If we are going to meet the need for food in regions most at risk from reduced yields due to global warming , " says Katherine Meacham-Hensold of the University of Illinois in the US , first author of the Global Change Biology paper . <p> " We need to produce crops that can withstand more frequent and intense heatwave events . <p> During photosynthesis a plant enzyme , rubisco , catalyses the fixation of carbon dioxide . But it can also catalyse a reaction with oxygen in a process known as photorespiration . <p> This is an essential plant process , but it also wastes energy produced by photosynthesis and produces a toxic byproduct -- glycolate . It also happens more frequently under hot and dry conditions . <p> " Photorespiration is a large energy cost for the plant , " says Meacham-Hensold . <p> " It takes away from food production as energy is diverted to metabolising the toxin . Our goal was to reduce the amount of wasted energy by bypassing the plant 's original photorespiratory pathway . " <p> Researchers were n't sure how the potatoes would respond to the high temperatures , but harvest showed the modified potatoes grew 30% more mass than the control potatoes . Credit : RIPE Project/Claire Benjamin <p> A separate study , published in the Plant Biotechnology Journal , looked at increasing the ability of plants to survive at high temperatures by engineering the enzyme at the final step in photorespiration . <p> In this study , researchers increased the thermostability of the enzyme glycerate 3-kinase ( GLYK ) , which is involved in the final step of photorespiration , in thale cress ( Arabidopsis thaliana ) . <p> They looked at the structure of the same enzyme in the alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae , which lives in acidic volcanic hot springs . After identifying the structural characteristics responsible for its greater thermostability , the researchers introduced these into Arabidopsis GLYK . <p> " By understanding the ' why ' of how C. merolae enzymes operate at higher temperatures , we can reengineer plant enzymes to be better prepared for a world with higher temperatures , " says Berkley Walker , associate professor at Michigan State University in the US . <p> The next step is to introduce these engineered , more thermotolerant enzymes into the model plant Arabidopsis to see how the plant reacts . <p> " Understanding how we can learn from nature and improve enzymes for a warmer future is critical since plants are faced with temperatures that they have not historically been exposed to , " Walker says . <p> " Some enzymes are going to be just fine , but others may not be able to take the heat . With this knowledge , we have a strategy we can try on any enzyme to increase its ability to operate under warmer conditions . "

Credit : Adobe Stock/Martin Villadsen - stock.adobe.c <p> People with hay fever may be more likely to crash their car when the pollen count is high , a study suggests . <p> Scientists have found that , on days when pollen levels are soaring , there is a six per cent increase in fatal road accidents . <p> For every one per cent rise in the amount circulating in the air from flowers , grass and trees , the number of crashes rose by two per cent . <p> This suggests that allergy symptoms , such as sneezing and itchy eyes , could impact driving ability in a similar way to drinking alcohol , the researchers said . <p> One theory is that a high pollen count may impair some people 's cognitive ability -- increasing the time it takes for them to react and shortening their attention span , so they are more distracted . <p> The researchers , from Wayne State University in the US city of Detroit , said : " This is the first study on the extent to which allergies due to seasonal pollen affect traffic fatalities . <p> " We find novel evidence that traffic fatalities increase on days in which the local pollen count is particularly high . <p> These effects are driven by cognitive impairments that arise as a result of seasonal allergies . <p> We hypothesise that exposure to pollen impairs cognitive ability and reaction time . " For the study , experts analysed 11 years of data on car crashes in the US , alongside other research about atmospheric conditions , including pollen counts . <p> They found there were 5.8 per cent more fatal accidents on days when the count was high , compared to when it was low . <p> The study , published in the Journal of Health Economics , states : " Given that driving requires high performance of both parts of the brain which deal with automated tasks and with reaction time , pollen allergies could temporarily impair drivers resulting in more traffic fatalities . <p> " Previous research has estimated that the cognitive impairment caused by seasonal allergies is comparable to that of being under 0.05 per cent blood-alcohol content , which is the legal driving limit in many countries . " The findings are significant as rising global temperatures driven by climate change are already causing the pollen season in the UK to become longer and more intense . <p> Around 10 million people in England -- one in seven -- have some form of pollen allergy . <p> Along with a runny nose , sore throat and itchy eyes , hay fever can also trigger wheezing and asthma attacks . 
@@118602044 <h> Australia needs to think outside the box on packaging <p> Camera IconAlmost half of Australia 's annual six million tonnes of packaging ends up in landfill . ( Jono Searle/AAP PHOTOS ) Credit : AAP <p> A proposed national packaging scheme could force manufacturers to start thinking outside the box on household waste and carbon emissions . <p> Australia uses more than six million tonnes of packaging every year at a rough cost of $15 billion , mostly paid for by consumers and with almost half ending up in landfill . <p> The nation 's environment ministers agreed to an overhaul by 2025 after an independent review found more should be done both to recycle plastic packaging and increase its recycled content . <p> Used milk cartons could become pallets to carry the next batch , for example , if they were designed for re-use from the get-go . <p> Consumers are also concerned about the impact of recycled materials on food safety but paper fibre could also be turned into construction materials or toilet paper . <p> " The system we have today is reaching the limits , " according to Tetra Pak managing director for Australia and New Zealand Boris Munster . <p> " Recycling rates are stagnating . " <p> But a lack of infrastructure after years of shipping waste to Asia means Australia needs to strike a balance that suits local sustainability and recycling requirements , the global packaging and processing company believes . <p> An approach known as extended producer responsibility ( EPR ) makes companies responsible for how they make products - for a circular and low-emission economy - but also what happens after the consumer has used them . <p> " What we 've seen from other countries where they launch an EPR scheme is that producers look for alternatives and look for lightweight packaging material or more renewable packaging material , " Mr Munster said . <p> When they are also required to report their greenhouse gas emissions , they start moving towards more sustainable options and rejuvenate their industrial base , he said . <p> A " life-cycle assessment " of packaging would measure emissions along the value chain from raw materials to the recycling stream and force the industry to look for more sustainable methods . <p> " We need to incorporate that into the eco-modelling or how EPR schemes could look , " Mr Munster said . <p> " If you 're going to apply it on the existing infrastructure , you 're not going to create that innovation towards a more sustainable and less emissions-driven industry . " <p> RMIT sustainability and industrial design expert Simon Lockrey said the ultimate goal of no packaging and no food waste would require a switch to micro-farms around suburbia and daily shopping . <p> People see packaging as an " unnecessary evil " but removing it would drive a worse environmental issue - greater food waste , he said . <p> " There 's a role for packaging as it gets food to consumers in a good condition and extends shelf life , " Dr Lockrey said . <p> " There 's still a lot more to be done to get the best out of the incumbent system ... it is actually designed most of the time to help people in the home , " he said . <p> But packaging reform wo n't be wrapped up before the federal election , which must be held by May . <p> The department of Climate Change , Energy , Environment and Water is analysing submissions on options , including legislating mandatory requirements and an extended producer responsibility scheme . <p> Producers will also be required to do more to eliminate harmful chemicals such as PFAS from food packaging . <p> Dubbed " forever chemicals " because of their long life , the PFAS group accumulate in water , soil and living organisms and have been linked to cancer , immune suppression and developmental issues . <p> " The consultation will support government consideration in 2025 of a preferred regulatory option and potential obligations under a reformed scheme based on international best practice , " a department spokesperson said .

@@118602242 <p> Angela Bishop has been struggling with what she describes as " the cost of everything lately . " Groceries are one stressor , although she gets some reprieve from the free school lunches her four kids receive . Still , a few years of the stubbornly high cost of gas , utilities , and clothing have been pain points . <p> " We 've just seen the prices before our eyes just skyrocket , " said Bishop , who is 39 . Although inflation , defined as the rate at which average prices of goods or services rise over a given period , has slowed considerably since a record peak in 2022 , consumer prices today have increased by more than 21 percent since February 2020 . Frustration over rising cost of living drove many voters to support president-elect Donald Trump , who campaigned on ending inflation . <p> Simply put , inflation was instrumental in determining how millions of Americans cast their ballots . Yet climate change , one of the primary levers behind inflationary pressures , was n't nearly as front of mind -- just 37 percent of voters considered the issue " very important " to their vote . Bishop said that may have something to do with how difficult it can be to understand how extreme weather impacts all aspects of the economy . " Climate change is an important part of the inflationary puzzle , " she said . <p> Food prices are another area where the inflationary pressure of warming has become obvious . A drought that engulfed the Mississippi River system in 2022 severely disrupted the transportation of crops used for cattle feed , increasing shipping and commodity costs for livestock producers . Those added costs were likely absorbed by consumers buying meat and dairy products . Grain prices jumped around the same time because drought-induced supply shortages and high energy prices pushed up the costs of fertilizer , transportation , and agricultural production . Not long after , lettuce prices soared amid shortages that followed flooding across California , and the price of orange juice skyrocketed after drought and a hurricane hit major production regions . <p> Though overall inflation has cooled considerably since then , the economic pressures extreme weather places on food costs persist . The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations reported that weather disruptions drove global food prices to an 18-month high in October . In fact , cocoa prices surged almost 40 percent this year because of supply shortages wrought by drier conditions in West and Central Africa , where about three-quarters of the world 's cocoa is cultivated . This can not only impact the price tag of chocolate , but also health supplements , cosmetics , and fragrances , among other goods that rely on cocoa beans . <p> " What we have seen , especially this year , is this massive price spike , " due to abnormal weather patterns , said Rodrigo C ? rcamo-D ? az , a senior economist at U.N . Trade and Development . <p> But the impact on consumers " goes beyond " the Consumer Price Indicator , which is the most widely used measure of inflation , said C ? rcamo-D ? az . His point is simple : Lower-income households are most affected by supply shocks that inflate the price of goods as increasingly volatile weather makes prices more volatile , straining households with tighter budgets because it can take time for wages to catch up to steeper costs of living . <p> Rising prices are expected to become even more of an issue as temperatures climb and extreme weather becomes more frequent and severe . In fact , a 2024 study found that heat extremes driven by climate change enhanced headline inflation for 121 countries over the last 30 years , with warming temperatures expected to increase global inflation by as much as 1 percent every year until 2035 . Lead researcher and climate scientist Maximilian Kotz noted that general goods , or any physical things that can be bought , broadly experienced " strong inflationary effects from rising temperatures . " <p> All told , the inflationary impact of climate change on cost of living is here to stay and will continue to strain American budgets , said Semenova .
