@@118851998 <p> Danny Price would like to disabuse those who think economic modelling is dull and wonkish , an arcane discipline peopled by number-crunching boffins who sometimes politely disagree . <p> " In the world of financial and economic analysis , it 's pretty rough and tumble . So if you ca n't stand criticism , get out of the debate , " says Price , founder and managing director of Frontier Economics , the federal Coalition 's current favourite economic modeller . <p> Price has probably played as rough as anyone throughout his long involvement in perhaps the most hotly contested field of modelling in this country : the cost and means of addressing the climate crisis . He seems to have had run-ins with almost everyone who 's anyone involved in climate policy . <p> Consider just a few examples from the past decade . <p> He once told a policy forum that reforms to the national electricity market recommended by Australia 's former chief scientist Alan Finkel would " lead us into an interventionist pit " . <p> He has called for the abolition of the Australian Energy Market Operator ( AEMO ) and accused its former head , Audrey Zibelman , of making an " audacious public grab for power " , by advocating a new strategic power reserve to avoid summer blackouts . <p> He dramatically quit the board of the Climate Change Authority ( CCA ) in protest at then prime minister Malcolm Turnbull 's " crazy " climate policies , which he claimed were frightening investors . He portrayed Turnbull 's decision to back the " Snowy 2.0 " hydro scheme as the epitome of half-baked policy . <p> Price has done work for both sides of politics and been accused by both sides of being a partisan hack . He is equally disdainful of those " who hold themselves out as experts but clearly are not " and those " too frightened to speak out against the orthodoxy " . <p> He wears the counter-criticism from those he despises -- such as the new CCA chair and former New South Wales energy minister Matt Kean -- as " a badge of honour " . <p> " Danny , " says Tony Wood , director of the energy and climate change program at the Grattan Institute , " has a habit of falling out with people . He has strong opinions and when someone disagrees with him he becomes very aggressive . " <p> " He loves a stoush , " says another expert . <p> Even by his past standards , though , Price has set himself up for an epic fight this time . He has made common cause with the federal opposition in its attempt to prove nuclear power a viable option for Australia . <p> When Opposition Leader Peter Dutton finally released his long-awaited nuclear plan on Friday , all the numbers cited were the product of Price 's modelling . <p> They are very big . But , according to Price and Frontier , the opposition plan would cost $263 billion -- or 44 per cent -- less than Labor 's between now and 2050 . <p> The Coalition wants renewables to provide 54 per cent of generation in the National Electricity Market by 2050 , with nuclear making up 38 per cent , and the remainder coming mostly from gas . <p> This compares with the government 's target of 82 per cent renewables by 2030 . <p> The assumptions behind the plan are also Price 's -- and they are even bigger . They provide for a very rapid rollout of nuclear , with the first reactor to begin operating just 11 years from now , if it is a small modular reactor , or 13 years from now , if it is a large conventional one . That compares with the CSIRO 's estimate of at least 15 years . <p> Importantly , the plan relies on Australia 's existing , aged coal-fired power stations operating for years longer than currently planned . <p> It 's fair to say Price is in the minority of experts who champion nuclear . In the view of most it is far too expensive , and the lead time for getting it up and running in Australia far too long , for it to be a practical means of addressing the urgency of the climate crisis . <p> The case against nukes was buttressed on Monday with the release of the latest annual GenCost report , produced by the country 's premier scientific body , the CSIRO , in collaboration with AEMO and energy industry stakeholders . <p> It found -- again -- nuclear was vastly more expensive than renewable wind and solar energy . <p> The 2024-25 draft report found renewables " to have the lowest cost range of any new-build electricity generation technology , for the seventh year in a row " . <p> Per megawatt hour , solar and wind , even with the costs of firming included , came in at $98 to $150 . Large-scale nuclear was $125 to $252 , and power generated by small modular nuclear reactors -- as yet globally uncommercialised but championed by the federal opposition -- ranged from $400 to $663 . <p> " What Bowen said about me was pretty scurrilous , suggesting that I cooked the books or something . Anyone who knows me knows that I 'd never do that ... The opposition , Ted O'Brien 's office , contacted me and said they 'd be interested in talking about my work . " <p> The report further noted that the price of renewables was still falling : the capital cost of large-scale solar photovoltaics had dropped 8 per cent for the second consecutive year . And the cost of battery storage , crucial to compensating for the intermittency of solar and wind , had fallen precipitously . " Battery costs recorded the largest annual reduction with capital costs falling 20 per cent , " it said . <p> The report was a blow for Peter Dutton 's opposition , which has made nuclear the key plank of its promise to lower power prices . All the more so because the GenCost report specifically addressed opposition complaints that its previous assessments had failed to adequately consider three relevant issues that could affect the cost competitiveness of nuclear . Those related to the longer operational life of nuclear facilities compared with renewables , their higher " capacity factor " -- the average time they operate at full capacity -- and the time it took to plan and build them . <p> In relation to the first , GenCost found no economic advantage due to longer life , because there were " substantial nuclear re-investment costs required to achieve long operational life " . <p> In relation to the second , GenCost reviewed its previous analysis and reconfirmed its estimate of nuclear 's " capacity factor range of 53-89 per cent was fair and remains unaltered based on verifiable data and consideration of Australia 's unique electricity generation sector " . <p> And regarding the third , it found " that global median nuclear construction times have increased from 6 years to 8.2 years over the last 5 years " , and overall development times , including planning and permitting , ranged from 12 to 17 years . <p> " Based on this analysis , GenCost maintained the total development lead time for nuclear in Australia will be at least 15 years , " it said . <p> The problem is , all of the nation 's geriatric coal generators are scheduled for closure by 2038 -- just 14 years away . <p> Coalition policy would see Australia rely heavily on gas generation while we wait for the promised nuclear generators to be built . GenCost 's numbers suggest that would be a very expensive way to go . <p> The estimated cost of unabated gas was in the range of $128 to $192 per MWh , or about 30 per cent more than renewables . With attached carbon capture and storage -- which is both technically problematic and necessary if gas generation is to be made carbon-neutral , that cost would rise to $187 to $284 . That is , even more expensive than nuclear . <p> The response of Peter Dutton and his energy spokesperson , Ted O'Brien , was to take aim at the messenger . No sooner did GenCost drop on Monday than Dutton accused the CSIRO of political bias . <p> " They have n't even seen our plan yet , and yet they 're out bagging it , " he said . " It just looks to me like there 's a heavy hand of Chris Bowen in all this . " <p> Actually , they were not bagging it . They were simply continuing an iterative process of assessing comparative energy costs , as they have done since the first GenCost report was commissioned under the former Coalition government in 2018 . <p> It was hardly fair to attack GenCost for its focus on the costs and timelines associated with nuclear , given the report had set out to answer questions posed by the opposition itself . The climate change and energy minister , Chris Bowen , took offence . Not on his own behalf -- he could n't give " two hoots " he said , about what was said about him -- but on behalf of CSIRO . <p> " It makes my blood boil when he attacks the integrity and independence of the CSIRO , which deserve better from the alternative prime minister of Australia , " Bowen said . <p> " To suggest that the CSIRO would let a government of any persuasion interfere with their work is deeply , deeply offensive ... He should apologise . " <p> Dutton did not apologise , of course . But in a televised debate on the ABC 's 7.30 program O'Brien took a different line of attack . He did not question the CSIRO 's political impartiality , but its expertise . And he sought to move the discussion on from the comparative costs of different power technologies to something called " total system cost " . <p> " Our focus as a Coalition is on getting prices down . You must calculate the total system cost because that 's what hits your bill at home , " he said . <p> Easy definitions of total system cost are hard to find . One expert paper published in the Journal Energy a couple of years ago summarised it as " the sum of all the investment and operating costs related to **30;3038;TOOLONG within system boundaries " . <p> " It is nonsense , " he says . " It is just the latest zeitgeist jargon term . " <p> In his debate on Monday night , O'Brien did not attempt a definition , but the essence of his argument was that the inclusion of expensive nuclear power as part of a " balanced energy mix " would make the whole system more economic . <p> " I can assure you that our balanced energy mix , which includes zero emissions nuclear energy , will come in cheaper , " said O'Brien . <p> This assurance , made in advance of any published costings , had the simple appeal of the old Bunnings ad : " Lowest prices are just the beginning " . <p> The detail is anything but simple , however . And for that the Dutton opposition is dependent on Danny Price , apostle of total system cost . <p> " Total systems cost analysis , " he tells The Saturday Paper , " is the job of a very complex mathematical optimisation tool . There 's a lot of the economics that go into it . The constraints of generation plant -- that is how they can ramp up , ramp down , variable operating costs at different heat rates , the reliability or unreliability of wind , the correlation between wind and solar . There 's enormous amounts of things that go into determining system costs . " <p> Enormous amounts of contestable data and assumptions , that is . The government began contesting them even before their release . <p> Just as Dutton accused the CSIRO of having a political agenda , so Bowen accused Price . <p> " The opposition have secretly asked Danny Price to do them a favour , abandon facts and evidence and cook up spurious numbers . They should open the books and have transparent costings , " Bowen said . <p> " What Bowen said about me was pretty scurrilous , suggesting that I cooked the books or something . Anyone who knows me knows that I 'd never do that , " says Price in response . <p> It 's at least a little prejudicial of Bowen to have called Price a " Liberal consultant " . For , as previously noted , he has done work for both sides of politics , including recently for the Labor government of South Australia . <p> Price says he is not being paid for his work modelling the Coalition 's energy policy . <p> As he tells it , he was motivated to do it simply because he was dissatisfied with the " really poor ways of thinking about the relative costs of power systems " that he says currently drive policy . <p> " What happened was I did an interview on the ABC about nuclear , because I was already doing some stuff in this area . And then the opposition , Ted O'Brien 's office , contacted me and said they 'd be interested in talking about my work . That would have been a few months ago . " <p> That said , he could hardly be called independent , either . When The Saturday Paper asked him on Tuesday when his work might be released , he could not say . <p> " Actually , I do n't know . You need to talk to the opposition about that . I do n't , I do n't know . " <p> Meanwhile , Price has been chipping away at the current numbers . Last month he produced his alternative calculation of Labor 's costing of the energy transition . Essentially it came down to different accounting methods , says Wood . <p> " AEMO said that the capital cost of the renewal generation , with some storage and some transmission augmentation , is $122 billion . Price said that the total cost , on his model , is $642 billion . That 's the total cost of supplying electricity from that system over the next 25 years . <p> " But they 're not comparable . That 's like comparing the cost of buying a car with the cost of ownership of that car over the next 25 years . It 's a nonsense comparison , " says Wood . <p> He does n't blame Price for this . " He just did the numbers , " says Wood . " Danny did n't make the comparison . " <p> It was the right-wing anti-renewables section of the media that made a big deal of that . Murdoch 's Daily Telegraph splashed an " exclusive " headline across page one : " Bombshell report : ALP ' hiding ' real cost of renewables-only grid . $500B GREEN HOLE " . <p> The opposition leadership has been retailing the false comparison ever since , to Wood 's great annoyance . " Dutton and co should not be allowed to get away with it , " he says . <p> Bowen 's office insists the government 's calculations followed the same accounting practice as its predecessor . <p> " Peter Dutton is a hypocrite , " says the minister . " If Peter Dutton has a problem with this method , he should take it up with his own shadow treasurer who put it in place . " <p> The government 's problem is that explaining the difference is complex , and a simple untruth beats a complex truth , particularly when the former is relentlessly pushed by a large section of the media . <p> When it comes to economic modelling , concepts of truth and untruth become complicated , because everything relies on the quality of the assumptions that feed into the model . " Garbage in , garbage out , " as former Liberal leader John Hewson was wont to say . <p> This is not to suggest Price 's work is bad . Indeed , most of his peers readily acknowledge he is very competent at what he does . <p> As Richard Denniss , executive director of the progressive think tank The Australia Institute and an economist with considerable background in the energy space , puts it : " What I 'd say is Danny Price runs a successful modelling firm , and that means he clearly makes his customers very happy . " <p> Bruce Mountain describes him as " a consultant first and foremost " . <p> " He focuses on his clients , and that 's the long history of his work . So there 's a difference between consultancy and academia and independent economic advice , and Frontier Economics is not an independent economic adviser . " <p> Matt Kean goes harder . " Ted O'Brien might as well have just written the costings himself , " he says . <p> Price is n't disturbed by the criticisms . Other people , he says , might be " afraid of having someone like Chris Bowen impugn you , or Matt Kean impugn you . It does n't bother me . " <p> Price is not motivated in the same way as the federal opposition -- he does not see nuclear as a way of deferring action on climate change . <p> " Planning for nuclear does n't mean that you stop building renewables , " he says . " Why do people automatically think that 's the case ? There 's no reason to think that . In fact , it 's wrong to think that because you 're planning to put nuclear in place , it means that there 's , you know , a discontinued investment in renewables . " <p> It 's clear , however , there are many in the Coalition ranks , particularly among the Nationals , who oppose renewables and in some cases still deny the reality of climate change . <p> Just last week Dutton promised that a Coalition government would " rescind " the declared offshore wind zone off the New South Wales Central Coast , which would torpedo a $10 billion two-gigawatt proposed development . <p> The promise of nuclear power is a way of papering over that rift between these people and the mostly urban Liberals who know their constituents want serious action on climate change , says Denniss , by promising a nuclear solution , a decade or so hence . <p> And the combative Danny Price , with his complex modelling and his optimistic assumptions and blinkered view of the realpolitik of the situation , is helping Dutton considerably . Maybe even helping him into government . <p> Whether he is ultimately helping the fight against global heating is another question . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " Coalition sets Price on nuclear costings " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take time , to doggedly hold to account politicians and the political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . @@118851999 <h> Stan Grant Seeking the soul of Christmas <p> The Christmas present I treasure most from childhood is a book of Greek myths . <p> We did n't have much and there were no grand gifts or holidays . Our cricket bat was carved out of a fence paling with a tomahawk . Our Christmas ham came out of a tin and chicken substituted for turkey . But that book took me to another world , a world of magic and wonder and gods . I must have been about 10 years old . <p> Christmas was celebrated at my grandmother 's house in Griffith , in south-western New South Wales . It was a small , tin house : two bedrooms , a lounge , a tiny kitchen . <p> There were no doors in the house , just beaded room dividers . Anyway , it felt like a palace to me . Nan 's house kept on giving . No matter how many of us came , there was always somewhere to eat and sleep . <p> The house sat on my grandfather 's soldier 's settlement block . Pa had been a Rat of Tobruk in World War II , one of many Black diggers who signed up to fight for a country that did not fully recognise them . <p> When he returned he was refused entry on a train to go back home . He was , like other Aboriginal people , barred from entering a pub with the mates he 'd served with . But he never lost his hope . He fought for a better country . <p> He battled for years for the block of land that was every soldier 's due , unless you were Black . He finally won his only a few years before his death . <p> I do n't remember a lot about my Pa . Sadly he was n't there for those Christmases . I am older now than he was when he died . <p> He left us the gift of the little tin house that held my world . It is the only place I truly call home . <p> That book of Greek myths spoke to the wonder in my soul . What a precious gift . Yet the greatest gift was my family and my culture and the Christmas miracle that spoke to the deepest truth : that the birth of a humble child could shine a light into the darkness and triumph over evil . <p> Nan had a big front yard , perfect for endless sweaty hours of cricket . If I did n't have a bat in my hand playing with my cousins and uncles , I was tucked up in the branches of a big old tree at the side of Nan 's house . I would daydream there and talk to God . My imagination was set free . <p> That 's why the book of myths meant so much to me . Over the years there were other presents : boxing gloves , a bike , some clothes . Nothing fancy . But that book stands out above all others . <p> The stories of Sisyphus and Icarus -- of being condemned to forever roll a boulder up a hill or the perils of flying too close to the sun -- were salutary . <p> I was transfixed by this world of wonder . They resonated with me because I came from a people of magic . My great-grandfathers were both magic men . They were men of tradition . My father told me how they would hypnotise and levitate . Dad said they could bilocate , sending their spirits to different places . <p> My people were people of deep culture and profound faith . There was no separation between being Wiradjuri and Christian . We have a word for God -- Baiyaame . He lives in Murriyang , the sky-world or heaven . <p> Among my earliest and most formative memories was attending the Black church , as we called it . It was a small church on the Three Ways mission -- an Aboriginal settlement on the outskirts of Griffith -- and we would cram in there singing old hymns accompanied by cowboy chords on the guitar . Some of my uncles were preachers , delivering thundering , fire-and-brimstone-style sermons . <p> The voices of my aunties would sweeten the air . In that church , God was alive . Faith fortified us against injustice and suffering . Jesus was an ancestor and saviour who took the evil of the world on his body and promised us salvation . <p> My people prayed with ferocity . <p> Christmas was the most magical time of all . It was a time of food and family , lifted by miracles . We never questioned the virgin birth . We never doubted that Christ healed the sick , fed the multitude and raised Lazarus from the dead . <p> The boy child born in a manger would become the crucified man of sorrows who pledged his dying breath to forgiveness . We gloried in his resurrection . <p> Our ancestors lived in the thinnest space between the mundane and the mystical . <p> My faith is a bedrock of being Wiradjuri . It is inseparable from family and Country . I fear that today Christianity has surrendered too much of its magic . It has made a bad bargain with modernity . <p> Rationality has become its own faith . Science has banished enchantment . Religion has been pushed into the private sphere . God is optional or dead . <p> The number of people of faith is dwindling in Australia . Aboriginal people are still holding strong , but only just . Among Indigenous people , more than half identify as Christians . Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are Australia 's fastest growing Catholic demographic . Yet faith is also falling among First Nations populations . Since 2001 , the number of Indigenous people declaring no religion has grown to 36 per cent . <p> The late Ngarinyin prophet and mystic Bungal David Mowaljarlai lamented that our world had lost the thread of the divine . " Money , " he said , " is more important than sacred testimony . " <p> In a remarkable book he co-authored with Jutta Malnic , Yorro Yorro : Everything Standing Up Alive , Mowaljarlai warned of what he called " identity man " , who " left his home shelter for the open Country , his totemic identity remaining locked away " . Mowaljarlai spoke of seeing the face of Christ and longed for God to return us to our ancestors . Without the sacred , " identity man " would weaken and wither . <p> If being Aboriginal is siphoned of the spirit , then all we have left is politics . What a miserable future . <p> Christianity was never the enemy of my people , modernity was . European Enlightenment , whatever its virtues , stripped the world of the divine and rendered God a mere thought experiment . Its cargo of relativism and rationality washed onto these shores with devastating impact . <p> Today I see more and more First Nations people -- especially younger people -- seduced by a fashionable nihilism that is utterly Western . It is the very triumph of " whiteness " . <p> It is the culmination of generations of Western philosophy that shears the mind from the soul . It has led us to a hyper-modernity where humans are incomprehensible . In place of wonder we have theory and critique . <p> I see it in the politicisation of the body . Among a fashionable cohort of intellectuals , the human is reduced to mere form . The Black body becomes an object onto which whiteness has inscribed its fear , lust or hate . <p> The Black body is reclaimed as a site of resistance . I appreciate the allure . Yet I refuse to see the body as the measure of existence . My dear family was more than their bodies . Hate and suffering were not the sum of their experience . <p> I want to reclaim the soul not the body . Pope Benedict said , " The body as a boundary makes us opaque , impermeable to each other . @@118852001 <h> The Administrative Review Tribunal , which was intended to restore transparency and trust , has released none of the decisions from its first two months of operation , owing to technical problems . By Rick Morton . <h> Exclusive : New tribunal yet to publish a single decision <p> A new federal tribunal established to increase transparency in government decision-making has not published a single decision in its first two months of operation . Its immediate predecessor routinely released as many as a dozen outcomes , with reasons , every day . <p> The Administrative Review Tribunal was partly designed to give effect to four recommendations from the robodebt royal commission by making the publication of " significant " decisions mandatory . It took effect on October 14 this year , replacing the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in the biggest reform of the quasi-legal body since it began in the 1970s . <p> The AAT published 21 decisions on October 11 , ranging across reviews of government decisions in migration , taxation , social security , Commonwealth compensation and tertiary education standards . No updates have since been made . <p> Upon the launch of the new ART , President Emilios Kyrou noted there would be some " 50,000 finalisations " each year from the very outset of its operation , though , as with the predecessor tribunal , only a fraction would be published decisions . <p> A spokesperson for the ART tells The Saturday Paper that the new agency has struggled with " technology issues " that have prevented it from releasing decisions . <p> " The Administrative Review Tribunal has not yet been able to publish decisions on legal database AustLII due to technology issues , " the spokesperson says , adding that the tribunal is " close to finalising updates to relevant systems and processes " to allow decisions to be published on the database . <p> " Publishing decisions helps us achieve our objective of providing a mechanism of review that improves the transparency and quality of decision-making , and promotes public trust and confidence in the tribunal . " <p> The nature of the technology issues is unclear . The ART took over the old infrastructure of the AAT -- including its website , as individual pages for the former tribunal simply redirect to the ART home page -- and no interim publication workaround has been released online . <p> The two-month gap in revealing what decisions are being made , and why , has raised questions about whether the new body will publish as many outcomes as its predecessor . <p> Design choices in the new legislation make this an open question . <p> Unlike the AAT , the new ART features a " precedent-like " Guidance and Appeals Panel ( GAP ) , whereby the tribunal president can refer matters to a senior multi-member panel for adjudication . Such matters and any others " involving a significant conclusion of law , and decisions that have significant implications for Commonwealth policy or administration " must be published . <p> For all other decisions , the tribunal has discretion as to whether to publish anything at all . This was also the case with its predecessor , but the AAT had set its own annual target of publishing a quarter of its decisions , based on a random selection of matters . The current ART is unable or unwilling to say whether it will commit to the same . <p> " The Tribunal 's performance measures are still under consideration and will be published in our first Corporate Plan , " a spokesperson said in a statement . <p> " At this stage , we are unable to quantify the initial number of decisions that will be published . A number of decisions made in the previous two months will be published , selected in accordance with our Publication of Decisions Policy . <p> " The public interest criteria in the publication policy are broad and include decisions that ' provide insight into , and/or are representative of , the conduct of reviews for the Jurisdictional Areas ' , that ' show how the Tribunal interprets and applies the law and policy ' and that ' reflect a range of outcomes and members ' . " <p> How the new ART brings such underlying matters to public attention will be critical to its goal of transparency and accountability . A fundamental feature of the previous AAT was a two-tier social security jurisdiction that allowed copious volumes of ordinary government welfare decisions to be quickly reviewed and decided , with the option of a second review . Former AAT member Terry Carney , who wrote multiple times in his first-tier tribunal decisions that the welfare compliance system known as robodebt was unlawful , noted that though the two-tier system was necessary , it could be " gamed " . <p> AAT1 decisions were never published , and only those that were appealed to the AAT2 were subject to publication . The departments of Human Services and Social Services never once appealed against any of the hundreds of lost robodebt cases , keeping all findings secret . <p> ART president Justice Kyrou told the ABC 's Law Report in October that the robodebt decisions made in AAT " never saw the light of day " . <p> " So what this new ART power basically does is to stipulate that if , for example , a social security matter does raise a significant matter of law , like a robodebt finding , then we would publish it , but we would de-identify it , " he said . <p> " We would take out all the personal information that was there previously , where there was no publication whatsoever . Now we would publish , so the conclusions would be out in the public , and governments would be accountable for those conclusions . " <p> A second social security review tier was added into the new ART after criticisms from people such as Terry Carney and legal groups . However , neither the first nor second decisions are capable of being referred to the GAP unless the president decides to do so . <p> " As with any new body , there are teething problems and there are structural problems that require vigilance . Publishing decisions is a critical function of what we do , and the fact we have n't done that yet , despite whatever issues have arisen , is simply not good enough . " <p> For matters that have only a single-tier review , parties can apply to have the decision referred to the panel , though in all cases the ultimate decision rests with the ART president . The decision to " refer or refuse " an application is not counted as an official decision of the tribunal , and so does not have to be published . <p> Where errors of fact or law are made , or likely made , the president may decline to refer these to the GAP , based on their assessment of whether those errors are likely to be repeated , and " the impact on the resources of the Tribunal and parties to the review of conducting a further review into the matter " . <p> Current and former tribunal members who have spoken to The Saturday Paper about the new body are broadly supportive of it . They say its creation ended the worst of what Attorney-General Mark Dreyfus called the " fatally compromised " AAT selection process , which saw the tribunal stacked with more than 80 Coalition-linked appointments . <p> " It 's a massive improvement on what came before , " one member says . <p> " As with any new body , however , there are teething problems and there are structural problems that require vigilance . Publishing decisions is a critical function of what we do , and the fact we have n't done that yet , despite whatever issues have arisen , is simply not good enough . <p> " These are decisions that inform the public about the scope and tenor of ART thinking and we need to take that seriously . " <p> A former member was surprised to learn that no directions on official practice had been issued regarding how decisions will be selected for publication . <p> A policy was made available , with a start date of November 1 . However , that was changed this week , following questions from The Saturday Paper , to December 11 , and now includes a list of other laws that prevent or restrict the publication of personal information -- twice as long as the one offered in the first version of the ART 's publication policy . <p> The tribunal may refuse to publish a decision if " the extent of the editing required to comply with non-disclosure requirements renders the written decision unintelligible " . <p> In hearings over the proposed ART laws earlier this year , Carney argued that " it 's very important that there 's a sufficiently high number of first-tier and second-tier decisions that become public knowledge , for instance . " <p> Though the government kept the two-tier review system for social security matters , there are no such benchmarks in the ART Act for publication of decisions . Other jurisdictions within the new tribunal -- there are eight , in total -- remain single tier , including the National Disability Insurance Scheme work area . <p> " As noted , a useful comparison can be made with review matters conducted in the AAT 's NDIS jurisdiction , which operates with a single tier , " Townsville Community Law told a parliamentary inquiry in a submission . <p> In that system of the AAT , they identified a " culture of confrontational adversarial conduct which delays decisions and traumatises applicants " . <p> A former tribunal member says fishing these cases out of the depths of the new tribunal will only be as effective as the agency 's processes are solid and its eyes sharp . <p> " In reality , it 's the staff who are bringing these matters to the attention of the jurisdiction leaders or list leaders , who in turn have to bring them to the attention of the president , who then has to decide if it should be published , " they said . <p> " That is a very hard process to get right , especially if the public do n't have eyes on the minutiae or , in your case , if journalists are less able to trawl through cases for hidden detail . Only time will tell us how they go . " <p> Though no decisions have been published so far , the ART is not able to say how many would have been published if its undisclosed technology issues had been rectified . <p> Introducing the legislation for the new tribunal , the attorney-general said it was the beginning of a new era . <p> " Unfortunately , the AAT no longer enjoys the trust and confidence of the Australian community it serves , and is not fit for purpose , " he said , noting that its problems extended " beyond the absence of a merit-based selection process " . <p> " Government inherited an AAT that is not on a sustainable financial footing , that is beset by delays and a large and growing backlog of applications , and an AAT that is operating multiple and ageing electronic case management systems -- a legacy of the poorly executed amalgamation of multiple tribunals into the AAT in 2015 . " <p> On October 14 , at the opening of the new ART , Emilios Kyrou said the decisions of the new tribunal " will have profound impacts on the lives of the individuals who seek review . In these circumstances , it is appropriate for the tribunal to be accountable to the public for its operations . <p> " If public commentators believe that the reasoning of a tribunal decision is unpersuasive or the outcome is incorrect , they will be able to critique the reasoning or the outcome , " he said . " If a party to the decision is not happy with it , they will be able to appeal against it or seek judicial review in the courts . <p> " The tribunal will welcome public and judicial scrutiny , " he promised . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " Exclusive : New tribunal yet to publish a single decision " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . @@118852005 <h> In an important case argued this week , the High Court is reconsidering whether the use of secret evidence in court proceedings is constitutional . By Kieran Pender . <h> The High Court challenge to using secret evidence in trials <p> This week in Canberra , two significant constitutional cases came before the High Court as its last hearings of the year . In the first , the nation 's best barristers sparred over whether the Albanese government 's legislation to put the CFMEU under administration was contrary to constitutional protections for free speech , beyond parliament 's legislative authority or undermined the separation of powers . The second set of hearings on Thursday and Friday was less heralded , but in many respects the outcome in MJZP v Director-General of Security could prove to be more constitutionally consequential . <p> At issue in MJZP is whether Australian federal courts can be permitted to consider secret evidence -- proffered by one party and seen by a judge , but kept out of view of the other party -- in reaching a decision . The case pits issues of national security against the integrity of our justice system . Is there a constitutionally protected baseline of procedural fairness ensuring that each and every party to court proceedings knows the case against it , such that secret evidence is unconstitutional ? Or should the dictates of justice bend to security considerations when Australia 's intelligence agencies are involved ? <p> The opacity of the nation 's court system has become particularly apparent in recent years . In 2019 , the ABC revealed that a former intelligence officer had been charged , pleaded guilty and sentenced to a term of imprisonment in Canberra in complete secrecy . The Witness J case , as it became known , prompted widespread alarm in legal circles -- open justice is a central democratic value . Even the former spy 's own mother did not know her son had been imprisoned . <p> An inquiry by the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor ( INSLM ) into " Alan Johns " , the spy 's official pseudonym , was damning . " Alan Johns shows how the relevant federal law can be used to conduct a federal criminal prosecution in ' secret ' from start to finish and to maintain this secrecy , seemingly , indefinitely , " wrote the then monitor , Grant Donaldson , SC . " This should not have happened in the Alan Johns case and it should never happen again . " <p> The Witness J saga was astonishing , the first fully secret process in Australian legal history -- in peacetime , at least . But it was not an entirely isolated situation . The prosecutions of former spy Witness K and his lawyer , Bernard Collaery , for allegedly exposing Australia 's espionage against Timor-Leste , was wrapped in secrecy . At first , Collaery 's trial was ordered to be held in a largely closed court ; that ruling was reversed on appeal , only for the appeal judgement to itself be kept secret for more than two years . Parts of the trial of David McBride , who leaked documents to the ABC that formed the basis of the landmark Afghan Files reporting , were also held in closed court . <p> In October last year , the INSLM delivered a review of the national security law governing court proceedings . It found that while the law does " good and laudable things " , these " come at too great a cost " . Donaldson made 40 recommendations . " It is critical that the public can scrutinise decisions of Attorneys-General seeking to impose secrecy , " he said in the report , " and understand the reasons of courts for ordering or rejecting secrecy that executive government seeks . " Attorney-General Mark Dreyfus , KC , has yet to respond to the review . <p> " As a British judge once remarked , ' even God himself did not pass sentence upon Adam before he was called upon to make his defence ' . " <p> The issue before the High Court in MJZP is distinct -- about secret evidence rather than secret hearings -- but all these cases share a common core . Where do we draw the line in balancing national security and vital democratic values ? <p> Procedural fairness is a fundamental common law concept . It requires that someone subject to a government decision , or the judicial process , knows the case against them and is given an opportunity to answer that case . As a British judge once remarked , " even God himself did not pass sentence upon Adam before he was called upon to make his defence " . In Australia , the principle has constitutional significance under the separation of powers -- procedural fairness is an inherent characteristic of the Federal Court system , and legislative attempts to undermine that feature may be unconstitutional . <p> The laws establishing the Administrative Appeals Tribunal , and its recent successor , the Administrative Review Tribunal , provide a mechanism to challenge adverse security assessments issued by the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation ( ASIO ) . In the predecessor case to MJZP , known as SDCV v Director-General of Security , an adverse security assessment by ASIO had been used to cancel the plaintiff 's visa on character grounds . The government 's reasons for cancellation included material that , because of a certificate issued under the ASIO Act , was given to the tribunal but withheld from the plaintiff . In other words , the individual 's freedom to remain in Australia was revoked for reasons they would never know . <p> These same laws provide for appeal mechanisms to the Federal Court , and for secret documents before the tribunal to be provided to the court . Once again , though , the plaintiff is not permitted to see the documents . SDCV challenged the validity of this scheme and the case came to the High Court two years ago . <p> " The question in this appeal is of a kind which has arisen in numerous national jurisdictions on numerous occasions since the notorious events of 11 September 2001 , " wrote Stephen Gageler , then a justice and now chief justice . " To what extent is the ordinary principle that a party to litigation is entitled to know the evidence relied on against them capable of legislative modification in the interests of national security ? " <p> The High Court split four to three on whether the law was unconstitutional for requiring the Federal Court to act in a procedurally unfair manner . Three judges found the regime caused " no practical injustice " to the plaintiff , while a fourth , Justice Simon Steward , interpreted the law as allowing a number of mechanisms to mitigate unfairness . To a majority of the High Court , the law was therefore valid . <p> The three dissenting judges were scathing . <p> Justice Edelman began his judgement under the heading : " The extremes of procedural unfairness and institutional injustice " . He followed with a 72-word question . " Could it ever be procedurally fair for a court to decide that a person was lawfully stripped of their permanent right to remain in Australia for reasons which the person will never be given , based upon specific allegations about which the person will never be told , involving evidence which the person will never see and will never be able to address , and without hearing from any counsel to represent the person 's interests ? " In the subsequent paragraph , Edelman offered a one-word answer : " No . " <p> Justice Gageler , meanwhile , took issue with one of the government 's submissions , which the majority had accepted . The government had contended that because the appeal regime established by legislation was beneficial to the plaintiff , in that it created appeal rights beyond the constitutional bare minimum , there was no injustice . " It can be no answer to an argument that a process required to be followed in the purported exercise of jurisdiction is unfair to say that something is better than nothing , " he wrote . " Chapter III of the Constitution which establishes the federal judiciary does not admit of ' grades or qualities of justice ' . " <p> Despite these critiques , the majority 's decision would ordinarily have been the final word on the validity of this regime . Two years on , however , the question is again before the High Court , and two of the judges in the majority have retired . Because Steward 's judgement was so distinct from the three-judge joint judgement , the plaintiff in MJZP argues that SDCV is not binding -- there was no majority four-judge agreement on the issue before the court . So this week , the High Court considered again whether the secret evidence regime is unconstitutional . A decision is expected by mid 2025 . <p> It would be a significant step for the High Court to depart from its judgement in SDCV . Strictly speaking , the High Court is not bound by its own precedent , but it does not rewrite the law lightly . In his written submission , the federal solicitor-general Stephen Donaghue , KC , warns the High Court against doing so , and four states -- New South Wales , Tasmania , Queensland and Western Australia -- are also resisting the challenge . <p> " All that has changed in the intervening period is the composition of the Bench , " Donaghue and his colleagues argue . " It would be highly destructive of the institutional authority of the Court were it to proceed ' as though the authority of the decision did not survive beyond the rising of the Court ' . " There is some irony in this argument from the government , as the Coalition attempted the same thing in relation to the landmark First Nations rights decision in Love in 2020 , only for the attempted re-litigation to be withdrawn following the 2022 election , before the High Court handed down a decision . <p> Similar issues to those in MJZP were litigated some two decades ago , in the aftermath of 9/11 . At the time , a judge accepted that " the potential prejudice to the interests of national security " in giving a litigant access to intelligence materials " appears to be such that the content of procedural fairness is reduced , in practical terms , to nothingness " . <p> Have things changed ? <p> In their final hearing of the 2024 term , the High Court was left pondering how to strike the right balance between national security imperatives and arch constitutional principles . They might take heed from the words of the current INSLM , Jake Blight . In a recent speech on secrecy laws , he offered a word of caution in these uncertain times : <p> " In the face of growing threats from espionage and foreign interference and perhaps a resurgence of terrorism driven by online radicalisation , it is tempting to think we need to ' strengthen ' our laws , " Blight said . <p> " Instead , we need to strengthen our democracy , including by ensuring our laws are clear , certain , necessary and proportionate . Intelligence and law enforcement agencies do important work , but we must always be careful that the secrecy and other laws relating to these agencies do not undermine the very democracy and rule of law that we want them to protect . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " Travail of secrecy " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take time , to doggedly hold to account politicians and the political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . In a country with a concentration of media ownership unlike anything else in the world , it is vitally important . Your subscription helps make it possible . <p> Kieran Pender A case before the High Court next week , concerning the conduct of a judge who jailed a man for contempt , will determine how much immunity some judges can claim from allegations of misconduct . <p> Kieran Pender Adverse weather conditions may have prematurely halted Omar Di Felice 's attempt to cycle solo across Antarctica to the South Pole but they did nothing to dampen his drive to raise awareness about climate change . <p> Kieran Pender In some areas , barely 10 per cent of the homes lost in the Black Summer fires have been rebuilt due to struggles with development approvals , insurance shortfalls and labour and material shortages . @@118852007 <h> Australia will soon seal an agreement with a group of Western nations to end public subsidies for fossil fuel export projects , drying up a key source of finance for new oil , gas and coal fields . By Royce Kurmelovs . <p> Australia is expected to take a significant , symbolic step towards entrenching a phase-out of fossil fuels under the United Nations agreements on climate change next week , as representatives meet at the OECD to finalise an agreement between a group of Western economies to end major public subsidies for international oil , gas and coal projects . <p> The path for this Clean Energy Transition Partnership ( CETP ) was cleared in the final sitting week of parliament , when Labor and the Greens struck a deal to pass the Future Made in Australia legislation -- a suite of policies to rebuild Australia 's industrial base to take advantage of the zero-carbon economy . The new laws include a commitment to ending public finance for new fossil fuel projects . Under the agreement , Australia will stop its export credit agency , Export Finance Australia ( EFA ) , from investing public money in new fossil fuel projects overseas . <p> The laws are n't a complete abolition of public financing for polluting industries . Implementation guidelines released by the government state that the laws apply to " projects wholly outside of Australia " and domestic projects that are geared exclusively towards export . That means taxpayer money can continue to fund domestic fossil fuel projects that include an export component . <p> Nevertheless , this is an important step towards choking off a key source of financing for fossil fuel companies . As banks and other financial institutions have scaled back private funding , increasingly wary of the reputational and financial risk associated with oil , gas and coal investments , export credit agencies such as EFA have filled the vacuum to prop up major new developments . <p> According to Oil Change International , US$41 billion in public money is spent globally each year via export credit agencies to help underwrite oil and gas expansion . These agencies are vehicles through which countries contribute public funds as " first investors " to help de-risk major infrastructure projects that would n't otherwise go ahead . Often these agencies direct their investment to support national goals , or domestic companies , such as fossil fuel producers , with new projects . <p> Australia 's new laws mean the government is now complying with its obligations under the CETP , which Labor signed in 2023 at COP28 in Dubai , two years after the Coalition declined to do so . According to the International Institute for Sustainable Development ( IISD ) , several nations to the agreement have already fulfilled their commitment , including the United Kingdom , Canada , New Zealand , France , Finland , Belgium and Sweden . As a result , IISD notes , " CETP signatories ' financing for fossil fuels dropped by two thirds to USD 5.2 billion in 2023 " . Norway and Australia had until the end of this year to honour theirs , while other members , including the United States and Germany , are yet to do so . <p> The decision to direct EFA to stop investing in fossil fuels represents one of the strongest efforts to implement the agreement among its signatories . A carve-out in Australian transparency laws means EFA transactions are shielded from accountability through mechanisms such as freedom of information , but a report by Asia-Pacific community advocacy group Jubilee Australia suggests the agency has sunk $1.7 billion into fossil fuel projects since 2009 . <p> These projects have mostly involved the construction of enabling infrastructure to support the extraction and export of Australian gas , such as ports , wharves and terminals , including the Gladstone and Ichthys LNG export terminals and the Wiggins Island Coal Export Terminal . <p> Though the agency has not been investing in fossil fuel infrastructure since the election of the Labor government , it had previously committed $500 million to build a large new gas import terminal in Papua New Guinea , being developed by Santos , ExxonMobil and TotalEnergies . <p> Campaigners have described the approval of the laws as one of the most significant and under-publicised government actions on climate change this year . The move also may strengthen the government 's pitch to host COP31 in 2026 , as its competitor , T ? rkiye , is not yet a CETP signatory . <p> " It comes back to the role of public money in driving investment in energy . We need this public money to be directed to clean energy . " <p> Jubilee 's James Sherley said Australia 's decision to formally end financial support for international projects raises pressure on major trading parties such as South Korea and Japan to do the same . <p> The finance agencies of these countries are heavily invested in Santos 's $5.8 billion Barossa gas project off the far north coast of Australia -- described by some critics as a " carbon factory with a gas field attached " . <p> " Money talks , " Sherley said . " Every dollar an ECA export credit agency spends on a fossil fuel project , a further $5 can be crowded in from the private market . <p> " There 's a lot of evidence to suggest that there are big fossil fuel projects that are only commercially viable because they 've been written by these credit export agencies . <p> " It comes back to the role of public money in driving investment in energy . We need this public money to be directed to clean energy . " <p> Annika Reynolds , national climate policy adviser for the Australian Conservation Foundation , described the new laws , and particularly the EFA decision , as a " huge win " and " the quietest major climate development this year " . <p> The ban on public funding appears to have taken Australian oil and gas producers by surprise . <p> Samantha McCulloch , chief executive of Australian Energy Producers , the oldest and biggest industry association representing oil and gas interests in the country , has described the deal as a " capitulation to the Greens " saying it was at odds with the government 's Future Gas Strategy and " further damages Australia 's reputation as an investment destination at a time when Australia urgently needs investment in new gas projects " . <p> " Natural gas is also critical to many of the Future Made in Australia 's strategic objectives , including growing our critical minerals industry and manufacturing capabilities , " she said in a press release issued after the deal was struck . <p> The new law follows another recent decision by the Albanese government to direct the Future Fund , Australia 's sovereign wealth fund , to stop investing in fossil fuels -- another significant development given the hundreds of millions in shares it holds with domestic and international oil , gas and coal producers . <p> These include $593 million in shares with Woodside Energy , $261 million in Santos and $138 million in ExxonMobil . Other holdings include a $26 million stake in coalminer Glencore . <p> " The institutions of the Australian government have been monetarily invested in the future of the fossil fuel industry for decades now , " says Annika Reynolds , " and the pivot away from investing in this industry is a monumental shift in how government is likely to think about and make policy with respect to the fossil fuel sector . <p> " Not only does it turn off the tap for a major fossil fuel subsidy , for this government and future governments , but it also positions Australia to play a more constructive financing role in a way that Australia has n't historically . <p> " It 's one of the strongest in the world -- this is a genuine moment of Labor leadership . " <p> Less inspiring was Australia 's other contribution to international efforts to address climate change this month , as Australian Solicitor-General Stephen Donaghue argued before the United Nations ' International Court of Justice that countries have no obligation to do anything about climate change beyond their commitments to the Paris Agreement . <p> The ICJ this month began hearings on what countries should be expected to do , following a campaign by Pacific Island nations and developing states to ask the court for an advisory opinion . <p> In his submission , Vanuatu MP Ralph Regenvanu , representing countries such as Fiji , PNG and Solomon Islands , called on the court to declare fossil fuel production and its associated pollution to be " unlawful , that it must cease and that its consequences must be repaired " . <p> " The conduct on trial here is that of states which have failed for over a century , despite increasingly dire warnings , to rein in the emissions from their territories , " he said . <p> Australia made submissions that closely resembled those argued by the bloc of nations belonging to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries ( OPEC ) and by the US , China and Saudi Arabia . <p> Donaghue argued that countries should only take the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement into account when thinking about how to address the existential threat of climate change . <p> " They are the primary source of states ' obligations under international law in respect of climate change , setting out both collective goals and aims alongside individual obligations and commitments , " the solicitor-general said . " They create the central co-operative framework for the collective action that is needed to address both the causes and the impacts of climate change . " <p> Shiva Gounden , head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia , said Australia had failed Pacific communities at " one of the most important moments " . <p> " Instead of standing with its Pacific family pushing for the most ambitious climate action , Australia chose to side with petrostates like the US and Russia , and presented arguments that shirk responsibility to take any action beyond the United Nations process -- a process we know is deeply flawed and heavily influenced by the fossil fuel industry . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " ' Huge win ' on climate " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . @@118852009 <h> Expectant and new mothers in prisons across Australia are not being provided with adequate healthcare or services due to poor implementation of state government policies . By Madison Griffiths . <h> Women inmates denied adequate healthcare <p> There is a mother and baby unit at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre , a maximum-security women 's prison in the Melbourne suburb of Deer Park , but it has n't accommodated any babies for several years . According to reports received by the advocacy group FIGJAM from pregnant women over the past year , inmates have been transferred from the prison to hospital to give birth and return days later to no medical attention or aftercare . <p> " It has come onto our radar , as there have been multiple instances of women coming back to Dame Phyllis Frost Centre either in severe pain and it not being attended to , or completely distraught because their child has been removed , " says Nina , a member of this collective of formerly incarcerated women , trans and gender-diverse activists , who did n't want to give out her last name . " A lot of those women are placed in solitary confinement when they do flag that they are either in complete distress or pain . " <p> In December last year , Eamon Ryan , Western Australia 's inspector of custodial services , declared the Melaleuca Women 's Prison in Canning Vale unfit to accommodate women , particularly those who are pregnant . The maximum-security prison " had just two standard accommodation blocks that were double bunked " , Ryan tells The Saturday Paper . The prison 's spokesperson declined to comment on the matter . " Women who are pregnant essentially had to live in those conditions , " Ryan says , noting that " almost all women in prison who are pregnant would fall into the category of high-risk pregnancy . That is consistent with what we hear from across the country . " <p> Rachel* , a former corrections staffer at Adelaide Women 's Prison , says in 2022 a room was set up in its health services building for a pregnant prisoner . " She did not have any other residents in that building , " says Rachel , explaining how isolating the experience was for the inmate . " There were allegedly plans for her to have access to socialisation both pre-birth and post-birth . But custodial staff would often prevent that from happening . " The inmate told Rachel that when staff came to do bed checks " they would rap on the window with their torch , waking the baby up . They would shine their torches directly into the crib . They were not supportive of this program , so they wanted to make it uncomfortable for this prisoner . " Whenever the baby left the prison to spend time with their siblings and grandmother , Rachel noted the infant 's re-entry was particularly punitive . " There would be very invasive checks and inferences that the family were smuggling things into the child 's nappy . This particular prisoner had no history of anything like that . " <p> " The Department of Correctional Services and custodial officers are not on the same page in terms of the mother and infant program ... There 's a lot of misogyny . " <p> A departmental spokeswoman from the South Australian Department for Correctional Services did not directly address these concerns . " There are a range of programs and services for mothers in prison , " she tells The Saturday Paper . " The department conducts individual assessments on prisoners throughout their term of imprisonment and ensures their level of care is tailored to their needs . " <p> Australia has no national prison healthcare standard to cover the more than 3168 women currently incarcerated across the country , as prisoners are not covered by Medicare . Prison advocacy groups in each state and territory note significant disparities in health literacy and access to care between populations in prisons and in the general community . For incarcerated women , these shortcomings can be especially dangerous if they need to navigate significant reproductive health problems , a pregnancy or a termination . <p> In some cases , inadequate provisions for women 's healthcare are due to poor implementation of state policies within the institution . The website of the South Australian Department for Correctional Services says it has committed to individualised birth plans designed to maximise bonding opportunities . At Adelaide Women 's Prison , Rachel tells The Saturday Paper , the policies lack support from custodial staff . " The Department of Correctional Services and custodial officers are not on the same page in terms of the mother and infant program , " she says . <p> She attributes this to a " particularly nasty culture " . <p> " There 's a lot of misogyny , " she says . The former corrections officer also recounts claims of harassment against a male custodial officer years earlier , who was alleged to have procured " multiple sexual relationships with female prisoners , from oral sex to intercourse to ' flash your tits and I 'll give you a Nicorette ' . " Despite raising concerns about the officer in question , Rachel says , no investigation ensued . <p> A spokesperson for Victoria 's Department of Justice and Community Safety tells The Saturday Paper " women in prison have access to community and specialist physical and mental health services , including access to contraceptive and reproductive medication and care as medically required " . A new primary healthcare model for public prisons was initiated in Victoria last year , and the women 's healthcare system in the state is now provided by Western Health and Dhelkaya Health . <p> Sarah Lorrimar , team leader of sexual and reproductive health at GenWest , a Victorian-based family violence support service that delivers programs focusing on gender equity , says that shift was very necessary . Alongside her team , she is in regular consultation with Western Health , providing education sessions that cover " a range of topics , including health screenings and discussions about healthy relationships , sexuality and pleasure " . Lorrimar is conscious , however , that there is a great disparity with " what women in prison are able to actually access , as well as the reality of wait times for seeing a general practitioner " . She says delays " can be weeks long , and there are many circumstances of medical trauma that people have had , so they approach healthcare with hesitancy " . <p> At Tarrengower Prison , a minimum-security women 's prison in Nuggetty , Victoria , conjugal visits are permitted but , according to Nina from FIGJAM ( Formerly Incarcerated Girls , Justice Advocates Melbourne ) , the only contraception available to inmates is " out-of-date condoms " . <p> Among the most urgent healthcare needs that are inadequately addressed , according to the advocates who spoke to The Saturday Paper , is abortion . Mary* , a community corrections officer based in New South Wales , says " abortions are available , but it 's a long process " . Given the time-sensitive parameters around terminations , any suspension has reverberating impacts on the patient in question . <p> At Adelaide Women 's Prison , Rachel says that while a prisoner is able to request an abortion , the procedure is often thwarted by custodial staff shortages and other discretionary hurdles . @@118852013 <h> Celebrations and trepidation in Syria after Assad ousting <h> Assad falls <p> The sudden fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria last weekend marked the end of 53 years of brutal rule by him and his father , Hafez al-Assad , and prompted euphoric celebrations , tempered by fears about the country 's future . <p> The regime crumbled after a swift advance towards Damascus led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ( HTS ) , a Sunni Islamist group , which was supported by Turkish-backed rebels . <p> For the past 13 years , Assad had clung to power during a disastrous civil war that cost as many as 600,000 lives and displaced 12 million people , about half the prewar population . In the end , he retained control of about two thirds of Syrian territory after securing the backing of Iran and Russia . <p> His fortunes turned when two key allies withdrew support : Russia , which faces a gruelling war in Ukraine , and Iran , whose main proxy force , Hezbollah , has fought a costly conflict with Israel . As rebel forces approached Damascus , Syrian soldiers and police , angered by the country 's failing economy after years of propping up the president , abandoned their posts . <p> Mehdi Rahmati , an Iranian analyst who advises Iranian officials , told The New York Times : " We can not fight as an advisory and support force if Syria 's army itself does not want to fight . " <p> The end of the regime was met with jubilation in Damascus , as statues of Assad were brought down and the city 's residents wandered through his palace . <p> In the city 's Umayyad Square , which has been a centre of celebrations , Khalid Kassah , a 27-year-old , told The Washington Post : " For the first time in my life , we are feeling freedom . " <p> At the notorious Saydnaya Military Prison , where an estimated 30,000 prisoners were killed between 2011 and 2018 and thousands were tortured and raped , the HTS threw open the doors , allowing prisoners to walk free , including some who had been there for decades . Families rushed to the prison to try to learn the fates of missing relatives . <p> Rana Aankir told the Financial Times this week she had been searching for her son Raed , who disappeared at the age of 16 , for 13 years . <p> Scouring through notebooks at the prison , she said : " He 's my entire world ... I need to know what happened to him . I need to find him . " <p> Since 2011 , Assad has overseen the disappearance of an estimated 100,000 people . <p> On Monday , the Kremlin confirmed that Russian president Vladimir Putin had given asylum to Assad and his family . <h> The new rulers <p> The offensive that toppled Assad was led by HTS , a group initially aligned with Al Qaeda but that broke ties in 2016 . <p> Ahmed al-Sharaa , the group 's leader , who uses the nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani , has increasingly tried to present himself as a moderate in an apparent bid to persuade Syrians and the West that he can unite the country . <p> The 42-year-old , who was born in Saudi Arabia but returned with his Syrian parents to Syria as a child , has given multiple interviews to Western media , telling Sky News on Tuesday : " People are exhausted from war . So the country is n't ready for another one and it 's not going to get into another one . " <p> Analysts remain divided over whether HTS has genuinely reformed or will -- like the Taliban in Afghanistan -- revert to extremism once its rule is secure . <p> For now , HTS , which is designated as a terrorist group by the United Nations , the United States , Australia and others , is the dominant group in Syria . <p> On Tuesday , the group said an interim government until March 1 will be led by Mohammed al-Bashir , who oversaw the administration of Idlib , a northern province that HTS controls . In Idlib , HTS showed religious tolerance , allowing women to work and study and granting religious freedom to Christians and other minorities , but it crushed political dissent , arresting and torturing journalists and opponents . <p> Parts of Syria remain under the control of other groups , and it is not clear whether they will accept HTS 's rule . <p> In northern Syria , anti-Kurdish forces backed by T ? rkiye this week attacked the Kurdish Syrian Democratic Forces , which has received US support to fight Islamic State . More than 200 people were killed , according to a British-based war monitor . <p> ? lham Ahmed , a Kurdish politician , told The National newspaper this week that the Kurds wanted to enter an agreement with HTS to transfer Syria to democratic rule . <p> " There 's a lot of grudges , people wanting revenge , so we are very concerned that it might slip into civil war , " she said . " It is very important to find a political solution . " <h> Foreign intervention <p> As the Assad regime fell , countries across the region with stakes in Syria 's future scrambled to secure their interests . <p> Israel this week launched a major bombing campaign across Syria , saying it was targeting military capabilities such as jets , ships , long-range missiles and chemical weapons sites to prevent them falling into the hands of extremists . On Tuesday , Israel said it had launched 350 strikes in the previous 48 hours . <p> " We have no intention of interfering in the internal affairs of Syria , but we certainly do intend to do what is necessary to ensure our security , " Israel 's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement . <p> Israeli troops this week entered a demilitarised buffer zone in Syria that was created by the United Nations as part of a ceasefire following a war in 1973 . Netanyahu said the deployment was a " temporary defensive position " that was necessary because the Syrian troops who normally oversee the zone had abandoned their positions . Qatar , T ? rkiye and Egypt criticised the move , but the US and the United Kingdom expressed support . <p> T ? rkiye is emerging as the major beneficiary of the removal of Assad . <p> The country is believed to have approved the rebel takeover , in the hope of establishing a secure zone along the Turkish -- Syrian border and containing Kurdish groups in the north . <p> Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan , who is facing pressure over his country 's poor economy , may try to encourage the three million Syrian refugees in the country to return home . On Tuesday , he announced the opening of a border gate " to prevent any congestion and ease traffic " . The move will allow up to 20,000 people to cross the border daily , up from 3000 . <p> Assad 's fall has dealt a heavy blow to Iran and Russia . <p> Iran , a predominantly Shiite country , was a strong backer of Assad , who is an Alawite , which is an offshoot of Shiite Islam . During Syria 's civil war , Iran and Hezbollah , an Iran-backed Shiite group based in Lebanon , each sent thousands of troops to support Assad . Iran has used Syrian territory to supply arms to Hezbollah and other militant groups across the Middle East . <p> Russia also helped to prop up Assad , who allowed Moscow to operate an air force base near the city of Latakia and a navy base at Tartus , giving Russia access to the Mediterranean Sea . The bases enabled Russia to transport supplies to Africa , where it conducts military operations . Russia this week said it intended to retain the bases and will negotiate with the rebel forces . <h> New Middle East <p> The regime change in Syria has prompted a push by the international community to prevent the country -- once a powerful force in the Middle East -- turning into an even greater source of regional chaos . <p> At a meeting of the United Nations Security Council this week , the members agreed to try to preserve the country 's territorial integrity . <p> Robert Wood , the deputy US ambassador to the council , told reporters : " This is an incredible moment for the Syrian people . Now we 're really focused right now on trying to see where the situation goes . Can there be a governing authority in Syria that respects the rights and dignities of the Syrian population ? " <p> The European Union 's foreign policy head , Kaja Kallas , told European lawmakers Syria risked a return of sectarian violence and extremism , saying " we must avoid a repeat of the horrific scenarios in Iraq , Libya and Afghanistan " . <p> The events of the past week are expected to transform the region 's balance of power , leaving the US-backed Sunni bloc ascendant in its contest for influence against an Iran-led Shiite bloc . <p> Joshua Landis , a Syria expert at the University of Oklahoma , told Politico the emergence of a Sunni state in Syria for the first time in 54 years marked " a new page " for the region . <p> " We do n't know who is going to be an ally of Syria right now , other than T ? rkiye , " he said . " America has wanted a Sunni-led state in Damascus in order to hurt Iran . And Russia ... Yes , they HTS are more Islamist than Washington would prefer to have . But that 's the reality of the Middle East . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " Celebrations and trepidation in Syria after Assad ousting " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers .
