@@118852015 <h> Ramona Koval The fight against anti-Semitism <p> Ten days before Christmas and the usual carols , jolly Santas and decorated trees colour my local Balaclava shopping strip in inner Melbourne . But this year they coincide with the aftermath of the terrorist attack on the nearby Adass Israel Synagogue in Ripponlea , a " fuck Israel " sign on the gazebo in my local park , " fuck jews " on a lamppost and , further afield , cars set alight and messages of hate scrawled on fences in Jewish areas of Sydney . Welcome to Australia in 2024 . <p> I spent the solemn first anniversary of October 7 in the company of family , friends and members of the Jewish community . Making our way to the commemoration venue -- a warehouse in an industrial precinct in Moorabbin , selected to foil disruption by angry activists -- all felt wrong . The location was disclosed with less than 48 hours ' notice as a security precaution , and there was a massive police presence . I was hiding in my own city . I had already avoided the central business district on Sundays because of the loud and aggressive protests marching weekly through our streets , with some demonstrators flying terror group flags , their faces covered with masks and keffiyehs . <p> The day before the anniversary , a highly educated and politically left old friend , who had remained silent for most of the year , emailed to tell me she had been thinking of me but had n't known what to say . With this introductory remark she went on with an account of her new book , her dinner with a mutual acquaintance and her plans to set off for an overseas holiday . <p> On her lack of communication over this past year , I reply to say I have been struck by how few of my old lefty friends have thought to check in with me as the rising tide of anti-Semitism has made it difficult to feel safe in my city of birth . I tell her I have had to contend with explaining to my grandchildren why their schools needed to bolster their security arrangements and why people angrily tear down posters of children held hostage by terrorists . I 'd asked myself why do many leftists now march with Hamas and Hezbollah supporters ? Is this a new thing or have they always supported Islamist terrorism ? I say I 'm not sure how to interpret the silence , but it feels like abandonment from where I sit . So many dinners , so many years of sharing family and laughter . What did it add up to in the end ? <p> Insulted , she retorts sharply about my questioning of my old leftist associates . She says two things really got to her -- my assumptions about people like her and " your relentless focus on your experiences of this terrible period " . <p> Focus on our , meaning Jewish , experiences might seem relentless for her , but it is a long-practised response of our community to threats from outside . Who else is going to focus and think and write about what is happening to us ? <p> Look at the drive-by shootings and firebombing of synagogues in Canada to get a taste of what is developing here . The rallies long ago crossed over from being anti-Zionist to anti-Semitic and fundamentally anti-Australian . We have always prided ourselves on a relatively harmonious population of multiple origins that does not carry overseas battles onto home ground . <p> The chief of staff to the Greens deputy leader , Mehreen Faruqi , suggested the Melbourne synagogue attack could have been a " false flag " attack , and is " counselled " . A journalist reports hearing the view that the Jews firebombed their own synagogue to keep the focus on them . Did we gas ourselves in the 1940s , too ? <p> In Perth , on the day of the synagogue fire , Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intoned , once again , that there is no place in Australia for anti-Semitism . He looked especially tired and regretful that this " ancient hatred " has somehow bubbled up again on his watch . It 's so hard to deal with an ancient hatred , he implied , like dealing with all those other perennial afflictions : bushfires , floods , plagues . <p> He pledged an extra $32.5 million over the next 18 months to increase security for Jewish communities . The schools my grandchildren attend already have parent-funded armed guards at their gates . What are we expecting now , tanks and rocket-launchers ? How about taking measures to reduce the threats ? <p> The government has banned Nazi salutes and symbols , passed anti-doxxing legislation after the doxxing of my WhatsApp group , and appointed an anti-Semitism envoy , so what more is there to do ? <p> Minister for Foreign Affairs Penny Wong , in her efforts to appease anti-Zionist sectors of her party , has diminished our relationship with Israel and makes mealy-mouthed pronouncements about Australia 's standing on these global issues . What Australia thinks and does in the Middle East has minimal impact internationally , compared with the impact these statements have in creating havoc at home . <p> But even that 's not good enough for the protesters . <p> When asked when the weekly demonstrations will stop , Nasser Mashni of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network , says " only after liberation " , by which he meant " decolonisation of Palestine -- a Palestine that 's free from the river to the sea " . He said this was a one-state solution -- not the federal government 's preferred two-state solution . He is calling for the elimination of Israel -- the only Jewish state in the world , surrounded in the region by 22 Arab Islamic states . You do the maths . <p> " Globalise the Intifada " means exactly what we saw at the Adass Israel Synagogue . Look at the drive-by shootings and firebombing of synagogues in Canada to get a taste of what is developing here . The rallies long ago crossed over from being anti-Zionist to anti-Semitic and fundamentally anti-Australian . We have always prided ourselves on a relatively harmonious population of multiple origins that does not carry overseas battles onto home ground . <p> These forever weekly marches , with a seemingly permanent booking at State Library Victoria and the city streets , are starting to morph into the " liberated " or " autonomous zones " tactics we saw in Seattle 's Capitol Hill and New York City Hall four summers ago , leading to arson and looting and violence . We have already seen this tactic on our university campuses this year . <p> Let 's think about what the desperation to land votes in a few seats where Muslim voters are active has led to in the wider society . Penny Wong and Tony Burke have bent over backwards to satisfy these communities , but it 's not enough to appease Senator Fatima Payman or the Greens . The Greens just announced their new candidate for the seat of Blaxland , Omar Sakr , who has reportedly called Zionists " angry Karens in a state of constant hysteria " , invoking the " Holocaust to shield their behaviour " . He has labelled this a " Zionist tradition " . <p> More than 80 per cent of Jewish Australians are committed to Israel 's continued existence , which is what Zionism is . Our connection to the land of Zion has been inextricably embedded in liturgy and practice for more than 2000 years . <p> State governments have allowed the relentless public expression of anti-Zionist sentiments in rallies , and the federal government 's critiques of Israel has created a climate where anti-Zionism crosses into anti-Semitism -- the explosion of abuse , intimidation and violence against Australian Jews , which has increased fourfold in the past year . <p> Make no mistake , for " Zionist " read " Jews " . That 's why Australian Jews are being targeted , all these thousands of kilometres from the war in the Middle East . A young couple running a gift shop in Northcote were forced out of the suburb with their child after harassment and threats of violence . He told me he will soon have to close down . <p> State governments must take control of the public order . They have to end . <p> If the government thought this would burn itself out , they were wrong . I know how they feel . <p> A year ago , I had a sad call from my then eight-year-old granddaughter . She had been following the horrible news of the pogrom in Israel . I reassured her that this time the difference is Israel has a strong army and would now be able to defend its citizens . I said we in Australia were a long way from the disturbing events of that weekend . My Holocaust-survivor mother chose to come here because it was as far away as possible from Europe and the ashes of her family . <p> The reports of celebrations in Australia by Hamas supporters at the Sydney Opera House made me nervous . How was it that followers of an Australian government-listed terrorist entity could take over our streets and celebrate the murder and rape and taking of civilian hostages with impunity ? I hoped that my reassurance to my little granddaughter was justified . <p> Now , a year on , I am older and wiser and for the first time in my life I am glad my mother is dead and ca n't see what is happening in her beloved Australia , the refuge that delivered to her the precious gift of the rest of her life in peace . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " The fight against anti-Semitism " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118852018 <h> Editorial Springing the parent trap <p> Anthony Albanese outlined his government 's first steps in a plan for universal childcare this week , and they were as sure-footed as any policy that has evolved through decades of setbacks . Labor 's policy clears a way to affordable care that takes into account all the hurdles to parents finding work and earning enough to support their families . <p> If Labor wins next year 's election , it will set up a $1 billion building early education fund . This is not a " cash splash " , as the Murdoch papers have described it . It 's to help provide centres in the 24 per cent of regions that a Victoria University study has identified as childcare deserts . The activity test -- which the Productivity Commission say is the biggest hurdle to entry for children from low-income households -- will be scrapped so that families earning less than $530,000 can access the childcare subsidy for three days a week . The costs are substantial , but there are offsets from higher tax receipts and lower welfare payments as more parents join the workforce . <p> Putting the politics aside , the science on early childhood education and care is about as exhaustive and close to consensus as any imaginable . Studies around the world have consistently found manifold benefits to children : they are more likely to undertake tertiary study and enter the workforce . They are less likely to skip school , suffer poor mental health and break the law . A Brookings Institution study that traced the development of children from early learning settings to the age of 26 reported that " the outcomes for these young adults from low-income backgrounds who experienced sustained high-quality care were statistically indistinguishable from their higher-income peers " . In terms of addressing inequality , few interventions are as cost-effective , given the far-reaching effects . <p> And here is the rub for the opposition . Peter Dutton is n't interested in addressing inequality . He is not interested in more people getting into " rich city universities " . His answer to inadequate supply is to cut demand . Not enough houses ? Cut migration . Not enough childcare ? Stay at home . As if housing , childcare and other essential resources should exist only within a shrinking circle of privilege . <p> The opposition wants the market to deal with it , and so it will , as it always does , by pushing up the prices of what is most needed and most scarce . From 2018 to 2022 , the cost of childcare rose by more than 20 per cent . <p> The plan has its flaws -- Labor is still eyeing a flat daily fee to replace the subsidies , because while they help in the short term , as the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has pointed out , costs tend to rebound as private centres respond by raising their fees . <p> No one knows this as well as Peter Dutton -- it 's barely five years since he fought allegations of a conflict over his stake in two childcare businesses . More recent reports say the Dutton family retains no such interest . So there is no excuse for having no better policy . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " Springing the parent trap " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118852019 <h> After a decade-long wait , the latest instalment of the Dragon Age franchise answers a lot of questions -- maybe even too many -- about this rich and complex world . By Katherine Cross . <h> Dragon Age : The Veilguard <p> The fiercest enemy you fight in Dragon Age : The Veilguard is your own nostalgia . <p> If you 're a longstanding fan of the 15-year-old Dragon Age franchise , your mind will reel with thoughts about what makes Veilguard different from its three predecessors , and you will find yourself pining for that old feeling of wonder , perhaps a decade or more gone , that haunted your first steps into the dark world of Thedas . <p> Thedas has no right to be this good , after all -- least of all because the setting 's name is literally derived from " The DAS " , or " the Dragon Age setting " , which was a placeholder name that lived on BioWare whiteboards in the mid-2000s before the acronym became a proper noun as legendary as Toril , Middle Earth or Westeros . This world of dark mysticism , darker politics and deep theology wowed from the first with elaborations of magic , might and mystery that felt fresh in 2009 . So , after a 10-year wait , does Veilguard bring you back to this place ? <p> Sort of . This is a game that needs to stand on its own terms and faces an impossible mandate : pleasing old fans like me and neophytes who might be playing a DA game for the first time . It should be both sequel and reboot . It certainly succeeds in opening vast new realms for the franchise , with gorgeously realised characters and vistas in parts of Thedas we only read about in previous games . But it also lacks aspects of the soul that made Dragon Age so effective as a franchise , with a particularly strange allergy to delving deep into its own theology . It 's an absence made all the more glaring by the nature of the plot . <p> You pick up where Dragon Age : Inquisition left off . The ancient elven mage Solas , having revealed himself to be the elven trickster god Fen'Harel , is off on a mad scheme to tear down the veil separating Thedas from the world of dreams and spirits . In his mind , this will right an old wrong and restore the gloriously magical world of ancient elves that he had to destroy . And you do stop him . Kind of . His ritual goes awry and you accidentally unleash two of the evil elven gods he 'd sealed away , Elgar'nan and Ghilan'nain , who begin to raise up armies of darkspawn to blight the world . You , and the eponymous Veilguard , have to stop them all . <p> This kicks off a globe-spanning RPG adventure where you at last get to travel through the network of eluvians -- ancient elven mirrors that act as portals -- hopping from one kingdom to the next , solving problems and chasing your enemies . On the way you gain a reputation with various factions across Northern Thedas -- whether old , like the darkspawn-slaying Grey Wardens or the suave assassins among the Antivan Crows , or new , like the treasure-hunting Lords of Fortune , led by an old friend in whom Dragon Age fans will surely revel . Taken together , it 's compelling stuff . Fast-paced combat , pleasurable RPG mechanics and snappy dialogue combine to make this an experience that feels like Dragon Age . <p> The characters are the heart and soul of this game . Like so much else in Veilguard , they start slow , but when they and their stories come to a boil it 's hard to imagine that even sceptical players wo n't have a favourite by the end . From the noir private investigator mage Neve and the charming Vincent Price-like Emmerich to fan favourite Dwarven scout Harding being promoted to a full and romanceable companion , the characters and their plot-relevant tales are all incredible . <p> This game most closely resembles Dragon Age II and Mass Effect 2 in structure . You have to get to know your companions and finish their quest arcs in order to ensure that they 're maximally effective in this game 's pulse-pounding finale , which will wrench tears from you no matter how perfectly you 've set everything up . Even something I 'd initially chalked up to weak writing turned out to be a set-up for a late game twist that moved me to a beautiful grief . The characters take up residence in the deepest places of your heart without you realising it , much as they build floating homes for themselves in the game 's base , the Lighthouse . <p> For better or worse , it answers some of the biggest questions about the Dragon Age mythos and in so doing shatters the sense of mystery that made the game 's world feel so rich and vast . <p> But ... you knew there was a " but " coming . <p> As with Mass Effect : Andromeda , it takes a while for the game to truly find its footing , and it 's a lot to ask to play five to 10 hours before " it gets good " . More importantly , this is a game that is about gods and their depredations . For better or worse , it answers some of the biggest questions about the Dragon Age mythos and in so doing shatters the sense of mystery that made the game 's world feel so rich and vast . <p> DA 's theology was lavish precisely because it was a fantasy version of our own world , where divinity is not self-evident and faith is required in order to believe at all . Contrast this with worlds such as Dungeons &amp; Dragons , where the existence of gods is an objective fact . The three previous games , especially Inquisition , embraced this mystery . Even your world-historical Inquisitor , with all her power and her ability to walk where few mortals dare to tread , found only questions instead of answers about the world 's cosmology . <p> Veilguard proposes to give you answers . These are often interesting and wind through the best parts of the game 's story -- engaging with Solas and his tragic history of war crimes in aid of a rebellion -- but no one seems to wrestle with them . In your party you have two Dalish elves who were raised to believe in gods such as Ghilan'nain and Elgar'nan as paragons of virtue , yet no one has a dark night of the soul about their revelation as mad , cackling villains . The Catholic-like Chantry , meanwhile , is almost nowhere to be seen in this game , despite frequent visits to one of the setting 's holiest cities . <p> Chantry believers worship the Maker , whose provable absence should be worrying to the faithful . If only we could hear from them . The revelations of the elven gods , meanwhile , call the most basic Chantry beliefs into question -- and no one seems to notice or care . The grey , horned Qunari , meanwhile , named for the collectivist Qun philosophy , are represented copiously , but almost none are believers in the Qun . It 's a glaring absence when a plot point involves a civil war among the Qunari , with the better part of their military breaking away from the Qun . How do Qun believers feel about this ? We do n't hear from them . <p> In previous Dragon Age games , the silence of the gods could be beautiful pauses in a cosmic symphony . In Veilguard the silence of believers is dissonant . <p> Not every question needs an answer . To that end , is Veilguard an excellent game ? That 's actually proved to be a fun mystery to wrestle with -- I do n't regret the struggle at all . I find myself hoping that any sequels to Veilguard rediscover the beauty of such unanswerable questions . <p> Dragon Age : The Veilguard is available for PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series X/S , and PC . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 12 , 2024 as " Hits and myths " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . @@118852020 <h> This year 's spectacular Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art at QAGOMA foregrounds indigenous artists from around the globe . By Stephanie Radok . <h> Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art at QAGOMA <p> Every Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art has been spectacular , and APT11 is no exception : 500 artworks by 70 artists and collectives from 30 countries are spread over the two gallery sites of Brisbane 's QAGOMA . <p> Its scale ranges from monumental sculptures by Brett Graham in Tai Moana Tai Tangata ( 2020 ) and the eight-metre weaving Fala Kuta e Toa Ko Tavakefai'ana ( 2024 ) by Tonga 's ' Aunofo Havea Funaki and the Lepamahanga Women 's Group to Persian and Pakistani miniature paintings by Abolfazl Harouni and Wardha Shabbir respectively . The range of media and concerns and the amount of attention required to see , learn concepts and digest the aesthetics of the art are extreme . In its many languages , untold histories , specific geographies and unseen lives , this year 's APT is overwhelming . Cultural resilience and innovation are constant themes . <p> The book of essays published in 1993 to celebrate the first APT was titled Tradition and Change -- and made a start at encouraging Australians to think of art in Asia and the Pacific as being as contemporary as art made anywhere else . As John Clark wrote in 1998 in his book Modern Asian Art : " We now begin to see each other , and no longer only the figments of force or imagination . " <p> Some previous APTs have been put together by large groups of curators spanning different countries , but this year 's is overseen by QAGOMA curators Tarun Nagesh , Ruth McDougall , Reuben Keehan , Ruha Fifita and Abigail Bernal , who have worked with local individuals , collectives and facilitators . The logistics are staggering , the result seamless and varied . <p> All artworks in APT11 have wall texts side by side in two languages -- English and that of the artist or artists -- which means that the theme of translation is visible and constant . A surprising number of different groups of indigenous peoples are represented , with resonant stories and histories of resistance , courage , knowledge and fortitude . <p> Joydeb Roaja , for example , hails from south-eastern Bangladesh , home to 11 different Jumma or indigenous peoples . His intricate artwork series , The future of indigenous peoples ( 2024 ) , are large ink-on-paper drawings showing pairs of indigenous people with large trees growing from their heads . They are surrounded by tiny figures with tripods and cameras , helicopters and drones who are non-indigenous observers : tourists , journalists , anthropologists . Emphasising an indigenous sense of belonging and relatedness to their place and the inquisitive intrusions of the coloniser or documenter , the work offers hope and " intangible power " in its portrayal of a close and enduring relationship with other life forms . <p> Curiously this fine , intense work is echoed in a large woodcut series , Sangiang Serri ( Goddess of Rice ) ( 2021 ) , made by Muhlis Lugis of the Bugis people of South Sulawesi in Indonesia , and in the woodcut History , Memory , Identity ( 2024 ) by Subas Tamang , of the Tamang people of Nepal . In each case human or divine figures appear to be holding power and knowledge that is emphatically local , historical and spiritual . <p> Lugis advocates a " return to tradition " . Observing the intense detail and scale of his work almost sends you into a trance . This is also the case with Tamang 's print , which shows figures engaged in a ceremony with their faces concealed by what look like drums . <p> Tamang 's work is part of a collection of works from TAMBA , a Nepalese collective of artists , writers , poets , researchers and activists formed for APT11 . Alongside his work , a video by Mekh Limbu , titled Mangdem'ma -- an invocation for the healing of Adivasi spirits and lands ( 2022-23 ) , tells a complex story of protest and revolution that splices the world-turning qualities of shamans with politics . <p> Another mesmerising video by Kiri Dalena from the Philippines , Mag-uuma ( Farmer ) -- Lamentation by Melfe Ebalang from Valencia , Bukidnon ( 2014 ) was filmed in Northern Mindanao . It is a spoken ballad by a young activist farmer about poverty and injustice . Its simplicity creates empathy -- we see her face , we read her voice , we hold her despair in our eyes . <p> Wang Tuo 's is a daring work in its criticism of the Chinese government and mentions " being asked to tea " as that moment when you are taken aside and warned ... <p> Papua New Guinea is represented in work from the collective Haus Yuriyal . It includes a garden of subsistence vegetables -- taro , corn , bananas and sugar cane , a meeting house with woven walls , as well as carved and painted tree ferns . There 's also a set of weavings including colloquial names such as " Back Page " and " White Horse " , and shield designs in earth pigments or bright house paint . <p> In another woven-walled sitting place a video is shown of some aspects of contemporary life -- people looking at photo albums , a ceremonial parade by young children dressed as men , people dancing wearing feathers , all accompanied by very gentle male voices softly singing . It is a collection of hope and time -- making shields not for defence , as they are no protection against bullets , but to hold energy and tradition . <p> The artwork Echo ( 2023 ) , made by Vietnamese artist L ? Thu ? , marries life and death in black , red and gold images of trees , plants and skeletons painted on nine wooden doors from a dismantled house in H ? i An . They are flanked by grey brush paintings on white silk showing lost rooms in empty houses , embroidered with the stitched calligraphy of a 19th century poem about returning home to H ? i An . On the ground a few bricks marked with gold leaf continue this story of the dismantling of the past and its lingering tenacity . <p> Chinese artist Wang Tuo 's The Second Interrogation ( 2023 ) includes three videos . Two are shown opposite each other and somehow slice and combine the same characters and their words in subtitles so that watching them is at once like being at a lecture and in a conversation . A more conventional video of a theatrical performance is in a separate connected bigger room . But it is the intimate conversation that compels you to sit and swivel your head from screen to screen while pondering all the questions it raises . The discussion about art and politics is between an intellectual young man and an older man who is an agent tasked with observing and reporting . Each are full of doubt and questions . <p> Tuo 's topic is contemporary art in China and its past history -- in particular the famous exhibition China/Avant-Garde , which was held in Beijing in February 1989 , just before the Tiananmen Square massacre , and how art might still act as an agent for political action and change . It is a daring work in its criticism of the Chinese government and mentions " being asked to tea " as that moment when you are taken aside and warned about your words or behaviour . <p> Up on the mezzanine in GOMA , several videos of the durational performances of Thai artist Kawita Vatanajyankur , mostly in red and white , show her using her head to wash dishes -- her hair acting as a brush , balancing and holding great trays of rice that are continually being filled , and unweaving a giant elaborate web of thread , among other situations . The work creates mesmerising metaphors for the exploitation of women workers . <p> Then in QAG there is Truong C ? ng T ? ng 's Khu Vu ? n L ? c Hu ? ng ( A disoriented garden ) , 2023-ongoing -- a scattered installation of gourds , pipes , bowls of bubbling water , soil , seeds and stones . Round lacquer paintings of fires and war hang in the air , while on the wall is a row of dusty and cobwebbed wooden grids once used in silkworm cultivation . They hold spheres of semiprecious stones and pebbles as a kind of memory storehouse . <p> T ? ng 's work is inspired by the makeshift farming methods of the indigenous Jarai people in the Central Highlands of Vietnam , which , in the words of Abigail Bernal , " contrast with the values of capitalism and ' progress ' ? " . Notably the wall label describes its materials as " a collaboration between humans , machines , plants , insects , light , darkness , soil , stone , water , wind , rain and the spirits " . To me this list suggest that such a collaboration does not privilege the human . If we are to learn from indigenous people how to look after the Earth , we must embrace seeing humans as caretakers not consumers . <p> In 2026 , a selection of works from APTs in the QAGOMA Collection will be travelling to the Victoria and Albert Museum in London . @@118852022 <h> Barrett Brown My Glorious Defeats <p> In 2008 , Anonymous arose from 4chan , the " arsehole " of the internet , to become a serious political adversary defending the central tenet of the hacker ethos : the free flow of information . Ostensibly a decentralised and non-hierarchical hacker collective , the targets of Anonymous were as diverse as the Church of Scientology , the Tunisian uprising and even the Australian government . <p> Like Julian Assange , Edward Snowden and Glenn Greenwald , the American journalist and online activist Barrett Brown has devoted his career to whistleblowing by exposing the surveillance state . Brown is known primarily as a gonzo journalist for the provocative , self-reflexive and drug-addled accounts of his involvement in the halcyon days of internet freedom . <p> My Glorious Defeats : Hacktivist , Narcissist , Anonymous is Brown 's expansive memoir , covering his involvement in Anonymous 's inner circle , junkie years , persecution at the hands of the United States Department of Justice , incarceration for circulating secret documents and eventual release in 2016 after Trump 's election victory . Much of the book is occupied by defining what he is not : he 's not a " hacktivist " ( he ca n't code ) ; he 's not the " spokesperson " for Anonymous , although he represented them to the media ; he 's not an altruist fighting for the freedom of the people but rather an " anarchist revolutionary with a lust for insurgency " whose attraction to insurrection and desire to become famous aligns with the public good . <p> Brown 's long-tongued narcissism is likely to alienate readers who are otherwise compelled by his valuable position as a documentarian of the subterranean ideological wars happening online . This signature style is partly a performance that co-opts the in-joke , meta-irony of anonymous forums . And sure , I get it : it 's funny when a nobody asserts on 4chan their authority over the subject . But taken into the public sphere , Brown 's self-aggrandising translates into passages of charmless boasting . By embracing his narcissistic urges , Brown also seems either unable or unwilling to distinguish between incisive critiques of deep-state surveillance and petty feuds with journalists and media representations . Much of the book is devoted to the latter and seems more personal than political . <p> In the empire of his memoir , Brown is a dictator . He presents an image of a high-functioning drug user and unreconstructed internet troll fighting against the military-industrial complex and moves from perceptive eloquence to stimulated rambling . Brown 's My Glorious Defeats sprawls across the 21st century and , despite its flaws , gives us a window into this transformative period of internet history and the emergence of hacktivism as an organised form of institutional subversion . <p> Farrar Straus Giroux , 416pp , $54.99 <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " My Glorious Defeats " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . The salad seems familiar at first , but the flavours have a Japanese lean and an interesting set of textures distinct from the Italian original . <p> The soft milk mozzarella is like a ball , often with a knot , its thin outer layer filled with cream and stracciatella . It is luscious and buttery , but with a little tang , and loves being doused in virgin olive oil . At this time of the year it is perfect with tomatoes at their best , ripe and sweet and with a little touch of tartness . <p> I am in love with the other flavours here , too : the tomato dressing spiked with a nuoc cham of sorts , the crispy fried garlic oil and the zippy , finely shaved spring onion and lemony sorrel leaves . <p> Over the top I 've been shaking shichimi togarashi , also known as Japanese seven spice , with its sansho pepper and nori , for a welcome hit of warm chilli and citrus . You can buy it in a little shaker at Asian grocery stores or most supermarkets . <p> This is a great little starter on its own , but it also sits really well with grilled or roasted beef , pork or chicken . <p> Ingredients <p> Time : 30 minutes preparation + cooking <p> Serves 6 as a starter <p> Crispy garlic oil <p> 10 cloves Australian garlic <p> 120ml extra virgin olive oil <p> salt <p> Method <p> Peel the garlic and slice thinly lengthways on a mandolin . <p> Add the oil and the garlic slices to a small saucepan and stir to separate the slices . <p> Place over low to medium heat and stir to gently fry the slices until a light golden brown ( about seven minutes ) . <p> Pull off the heat and quickly tip all contents into cold saucepan . <p> Once cool , season with a little salt . <p> Ingredients <p> Nuoc cham <p> 300g caster sugar <p> 200ml water <p> 175ml fish sauce or garam <p> 3 red bullet chillies , chopped into fine rings <p> 2 cloves garlic , sliced in half <p> Method <p> Add all ingredients to a saucepan and bring to simmer for three minutes , then turn off and allow to cool . <p> Ingredients <p> Nuoc cham , vinegar and tomato dressing <p> 250g whole over-ripe tomatoes <p> 50ml quality fermented brown rice vinegar or rice wine vinegar <p> 250ml nuoc cham ( recipe above ) <p> Method <p> Blanch and skin the tomatoes and blitz in a high-speed blender . Add the halved cherry tomatoes . <p> Spoon over the tomato dressing and then the spring onion slices and the sorrel . Position the Thai basil leaves . <p> Position the burrata and season with a little salt . Spoon over the crispy garlic oil . @@118852024 <h> Why ' big data ' has n't made randomised trials unnecessary <p> In 1747 , 31-year-old Scottish naval surgeon James Lind set about determining the most effective treatment for scurvy , a disease that was killing thousands of sailors around the world . Lind selected 12 sailors suffering from scurvy and divided them into six pairs . Each pair received a different treatment : cider ; sulphuric acid ; vinegar ; seawater ; a concoction of nutmeg , garlic and mustard ; or two oranges and a lemon . In less than a week , the pair who had received oranges and lemons each day were back on active duty , while the others languished . Given that sulphuric acid was then the British Navy 's main treatment for scurvy , this was a crucial finding . <p> The trial provided robust evidence for the powers of citrus because it created a credible counterfactual . The sailors did n't choose their treatments , nor were they assigned based on the severity of the ailment . Instead , they were randomly allocated , making it likely that differences in the sailors ' recoveries were due to the treatment rather than other characteristics . <p> Lind 's randomised trial , one of the first in history , has attained legendary status . Today , new medical treatments are routinely subjected to randomised trials . When a pharmaceutical company is testing a new wonder drug , it will typically be administered to two groups -- randomly chosen so they are as similar as possible . Only if the outcomes are significantly different between the groups will the drug be judged a success . Companies such as Amazon and Netflix routinely conduct randomised trials to improve their products . <p> Yet some are now arguing that " big data " makes randomised trials unnecessary . Between large-scale surveys and extensive administrative datasets , the world is awash in data as never before . Each day , hundreds of exabytes of data are produced . Big data has improved the accuracy of weather forecasts , permitted researchers to study social interactions across racial and ethnic lines , enabled the analysis of income mobility at a fine geographic scale and much more . <p> The problem is , big data can produce the wrong answer . Take the example of hormone replacement therapy ( HRT ) for post-menopausal women . In 1976 , the Nurses ' Health Study began tracking some 100,000 registered nurses . The study found that women who chose to use HRT halved their risk of heart disease . <p> Largely as a result of this non-randomised study , HRT usage rates soared . By the late 1990s , about two fifths of post-menopausal women in the United States were using HRT -- mostly to reduce the risk of heart disease . However , no randomised trial had evaluated its impact on heart health . <p> Lind 's randomised trial , one of the first in history , has attained legendary status . Today , new medical treatments are routinely subjected to randomised trials . <p> Then the US National Institutes of Health funded two randomised trials , comparing HRT against a placebo . The trials , which began in 1993 , did not support menopausal HRT to prevent coronary heart disease . Indeed , one of the randomised trials was stopped early because the data and safety monitoring board concluded there was some evidence of harm . <p> With the health of millions of women at stake , the early observational data had presented an inaccurate picture of HRT 's impact on postmenopausal women . The fact that the observational studies had a larger sample size than the randomised trials did not help . Lacking evidence from randomised trials , many women took a treatment that may have had an adverse impact on their health . Subsequent research has shown a far more nuanced picture around the potential uses and benefits of HRT , and has improved medical understanding of ways to alleviate the symptoms of menopause . <p> Researcher Rory Collins and his co-authors refer to this as the " magic of randomisation " . Large datasets are a valuable complement to randomised trials . But big data is not a substitute for randomisation . <p> In a 2023 joint statement , the European Society of Cardiology , American Heart Association , American College of Cardiology and the World Heart Federation concluded : " The widespread availability of large-scale , population-wide , real-world data is increasingly being promoted as a way of bypassing the challenges of conducting randomised trials . Yet , despite the small random errors around the estimates of the effects of an intervention that can be yielded by analyses of such large datasets , non-randomized observational analyses of the effects of an intervention should not be relied on as a substitute , due to their potential for systematic error . " <p> The same is true in policymaking , where low-quality evaluations can produce misleading answers . Randomised trials provide a more rigorous way to evaluate what works . For example , Scared Straight , a program aimed to deter young people from crime by exposing them to prison life , was found in randomised trials to increase offending rates instead . Similarly , randomised evaluations of abstinence-only programs aimed at reducing rates of HIV among young people found no evidence that the programs curbed behaviours associated with higher risk . <p> In other cases , randomised trials produce powerful evidence of effectiveness . Job training programs Year Up and Per Scholas , targeted at low-income adults , focus on fast-growing industries with well-paying jobs , and provide paid internships with local employers . Randomised trials find that these programs boost long-term earnings by 20 to 40 per cent . Saga Tutoring , an intensive schoolwide program for 9th and 10th graders , was shown in randomised trials to raise achievement in maths among high schools with the most socioeconomically disadvantaged students by more than two thirds of a grade level . <p> Randomised trials have also helped temper the claims of advocates . Despite assertions that police body cameras would transform officers ' interactions with the public , randomised trials of body cameras suggest the cameras produced only small and statistically insignificant effects on police use of force and civilian complaints , though they may provide better evidence when cases go to court . <p> Contrary to the belief that microcredit would transform lives , randomised trials have shown little evidence that this practice of providing small loans to entrepreneurs in emerging economies boosted spending on education or health , or empowered more women . <p> And despite bold claims for the impact of universal basic income on recipients , a recent randomised trial of universal basic income in two US states found that a payment of US$1000 a month over three years has fairly modest impacts on job quality and health . <p> Some of these findings surprised me , and I hope you had the same reaction . People are complex and it would be strange if theory alone predicted which programs will work . <p> Surprises are also common in medicine , where a recent study concluded that the overall success rate of clinical trials for new drugs is 8 per cent . Nonetheless , global spending on clinical trials exceeds US$30 billion a year , because such trials identify which treatments work and which do not . Clinical trials have extended life spans by proving effective treatments . Clinical trials have saved lives by weeding out ineffective treatments . <p> James Lind 's scurvy trial was groundbreaking . Alas , his write-up left something to be desired . Six years after his experiment , Lind published the 456-page tome A Treatise of the Scurvy . His experimental results were spot-on , but Lind 's theoretical explanations for why citrus worked were hocus-pocus . The treatise was largely ignored . <p> Finally , in the 1790s , a follower of Lind , surgeon Gilbert Blane , was able to persuade senior naval officials that oranges and lemons could prevent scurvy . In 1795 -- almost half a century after Lind 's findings -- lemon juice was issued on demand ; by 1799 it became part of the standard naval provisions . In the early 1800s British sailors were consuming 200,000 litres of lemon juice annually . <p> The British may have been slow to adopt Lind 's findings , but they were faster at curing scurvy than their main naval opponents . An end to scurvy was a key reason why the British , under the command of Admiral Lord Nelson , were able to maintain a sea blockade of France and ultimately win the 1805 Battle of Trafalgar against a larger force of scurvy-ridden French and Spanish ships . Nelson had clever tactics , but it also helped that scurvy was n't ravaging his crew . <p> His victory is just a part of the legacy of James Lind . His example reminds us even today , in our world awash with data , that a curious mind can change the course of history . <p> This is an edited extract of a speech delivered at Oxford University . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " When a coin toss saves lives " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@118852025 <h> Soccer 's true role in the Great War Christmas truce <p> The Great War was just six months old and the trenches that would define it were still relatively crude . Carved from muddy earth and fortified by razor wire , their sides were strengthened by sandbags and planks . Machine guns sat above them . " Those were the early days of trench warfare , the days of the jam-tin bombs and the gas-pipe trench-mortar , " Robert Graves , a British officer in the war , wrote in his famous memoir Goodbye to All That . " Still innocent of Lewis or Stokes guns , steel helmets , telescopic rifle-sights , gas-shells , pill-boxes , tanks , well-organised trench-raids , or any of the later refinements of trench warfare . " <p> Even then , just months into an almost four-and-a-half-year war , the space between the Western Front 's opposing trenches -- No Man 's Land -- already had its forsaken quality . This was the place of unclaimed corpses , charcoal stumps and swampy shell craters -- the place surreally rendered on canvas by the British officer and war artist Paul Nash . The landscapes he would later describe by brush were first described by pen in a letter to his wife . Flanders , he wrote , is " the most frightful nightmare of a country , more conceived by Dante or Poe than by nature , unspeakably , utterly indescribable . No glimmer of God 's hand is seen anywhere . " <p> Those opposing trenches , mostly carved through France and Belgium , were often made within intimate proximity of the other . In some places , only a hundred metres separated them -- soldiers could hear the enemy and smell their cigarette smoke . As Christmas approached , already four million people were dead , and the scene of combat became heavily frosted . <p> It was here , in various places along the Western Front on Christmas Eve 1914 , that a brief truce was spontaneously conceived . It 's a true story , and remarkable , but one that has attracted countless barnacles of myth ever since -- including one about soccer that was promoted by Prince William , as president of England 's Football Association , and the French football legend and then UEFA chief Michel Platini . <p> The candles and carols of the German trenches recurs , in the letters and recollections of soldiers , as the tender catalyst for the brief truce . <p> The Christmas truce was not formally sanctioned but was rather a series of improvised and local events that happened sporadically across the frontline between combatants , and as such we have only the letters and recollections of soldiers -- the sum of which does n't always cohere . The candles and carols of the German trenches recurs , in the letters and recollections of soldiers , as the tender catalyst for the brief truce . " All of a sudden , lights appeared along the German trench , " British rifleman Graham Williams told the BBC 50 years later . " And I thought : ' This is a funny thing . ' And then the Germans started singing ' Stille Nacht , heilige Nacht ' . " <p> It 's really something to contemplate : stirred by " Silent Night " , shell-shocked soldiers -- living with rats , dysentery and decomposing friends -- were now anxiously calculating the sincerity of the other side 's promise of a temporary peace . So white flags and hand-written signs were held above the trench lines -- " Tomorrow you no shoot , we no shoot " -- and the next morning some brave heads rose above their own threshold to test the proposition . <p> These local truces were improvised and tentatively wrought , but in several places across the front , soldiers indeed climbed from their cesspits and crossed No Man 's Land to meet the enemy . Once there , rival soldiers exchanged modest gifts -- bread , biscuits , tobacco , whatever their rations might afford -- and allowed the other side to bury their dead , the ones left rotting in the wasteland between their trenches . <p> " They were only fifty yards away from us in the trenches , " Private Frederick Davies wrote to his mother . " They came out and we went to meet them . We shook hands with them . They also gave us cigars but they did n't have much food . I think they are hard up for it . They were fed up with the war . " <p> As a spontaneous and idiosyncratic event , the Christmas truce was not realised even kilometres from where those combatants were peacefully exchanging cigarettes . Plenty of fighting was recorded on Christmas Day 1914 , and so too the deaths of men who walked into No Man 's Land and suffered head shots from snipers . Today , we receive the Christmas truce as something sweeter and more uniform than it was . <p> One large part of the mythological swelling of the Christmas truce is the place of soccer in it . The most popular rendering , and the least credible , is that a game broke out between English and German soldiers who used No Man 's Land as a pitch and their stretchers for goalposts . That a heavily cratered and frozen land strewn with bodies and barbed wire might accommodate a soccer match seems unlikely , as is the convenient discovery of a soccer ball . <p> The fact that the ceasefire was not singular or organised , but multiple and spontaneous , also discredits the romance of a large soccer match around which combatants gathered . Instead , the few references to soccer in soldiers ' letters home refer to brief and silly kickabouts with improvised balls made from socks and tins of meat . <p> But over time , the idea that an organised match occurred between England and Germany became intoxicating . Oddly , it 's the fiction of a man who was there , and famously recorded his experiences in a memoir , that may have helped inspire it . In 1962 , the poet and novelist Robert Graves published a short story about an imagined soccer match between opposing troops during the Christmas truce . In the story , the Germans win 3-2 -- a score often given by those who tell the tale as fact . <p> Paul McCartney , strangely , may have helped too . The film clip for his 1983 single , " Pipes of Peace " , is based on the Christmas truce . McCartney plays both a German and British officer , each man resigned to his respective trench on Christmas Eve while clutching a photo of his beloved . Tentatively , each rises from his muddy gutter , approaches the other in No Man 's Land and shares his photo . A soccer ball emerges and the combatants -- now entwined by their shared humanity -- play joyously like children . Until , that is , the crash of a mortar shell and each side 's panicked retreat . <p> In 2014 , on the centenary of the truce , the British supermarket chain Sainsbury 's spent millions on a televised commercial that seemed to borrow heavily from McCartney 's video . The war 's deathly squalor was sweetened again , and the military adviser to the commercial advised against the use of the soccer game . This request was , apparently , partially indulged . " It is a lot more accurate than it could have been because , I understand , of the involvement of a historical adviser who knows his stuff and was able to get the makers to tone down the football element so as to include some of the more mundane things that took place -- such as the soldiers showing each other photographs , " Professor Gary Sheffield , a military historian from the University of Wolverhampton , said at the time of the commercial . <p> " The role of football in the truce is very much overhyped . There is a common assumption that some sort of big match took place but there is scant evidence of this actually occurring ... Football has become emblematic of the truce and distracts the attention away from why the truce was important . " <p> This was not apparent to Prince William , however , who as the FA 's president marked the centenary and the unveiling of a statue of two opposing soldiers shaking hands with a soccer ball between them , by saying : " Football had the power to bring people together and break down barriers . It is vital that 100 years on we keep the Christmas truce story alive . For future generations , this memorial will help ensure that not just football but also a nation remembers . " <p> It would seem the combatants were n't moved to jointly sanctify soccer but merely to stretch their legs , bury their friends and enjoy a day off from warfare . Prince William was not the only football administrator to ratify the myth with sickly platitudes . " I pay tribute to the soldiers who , 100 years ago , showed their humanity by playing football together , opening an important chapter in European unity and providing a lasting example to young people , " Michel Platini said in 2014 at his own unveiling of a monument . <p> We might wonder what it is that we 're asked to remember . Still , sweetened as the truce has become , and as encrusted by myth and exploited by shopping chains as it has been , there remains the image of Germans singing " Silent Night " on Christmas Eve and prompting , accidentally , a brief lull in the vast , attritional violence . <p> Nothing else like it would be seen again for the remaining four years of the war , in which about another 12 million souls would die . " On Christmas Day the greatest thing took place here -- Somehow or other a friendly feeling got up between the Germans and us , so we both left our trenches unarmed and exchanged greetings about 300 yards apart , " Corporal T. ? B. Watson wrote home . " This took place in the forenoon . After dinner we were firing and dodging as hard as ever ; one could hardly believe that such a thing had taken place . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 14 , 2024 as " The whole truce " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . temperatures across summer , with an increase in unusually high temperatures during the night . <p> Heat stress kills more people than any other natural hazard , according to the World Health accidents and transmission of some infectious diseases " , WHO says . <h> READ MORE <p> Around 47,000 deaths were attributed to high temperatures in Europe in 2023 and -- according to the European Union 's Copernicus Climate Change Service -- heat-related mortality has increased by around 30 per cent in the last two decades . <p> Dr Arnagretta Hunter , a physician and public policy researcher from the Australian National University , told SBS News that Australians may have difficulty understanding the risks posed by heat because heatwaves are part of our " national psyche " . <p> " I do n't think we have really built into our brain just how dangerous it can be . And particularly as climate change starts to be a more prominent feature of seasonal variation , " she said . <h> READ MORE <h> What to do in a heatwave <p> Individuals can take action to cool down and avoid the serious health consequences of heat . <p> The Climate Council recommends steps such as spending time in cool indoor areas with fans or air conditioning , including homes or public areas such as libraries or shopping centres ; completing outdoor tasks early in the day ; staying hydrated ; avoiding alcohol or caffeinated drinks , and checking the heatwave plans of local councils . <p> Hunter said that proactively staying on top of weather forecasting and understanding the impacts of both heat and humidity are important safety behaviours for heatwaves and will become more necessary as temperatures rise . <h> READ MORE <p> While children and older people are known to be more vulnerable to heat , anybody can be affected , and people who work outside are particularly prone to heat-related health issues . <p> Because outdoor workers take on the burden of heat , Hunter said it 's important for industries to consider the health impacts and ensure workers are protected . <p> " That means not working for long periods in very hot temperatures , making sure that there 's access to ambient and cool environments , making sure that temperatures are checked and making sure that hydration is attended to . " <p> Hunter said it is also important to consider the communities around us in times of extreme heat . <p> " It 's about taking care of each other . So , it 's about keeping environments cool and making sure that people have access to a cool environment , " she said . <p> " There 's an advantage to us knowing our neighbours , knowing our communities , knowing who 's on our streets and thinking about them when the weather events are extreme . " <h> What cities need to do as temperatures rise <p> Ian Wright , an associate professor in the School of Science at Western Sydney University , told SBS News he believes cities need to think more carefully about long-term solutions to help people deal with heat , including cool refuges and more access to swimming in waterways . <p> Wright said a lack of monitored swimming areas is a particularly big issue in western Sydney . <p> " We have the rivers but we do n't have that safe community access and the parks and swimming areas that go with it like we do on the coast -- I think it 's quite inequitable . " <p> More equitable access to swimming in waterways has been suggested as a long-term solution to rising heat . @@118854695 <h> We now have the election 's defining issue . Here 's how Labor will stuff it up <p> The release of some Opposition nuclear policy detail , such as it is , will define the federal election . It represents an opportunity for an unimpressive government to grab the issue , to make it what the election is about , and , having demolished the Coalition 's assumptions and mathematics , to win an improbable victory . <h> Subscribe now for unlimited access . <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of Today 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> Interactive Crosswords , Sudoku and Trivia <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> But if the Coalition has its strategy and its tactics right , one can see Labor taking the bait to bore the electorate witless with niggles about detail , gotchas about costings , timetables and unknown future events , including the attitude of potential partners and climate disasters . <p> I fear the worst . Six weeks of exposure to the relentless - and ever so successful and persuasive - policy logic of Chris Bowen , the Napoleon Pig of Anthony Albanese 's menagerie , and the blather of Ted O'Brien making points proving that perpetual motion technology is around the corner . Peter Dutton and David Littlemore simultaneously speaking of prudence and fiscal rectitude , scorn for the uncertainty of rain , and promising that their established managerial excellence and network of cronies would produce umpteen new power plants on time and on budget , a long time away . <p> Meanwhile old Labor warriors such as Anthony Albanese will speak with passion and horror of the struggles at the 1983 conference of the federal ALP , which irradiated most of the Left of the day . <p> Some nation-builders will weigh , count , measure and audit every Opposition proposition in a very thin program and outline of costing . They will be able to write whole theses on false assumptions , undercounting , overcounting and double counting of inputs , and over , under and double guesstimates about outputs . <p> Each side will produce umpteen consultants , experts and scientific bodies to prove that black is white , if that is what suits the interests of the group paying the bill . Some will probably be right , and others will appear to be substituting hopes , belief and ideology for scientific information . Labor , in particular , will assume that voters will soon be carefully weighing up the evidence and coming down to formal judgement about the facts . Or the concerns that ought to be associated with the fact that there are atoms in those durned pieces of uranium . <p> In fact , most voters have already made up their minds and are unlikely to be swayed by facts , new or invented . Or economic arguments , including those made by Treasury or CSIRO , or scientists imbued with the urgent need to do something about global warming . Most particularly taken with a grain of salt will be all mathematics , tables and graphs presented by economists or engineers . <h> Most of the public knows enough <p> This is not to say that the public is ignorant of , or uncaring about , the wider issues or agendas . If the proposition were merely about whether now was the moment for clean safe nuclear energy , a plebiscite might come out in favour . That might not be a judgement about the uncertainties of alternative power ( or the need for a range of options given droughts , storms and difficulties on electricity grids ) . It might also reflect a canny view that the economics of different power fuels ( including wind , sun , tides and rain ) might change over time , just as they have over the years with coal and gas . It might reflect an opinion that in time , a need for more urgent actions might involve effective taxes , paid by suppliers , on carbon . All of these could be plausible views for wanting nuclear power as a possibility , especially given the ready supply of potential nuclear fuels in Australia . <p> But most of the population believes in firm action on climate change and see the nuclear debate as fitting in that framework . Repeated polls over the past 15 years have demonstrated that they recognise political equivocation and prevarication on the subject . They know the broad positions of each of the parties , including of independent groupings such as the teals and David Pocock , on the subject . <p> Many - the 60 per cent of the electorate who were about in 2007 - remember phrases such as Kevin Rudd 's about climate change being one of the great moral issues of our time . Typically , also , they have been through several iterations of Labor 's talking bravely then letting everyone down , so they are mostly not astonished , if disappointed and saddened , by fresh betrayals and cowardice . Even more the party loses credit and moral authority out in the electorate by its craven surrender to Labor premiers who have become instruments of powerful lobbies . <p> So , for many voters , the issue is not a theoretical one . Nor is it a judgement , objective or subjective , about the dangers of climate change , or the way the nation 's resources ought to be spent in addressing it . If Labor lets itself get stuck in such a debate , it is unlikely to be allowed to emerge to fight a much more important debate about the urgency of practical action . All the more so because Labor , and Albanese , are not well credentialled on the subject . They have made too many compromises with powerful interests to be regarded as noble in purpose , if necessarily required to be pragmatic and to move more slowly than some would like . <p> They are often , instead , in a duplicitous position , just as they are on banning gambling , on respecting the human rights and dignity of refugees , or in being in thrall to American defence ideology . They must do their best , including by being unsettled by clever Coalition wedging and shameful pre-emptive kowtowing to deal with the political pressures upon them . But they can not feel pure , and they are not regarded as pure . <p> David Pope 's view . <p> This compromises any attempt to treat nuclear power as a moral issue . Many people who might have been inclined to follow Labor on the subject have already shifted their political support to groups such as the Greens and the teals . Others , including many instinctive Labor supporters , can barely conceal their disgust for the party 's leadership and lack of bottom on the subject . <p> It is far too late to run an education or advertising campaign seeking to persuade supporters that Labor has correctly weighed the importance and significance of serious action on climate change . If it is to mobilise support on the matter against Dutton , it must have a flag under which every opponent of the Dutton plan can unite . That would have to include groups - 30 per cent or more of the electorate - who regard Labor policy as weak , pathetic and unprincipled . People who are not impressed by Labor 's low targets and poor performance , and the excuses it has made for continuing with coal mining . People who wonder why Labor continues to give massive subsidies to the hydrocarbon industries , and allow the opening of fresh coal fields for export of pollution abroad . <p> The same voters are well aware of an even more dismal record by the former Coalition governments , and the fact that going for nuclear power is all about burning fossil fuels for as long as possible . If anything , Dutton has promoted an approach even more retrograde than that pushed by Scott Morrison . <p> The public understands that the Coalition 's conversion to the need for nuclear options is a search for more delay and retreat in dealing with hydrocarbon emissions . It has been done at the behest of the hydrocarbon industry , particularly from pressure by the National Party , which generally behaves as a wholly owned subsidiary of big energy , even at a cost to farmers and regional areas . <p> Most voters , in short , understand well that most of the pretend arguments advanced for nuclear power stations are designed to produce delay . To do less with a pretence of planning to do more , later . The Coalition have rehearsed arguments intended to obscure the desired end point , with quibbles about the unreliability of alternative power , the allegedly uncalculated costs of grid extensions to make their own case seem more compelling . But those who get sucked into and distracted by such arguments are missing the real point . Labor has to cut through to the Coalition 's real agenda . It has to be frank , in admitting that its own performance has been " less than optimal " so as to invoke some sympathy or support from those ultimately on its side . <h> Labor needs inspiration from its supposed enemy <p> Prime Minister Anthony Albanese . Picture by Gary Ramage <p> The centre of those wanting climate action is not in the Labor party , but it is Labor fighting the election . Its own underwhelming record hardly inspires people to join its crusade . Voters will see only minor differences - about the shape of determined minimal action - between Labor and the Coalition . They can not get motivated by the struggle or the fight , especially given the risk they see of Albanese himself losing spirit or commitment and walking away from serious action - as he has done over Indigenous affairs . <p> The need for some political alliance is greater given that neither Albanese nor his senior ministers and the party organisation have shown themselves up to serious political struggle on climate change . They have run away from fights . Ministers , particularly Albanese , have failed to explain to voters what Labor is doing , and why it is responding in a particular way . <p> It is not , as some think , merely a communications problem . It is their record in government . <p> Dutton 's nuclear plans provide an opportunity for a campaign Labor could win . But it wo n't be won without girding for war . Labor has yet to do this , even if it is secretly trying out a few new promises and programs , as with increased access to preschool education . Neither the backbench nor the Labor Party at large is poised for battle . They do not even know what they are fighting for . And showing none of the " flexibility " and nimbleness that a campaign already in desperate straits now badly needs . Albanese has so far failed to rev up his party . <h> The campaign has begun <p> David Pope 's view . <p> Some circumstances are against them . Dutton 's opening artillery shots , for example , come just as the nation subsides into the Christmas break and January holidays , when most voters are not much focused on politics . That also has risks for Dutton of his attack 's fizzling out . <p> But Dutton can change tack , or concentrate on his exploitation of events , including events in the Middle East , and the advent of Donald Trump . He also has the electoral appeal of cultivating sentiment against migrants and exploiting national security uncertainties . He has , as Albanese has recently complained , the full support of the Murdoch media operation . ( It 's a wonder why Albanese responds by then favouring it for leaks , perhaps in the hope that the tiger will eat him last . ) <p> Albanese faces the risk of Labor 's response to Dutton going largely unheard , or of its losing its emotional pitch and getting bogged down on details . Dutton will jump enthusiastically into such arguments because they do not matter to the outcome . Perhaps Labor has a secret policy that will knock everyone out . There has been little sign it is on the way - even less that it is foolproof . There 's always an element of risk in making the Opposition Leader the issue - as Paul Keating did with John Hewson in 1993 and Morrison did with Bill Shorten in 2019 . But it sometimes works , especially when there 's not much of a record to boast about . Nuclear is as good as it gets . <p> If Albanese can not invest Labor 's campaign with moral fervour , he will be doing what he has all too often done over the past five years - playing the game on the opponents ' field , by its rules , on its timetable . It 's not the public 's fault that he has so little material to rally or inspire a followership. 
@@118854940 <h> These are our ' sweatiest suburbs ' , putting vulnerable at risk in heatwaves <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> A shortage of tree cover and poor-quality housing in Melbourne 's most disadvantaged suburbs are putting vulnerable people at greater risk of harm in a heatwave , councils and health agencies warn , as the city braces for its hottest day of the summer . <p> A new ranking of Melbourne 's hottest and most humid council areas has found that inner Melbourne -- also the epicentre of rough sleeping -- is the wider city 's most uncomfortable place to be on days of extreme heat , closely followed by the northern suburbs and the outer south-east . <p> The cities of Melbourne , Merri-bek , Greater Dandenong , Darebin and Casey ranked highest on the new " sweatiest cities " metric , while the Yarra Ranges and Whittlesea , both in the outer north-east , were found to have the driest conditions in summer . <p> The new ranking , by Sydney-based Alliance Climate Control , assessed Australia 's 80 largest local government areas by their average summer temperatures , humidity , tree coverage , wind speeds , population density , average cooling costs and distance to a natural body of water . <p> Six Melbourne councils were not assessed due to their smaller populations . <p> Councils in some of the worst-ranked municipalities are preparing extreme heat emergency management plans that include opening libraries and community halls as refuges , as well as longer-term tree planting goals . <p> Teams of health workers will also walk CBD streets and laneways on Monday in a new heat relief outreach program , which will assist homeless people who may be caught in the forecast 40-degree heat . <p> Cohealth director of community-based drug and alcohol responses Andrea Fischer said the organisation had set up a " pop-up " heat relief centre last summer but had learnt that the service works better when staff met rough sleepers where they are . <p> Advertisement <p> " Often if you are a vulnerable person you are a bit wary about going to places , so you need someone to guide you and just let you know it 's OK to go there and you will be safe , " Fischer said . <p> Loading <p> Dandenong , Casey , Merri-bek , Darebin and Melbourne have among the least tree canopy cover in Melbourne , according to planning department analysis . <p> The peak body for Victorian councils called for a greater state government commitment to cooling the suburbs , days after the Allan government dropped a proposal to mandate lighter roofs on some new homes . <p> Melbourne 's two largest councils , the cities of Casey and Wyndham , had backed a Victorian Planning Authority proposal to restrict dark roofs on new homes in Melbourne 's growth areas , which rank poorly in analysis of places that experience the so-called " heat-island effect " . <p> But the government 's small lot housing code , released this month , omits the draft version 's reference to mandating lighter-coloured roofs . <p> The Municipal Association of Victoria said reflective roofs were an important way to reduce urban heat retention . <p> " Sustainable building design experts see roof reflectivity as a significant opportunity to reduce heat absorption in dwellings , " said association president Jennifer Anderson . <p> Anderson said growth-area neighbourhoods were some of the hottest parts of the city . New homes should be designed for a warmer climate , and councils given state funding to create and maintain parks , forest , wildlife corridors and waterways , she said . <p> Greater Dandenong , which ranked third in the new sweaty cities ranking , held its first heatwave preparedness summit late last year . <p> Rhonda Garad , a Greens councillor who successfully pushed for the summit , said it was confronting to learn how ill-equipped Dandenong was for a heatwave . <p> " Our open spaces are very concrete bound , hot , many people simply do n't have the resources to remain cool and if there were a blackout , which is going to happen in those prolonged heat events , we are in real trouble , " she said . <p> Dandenong has Melbourne 's largest homeless population , as well as a high refugee population , and Garad said many of the poorer parts of the city had housing that was not fit for staying cool . <p> Loading <p> " In our areas where there is less income a lot of the houses do n't have a lot of insulation , they 're small houses , with not a lot of tree coverage and even if they do have air-conditioning , a lot of people ca n't afford to run it for a long time , " she said . <p> In a statement , the government said extreme heat killed more people than natural disasters , but simple steps could help , such as drinking lots of water , seeking out air-conditioned spaces , staying in the shade and checking in on those at risk . <p> Merri-bek Mayor Helen Davidson said the council had set a goal of doubling tree canopy by 2050 , and had planted 3500 additional trees this season . It has added seven new parks through a mix of council funding and developer contributions , she said . <p> A City of Melbourne spokesperson said climate change was causing Melbourne to have more frequent and severe heatwaves , impacting the health of the city 's most vulnerable . <p> The city has created an interactive map of cool , shaded paths through the city and will distribute cool kits to at-risk people in libraries and community centres . <p> Adam Carey is senior city reporter ( suburban ) . @@118855473 <h> The very worst day in an annual surge <p> The 2016 severe thunderstorm asthma event seemed to come as a surprise , but it should n't have . <p> Thunderstorm asthma events have been reported about every seven years in Melbourne since 1984 . With population increases , there are many more people living in the north and west of the city who are exposed to the particular weather conditions that cause thunderstorm asthma . <p> In Melbourne , thunderstorm asthma events happen when severe storm fronts travel across from the north and west of the city in the spring -- and especially after a day or more of high grass pollen counts . <p> But not all storms cause thunderstorm asthma : so , there are probably additional weather factors that are worth exploring . <p> Now , in 2024 , there is a Victoria-wide pollen reporting service and detailed meteorological monitoring for weather events that are likely to lead to asthma epidemics . <p> Hay fever -- or allergic rhinoconjunctivitis -- affects one in five people in southeastern Australia . Picture : Getty Images <p> Pollen counts are now distributed throughout the state as an early warning for both city and rural dwellers who are exposed to high levels of grass pollen . <p> The warning system includes notifications through the Victorian Emergency Services website and the VicEmergency app , as well as websites and apps that report on pollen , like Air Health . <p> If we look at information over 25 years of Victorian emergency department presentations for asthma , it shows us that there is a reliable seasonal surge of emergency asthma presentations in children and younger adults between October and December every year , usually , but not always , associated with thunderstorms . <p> So , the major thunderstorm asthma events are the worst days of this seasonal surge . <p> Climate change in Australia is likely to lead to higher levels of more potent grass pollen . Picture : Getty Images <p> One of the easiest ways to keep people safe is timely public warnings and advice to keep people out of thunderstorms . <p> Most of the grass pollen that triggers thunderstorm asthma is right at the storm front .
