@@119108933 <p> The nurse said , ' Try getting some sleep . ' ' I do n't need any sleep . ' ' You do n't , but it 's easier to run a hospital with all the patients sleeping . ' <p> The Final Programme , 1968 <p> " Easiest way to run the world , for that matter , " Jerry Cornelius replies in the film version of The Final Programme , made several years later when reality had caught up a little with the imagination of British new wave writer Michael Moorcock . Swinging London had by then given way to the three-day week , an oil shock and rampaging inflation -- a world far closer to the crumbling dystopia Moorcock had set his " urban adventurer " Cornelius loose in in the mid-1960s . <p> Moorcock offered Cornelius as a kind of template for other writers to use in the growing experimentalism that marked his editorship of New Worlds magazine and the emergence of JG Ballard , Brian Aldiss and then Moorcock himself at the forefront of a new kind of " speculative fiction " entirely at odds with traditional , American-style science fiction . Jerry Cornelius initially appears as an immaculately dressed , Bond-style action hero , not to mention a guitarist , physicist , former Jesuit , serial bisexual seducer and the putative messiah to the age of science . He totes a lethal " needle gun " , drives beautiful 1930s cars , flies his own aircraft and has apparently endless supplies in his fortress in Ladbroke Grove and scattered across the world . As becomes clearer as the novels progress , Cornelius is also a time traveller , or perhaps multiverse traveller , dipping into and out of various worlds , which only have in common their incipient surrender to that beloved trope of sixties sci-fi , entropy . <p> But whatever his trappings , Cornelius is no traditional hero : his passivity soon becomes apparent even in the first , most straightforward novel . The Final Programme ends with Jerry fused with the formidable , vampiric Miss Brunner -- the computer engineer who drives the entire plot -- into a self-replicating " final human " produced by a supercomputer in a cave in Lapland . The second , and most explicitly political , of the novels , A Cure for Cancer , sees Cornelius , now unsubtly wielding a " vibragun " ( and continuing his pansexual conquests ) , in the midst of a US invasion of Europe , with London -- he sees the apt graffiti " Vietgrove " near his HQ -- eventually enveloped in Vietnam-era sheets of napalm . <p> In the third , set in alternate , steampunk realities familiar to readers of Moorcock 's A Nomad of the Time Streams novels -- worlds of ceaseless , century-long wars between empires that never fell , armed with vast fleets of airships and suburb-sized tanks -- Cornelius ' lack of agency is near-total . He spends most of the novel dead , his corpse the occasional MacGuffin for , but mostly a backdrop to , the adventures of a developing ensemble of characters , including Jerry 's joyously slatternly mother . When he eventually emerges at the end , it 's to establish the Commedia dell'arte framing that will dominate the fourth novel , abandoning his role as Harlequin to adopt the guise of Pierrot to his sister 's Columbine ( Jerry 's two persistent motivations are his pursuit of chaos and his incestuous love for his sister , who herself spends much of the tetralogy dead ) . By The Condition of Muzak , we 're not even sure Cornelius exists at all or whether he 's the projection of a London teenager anxious to find a gig for his band ( " The Deep Fix " ) . * <p> Or perhaps not . It 's rarely clear ; Moorcock 's dialogue is often elliptical and riddled with non-sequiturs , as if any attempt at communicating information is being broken down by the ever-encroaching entropy ; in the film version of The Final Programme -- the only film made of Moorcock 's vast output -- the dialogue is transformed ( as per that hospital gag above ) into an exchange of arch drolleries , especially between Miss Brunner and Cornelius , played , not without some success , by Jenny Runacre and Jon Finch , in what might be termed the first screwball apocalypse . <p> Indeed , across the books , the end of the world and societal collapse are always just around the corner , and just a pogrom away ; populations abandon cities , insurgents topple regimes , colonial rebellions overwhelm empires , ships shell seaside resorts ( try saying that drunk ) , refugees ebb and flow across lands , millions of military " advisers " overrun and incinerate capitals . But Cornelius , indeed the entire cast , are rarely troubled by such disasters -- those they themselves have n't caused -- as if permanent catastrophe and dislocation are the norm wherever you end up in the multiverse . " I have it on very good authority that the world is coming to an end , " Jerry says in the film . " I thought I 'd go home and watch it on television . " <p> Climate change is one of the catastrophes , but the kind resulting from the heat death of the universe ( entropy , again ) , not the greenhouse effect -- -- A Cure for Cancer ends with a frozen world from which Cornelius has sucked all energy in order to briefly restore his sister to life . The end of the world was an atomic-fueled staple of fifties and sixties sci-fi , but for Moorcock , at the end of the world , the screaming terror of end-times is replaced with insouciance , pragmatism and a bemused acceptance that catastrophe is the price to be paid for modernity . Cornelius ' only complaint about the oncoming collapse of civilization in The Final Programme is that it 's happening more quickly than he expected , but he 's well-prepared for it anyway . <p> This indifference toward catastrophe is more than just sixties cool -- swinging London in the shadow of the mushroom cloud -- it seems prescient given it is formal government policy now in response to heat death of another kind , as we know from the relaxed response of the political class to the climate emergency : even as cities flood and refugees begin to shift en masse , we too are invited to simply watch it on television . <p> That Cornelius sprang forth , at least in novel form , in 1968 also seems apt over recent weeks . The US conducted its own bizarre version of the 1968 election ( is not Trump a perfect embodiment of the 1960s presidents minus their virtues -- Kennedy 's sexual predation , LBJ 's vulgarity and corruption , Nixon 's paranoia and criminality ) . A health insurance CEO was assassinated on a New York street . A Middle Eastern regime collapsed overnight , in the manner of the ceaseless Third World coups d ' ? tat of the 1960s -- all while a US-sponsored war immiserates the Middle East . <p> Even now , we 're still playing catch-up to Moorcock 's dystopias . In A Cure for Cancer -- the cancer being the communism the US must burn out wherever it 's found -- President Teddy " Angel Face " Paolozzi dispatches 3 million " military advisers " to Europe ( partly to confront an expansionist Israeli empire gobbling up eastern Europe ) before being replaced with Ronald Boyle of the " Greater American Party " , who announces a special militia to reestablish law and order in the US ( " I 'm sure you will be prepared to suffer a little inconvenience for a short time so that the president can make sure there 's plenty of law and order in the future ? " the arriving inmates of a concentration camp are told ) . <p> By the third novel , The English Assassin ( Jerry does little assassination , or anything else ) imperialism , and especially British imperialism , becomes the primary backdrop for the adventures of the growing cast , with much of the story 's disparate scenes -- you 're never sure if you 're in the same universe as the one on the previous page -- having a decidedly Edwardian , or perhaps Wellesian , air . Una Persson , Jerry 's rival for Catherine 's affection -- Harlequin , eventually , to his Pierrot -- appears as a jobbing music hall songstress when not leading revolutions ( whether music hall or The Beatles , the books are steeped in English music ) . The atmosphere sticks even as the global conflict rages across much of the twentieth century and the cast variously fights with and against each other amid revolutions , occupations and invasions . <p> Imperialism , both old and new world , persists like radioactivity across the novels , making the experience of reading them a crystallisation into plain view of the imperialism that continues to dictate terms for much of the contemporary West , in both domestic and international politics . The West 's support of , or at least readiness to turn a blind eye to , Israel 's genocide and radically accelerated program of occupation and apartheid , all armed and funded by US taxpayers , continues the great tradition of Anglophone settler colonialism . <p> Here in Australia , after spending most of 2023 debating , ostensibly , how to integrate Indigenous communities into policymaking , but in fact debating and legitimising white resentment , we persist in our own settler colonial fantasy of terra nullius , with a formal constitutional position that Indigenous peoples do n't and have never existed here except as incidental features of the landscape . First Nations peoples vanished into a great political silence in 2024 , perhaps henceforth to be mentioned only in February each year when yet another Closing the Gap report is issued , with politicians from both sides joining together to regretfully discuss how , yet again , there 's been little progress . You can watch it on television . <p> And once you start examining events through the persistence of imperialism , other things slot into place . Imperialism dominates Australia 's strategic priorities : we 're caught between the decline of the United States , a democratic empire prone to invading other countries and supporting genocide , and the rise of China , a monstrous tyranny rather less interested in invading anyone else or supporting the extermination of other peoples . Navigating this imperial seesaw will be Australia 's lot for decades to come ( anyone for Moorcock 's " Australasian-Japanese Federation " , a major imperial player in his steampunk adventure The Land Leviathan ? ) , especially as American policymakers become more and more obsessed with containing China and less and less interested in the costs -- to themselves and everyone else -- of doing so . The US is already knee-deep in bipartisan tariffs aimed at choking off China 's strategic advantages and returning president Boyle Trump promises more , so much more in terms of a trade war , with the chance of a real war between empires thrown in for good measure . We can only hope for some military technology as elegant as heavily armed airships . <p> But as veteran sci-fi historian and critic John Clute observed in his introduction to the series in the late 1970s , the Cornelius books are primarily urban novels . <p> Jerry Cornelius is the paradigmatic native of the inner city ; his r ? les constitute a genuine paradigm set of strategies for living there . His inner city is London ( but could be New York ) , his patch is Ladbroke Grove . His real story ( I believe ) runs from about 1965 to about a decade later , a period during which London had been destroying itself as a place to live ... <p> Indeed , this " urban adventurer " ( Moorcock 's term ) spends a lot of time in cities that have been burnt , bombed , shelled , depopulated , or invaded . London landmarks like Buckingham Palace are invariably occupied by figures like General Cumberland in A Cure for Cancer ( a pun on Vietnam-era general William Westmoreland obvious to anyone familiar with England 's pre-1973 counties ) . In the most eerie moment of the entire series , Jerry returns to an increasingly deserted London midway through The Final Programme and visits one of his favourite haunts , only to be pursued by a blob-like crowd that tries to envelop and consume him . The ruined urban landscapes persist into the final novel : the teenage Cornelius seeks recognition , if not fame and fortune , in a filthy contemporary metropolis ; later , Jerry will be crowned King of the city-state of London in an England now controlled by scores of small statelets and its former dominions , which have reverse-colonised the country . <p> In that regard , the books serve not only as a prescient nightmare of dystopias to come but an almost heartwarming evocation of a simpler era . It 's not cities themselves that have been depopulated by cataclysm , but the communities within them . The London of the 1970s , like other Western cities , has n't morphed into either deserted dystopia or garbage-strewn , Winter-of-Discontent capital of a lost empire , but something arguably bleaker and more sinister : a global city in which the nightmare is not to be absorbed by the mob but to be left behind . <p> The modern experience of residing in the cities of the West is now one of permanent competition , for things far more important than a gig for The Deep Fix : competition for housing , competition for the job sufficient to pay for housing , competition for educational opportunity , competition for infrastructure , for services . One fears not being absorbed , but missing out -- on that house , that apartment , that job , that childcare place , that parking spot , that space in the next lane . And you can barely compete with the people already around you , let alone the tens of thousands of people that will arrive in coming years , who threaten to out-compete you and lock you or your children or your grandchildren out of a house , or out of a school , or out of a high-paying job . <p> In the post-neoliberal city , the most quotidian things of life -- paying the rent , paying the mortgage , sending your kid to school , going to hospital , getting to your job -- are a battle of all against all , with most of us barely keeping our heads above water while a precious few -- the true elites -- enjoy the perks of the system : asset owners , large corporations , scammers , developers , ticket clippers , every genius who has spotted an economic interstice in which to insert themselves and make money from the hundred or thousand micro- and macro-transactions we all have to make every day and every year , soaring above our dystopia in airships fueled by greed and the capacity to get away with it . <p> The resentment and exhaustion this breeds in all of us channels not into communitarian sentiment but tribalism , not generosity of spirit but rejection of the other , not fellow-feeling for the fact that we 're all in this together , but resentment that the system delivers us so little for so much striving for those who play by the rules . This curdling of the individualist economic value system of neoliberalism into a sour resentment of others , of the elite ( like health insurance executives ) , of migrants , of minorities , of anyone and everyone because they 're not missing out and we are , is all nimbly exploited by the clever Harlequins of post-neoliberalism . The Trumps , the Johnsons , the Duttons , the Le Pens , offering themselves as messiahs to deliver salvation , justice and retribution to the disaffected , the aggrieved , the angry . <p> Inevitably , they prove empty idols , offering nothing but more rage and hate , pushing to turn the city into something still more tribal , violent , and divided . At the end of The Final Programme , Cornelius Brunner , the computer-created Messiah , gathers the remaining peoples of Europe into a vast throng and leads them to drown themselves , lemming-like , in the Black Sea . " A tasty world , " Cornelius Brunner reflects . " A very tasty world " , as if it was just one of many sampled and enjoyed , before the inevitable transition to another time and place . <p> Dystopias are rarely as bad as those who insist they can save us from them , especially for those of us without somewhere else to flee in the multiverse . <p> *I 'm skipping Moorcock 's post-Brexit , Trump-era Cornelius effort , Pegging The President , which he 's now more or less disowned as having been written in too much anger . <h> Topics <p> Crikey is committed to hosting lively discussions . @@119108937 <p> We suspected oil and gas lobbying was reaching cyclonic intensity , pressuring governments to approve the final components of one of the largest fossil fuel developments in the country 's history . At the centre of the storm lies Scott Reef , a remote and breathtaking ecosystem that could arguably claim the title of Australia 's least known , yet most globally important , natural wonder . <p> With an actual cyclone season looming , it was now or never to amplify the reef 's story . So a group of us -- a dozen marine scientists , filmmakers and conservationists , including my old friend Tim Winton and guitarist and singer John Butler -- pooled resources to charter a vessel to the reef to document the threats posed by Woodside 's Browse gas proposal . <p> It 's a privilege to visit places like Scott Reef , and despite having first advocated for its protection nearly 20 years ago , I doubted I 'd ever be able to dip a fin in its waters . It 's halfway to Indonesia and a long overnight voyage from the closest point on Australia 's mainland . <p> Scott Reef ( Image : Nush Freedman Photography/Supplied ) <p> Departing from an old pearling base on the remote Kimberley coast north of Broome , we waded through the turbid water , transferring swags and special camera equipment from a 4WD buggy to a big catamaran 's tender . Joining the campaign leads as we headed offshore into the tropical night was a group with deep experience in marine biology and filmmaking . <p> An expedition certainly was n't in Tim 's diary , but I had rung him anyway , despite his erstwhile plans to decompress after touring his new climate-themed novel , Juice . ( He keeps a relentless schedule that would have even a young rocker reaching for the uppers . ) His involvement would help to get the word out , and I knew he 'd want to experience the place directly . Being the trooper he is , Tim breathed deep and agreed to join the crew . Another dedicated environmentalist , John Butler , also beloved by many , wedged the trip into his end-of-year crunch . <p> Scott Reef does not disappoint -- even for those of us , like Tim and I , who 've been fortunate to experience Ningaloo Reef 's majesty , and for the Ningaloo-based filmmakers with us whose adventurous lives are akin to a perpetual nature documentary . <p> Scott Reef ( Image : Nush Freedman Photography/Supplied ) <p> Scott Reef is like a skyscraper of coral rising from the ocean floor . Approaching it , one minute you 're in sleepy reverie , watching the cat 's hulls slice the surface of the endlessly deep , dark blue , with flying fish and narrow-winged seabirds the only hint of life . The next you 're scrambling into tenders , leaving the mothership behind -- the only vessel for 100km or more -- picking the moment between oceanic swells crashing onto the giant crescent of coral , then tracking inside Scott 's sheltered coral lagoon . <p> The water in here shifts and ebbs languidly , like gel . It 's all kinds of turquoise , and you do n't need a mask to see the carpets of coral and the fish scattering under the bow . Still , every fibre wants to be in that water . Tim and I share that compulsion . In two days we saw and filmed manta rays , sea snakes , vast clouds of fish , and corals and sponges of impossible hues and shapes , as well as dolphins , turtles and reef sharks . <p> It is a spectacle like the famed atolls of Australia 's east coast , but Scott Reef is inevitably categorised differently in our national psyche . That 's because it 's off WA , a cultural Bermuda Triangle where different norms and values seem to apply . We were determined not to allow Scott 's misfortune of being on the wrong side of the country , and its consequent " out of sight , out of mind " handicap , to render it vulnerable to fossil fuel exploitation . <p> Woodside leads a consortium -- its main shareholder is BP , no stranger to controversy after the Gulf of Mexico disaster -- which is seeking to drill 50 wells around Scott Reef and noisily suck out fossil fuels via all manner of industrial equipment , including a de facto port where enormous vessels would be permanently anchored to store and export petroleum products . Climate change-inducing gas would be piped south , past yet more reefs , for processing and export at the Burrup Hub , adding to the unconscionable acid pollution already damaging rock art at World Heritage-nominated Murujuga . <p> Not far from where we marvelled at Scott Reef is the site where the Montara oil and gas operation blew out 15 years ago -- despite the reassurances of industry -- spewing millions of litres of toxicity into the ocean . A spill of any kind around Scott Reef would be shameful for Australia . Such profound disrespect for a thing of beauty and wonder like a coral atoll would persist in our collective memory forever , like the indelible imprint of oil-cloaked , suffocating seabirds of the Exxon Valdez disaster . <p> Even if ministers can somehow convince themselves that it 's worth rolling the dice on the risk of an accident , they 'd still be endorsing industrialisation of this place and its impacts on threatened animals like sea turtles , pygmy blue whales and sea snakes . And while Scott Reef is still a kaleidoscope of colour and life , scientists know that successive climate-induced underwater heatwaves will push it to the brink . <p> If arguing about whether to drill around a coral reef for the very substance that 's already cooking it does n't capture the madness of the moment we 're in , what does ? <p> Postscript : The WA government has just approved Woodside 's North West Shelf extension for a half-century , which would process vast quantities of gas from the Browse Basin around Scott Reef , as part of the giant Burrup Hub processing plant . The final decision rests with Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek . The WA and federal minister 's decisions on the separate environmental assessment of the Scott Reef-Browse Basin component are also due . <p> Share <h> About the Author <p> Paul Gamblin is WA director of the Australian Marine Conservation Society , of which Tim Winton is a patron . " <p> As the federal election looms , Mr Dutton has used modelling commissioned by the LNP to reveal renewable energy would compose only 52 per cent of the national electricity market by 2050 under its " progressive change " agenda to replace Australia 's fleet of ageing coal-fired power plants . <p> This compares to Labor 's " step change " plan for energy from the sun and wind , backed by storage like pumped hydro and batteries , to contribute 82pc to the grid by 2030 and at least 90pc by 2050 to achieve net zero emissions by 2050 . <p> The Coalition 's vision for what critics have labelled a " smaller Australia " was outlined in the Frontier Economics analysis that assumes 30 to 40 per cent less power will be needed than the 410 terrawatt hours of electricity the Australian Energy Market Operator believes households and businesses will require each year by 2050 . <p> In simple terms , given it proposes only a 52pc renewable energy contribution into the grid by 2050 , the Coalition would add only a little more green energy to the grid in the next 26 years . <p> Instead , it would rely coal-fired power staying switched on until nuclear plants are built and Australian 's using that 40pc less power from the grid . <p> This would partly be achieved with just 63pc of motorists using electric vehicles , with 37pc still running gas guzzlers , and fewer than expected property owners installing rooftop solar by 2050 . <p> Mr Dutton also plans to unveil a new gas strategy before Australians go to the polls . 
@@119120177 <h> Pink zones threaten West Wyalong livelihoods <p> Logan and Bailey Lynch are continuing on a 50 year long family tradition of harvesting broombush in West Wyalong , however that is now at risk with the draft Native Vegetation Regulatory map . Picture supplied by Bailey Lynch <p> For three generations Bailey and Logan Lynch have been harvesting broombush at West Wyalong but now their business is at risk due to issues with the draft Native Vegetation Regulatory map . <h> Subscribe now for unlimited access to all our agricultural news across the nation <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of This Week 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> Bailey Lynch said he had been harvesting the vegetation since he was 17-years-old and together the brothers started their own business Lynch Brush and Panel Supplies about two years ago . <p> They were harvesting broombush on various landholders properties in the West Wyalong area and sell the brush wood panelling produced to buyers in Sydney , Byron Bay and Melbourne . <p> However , due to large areas of broombush in the West Wyalong area having been marked as Category 2 - sensitive regulated land or pink on the draft NVR map , harvesting is no longer permitted . <p> " About 80 per cent of our business is affected , " he said . <p> " There are a couple of areas that are n't affected where I 'm still allowed on but we do n't know for how long . " <p> He said they were now travelling up to 200 hundred kilometres away to find broombush able to be harvested , which was not a viable solution in the long term . <p> Mr Lynch said they had been cutting and bundling the broombush by hand before it was put through the panelling machine . <p> " When it comes to looking after the land we are always extremely conscious , as we do n't actually own it and are always doing right by the landholders , " he said . <p> " We pick and choose where to cut and how much we take from each patch . Because everything we do is done by hand we are able to be very particular in doing so . " <p> Mr Lynch said the patches of broombush were not being cut for anything except the panel production and the term clearing was a misconception . <p> " Once the brush has been cut it starts to regenerate within a few months depending on the season , " he said . <p> " After we are finished with that particular patch it is actually left for several years before even approaching that area again . <p> " With all that being said the broombush always comes back and usually better than ever . If anything we are helping the bushland continue to flourish by exiling much of the Mallee Strangle-vine which is known to smother Mallee and other plant species . " <p> Mr Lynch said the map had left them shocked and uncertain for the future . <p> Both brothers have young families and had spent $250,000 on a truck panel machine and along with the normal cost of living and house repayments he said financial stress and pressure was a struggle . <p> " It 's certainly taking a toll on our mental health and young families with no extra time or money to spare , " he said . <p> " If we can free these areas back up for us to get back to work and make money that would be much appreciated . " <p> Mr Lynch said broombush harvesting was in his blood . <p> " My late Grandfather and my Dad were also brush harvesters so I guess you could say it 's all I 've ever known , " he said . <p> " It started in 1974 in West Wyalong with my grandfather and my Dad started cutting at 14 . The Lynch name has been the longest serving name in brush . " <p> A Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water spokesperson said the department acknowledged the concerns and was committed to working through any mapping or compliance issues with landholders. 
@@119120414 <h> The Coalition 's nuclear proposal offers no outlook for lower household bills , and the political debate obscures the fact that the plan is undeliverable . By Mike Seccombe . <h> The Coalition 's coal-keeper plan <p> There are really only two possibilities . Either Peter Dutton and Angus Taylor do not understand the basics of the Coalition 's signature nuclear power policy or they are deliberately , repeatedly broadcasting a falsehood . <p> At December 13 's Brisbane press conference where the opposition leader and shadow treasurer released the long-awaited costings of the Coalition 's nuclear plan , contained in modelling by Frontier Economics , both men said it showed their policy would cut electricity bills by 44 per cent . <p> Dutton did it again on Tuesday at a press conference in Adelaide , called to promote the candidacy of Nicolle Flint , a member of his hard-right faction , for the seat of Boothby at the coming election . <p> " The work of Frontier says that over time electricity prices will be 44 per cent cheaper under our policy than Labor 's , " he said . <p> On Wednesday , Taylor repeated the claim . The opposition plan , he said , " will bring down electricity bills by 44 per cent . There 's no doubt about that . " <p> It 's not true . In fact , the Frontier report specifically says , on page 18 : " We do not , at this stage , present any results for the prices , as this will depend on how the cost of new capacity will be treated in the future . " <p> What the Frontier modelling actually concludes is something quite different : that the total cost of upgrading and running the national electricity market out to 2050 -- when we are committed to reaching net zero greenhouse emissions -- would be 44 per cent less under one scenario including nuclear power than under another not including nuclear . <p> That claim , too , is misleading , according to many economists and energy experts , because it compares " apples and oranges " -- that is , two dissimilar scenarios labelled " step change " and " progressive " . <p> The first scenario , step change , is premised on Australia electrifying its economy in a big way between now and 2050 , largely using renewable energy to power vehicles , homes , existing industries and energy-hungry new ones , such as data centres and AI services , in a robustly growing economy . The other is premised on a future in which that transition away from coal , gas and oil is slower and growth is significantly smaller . <p> " This is unequivocally about politics , not policy . The Coalition 's $331 billion nuclear fantasy is a coal- and gas-keeper energy transition plan for Australia , funded by taxpayers . " <p> According to the modelling produced pro bono for the Coalition by Danny Price , managing director of Frontier , the step change scenario without nuclear would cost $594 billion . The progressive scenario with nuclear would cost $331 billion , a difference of $263 billion , or 44 per cent . <p> But that does not equate to a similar reduction in prices for consumers . Not if the economy ends up being smaller , with less demand for electric power . <p> Simon Holmes ? Court , businessman , energy analyst and director of pro-renewables body The Superpower Institute , summarises the opposition 's case as " we 're going to pay $263 billion less for electricity , but it 's for a lot less electricity " . <p> " And meantime , we have to pay an extra $500 billion for fossil fuels . " <p> His calculation factors in the long lead times involved in building nuclear capacity . The Price model would see 13 gigawatts of nuclear commissioned across Queensland , New South Wales and Victoria by 2050 . The first unit would not come online until 2036 -- and even this is a highly optimistic forecast . According to the CSIRO , a more realistic timeline is 15 years , not 11 , to get the first one up and running . Other experts suggest even longer . <p> The Price model would see only a small amount of nuclear power before 2039 and the whole 23 gigawatts not operational until 2049 . <p> In the meantime , his report says , Australia would have to extend the life of its fleet of coal-fired power plants . <p> " Already , " says Nicki Hutley , economist , former banker and now a councillor to the Climate Council , " at any one time , about 25 per cent of coal is down because it is ageing and is either under planned or unplanned repairs . What does that do to power prices when you do n't have enough supply to meet demand ? " <p> In his report , Price suggested the problems with coal-fired plants could be ameliorated by introducing much more gas into the grid , but the cost of that , he wrote , " has not been modelled " . <p> Nor would the extra costs incurred by a delayed transition to renewables only be financial . More fossil fuels would be burnt , so more planet-warming gases would be emitted . <p> According to Price 's own modelling , the emissions intensity -- the amount of greenhouse gas produced per unit of power generated -- remains vastly higher under his plan than the government 's , all the way out to 2046 . <p> The fact that emissions under the Price -- Dutton nuclear plan eventually come down to the same level as the government 's renewables-heavy plan is beside the point , says Dylan McConnell , an energy systems analyst at UNSW Sydney . <p> " The pathway there is more important than the destination , in some respects , because it 's the cumulative emissions that matter , " he says . <p> By his calculations , as well as those of Hutley and the Climate Council , Steven Hamilton of the George Washington University , and the Tax and Transfer Policy Institute at the Australian National University , the extra cumulative emissions under the Coalition policy would be enormous . <p> The Price -- Coalition plan would produce about 2.5 times the emissions of the government 's preferred step change model -- 1.65 billion tonnes , compared with 0.6 billion , according to Hamilton 's analysis , which was published in The Australian Financial Review this week . <p> And that is in the electricity sector alone , Hamilton wrote . <p> Add in the costs outside the generation sector , arising from things such as greater consumption of petrol and diesel resulting from the slower take-up of electric vehicles under the Coalition plan , and the cumulative emissions rise even more . To a total of more than 1.7 billion tonnes , according to Holmes ? Court . <p> Scrapping that 2030 reduction target set by the current government would breach the Paris climate agreement and make Australia an international " pariah " , she says . <p> Hutley stresses that she has no objection to nuclear power , per se . <p> " It 's not ideology . It is purely and simply about the numbers . And I just ca n't make them add up . You ca n't just say we 're going to produce a grid with a whole lot less energy and that 'll cost us less . " <p> A large part of the problem in trying to make sense of the Price modelling , Hutley and others say , lies in the assumptions that underpin it . Some , like the capital cost per kilowatt of installed capacity , are generally seen as implausibly low . <p> Price factors in a cost of $10,000 a kilowatt , although the actual delivered costs of nuclear plants in comparable Western countries are about double that . <p> Others are simply mystifying , such as his assumed " capacity factors " for nuclear generation compared with wind and solar . Skipping the technical details , the essence of the issue is that nuclear runs more or less continuously , producing a constant amount of relatively expensive electricity . Renewables , by contrast , are intermittent , depending on the sun and wind , but produce cheap electricity . <p> The widespread concern among energy experts is that the introduction of nuclear into the power system would result in renewables , including rooftop solar , being switched off for extended periods , lest the grid be overwhelmed with power , and to assure the financial viability of nuclear generators . <p> According to analysis by the peak body for the renewables industry , the Smart Energy Council , " up to five million rooftop solar systems will be switched off , and the average power price bill will more than double " as a result . <p> In fairness it should be noted the council has a big vested interest , but the fact remains that Price 's published modelling appears to ignore the impact of nuclear on renewables . As Hamilton noted , in Price 's modelling " these capacity factors that is , the amount of time renewables are generating power do not change with the introduction of nuclear producing 38 per cent of generation nearly 24/7 . " <p> In response to the Hamilton critique , Price argued it was already the case that renewables were sometimes turned down or off because there is too much generation . He said this problem would increase as the share of renewables increased . <p> " This is because you have to build vast amounts of renewables to produce enough electricity to meet demand , and since you never know whether they will produce at the same time or at different times , inevitably you end up at times with too much electricity . " <p> He did not , however , address the cost issue . And he conceded that under his model , less renewables infrastructure would be built . <p> The broader point , however , is that this was not apparent in his published work . <p> Normal protocol in the modelling world is to provide detail of the data on which a model is built , says Professor Warwick McKibbin of the ANU Crawford Centre . <p> " You should be transparent . That 's just standard good practice . If you ca n't see that data that underpins the work , then how do you know what 's been assumed ? How do you assess the value of it ? " he says . <p> It does n't take an internationally renowned economic modeller to tell us that -- every primary-school maths teacher instructs their students to show their work . But when the Smart Energy Council contacted Price , seeking the data underpinning his assumptions , the reply was a single word : " No . " <p> An approach to the shadow minister for climate change and energy , Ted O'Brien , seeking the data got no response at all . <p> Experts interviewed by The Saturday Paper noted other worrying or peculiar aspects of the opposition 's policy , including the party of business 's vision of a nuclear industry wholly funded by government . <p> They say the reason is that the private sector would not risk investing . <p> But perhaps the biggest mystery , says Holmes ? Court , is why Dutton and co chose to bring on this fight . <p> Opinion polling shows nuclear is not a popular option with the public , in contrast with wind and particularly solar . More pertinently , it is a policy that almost certainly ca n't be implemented any time soon . <p> The Dutton Coalition would have to win both houses of federal parliament in order to overturn a ban on nuclear legislated under the Howard government in 1998 as part of a deal with the Greens . The odds of that happening are very long . <p> On top of that , Queensland , Victoria and NSW also have bans on nuclear power and show no inclination to reverse them , even though the Liberal National Party of Queensland now holds government . <p> " A little-known fact , " says Holmes ? Court , " is that Queensland made it a requirement that there be a plebiscite to un-ban nuclear . That 's a lovely little poison pill that they left in the legislation . " <p> That being the case , why pursue it ? <p> Because it is a means of exploiting voter concerns about the cost of living , even if it relies on the untrue promise of a 44 per cent reduction in electricity prices . <p> And because it avoids another round of the climate wars that have riven the conservative parties for decades . Those wars played a major part in the demise of several Coalition leaders , including Malcolm Turnbull , twice -- the second time as a consequence of the plotting of Peter Dutton . <p> What the nuclear policy actually does is kick the energy-policy can down the road . It promises to get to net zero by 2050 , but in the meantime to keep the electricity system running on fossil fuels for another decade or more . <p> Indeed , says Stephanie Bashir , of the energy consultancy Nexa Advisory , it is a mistake to consider it a serious policy at all . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " The Coalition 's coal-keeper plan " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take time , to doggedly hold to account politicians and the political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . @@119120415 <h> Thomas Mayo Young men and the far right 's influence on them <p> My first three children were born in the first years of my 20s . As a young father , the lessons , both good and bad , both intentionally taught to me and subliminally absorbed , shaped how I raised them and how I treated their mother . <p> Men are undoubtedly influenced by their father-figures . My father expected my mother to stay at home while he worked , and I expected the same of my partner . When our little son was upset , I told him not to cry like a girl , as my dad had told me . My misconception of what it was to be a boy and a man compelled me to tell my son how to dress , what sport he should play and how he should withhold his feelings and empathy , lest he be thought of as soft . I 'm saddened to think about how I treated him when he was reaching puberty : I stopped holding his hand in public , though he still wanted to hold mine . <p> Through the influences of my union sisters and brothers , who were on the frontline against inequality , and through a changed perspective as a single father in my late 20s , my one-dimensional views about masculinity and a mother 's and father 's role shifted . Society was shifting as well . <p> As a child , I remember it was common to hear misogynistic , derogatory and racist remarks about women , gay people and minorities . Such language is barely heard in earshot these days . Yes , the vitriol is rife on social media . Yes , these harmful acts are still too frequent , and I am a man who might seem intimidating to some who would otherwise be loose with their tongues . However , the movement towards respect for our differences has certainly made headway . <p> These gains towards decency and respect are under threat today . The bad actors in our midst -- the people who will intentionally harm others to achieve personal gain and power -- see progress towards genuine fairness and equality as a hindrance to their own selfish goals . <p> Men are undoubtedly influenced by their father-figures ... I 'm saddened to think about how I treated my son when he was reaching puberty : I stopped holding his hand in public , though he still wanted to hold mine . <p> The Coalition is rife with such bad actors . The Liberals and Nationals have become bereft of true centrists , lurching ever further to the far right under Opposition Leader Peter Dutton . Indigenous Australians , who overwhelmingly voted " Yes " in the referendum , can attest to their cruelty . Now Dutton disrespects the Aboriginal flag , saying that if he is prime minister , he will not stand to have it displayed behind him . <p> Such is the nature of right-wing political players . They claim to be conservatives , but their politics is radical and reactionary . Nothing they do is about helping Australians to live full and healthy lives . They attack Medicare , welfare , superannuation and workers ' and women 's rights at every possible opportunity . Conservative politics in recent decades has been about regression . The only thing it conserves is the widening gap between the wealthiest 1 per cent and the rest of us . <p> My concern of late has been the realisation that the far right is targeting boys and men in its campaign for power . I have observed how material on social media is exploiting men 's propensity to be protectors of their families , especially when they are led to believe there is an enemy at their door . Cue Dutton and a scary minority . <p> Throughout the year I have seen content that even my progressive algorithm did not keep out . I have seen subtle nudges towards ignorance and the ill-treatment of women in what my son teenage son watches as well . The memes and videos are designed for younger male consumers , in both how they are visually presented and how they cater for limited attention spans . They often tell stories about unfaithful , lazy or conniving women , pitched as if the scene were candid . The effect is the promotion of the right-wing complaint of male victimhood and the anti-woke campaign . <p> Racist content -- again , not always blatant -- also reaches my feeds . The massive volume of footage of people of colour drinking , fighting , committing crimes or being disrespectful is reinforcing stereotypes about us . This insidious content , like the content that degrades women , is sometimes acted out , yet the video appears to be spontaneous . <p> As a parent I worry what this type of content does to an adolescent 's mind . Where my generation was influenced by the adults we looked up to -- who threw around racist or sexist tropes , often unwittingly -- today we are all being fed such ignorant views through our phones . <p> As part of the global right-wing movement , the Coalition is aware of this material and its power . All Peter Dutton needs to do is make seemingly benign comments about scary Black people or man-hating women to trigger the fears , outrage and prejudices that have been planted in our minds online . <p> When anyone complains about the stereotypes and how hurtful they can be , they are labelled woke . Woke means aware . Online , however , the meaning has been hacked and susceptible minds now see " woke " to mean elitist , anti-free speech and excessively sensitive . They want us to believe that it is shameful to be aware of each other 's feelings and perspectives . <p> The anti-woke movement reminds me of how those older men in my life taught me that it was wrong to show empathy to others . At my recent book launch , Leigh Shears from Hunter Workers , formerly the Newcastle Trades Hall Council , shared a story about dispelling his prejudices . He said that in the 1970s , when he was a youth , he was taught to hate everyone equally . <p> This is what anti-woke is . Anti-woke is anti-empathy . Anti-empathy is a denial of humanity , a rejection of fairness ; it is selfish , and that is who Peter Dutton is . He may not want to stand before an Aboriginal flag . I do n't want him standing before an Australian flag . He does not represent our values . He is not interested in a fair go . <p> When I travel overseas , from the moment I land in a foreign country I miss home . This had never been a problem before . Perhaps I feel this way because I have seen so much of our great continent in recent years , from the green and turquoise waters of my tropical homes in the north , to the freezing , for a Darwin lad , deep blue waters in the south , from the waterside cliffs in the east to the low sandy country in the west , and all the ochre , green and gold in between . In many ways it was a privilege to see our country . I have met thousands of Australians I adore . <p> I love this country . Not just because this is where my ancestors have been for millennia , but also because it is where other ancestors have found safety and prosperity . They intermingled , worked hard and saw our nation progress from a colony to an inclusive multicultural gem in the southern hemisphere . Compared with when I am in other nations , it is here that I feel loved and secure . I want this feeling of security to be felt by all Australians . <p> My Christmas begins on the afternoon of Christmas Eve at my mum and dad 's place . This year , four of my five children will be home . My eldest son , the one whose hand I stopped holding , needs to stay in Broome for work . <p> The festivities begin in the afternoon with some cooking , drinks and a swim in the pool . Mum does the turkey . Dad might cook a semur , an Asian-influenced Islander favourite -- a chicken dish made with vermicelli , ginger , garlic , Chinese mushrooms , bamboo shoots and lots of soy sauce . I usually do a sambal -- ginger , garlic , onion and chilli , and either offal , squid or the fat from prawn heads , all chopped up small and cooked with pungent belacan ( shrimp paste ) . <p> Christmas Day is lunch at my place with my wife 's family , a tradition we started about 10 years ago . We squeeze tables and chairs into our tiny living room . With all the newborns , this seating arrangement may be impossible by next year . We have a European-style spread of lamb roasts and ham . Good food , good fun and a food coma in the afternoon will be the order of the day . <p> This year , I suggest we check in with our boys and men during the Christmas break . Men should note , this is not for the women in your family to do -- it is for the father-figures , the strong men who love these boys , to be a greater influence in their lives than the veiled and blatant bigots online and in politics . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Young men and the far right " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . It has announced more concrete changes to Indigenous affairs than it has in most other portfolios . <p> " I 'm absolutely baffled as to why a very senior politician in this country would focus on a group of people , in this case Aboriginal people and Torres Strait Islanders , who have come through and survived the most horrific things that happened to our people through colonisation -- and yet he wants to bring us down every opportunity , " says Jill Gallagher , chief executive of the Victorian Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation . <p> " If we 're split into different groupings or different tribes , we 're not going to be the unified country that I think we need to be , " he told 3AW in an interview that followed the flag announcement . <p> On the national flag , he was resolute . <p> " We 're a country united under one flag , " he told Peta Credlin , Tony Abbott 's former chief of staff and now a Sky News host . <p> " If we 're asking people to identify with different flags , no other country does that , and we are dividing our country unnecessarily . Now we should have respect for the Indigenous flag and the Torres Strait Islander flag , but they are not our national flags . <p> " I think the prime minister sends a very confusing message . " <p> Dutton also revisited his position on big business and what he called " corporate virtue signalling " . <p> " The prime minister 's not out there calling out Woolworths and not out there calling the pubs who do n't want to celebrate Australia Day , " Dutton said . <p> It is a strategy that attacks Anthony Albanese 's leadership and riffs on the success of Dutton 's opposition to the Voice referendum . <p> Pollsters say voters never raise First Nations flags as an issue of concern -- in focus groups all conversations are about cost of living , housing and health access -- but acknowledge that Dutton is trying to pick a " woke " fight with Labor . <p> Tacticians say the opposition leader 's plan is to get the Albanese government to talk about anything other than helping with cost-of-living relief , while " throwing red meat " to the right of the party 's base . <p> One Labor figure said Dutton is trying to " re-create the Voice " and a " Trumpian backlash against woke culture " . <p> Labor 's response has been measured and dismissive . <p> The minister for Indigenous Australians , Malarndirri McCarthy , was quick to post on social media that Dutton was " proving himself unfit to be prime minister " . <p> Minister for Education Jason Clare said it was a distraction from Dutton losing two senior colleagues to retirement and from opposition policies he does not want subjected to scrutiny . " <p> The opposition leader has confirmed recent reporting in Nine newspapers that he is taking regular advice and encouragement from Abbott and Credlin , 10 years after Abbott left the top job , but he 's downplayed the frequency and impact of the contact . <p> The MP questions how going hard on First Nations flags will help the Liberals hold on to a city seat such as Bradfield in northern Sydney , which is being vacated by senior moderate Paul Fletcher and is being seriously challenged by two-time independent teal candidate Nicolette Boele . <p> The Liberal says Dutton 's instinct comes from being a Queensland cop and from being in national security " strongman " portfolios . <p> " I do n't mean flags are n't important . I mean , which flags the prime minister stands in front of is certainly not an issue that I 've heard in my electorate . " <p> For Indigenous people , it is about being seen and knowing there are ongoing efforts being made towards reconciliation . <p> " We are one of the oldest living cultures on the planet and everything that happened to us was swept under the carpet . We were disempowered , " Jill Gallagher says . <p> " Whatever wealth we had , in the sense of wealth from a cultural perspective , was taken off us . Our language was forbidden , it was illegal . And we lived by a rule that you get told when to go to bed , when to sleep , when to eat and when to get up and whether you can leave a mission or not . <p> " Every aspect of our lives was controlled . Our culture was almost destroyed ... We were becoming invisible in our own country . We were invisible in our own country . We 're trying to be visible in our own country . Is that too much to ask for anyone ? " <p> Gallagher cites a similar push in New Zealand to reduce the presence and recognition of Maori culture . Under the Christopher Luxon conservative government , a series of policies that enshrine the special status of Maori people have been or are being unwound . This includes seeking to reinterpret the nation 's founding document , the Treaty of Waitangi . <p> " It seems they have views only about First Nations people -- and those views are divisive -- and they do n't have views on how they are going to fix the housing crisis , " Gallagher says . <p> " Where 's their policies on Australians having access to affordable , healthy food , and the list goes on ? Where 's his policies around that ? Why is n't he doing his job and actually holding the current government accountable ? Where 's the affordable housing ? " <p> Marcia Langton says the fixation on Indigenous people will achieve nothing other than division . <p> " Nobody 's mortgage is going to be reduced by these measures . Nobody 's cost of living is going to come down by these measures . It costs nothing to stand in front of an Aboriginal flag , " she tells The Saturday Paper . <p> " In fact , it gives the nation hope that there is an end to the vicious racism against Aboriginal people . It gives Aboriginal people hope and the six million Australians who voted ' Yes ' who want a cohesive society , who want rid of racism . <p> " Shifting the goalpost to say that you despise anti-Semitism does n't remove the burden of Australia 's own history . @@119120417 <h> Exclusive : ' Catastrophic errors ' seen in rushed NDIS reform <p> The largest reforms to the National Disability Insurance Scheme are moving so fast that promises made to people with disability are already " being broken " to secure billions of dollars ' worth of budget savings . The rush is to deliver a new needs assessment model that will dictate funding in NDIS plans for hundreds of thousands of participants . <p> Pressure from the federal government -- and especially the central agencies of Finance and Treasury -- has locked in a timeline for the next tranche of reforms that is " impossible to meet " without introducing " catastrophic errors " , disability advocates given confidential briefings tell The Saturday Paper . <p> New legislation was approved in August that gives the agency more powers to remove people from the NDIS , overhaul the planning process and explicitly prevent participants from spending NDIS money on banned items and services . However , much of the heavy lifting in these new laws will be done by subordinate legislative rules , instruments and tools that are still being designed or yet to be agreed between states , territories and the Commonwealth . <p> The race is now on to introduce these elements ahead of outgoing NDIS Minister Bill Shorten 's September 2025 deadline for the new planning framework to go live . The framework , which is being sold as introducing simplicity and flexibility for NDIS participants , will shave more than $60 billion from scheme growth over the next decade and reduce actual payments by $1.4 billion over the next four years . <p> To do this , the National Disability Insurance Agency must introduce a so-called " needs assessment " tool or tools that can be administered by an assessment workforce in a standard way across 700,000 people . This will assess needs -- not function -- so that a person who can not get out of bed unassisted , for example , will be assessed for how often they need support to get out of bed . It 's a subtle but important distinction , because this needs assessment will become the sole input into NDIS budgets for participants , converting assessment scores into funding amounts that the agency says will eliminate inconsistency in the planning workforce . <p> On Monday , Department of Social Services and NDIA officials briefed disability and carer representative organisations on updates to an assessment model that seemed , to those in the room , predetermined . They learnt the government will soon engage an external firm to report on options by February . <p> A presentation given to those briefed , marked " Confidential : do not share " and obtained by The Saturday Paper , sets out the new assessment process and its final stage : " The delegate inputs the information in the assessment report into the budget model , which determines all funding outcomes . " <p> A sector working group on assessments and budgeting , supposed to fulfil promises of " co-design " with the disability community , had only met twice before the third briefing was given on Monday . <p> " This is not something they can do individually for 700,000 people , " a source familiar with the briefing says . <p> " I 'm not going to get outraged ... just be honest and say , ' we ca n't co-design this model because of this highly confidential procurement process ' , plus , ' assessment tools and whatever ca n't be co-designed , because that would take 10 years for us to design our own and test it and validate it ' . <p> " Is it a mammoth task ? Absolutely . Will they get it right ? No , no , no , absolutely not . " <p> Others familiar with the discussions are less forgiving . <p> " The biggest concern right now , for me , is the timeframe that 's been imposed by the government . It 's completely unreasonable . We 're burning out good DSS and NDIA staff , and if they go , frankly , people are fucked . " <p> People with Disability Australia released a joint statement with three other representative organisations on Wednesday , stating they had been " caught off guard " by government announcements . They raised the spectre of Independent Assessments , the Coalition-era attempt at NDIS reform led by then minister Stuart Robert , which was killed off by a grassroots campaign skilfully leveraged by Bill Shorten . <p> " There could be some benefits to this model if the support needs assessments tools are co-designed with disability representative organisations , incorporate the whole-of-person support needs and are flexible , allowing participants to use their preferred providers , " PWDA president Trinity Ford said . <p> " However , we are seeing little evidence that timeframes will allow for this to be done well and need stronger assurances from government that this wo n't include concerning elements of independent assessments like automation and reduced choice and control . " <p> The briefing documents are almost apologetic about the timeframes , noting they are set by the government , states and territories . Parameters for consultation list agency " guardrails " , stating that " part of our transition considerations will also be how we test and validate the new planning framework approach ( tool and budget model ) as it is introduced " . <p> " The NDIS needs to identify a validated off-the-shelf assessment tool(s) that would be suitable to use as part of the new planning pathway . We are not going to build our own tool . Using an existing , validated tool means we can meet our project deadlines and be confident the tool meets our needs . " <p> Despite changes in rhetoric , some well-informed officials in the disability sector are unimpressed by the " commitment " to co-design from the senior leadership . <p> " The staff that we 're dealing with at the NDIA , they do want to co-design this with us , but the timeframe that they 've been given does n't allow it . It does n't even allow consultation , " the source said . <p> " The biggest concern right now , for me , is the timeframe that 's been imposed by the government . It 's completely unreasonable . We 're burning out good DSS and NDIA staff , and if they go , frankly , people are fucked . " <p> The government 's commitment to designing reforms with the disability community only relates to allowing them to " provide advice on key design features of the new assessment process relating to participant experience " . <p> This is careful wording , with a history . <p> In 2021 , when then Coalition minister Stuart Robert was trying to ram through wholesale changes to the NDIS -- authored in large part by McKinsey &amp; Company consultants and agents seconded to the NDIA -- one of the suggestions was to add a principle in the legislation that would give a nod to including people with disability in a " co-design capacity " . <p> Then general manager of national delivery Scott McNaughton queried whether this would hinder the agency . <p> " Does this need to be in the Act ? What will this mean in actual practice ? Legislating co-design could cause issues down the track with key policy and practice changes , " he wrote in a comment on the draft legislation . <p> McNaughton , now deputy chief executive of the NDIA in charge of service delivery -- including all elements of the participant pathway through the scheme -- lost the argument . That clause is in the new legislation , however , alongside others that effectively balance it out , including that all decisions made regarding the scheme must have regard to its financial sustainability . <p> Back in 2021 , McNaughton had also flagged a concern about the draft wording on the assessments process . <p> " Query : assume this provides enough cover ( i.e. is strong enough ) for us to determine who provides the assessment under 1 ( b ) , and they can not choose to undergo an assessment by a provider of their own choice , " he wrote . <p> Last year , while these NDIS reforms were reheated under the Labor government , McNaughton had his fees paid by the NDIA to attend a McKinsey &amp; Company executive leadership program . <p> While Stuart Robert 's reforms were torpedoed , Shorten 's efforts have left nothing to chance . Throughout 2023 , the social research and polling body RedBridge Group worked with the NDIA on a $250,000 engagement to come up with a narrative to sell proposed changes . <p> Documents released under freedom of information this week reveal the nature of the conversation the researchers had with key agency personnel , and briefings given to Shorten and the then ongoing NDIS Review co-chaired by Bruce Bonyhady and former senior public servant Lisa Paul . <p> That research advised the government to lead with genuine concerns about rorting in the system to help push through other major reforms . <p> " The disability community is definitely winnable , " a presentation prepared for the minister and reviewers said . <p> " General population wants to know we have values of fairness and equity at heart ... humanising and tackling rorts can tell that story better . " <p> About the same time , the researchers were worried about proposed changes that were less popular , including the shift to " evidence-based supports , changes to access for kids and SIL supported independent living " . <p> " I also think we need to see how those issues play out in the context of all the stuff that participants like , " a researcher wrote . <p> The NDIA had been keen to remove children from the scheme , as the growth in this cohort has far exceeded modelling for most of its lifetime . <p> " How can we effectively communicate the benefits of providing early childhood supports outside the NDIS , extending help to a broader audience , without appearing to abandon young people , " one official asked the researchers . <p> It appears information from the unfinished NDIS Review was also communicated to the RedBridge Group researchers , who asked for more detail about the decision to recommend support arrangements for people with disability living in group homes at a ratio of one support worker to three clients . <p> This was a huge budget concern for the agency , and RedBridge provided recommendations . " Qualified tolerance " could be found for these changes , they wrote . <p> Bill Shorten has followed that script almost to a tee . His legislation passed , became law and granted the NDIA new powers almost immediately . Alongside the recruitment of new " eligibility assessments " staff , the agency has already begun a mammoth campaign to remove people from the scheme by sending automated template letters demanding unspecified " evidence " and giving people just 28 days to respond . <p> Since The Saturday Paper first revealed that practice in November , the agency has sent letters via snail mail with no follow-up phone calls , demanding evidence that falls due on Christmas Day and Boxing Day . Those letters have gone to families of children with disabilities and to adults with permanent and profound impairments , alleging the scheme has information suggesting the person may no longer be eligible for support . <p> On Wednesday , Shorten announced $280 million in funding to develop a 1000-person needs assessment workforce to deliver the tools that are still being determined . <p> " This new workforce of dedicated support needs assessors will put participants ' needs at the centre and improve the NDIS experience for people with disability , " Shorten said in a statement . <p> " This will also free up allied health and medical professionals time to deliver supports -- putting downward pressure on waiting times across the country over the next five years for allied health professionals , who have a crucial role in the Scheme . " <p> A spokesperson for the NDIA said the new planning framework " will mean that participants will no longer need to source their own reports and provide evidence that they need a range of supports , which imposes costs and time burdens , receive more equitable budgets , reflecting their individual support needs and have increased flexibility with how they use their plan budgets " . <p> Come September , Shorten 's reforms will be all but completed and he will be long gone from parliament . He takes up his new role as University of Canberra vice-chancellor , under Chancellor Lisa Paul , his NDIS co-reviewer , in February . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Exclusive : ' Catastrophic errors ' seen in rushed NDIS reform " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120419 <h> Despite passing an ambitious suite of legislation in the final sitting week of parliament , Anthony Albanese is seen by focus groups as greedy , timid and too close to corporate Australia . By Jason Koutsoukis . <h> Exclusive : Albanese 's satisfaction ratings as bad as Morrison 's <p> Anthony Albanese visiting a Melbourne childcare centre on December 12 . <p> Focus group research by RedBridge indicates that voter perceptions of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese are as bad as they were for his predecessor Scott Morrison , strengthening the growing belief that Liberal leader Peter Dutton is the frontrunner to form government after the next election . <p> The RedBridge qualitative research aligns with recent private polling commissioned by the Liberal -- National Coalition , which internal party sources say dispels the narrative that Peter Dutton is unelectable . <p> " They 're probably at the worst position electorally now than they 've ever been since the election in May 2022 . There is a perception out there in parts of the electorate that Albanese 's government has not been completely focused on their needs , right or wrong , " says RedBridge Group director of strategy and analytics Kos Samaras , who has overseen more than 450 political focus groups this calendar year . " His satisfaction ratings are on a par with Morrison now . " <p> The polling caps a bruising year for the prime minister , with voters penalising his government for not doing enough to ease the cost-of-living crisis and turning their ire on him personally . <p> Criticism sharpened around his purchase of a $4.3 million home on the New South Wales Central Coast . According to focus groups , voters were also unhappy at his cosiness with corporate leaders such as former Qantas chief executive Alan Joyce and his perceived fondness for " freebies " . Among progressive voters there was deepening disappointment at his apparent timidity and lack of courage . <p> " He has spent the greater part of 2024 explaining to Australians why he has made some personal choices like buying a mansion , taking flight upgrades , but he seems to have not really worked that hard on making sure that whatever perception Australians have of him , that it 's of a positive nature , " Samaras says . <p> While the government succeeded in getting the bulk of its legislative agenda through parliament in the final sitting week of the year , including more than 30 pieces of legislation on the last day , Samaras believes that voters remain dissatisfied because whatever the government has achieved has not been enough to address what they see as the institutionalised and ingrained inequalities they face . <p> Paul Strangio , emeritus professor of politics at Monash University , makes a similar point . <p> " The deluge of legislation in the final week of the parliamentary year did nothing to fundamentally alter the picture that in 2024 -- following the failed endeavour of 2023 to land a totemic change through the Indigenous Voice referendum -- Albanese and his team fell back to a practice of eking out well-intentioned but modest measures , " Strangio says . <p> The author of a September essay for Inside Story that highlighted the entrenched public perception of Albanese as well-intentioned but insipid , weak and more a hostage to events than a shaper of them , Strangio argues that three months later his assessment of Albanese 's performance remains largely unchanged . <p> " Now in sight of the 2025 election , it means that the government will end its term with no signature landmark reform , " Strangio says . " The impression is of a government engaged in a maintenance project rather than embarked on an ardour-filled mission -- an issue bedevilling social democratic parties worldwide . " <p> Nor has the prime minister 's performance in the final months of the year suggested he is getting any better at creating a narrative that connects the government 's current actions with where Labor is intent on taking the nation . <p> " Throughout it all , the prime minister stubbornly refused to distance himself from Joyce , doubling down instead of cutting ties . That was a misstep , I think , and it marked a turning point for Dutton . " <p> " Growth in office has been a hallmark of many of Australia 's best-performed prime ministers , but Albanese is yet to demonstrate that capacity , " Strangio says . <p> " He was a keen observer of Howard 's prime ministership , but perhaps the lesson he ought to have drawn from watching from the opposition benches is that when Howard was in trouble during his first term , he drew upon his deep-seated convictions to strike out on a bold direction -- taxation reform -- to invigorate his government . " <p> Whether or not Albanese has a commensurate reservoir of convictions is a question that lingers uncomfortably , according to Strangio , after nearly a full term of his prime ministership . <p> What is even more disturbing and demoralising for the government is feedback from focus groups and sliding poll numbers that show voters struggling to nominate any measures the government has implemented . <p> " Three things occur : one , the lack of salience of the government 's nips-and-tucks approach , especially in an environment in which there is electoral impatience with the status quo ; two , Albanese 's deficiencies as a ' communicator-in-chief ' ; and three , the confounding problem of reaching voters in a fragmented and polarised media landscape , " Strangio says . <p> " In sum , it 's fundamentally been more of the same from the prime minister and his government this year , despite the evidence that the formula is leaving the government in a political position of little better than muddling through . " <p> Liberal Party insiders believe that momentum started to shift to Peter Dutton in September last year , halfway through the current three-year parliamentary term and about a month out from the October 14 vote on the Voice . <p> " As the ' Yes ' campaign was hitting rock bottom , one of its few big allies was corporate Australia , led by none other than Alan Joyce , not just the nation 's most unpopular CEO but arguably its most disliked public figure , full stop , who was at the time embroiled in a litany of controversies , " says one Liberal adviser . <p> " Yet , instead of distancing himself from this liability , or even taking a swing at him , Albanese doubled-down on a relationship that amplified the belief that he was not interested in the issues that mattered to ordinary Australians struggling to pay the mortgage . " <p> When Albanese appeared with Joyce on August 14 last year for the unveiling of three Qantas aircraft painted with the " Yes23 " logo in support of the Indigenous Voice to Parliament , and praised Qantas as representing " the spirit of Australia " , Coalition insiders thought it was the beginning of something . <p> At the time Albanese was facing criticism over the government 's decision to block Qatar Airways from launching 28 new flights a week between Qatar and Australia , as well as reports that Joyce had granted a Qantas Chairman 's Lounge membership to Albanese 's son . <p> " Over the next four weeks , Albanese and his ministers found themselves on the defensive , unable -- or unwilling -- to take on Qantas amid mounting controversies , " the Liberal adviser says . <p> " These included the Qatar Airways decision , Alan Joyce 's exorbitant pay , an ACCC lawsuit against the airline , and the High Court 's damning ruling that Qantas had illegally sacked nearly 2000 baggage handlers who were all their own people , union members . <p> " Adding to the backlash was an Aviation Green Paper widely dismissed as a token effort with no real intent to improve competition in the sector . Throughout it all , the prime minister stubbornly refused to distance himself from Joyce , doubling-down instead of cutting ties . " <p> The latest Freshwater Strategy Poll , commissioned by The Australian Financial Review and published on Monday , showed the Coalition leading Labor on a two-party preferred basis by 51 per cent to 49 per cent . The poll also found the majority of voters now expect Peter Dutton to form government after the election . <p> Liberal Party operatives are heartened by this and other poll averages , and believe Dutton stands a realistic chance of winning more lower house seats than Labor -- although still likely to be looking at minority government . <p> " This notion that Dutton is unpopular is simply not true , and that 's being reflected in the public polling that 's out there , as well as the private polling , " says one Liberal operative familiar with the Coalition 's internal research . They 're not anti-renewables , per se , but they do n't necessarily trust what they 're hearing about the renewable solutions . <p> " Cost of living is still the No. ? 1 issue , like , two to one over the next issue , which is housing , and that is largely about affordability and rising rents , and the third issue is management of the economy . " <p> So can Dutton actually win ? <p> " There is a growing narrative , emanating from right-of-centre commentators , of progressives repeating the mistake of history by construing Dutton as unelectable and by underestimating the electoral appeal of his muscular , populist-hued conservatism . Electoral mathematics dictates this as much as anything else . The path to government for the Coalition is very steep in the absence of the Liberals reclaiming the teal seats , and Dutton 's political and electoral strategy has been undeniably focused on outer-suburban and regional-rural areas . <p> " He is embarked on an electoral realignment , albeit one that has been running since Howard 's era . I continue to also believe that women and young voters loom as substantial hurdles to his prime ministerial ambitions . " <p> A more interesting question , Strangio argues , is what kind of government will Dutton have set himself up for , if he does manage to win ? <p> " How would the Coalition 's paucity of credible policy development , the populist technique of crude reductionism -- simple answers to complex problems , e.g. the nuclear energy fig leaf -- and Dutton 's divide-and-conquer strongman leadership style translate into office ? I doubt it would be a basis for sustainable or productive government and so the cycle of instability and discontent would continue . " <p> Samaras , for his part , believes that while it will be hard for Albanese to turn perceptions around between now and the election , which must be held by the end of May , it 's far too early to make a prediction on who will end up being able to form a government . <p> " The possibility of a change of government is present in our research right now ... It is n't huge , but it 's present , " says Samaras . " Will that presence grow ? Maybe . We 'll just have to wait and see . We just do n't know yet .
