By Peter Martin . <h> Jim Chalmers ' missing surplus marks grim tidings <p> If this week 's Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook ( MYEFO ) turns out to be Treasurer Jim Chalmers ' last budget statement before the election , it 'll be one of the grimmest sets of pre-election forecasts on record , and certainly since the mini-budget on the eve of the early 1990s recession . <p> Chalmers ' December update shows the outlooks for economic growth , wages and consumer spending have all deteriorated since May . <p> The update has the economy growing 1.75 per cent this financial year instead of 2 per cent , wages growing by 3 per cent instead of 3.25 per cent , and household spending growing just 1 per cent in real terms instead of 2 per cent , which , given the rate of population growth , will see buying per person shrink . <p> It 's an environment that , even if there was n't an election due within months , would make it wise for the government to offer extra support . The treasurer 's problem is that this time the bounty usually built up for extra spending in December is n't there . <p> This year , these sources handed it nothing , largely because the price of iron ore fell . Combined , they weakened the four-year position by $4.2 billion . <p> Moreover , the extra spending confirmed by Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher on Wednesday will cost $17.5 billion . Gallagher said much of the extra spending was " unavoidable " . The Coalition had failed to properly fund the Veterans ' Affairs teams responsible for processing claims . Labor put on more staff to clear the backlog and had to pour in an extra $6.5 billion in the May budget and an extra $1.8 billion in MYEFO . <p> Most of the other measures were post-budget decisions already announced , including paying childcare centres $3.6 billion to boost carers ' wages by 15 per cent as a downpayment on a work value case before the Fair Work Commission . <p> " It 's an environment that , even if there was n't an election due within months , would make it wise for the government to offer extra support . The treasurer 's problem is that this time the bounty usually built up for extra spending in December is n't there . " <p> Some are " off-budget " , not appearing in the usually quoted measures of government spending , including $19.9 billion to wipe 20 per cent off student loan debts and an extra $19.3 billion in loans by the Clean Energy Finance Corporation . <p> Others are yet to be revealed . MYEFO allocated $5.5 billion for spending decisions " taken but not yet announced and not for publication " , a sum that includes money set aside for measures to be unveiled before the election , as well as commercial-in-confidence and national security contracts . <p> Chalmers said the allocation was relatively small , " particularly in the lead-up to an election " , but he made it clear he was prepared to spend more than that allocation as the election approached . <p> The electricity bill rebates announced in the May budget finish in June . The Treasury believes they have pushed down the consumer price index by half a percentage point . Keeping them for another year would extend that downward pressure on inflation ( and perhaps give the Reserve Bank greater confidence to cut interest rates ) , at the cost of another $3.5 billion . <p> Chalmers said he would consider doing more if he could " afford to do more and there is a case to do more " . <p> As it is , MYEFO envisages an end to two years of budget surpluses with a deficit of $26.9 billion this financial year ( 1 per cent of GDP ) , jumping to $46.9 billion ( 1.6 per cent ) next year . That gap is expected to slowly narrow over the next decade , on the delicate assumption that spending grows more slowly than income . <p> Shadow treasurer Angus Taylor said the projections showed " red ink as far as the eye can see " . <p> Asked to specify the spending he objected to , he said it was too soon , but spoke about spending on bureaucrats , on housing programs that did n't produce new houses . He also mentioned spending on powerlines that would n't be needed with nuclear power , in a week in which the Coalition 's costings on its nuclear plan have caused much controversy . <p> The parliamentary calendar has the budget pencilled in for March 25 , two months earlier than usual to allow an election to be held by the deadline of May 17 . But if the prime minister picks a date in April and calls the election in March , there wo n't be a budget before the 2025 election , making this week 's statement the last before Australians vote . <p> Unveiling the numbers , Chalmers indicated both nervousness about the state of the economy and sensitivity to claims he is spending too much . <p> " We have always said we are trying to manage a soft landing on a bumpy runway , " he said , noting that Australia had " escaped negative economic growth to date " . <p> He buttressed his credentials on spending by pointing to earlier years when he banked rather than spent revenue upgrades . He also , somewhat irrelevantly , compared this economising with the Coalition 's big-spending years during the pandemic <p> Slashing spending right now , he said , would be " diabolical for an economy that is barely growing " . <p> Part of Chalmers ' strategy is to use small amounts of government spending to underpin larger amounts of private spending . <p> Among the measures are $529 million in grants to help private operators set up childcare centres in underserved locations and $336 million in a Future Made in Australia program co-funded with the German government that will connect Australian hydrogen producers with overseas customers . <p> What Chalmers really needs is for the Reserve Bank to cut interest rates after the next set of quarterly inflation numbers due at the end of January . While economists at the Big Four banks have scaled back their expectations for a cut at the RBA 's first meeting in February , markets anticipate a move in April . <p> Longer term , Chalmers needs more money , and on Tuesday he published a road map showing where to find it . <p> Each year , the government is required to produce a tax expenditures and insights statement , setting out the cost to the budget of each large tax break and tax deduction . This one identified 40 that cost more than $1 billion a year . Combined , they amount to $250 billion a year . <p> Some are politically hard to touch , including the capital gains tax exemption for the family home . Others involve superannuation . The concessional taxation of employers ' contributions costs $29 billion a year . <p> At the moment super contributions are taxed at 15 per cent regardless of tax bracket . This means high earners get big discounts while low earners get scarcely any . <p> The government has been pushing for legislation on the separate concessional tax treatment of super earnings , which the statement costs at another $22.2 billion a year . At the moment earnings are taxed at 15 per cent for most Australians and zero for super accounts paying out in retirement . In February last year , the government proposed a 30 per cent rate on earnings on balances above $3 million , and Chalmers committed again this week to moving this bill . <p> Eslake also suggests removing the complete exemption from tax for the earnings of funds paying pensions to retirees . He says the tax rate of zero on what are often very large earnings accumulating in the accounts of well-off retirees is " excessively generous " . <p> On Tuesday , Chalmers stressed that the tax expenditures and insights statement was an " important piece of analysis " rather than a " statement of policy intent " , but it is an analysis he has helped shape . <p> Rental deductions -- for the expenses associated with maintaining and financing rental properties -- were n't in the statement until Chalmers became treasurer . <p> The statement says 2.4 million landlords use rental deductions to cut tax by $16.9 billion a year . About $2.2 billion goes to landlords who negatively gear , claiming more in deductions than they make in rent . <p> Outlawing negative gearing , except perhaps for newly built homes as Labor proposed in the 2016 and 2019 elections , would save the best part of $2 billion a year . Winding back the much larger capital gains tax concession -- as Labor also promised to do in 2016 and 2019 -- could save half of the $22.7 billion the statement says the concession costs . The statement makes the point that almost all of that sum ( 82 per cent ) goes to the top 10 per cent of earners . <p> In October , Chalmers ruled out taking changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax to the election after it became public that he had asked his department for advice about how such changes could work . <p> They are off the agenda -- for now -- but after the election , should Labor win , the weakening state of the government 's finances and the ever-growing need for spending on priorities including the energy transition and an ageing society may make these solutions more palatable . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Grim tidings " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take time , to doggedly hold to account politicians and the political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . In a country with a concentration of media ownership unlike anything else in the world , it is vitally important . Your subscription helps make it possible . 
@@119120425 <h> The year in review <p> I can say precisely when the last measure of my respect for the prime minister evaporated . It was October 3 , the day Anthony Albanese asked each of us to look inside a bag of salt-and-vinegar chips and contemplate the emptiness therein . " Ever found more air than chips in your chip packet ? " he asked on social media . " More air , less product , same price . It 's called shrinkflation , and it 's ripping Australians off . " <p> Here , just two years into his prime ministership , the great mountaintop he 'd dreamt about for most his life , was an appeal of such exquisite triviality that I was overcome by the fumes of his exhausted imagination . That said , shrinkflation is real : symbolically , the size of the prime ministerial office remains the same , but its occupants keep getting smaller . <p> Contemptuous of his predecessor , Albanese nonetheless shares much with Scott Morrison . Each man is a career politician and the product of decades of backroom whispering . Both men refined their political manoeuvring much more than their imagination , intellect or charm and , having found the summit , their vacancy was quickly revealed . Governance , it turns out , requires very different skills from the ones needed to get there in the first place . <p> This month , Albanese groused to senior colleagues that the Murdoch press was out to get him and the conversation was duly shared with the media . If there were ever two signs a Labor government was slouching towards defeat , it 's the bitter blaming of the old mogul and a leaky cabinet . <p> This year , Albanese was aggrieved that he might be asked questions about enjoying privileges from the airline he once regulated . He banned social media for kids while capping the number of international students to our universities . He tried to introduce laws that would authorise one individual to determine what might be " disinformation " . He picked a fight with Elon Musk , then retreated , never able to explain why footage of the stabbing of a Sydney priest should be barred from X but footage , say , of the planes hiting the Twin Towers might remain . He outlawed vapes , while cigarettes can still be bought at any servo -- albeit at such extravagant prices that a violent black market for tobacco flourishes . <p> Albanese 's achievements were often defined by the restriction of things . Even this , he does n't do well . The legislation that bans those under 16 from accessing certain apps is silent on how the restrictions might actually be enforced -- that responsibility has been pushed to the companies . <p> Elsewhere , long-promised restrictions to what have become notoriously ubiquitous sports gambling ads were slowed by " vested interests " , as independent MP Andrew Wilkie described it , as the government announced it would not introduce a bill until next year . <p> If vested interests had stymied gambling ad reform , they at least did n't seem to have had the same effect on industrial relations . The Albanese government passed legislation this year making it easier for casual employees to claim permanent status , while its " right to disconnect " provision outlawed -- within reason -- employers contacting workers outside established hours . <p> Long overdue , the government also substantially reformed the Reserve Bank of Australia 's structure . From March , the RBA will have two boards : one responsible for monetary policy , and the other for the bank 's governance . An independent review reported last year that this reform was necessary to correct for an impassive board too reluctant to scrutinise the governor 's decisions ( a contentious finding that was naturally rejected by then governor Philip Lowe ) . <p> The RBA board has typically been dominated by corporate executives -- that is , non-economists -- but under the new composition , the monetary policy board will be made of subject experts , something borne out by the two appointments announced by the treasurer this month , of Ren ? e Fry-McKibbin and Marnie Baker . The review 's recommendation , however , for the removal of the treasurer 's veto power over RBA decisions was dismissed after widespread opposition from former RBA governors and academics . <p> As I write , further proof the labour market remains piping hot has been released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics . The unemployment rate declined to 3.9 per cent in November , close to record lows , while government expenditure remains historically high , as underlying inflation remains stubbornly above the RBA 's comfort level and economic growth is anaemic . Combined , this suggests an economy operating well beyond its capacity . <p> Inflation has not been solved . While both core and headline inflation has declined , only the latter has fallen within the RBA 's target band . And so , in September , Jim Chalmers celebrated the decline of headline inflation . " Monthly inflation was 2.7 per cent in the year to August 2024 , down from 3.5 per cent in July 2024 , " he said . " It 's now less than half the 6.1 per cent we inherited and less than a third of its peak . " <p> This was highly selective , and while partisans cheered , and the public may have anticipated rates relief , Reserve Bank officials ground their teeth . " Headline inflation is expected to fall further temporarily , as a result of federal and state cost-of-living relief , " the RBA said in September . " However , our current forecasts do not see inflation returning sustainably to target until 2026 . " <p> It 's true that Albanese inherited high inflation , a consequence of war-crimped supply chains and what turned out to be the overly generous floats of the Morrison government during lockdowns -- a generosity that seemed justified at the time , and which enjoyed broad support , including Labor 's . <p> But nearly three years have passed since this awkward inheritance . " My reading , when I speak privately to the treasurer and when I hear him speak on television and radio , " the RBA governor , Michele Bullock , said last month , " is that he 's fully aware of the inflationary implications of his own policies . " <p> " Every time we accelerated , whale juice would pour into the windows of the car ... We all had plastic bags over our heads with mouth holes cut out , and people on the highway were giving us the finger , but that was just normal day-to-day stuff for us . " <p> In 2024 , it seemed many journalists had learnt nothing from 2016 . That the president of the United States was seriously mentally impaired was obvious to his own staff , of course , but also to many Washington journalists -- and also suspected by a large percentage of the American public , who had consistently expressed as much in polls for at least a year . <p> Yet few " liberal " journalists this year -- or last -- took seriously his cognitive decline , despite explicit evidence . When the US Justice Department released transcripts of its interviews with Joe Biden , who had been questioned for his improper removal of classified documents from the White House , they revealed the president 's alarming confusion . Biden could not recall the year he became vice-president nor the year his son died . " And his memory appeared hazy when describing the Afghanistan debate that was once so important to him . " Biden 's brain was so clouded that those writing the report suggested any criminal trial would likely feature a defence that Biden simply could n't remember anything . <p> How did certain journalists respond to what seemed like an extraordinary revelation of the president 's unfitness ? Here 's Emily Bazelon of The New York Times : " This has all the hallmarks of over-covered problems . " <p> Her podcast partner , John Dickerson , who anchors CBS News , offered this : " The age obsession is a part of the obsession with the performative aspects of the presidency . " <p> The " performative aspects " that Americans were " obsessed with " were thinking and talking , but for a long time Democrats and a sympathetic press chastised the public for their " ageism " or superficiality . <p> Then came the televised debate between Biden and Donald Trump . Within seconds the president resembled the melting face at the end of Raiders of the Lost Ark , his eyes widened by fear . Here was explicit proof that the president was unwell , and the long-held suspicions of Americans could no longer be denied , ignored or sneered at . <p> Regarding the lack of reporting on Biden 's decline , former executive editor of The New York Times Jill Abramson said : " If enough reporters had pushed , the story was reportable . I worry that too many journalists did n't try to get the story because they did not want to be accused of helping elect Donald Trump . " <p> I would go further : the failure to do so was not only ineffectual but also civically destructive . It hardened the public 's distrust of journalists -- the same ones , incidentally , who are alarmed by plagues of disinformation . <p> The basic concerns of Americans , expressed consistently in years of polling , were rarely acknowledged by Democrats . Trump 's return , while seeming inevitable to me some 18 months ago , surprised too many who would write about such things . <p> Back home , we kept speaking in circles about the " housing affordability crisis " . This month the federal housing minister , Clare O'Neil , said on triple j , " We 're not trying to bring down house prices ... we want to see sustainable price growth . " <p> That was revealing , though , to be fair , that no politician will effusively support falling house prices . If we genuinely want to improve affordability , we need to build many more homes , remove local restrictions to doing so , and accept the screams of those objecting to improved density and the idea their assets might depreciate in value . <p> You have to choose . O'Neil , on behalf of the government , seemed to choose the Boomer asset class . Other generations are being alienated , and it will reverberate soon enough . <p> Of Middlemarch , Virginia Woolf wrote that it was the rare novel written for grown-ups , and with Perfect Days , released in Australian cinemas this year , Wim Wenders made a film for those whose attention spans could accept it . Radically slow , very little happens -- except for life itself . <p> Perfect Days follows Hirayama , a cleaner of Tokyo 's public toilets , on his daily routine . Few notice him , but he notices much : the outline of trees against the sky , the dappled light they help cast on bathroom walls . He reads avidly , nurtures saplings , and commits fastidiously to the cleaning of toilet bowls . He loves music and pauses each morning in his van to select the cassette tape he 'll play while driving to his first job . We 'll hear Otis Redding , Nina Simone and Lou Reed , the man whose song gives the film its title . <p> Hirayama speaks little but is warmly attuned to those around him . His habit of taking photos of things that please him -- most often the large maple tree before which he takes his lunch each day -- substitutes for human intimacy . Later he opens a cupboard filled with boxes , each stuffed with photos of the same tree and labelled by month . This obsessive archiving is not the work of a man blissfully wedded to the present . <p> Admiring reviews have celebrated Hirayama as a paragon of gracious contentment and decency , and it 's true he 's a beautifully sympathetic character , but his careful noticing of the present in this case is also a way of ignoring his past and his equanimity has come with great sacrifice . He is estranged from his family -- so severely that he can not bring himself to visit his dying father . <p> The film subtly suggests Hirayama 's past injuries and his decision to move beyond them . But he achieves this principally with avoidance , rather than transcendence . Most critics missed this melancholy quality . The final , remarkable scene shows a man quietly oscillating between contentment and pain . <p> The past clings to Hirayama , as it did with Shalom Nagar , who died last month . One of Adolf Eichmann 's prison guards , Nagar also became his reluctant hangman after being chosen by lottery to pull the trapdoor 's lever . <p> It was the midnight of May 31 , 1962 , when the logistics chief of the Final Solution stood upon the gallows . Eichmann had just finished his requested cigarette and cup of wine and Nagar was standing so close to him that he could smell both on his breath . <p> Eichmann 's hands and feet were tied , and the noose placed around his neck . " It was just me and Eichmann , " Nagar remembered decades later . " I was standing a few feet from him , and looked him straight in the eye . He refused to have his face covered , and did n't resist when he was told to stand on the floor that would open under him . Then I pulled the lever and he fell , dangling by the rope . " <p> Nagar objected -- there were colleagues , he argued , who wanted to pull the lever -- but he was stuck with his role . This included unfastening the bloodied corpse and transporting it to the oven . He had nightmares and panic attacks for years afterwards . <p> He remained a guard at the prison for many years and avoided Eichmann 's old cell . He became embarrassed by his fear of " a dead man " and one night walked past it alone . Seeing his own reflection in the cell 's glass door , he panicked . " I thought his ghost was coming to get me , and I fell down the stairs . " <p> In December , the South Korean president , frustrated by his party 's parliamentary minority , found a novel way to resolve democratic obstruction : by declaring martial law . At 10.30pm on December 3 , the clownish Yoon Suk Yeol appeared on television to announce the country 's grave but unspecified infiltration by North Korean agents , and the " paralysis " of parliament , as justification for suddenly outlawing political activity and assuming control of all media . <p> The declaration of martial law in South Korea is governed by strict constitutional thresholds , few of which were met , and within hours parliamentarians had nullified the declaration through an emergency vote -- despite the military blocking the entrance of parliamentarians to the National Assembly . <p> Yoon consulted little before his decision , and did n't warn the country 's " great friend " , the US , who have 30,000 troops stationed there . The declaration was swiftly responded to by both politicians and a public angered by the sudden revival of an authoritarian past . <p> Yoon has since been impeached , barred from leaving the country and will likely face prosecution for high treason . At the time of the declaration , US president-elect Donald Trump remarked , " The world is going a little crazy right now . " <p> In Syria , the Bashar al-Assad regime collapsed the way Hemingway once described going broke : slowly , then all at once . Rebels seized Damascus , liberated prisons and torture cells , and found the state-controlled amphetamine factories . Before they did , the Assad family flew to Russia to hide , as Russian troops , once critical to upholding his regime , withdrew from the country . <p> Bashar and his father , Hafez al-Assad , had held the presidency since 1971 . There is now a power vacuum with no coherent coalition among the rebels , and recent history -- specifically that of Iraq and Libya -- suggests a violent jostling for primacy , including among jihadists , as well as the assumption of vast and untended arsenals . The prospect of former Al Qaeda and ISIS forces acquiring chemical weapons and machinery has compelled Israel to bomb various sites since the collapse of the regime . <p> A little further south , Israel and Lebanon signed a ceasefire in November after months of missile exchanges , Israeli ground incursions and Mossad 's sophisticated targeting of Hezbollah 's leadership . The ceasefire , though fitfully honoured , helped further isolate Hamas , which , through more than a year of uncompromising Israeli air strikes , has lost several leaders and now governs a Gaza Strip comprising blood and rubble . Since the October 7 , 2023 , attack on Israel , in which Hamas militants killed 1200 Israelis and took about 250 hostages , local authorities say Israel 's bombardment has killed more than 45,000 Palestinians in Gaza . <p> Egypt , long contemptuous of Hamas , have recently mediated talks between the group and its once-rivals Fatah , a major part of the Palestinian Liberation Organization , about a new alliance after the war . Israel will emphatically reject any coalition involving Hamas , and Trump will likely be influential when he returns to office . <p> It was not a good year for Iran , whose threats against Israel proved largely theatrical , and whose " axis of resistance " suffered the loss of the leaders of Hamas , Hezbollah and now Syria . More than one geostrategist wondered publicly if this new insecurity would spur Iran to acquire nukes . <p> In Melbourne , the Adass Israel Synagogue was firebombed in December while worshippers prayed inside . Later , in a Jewish neighbourhood in Sydney , a car was torched and anti-Israeli graffiti sprayed on homes . <p> In the days after the synagogue 's torching , a senior staffer for the federal Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi mused publicly that the attack could have been committed by Jews themselves . " It could very well be a white supremacist or someone enraged by the genocide or a Zionist false-flag , " he wrote . " They 've done this before . " <p> Just what , exactly , had been " done before " was not explained . <p> The Notre-Dame cathedral reopened in Paris , five years after it was substantially damaged by fire , and the Crown of Thorns relic , salvaged by firefighters in 2019 , was returned there . In October , NASA launched its Europa Clipper spacecraft on its mission to the moon of Jupiter that gives it its name . It 's scheduled to enter Europa 's orbit in April 2030 , after a three-billion-kilometre journey , when it will perform close scans of the moon 's surface and analyse the oceans beneath its icy crust . <p> In Vancouver , Taylor Swift finished her almost two-year , 149-show Eras tour -- earning $2 billion in gate receipts from 10 million attendees in five continents and inspiring a shadow industry of torturously embittered think pieces . <p> Neil Young 's music returned to Spotify after a two-year boycott to protest against Joe Rogan 's podcast , while a federal agency confirmed it investigated Trump 's nominee for health secretary , Robert F. Kennedy Jr , after a 2012 interview with his daughter resurfaced in which she described her father once decapitating a beached whale with a chainsaw and then securing the head to the roof of the family 's car . @@119120427 <h> Great power rivalry <p> Syria : Ahmed al-Sharaa , the leader of the Islamist group in Syria that oversaw the ousting of Bashar al-Assad , has unveiled plans to disband his and other rebel groups and form a national army under the control of the defence ministry . <p> As the United Nations warned that the war " has not ended yet " , Sharaa , who heads Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham ( HTS ) , said Syria must " remain united " and find a place for all sects . He said forced conscription will end and only the army will be allowed to carry weapons . <p> " We have to adopt a state mentality , not an opposition mentality , " he said during a meeting with leaders from the country 's Druze minority . <p> Sharaa has been seeking to gain international legitimacy for HTS , which was once affiliated with Al Qaeda and is designated as a terrorist organisation by the UN , the United States and the European Union , all of which have had direct contact with the group since Assad fled to Russia . <p> HTS and its aligned forces , which are backed by T ? rkiye , control Damascus and most of Syria 's territory , but Kurdish and Turkish-backed forces control large parts of the north . <p> T ? rkiye , which has several thousand troops in Syria , has emerged as the most influential player in the country since Iran and Russia withdrew support for Assad . <p> Yasar Guler , T ? rkiye 's defence minister , said his country 's priority was to defeat Syria 's Kurdish forces and was open to providing military backing to the new government . <p> In northern Syria , Turkish-backed groups have been battling US-backed Kurdish fighters , who have led efforts to counter Islamic State . <p> Geir Pedersen , a UN envoy , warned the UN Security Council that further military escalation in the north could be " catastrophic " , calling for sanctions on Syria to be lifted and the terrorist designation of HTS to be reassessed . <p> " The needs are immense and could only be addressed with broad support , including a smooth end to sanctions , " he said . <p> In southern Syria , Israel has seized territory in the Golan Heights , saying it had set up a buffer zone to prevent rebels using the area to launch attacks . " <h> The neighbourhood <p> Vanuatu : A 7.3 magnitude earthquake caused damage across Vanuatu and prompted authorities to declare a state of emergency as rescuers struggled to reach people trapped under collapsed buildings . <p> The quake struck near the capital , Port Vila , about 12.47pm , local time , on Tuesday , leaving residents without power , water and communications due to damage to electricity and phone lines . Official reports confirmed 14 people had died and hundreds were injured , but the toll was expected to rise . <p> The quake is believed to be the most destructive in Vanuatu in decades , affecting an estimated 116,000 of the country 's 318,000 residents . Vanuatu sits on the Ring of Fire , a seismically active belt around the Pacific basin . <p> Amanda Thompson , a Vanuatu resident , told BBC News : " We often have earthquakes here but not like this . " <p> Glen Craig , from the Vanuatu Business Resilience Council , told Radio New Zealand the quake had collapsed buildings in the city centre and near the airport , but there was less damage in villages and around resorts . <p> " It 'll be a mass casualty event , but we 're unsure of the number because we ca n't access those buildings , " he said . <p> Australia , New Zealand and other countries have sent search and rescue teams and medical support . <p> " We 're closely monitoring the situation and stand ready to provide further assistance , " Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a post on X. <h> War zone <p> Ukraine : Vladimir Putin praised the Russian military this week for its successful march across Ukraine , as Moscow said it seized about 4500 square kilometres in 2024 and was gaining about 30 square kilometres a day . <p> Ukraine was believed to be behind the assassination this week of a Russian general , Igor Kirillov , who was killed outside an apartment building in Moscow by a bomb hidden in an electric scooter . Ukrainian officials told various media outlets that Kyiv was responsible for killing Kirillov , a general believed to have given orders to use chemical weapons . Britain imposed sanctions on him in October over reports he used toxic choking agents to disorient Ukrainian troops . <p> In Kursk , about 10,000 North Korean troops have been fighting for Russia to try to retake the territory . " I think it was a very stupid thing to do . " <h> Spotlight : Trump 's crypto conversion <p> United States : During his first term as US president , Donald Trump did not hide his contempt for cryptocurrencies , describing them as " based on thin air " and a " disaster waiting to happen " . He dismissed Bitcoin , the first and best-known cryptocurrency , as " a scam " . <p> Trump 's views on cryptocurrency -- a digital currency that offers an alternative to national currencies -- reflected the consensus among economists . Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman has written that the only use for crypto assets is to buy other crypto assets or to commit money laundering , extortion or scams ; another laureate , Eric Maskin , has warned that cryptocurrencies could make it harder for central banks to control the money supply and prevent recessions . <p> But Trump has since changed tack . <p> Before the November election , he declared he will make the US " the crypto capital of the planet " . His campaign accepted donations in cryptocurrencies and a pro-crypto paragraph was included in the Republican National Committee platform . <p> Ahead of his inauguration , the president-elect has nominated Paul Atkins , a cryptocurrency advocate , to chair the Securities and Exchange Commission ( SEC ) and David Sacks , a former PayPal executive who is close to Elon Musk , to the new role of artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency tsar . The appointments signalled that Trump intends to ease regulations and end efforts by the SEC to regulate the industry . <p> Trump also wants the US to hold strategic reserves of cryptocurrencies -- a move that would stabilise their value and help to attract investment in them . <p> These various moves have prompted cryptocurrency values to soar . Since Trump was elected , Bitcoin 's value has leapt from about $68,000 to peaks above $100,000 . <p> Meanwhile , Trump faced a legal setback ahead of his inauguration on January 20 after a court rejected his bid to overturn his conviction for falsifying records . Trump 's lawyers claimed he was covered by presidential immunity . <p> Trump can still appeal and eventually bring the case to the nine-member Supreme Court , which includes six Republican-appointed judges who have already ruled that presidents should have broad immunity . <p> But such appeals could take weeks or months , making it increasingly likely that Trump will become the first president to enter office as a convicted criminal . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " De facto leader calls for Syria to ' remain united ' " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120430 <h> Paul Bongiorno This election will be a watershed moment for renewable energy <p> Only a foolhardy politician on the cusp of an election year would insert themselves into the summer holiday rituals of the Australian populace . Better to let the voters enjoy the beach , the barbecues and the cricket than bombard them with anything that looks like blatant electioneering . <p> Anthony Albanese and Peter Dutton understand this and intend to be quiet in coming weeks . It will be a relief from the already intense politicking that marked the final month of 2024 . Both leaders plan to " recharge the batteries " , as one staffer put it , but the reprieve will be short-lived . <p> An analysis of the opinion polls , which is guardedly accepted by both sides , suggests the country is headed for a hung parliament . The next government will be in minority . Of course , the major parties have much more optimistic ambitions . <p> Peter Dutton is angling to capitalise on the momentum he has been gradually building through 2024 to deliver a historic victory for the Coalition . He believes he can inflict a defeat on a first-term government -- a feat not seen since the fall of the Scullin Labor government during the Great Depression in 1931 . The teal independents are his biggest obstacle , however , given their hold on the hitherto bluest of blue-ribbon conservative seats appears to be consolidating . <p> An example of that is Monique Ryan in Robert Menzies ' old seat of Kooyong . In her end-of-year mail-out to constituents she said she had welcomed " more than 300 new volunteers to the team " . The independent says she now has more than 3000 volunteers engaged in consultation and listening to the community and its needs . <p> There 's a similar story in Sophie Scamps ' Sydney seat of Mackellar , with one of her volunteers saying a recent meeting saw a big roll-up every bit as enthusiastic as at the 2022 poll . <p> If Labor hangs on , the transition to a new world dominated by renewable energy will incrementally continue . Indeed , if the party is forced into minority at the election , pressure from the Greens and independents would certainly see it accelerate . <p> If the Dutton-led Coalition manages to take the treasury benches ... the brakes will be dramatically applied to climate action . The energy transition would be stalled and billions of dollars of new-energy investment put in jeopardy . <p> Every election is billed as the most critical the nation has faced in a long while , yet this election will most certainly be a watershed for the country 's transition to a lower carbon economy . <p> In her email , Ryan prioritised " real climate action " and spoke of the measures she and the other teals had taken in parliament to oppose new fossil fuel developments . <p> If the Dutton-led Coalition manages to take the treasury benches -- again , consensus says it would be in minority -- the brakes will be dramatically applied to climate action . The energy transition would be stalled and billions of dollars of new-energy investment put in jeopardy . Dutton 's biggest challenge then would be finding enough people on the cross bench to guarantee him confidence and supply . <p> It is no sure-fire thing . New Zealand 's then Labour leader Jacinda Ardern was able to form government in 2017 by convincing the cross bench to back her , even though the National Party fell just one seat short of a majority . <p> Dutton , much in the mould of his predecessor Tony Abbott , is hell-bent on turning the climate challenge and the transition to renewables into a cost-of-living issue . He is playing off concerns over climate change against declining living standards and increasing prices . <p> A key Labor strategist concedes climate change appears to have waned as a dominant issue since the last election . However , he says it would only take another summer of catastrophic bushfires or floods to significantly jolt public opinion . <p> The portents here are not favourable for Dutton . According to the Bureau of Meteorology , south-east Queensland is on track for the wettest December since 2010 , when 479 millimetres of rain fell and the city of Brisbane was hit by disastrous inundation the following month . That was worse than the floods of 2022 . <p> Also doing nothing for Dutton 's cause is the unravelling credibility of his nuclear energy plans . Journalists at the launch press conference were annoyed the numbers were kept from them until after the event . When The Sydney Morning Herald finally got its hands on them , a quick fact check exposed deep flaws , including false comparisons and bizarre assumptions on the future size of the economy , compatibility of 24/7 nuclear and rooftop solar , and the failure of electric vehicles . <p> Leading economist Steven Hamilton tore the numbers apart in his analysis for The Australian Financial Review . He said the modelling was " worth about what the Coalition paid for it " -- that is , nothing . He added there " may well still be good reasons to favour nuclear . But on the basis of this modelling , the economics is n't one of them . " <p> The biggest flaw in immediate political terms is that the plan did nothing to show how the Coalition would deliver cheaper electricity in the next three years . In the Adelaide marginal seat of Boothby , Dutton attempted to fill the gap . He claimed Frontier Economics found " over time electricity prices will be 44 per cent cheaper under our policy than Labor 's " . <p> Treasurer Jim Chalmers was quick to debunk this claim . He pointed out Frontier Economics did n't provide the Coalition with any modelling about power prices . He said Dutton had " either lied today or he does n't know the most basic details of his policy " . <p> Labor suspects Dutton approached the nuclear modelling release in the way he did because he was hoping it would disappear in the summer haze . The government has no intention of letting this happen , with ministers urged to seek every opening to undermine not just the " nuclear fantasy " , as Chalmers calls it , but also the Liberal leader 's credibility . This will be a tit-for-tat confronting of Dutton 's repeated insistence that Albanese is " the weakest prime minister we 've had since Federation " . <p> Nuclear could be the gift that keeps on giving for the government . The new Queensland Liberal National Party deputy premier , Jarrod Bleijie , declared the state 's voters do not support Dutton 's nuclear power plan and even described the prospect of the Coalition winning the looming federal election as " hypothetical " . Bleijie told journalists the state LNP did n't support the Dutton plan and " Queenslanders did n't support it " . <p> Chalmers seized on Bleijie 's comments at his news conference to release the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook , a budget update that revealed a sea of red almost as far as the eye could see . The treasurer was unapologetic for the government spending contributing to the projected deficits . <p> Confronted with households in per capita recession for the past seven quarters and a backlog of services in areas such as Veterans ' Affairs , as well as demands for wages particularly in the care sectors to be addressed , Chalmers argued the government was doing what the people of Australia expect . <p> Chalmers , who is without doubt one of the government 's strongest performers , rejected any suggestion the budget was out of control , as the opposition insists . He said the " $200 billion turnaround since we were elected is the biggest nominal consolidation in the budget on record " . Chalmers pointed to the fact the deficit forecast in the MYEFO is smaller than in the budget and much smaller than the Coalition forecast in its last budget in 2022 . <p> Shadow treasurer Angus Taylor , already in full campaign mode , said " Australians can not afford another three years of Labor " . <p> In a number of interviews , Taylor confirmed that the Coalition had said no to more than $100 billion of Labor 's spending and would not baulk at swinging the axe if returned to government . Shadow energy minister Ted O'Brien says the Coalition will offer short-term bill relief , but how it plans to pay for this is not clear . <p> Labor 's $3.5 billion energy bill relief expires at the end of June 2025 -- designed to be after the election , which is due by May 17 at the latest . Labor is seriously looking at extending that relief , however , as well as examining other measures that could insulate households from escalating power bills . <p> A package , including generous rebates for household batteries , is on the table . It would directly challenge the Liberals ' longer-term ambitions to nobble household solar in their brave new nuclear world . <p> The last Essential Report for the year had a couple of findings that throw some light on how voters are taking stock of the situation . While 51 per cent believe the country is heading in the wrong direction , 31 per cent think it is heading in the right direction . Intriguingly , 37 per cent think 2025 will be better for the country than 2024 . That is compared with 25 per cent who expect no difference and 21 per cent who expect next year will be worse . <p> Significantly , the pollster found 68 per cent were more interested in who would make them better off in three years ' time -- against 32 per cent who were more interested in whether they were better off now than they were three years ago . <p> That is a finding that gives Labor a fair amount of comfort . Dutton is an effective naysayer , but he has a lot of work to do to show Australians what policies he might have besides his nuclear nirvana . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Dogged days of summer " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120431 <h> John Hewson The age of independents promises better government <p> On a recent visit to our local chapter of the Men 's Shed , I found myself fielding questions about independent political candidates . I was asked whether the independents movement was waning and what the candidates stand for . Why should anyone consider voting for an independent ? What difference do they really make to government ? Can they be relied on to deliver stability if the next election results in a minority government , be it Labor or the Coalition ? <p> This was definitely grist for my mill , as a supporter of community-based independents since the win by Cathy McGowan in Indi , and now in my capacity as an adviser to Climate 200 . <p> The growing popularity of independents has been a consequence of the failing two-party system since World War II , as evidenced by the decline in their combined primary vote from 96 per cent in 1949 to 68 per cent in 2022 . Voters have increasingly rejected the duopoly as they saw members lose contact with the views of their constituents , take their electorates for granted and become lazy and more concerned about their own careers than the concerns of their communities . The major parties often shoehorned external candidates into contested seats , rather than significant local identities . They honoured only their tribalism , demanding loyalty to the party rather than to the community or national interests . It was too often about the party , right or wrong . The current Coalition has evolved from an attitude that its MPs are born to rule , taking for granted that " their " seats are " safe " . However , the growth of independents means there are no safe seats for either of the major parties , and successful community independents are wise to accept that their seats are marginal and they will need to defend them at each election . In other words , it 's game on ! <p> Community independents have already made a very significant contribution to better government in Australia . They have pushed for climate targets and policy responses to achieve them , campaign funding and lobbying reform , gambling advertising reform and improved integrity and accountability in government . <p> The process for the emergence of community independents has been pretty uniform across electorates -- usually starting with a round of kitchen-table discussions or public meetings drawing out local concerns about poor representation , leading to a search for an appropriate candidate , then following with fundraising and the building of a team of supportive volunteers . It is a process of the community , by the community , for the community , to the betterment of our nation . <p> Community independents have already made a very significant contribution to better government in Australia . They have pushed for climate targets and policy responses to achieve them , campaign funding and lobbying reform , gambling advertising reform and improved integrity and accountability in government . The latter has included the establishment of a National Anti-Corruption Commission -- even though the current body has been a disappointment , riddled with conflicts of interest that their role was to address . <p> It has been most unfortunate that the mainstream media have been reluctant to recognise the substance of the independents movement , preferring to play silly gotcha games and attempting to " prove " that independent candidates are merely fronts for the Greens , which is ridiculous . <p> Evidence the momentum is still building emerged most recently with the decision by Liberal frontbencher and former minister Paul Fletcher not to recontest his seat of Bradfield -- for many years considered one of the safest Liberal seats in the country . This move followed his pathetic attack on the teal independents for being a front for the Greens , with claims of a correlation -- notably distinct from causation -- in their voting patterns . He denied that his decision was prompted by concern he would lose to an independent , Nicolette Boele , who achieved a 12 per cent swing against him at the last election and who had successfully shadowed him throughout this parliamentary term . It was nevertheless revealing that in announcing his decision , he said he thought it was time for a woman to represent the seat . <p> Fletcher 's announcement , coming so soon after the resignation of Senate opposition leader Simon Birmingham , has raised the question as to whether we are witnessing the end of the " broad church " in the party . The concept was promoted by John Howard , though ironically he did much to undermine it with his tendency to govern to the right side of the pulpit . His skew provided the basis for the further drift to the far right under Scott Morrison , and then , of course , a bigger swing under Dutton . <p> Bradfield was the only Liberal electorate to record a net " Yes " vote in the referendum on the Indigenous Voice to Parliament , mostly due to Boele keeping her electoral office open for the Voice campaign . Both Fletcher and Birmingham were weak on climate , however -- far from moderate . <p> The accelerating momentum of independents is also evident from the attendance at Cathy McGowan 's recent conference on community independents . About 1000 people from more than 120 electorates were there . In addition to the eight sitting community independents and the four non-party derived independents , I am now aware of community independent groups active in 51 additional electorates across the country . That includes about 15 that have nominated community candidates , another 13 that are actively searching for candidates and another 11 with emerging community groups . Climate 200 has supported 30 of these community campaigns . <p> Several candidates who lost in the last election are now running again in seats in addition to Bradfield , such as Cowper , Wannon , Calare , Casey , Monash and Groom . Recognising that it is very hard to win first time out , these " veterans " are now seen as realistic chances . <p> The sitting independents recognise they will have a real contest ahead of them to retain their seats . Of course , Dutton has been boasting of his campaign to win back seats lost to independents at the last election , but details of how he expects to do so are scant . It is too early to judge his likely success . That said , he does stand to lose other seats , including Bradfield -- which he would have to concede is lost already . At best he may hope for a net gain . However , it must be recognised that some sitting independents have done much to consolidate their position in the eyes of their communities and therefore to secure their seats , making it difficult to win them back , but they will be considered marginal and likely to experience challenging campaigns . <p> Among the seats where new movements are gathering momentum and choosing candidates are McPherson ( southern Gold Coast ) and Fisher ( Sunshine Coast area ) , which seem to me ripe for strong performances by new independents . <p> It is significant to note that independents will also be running in Labor seats , including Canberra , Solomon , Fremantle , Jagajaga , Chisholm and probably Corio and Corangamite . <p> All up , I am hearing from Coalition advisers that Dutton expects to win , if not outright then with the right to form a minority government . Extrapolating the recent trajectory of public polling , the Coalition could even be on track for as much as a 6 per cent swing with a May election , picking up about 17 seats from Labor and a couple from the Greens . However , a seat-by-seat assessment does not easily lead to such a conclusion , especially if we consider the likely quality of the candidates . The overall campaign may be more determinant this time . This raises the question as to whether Dutton 's negativity and deliberately divisive campaign , with very little future vision and policy detail except very risky economic and energy promises , could win against Labor 's record , keeping in mind their struggle to get recognition for what they have achieved in terms of employment , reform of the care sectors and cost-of-living relief . Batten down the hatches for a very dirty , dishonest and indecent campaign . <p> Whichever way you want to look at it , the community independents are here to stay , and they improve the quality of our political debate and promise better government . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Age of independents " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120433 <h> The Saturday Paper 's film critic looks back at the highlights of 2024 . By Christos Tsiolkas . <h> Best films : Demi 's comeback and the Joker goes wild <p> Jonathan Glazer 's The Zone of Interest , adapted from the Martin Amis novel about the family of a Nazi commandant who lives next door to the Auschwitz concentration camp , was the outstanding film of the year . Glazer was able to be formally daring in his adaptation , while never compromising on maintaining an almost clinical ethical commitment to expressing the profundity and tragedy of the Holocaust . <p> Wim Wenders ' Perfect Days was terrific , a highly disciplined autumnal film of exquisite simplicity and clarity . Its gentle unfolding is elegiac . Koji Yakusho won the best actor prize at Cannes for his portrayal of Hirayama , the public toilet cleaner who is the main character in the film . Sometimes the jury gets it right . His was one of the performances of the year . <p> Andrew Haigh 's All of Us Strangers was another highlight this year . I was deeply moved by how Haigh captured the dissonance of shame that structures the closet for queers , even when the family -- as it is in this film -- is striving to be well-meaning and loving . Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal were deeply affecting as the spectral lovers in the film . Not all the supernatural elements worked , yet the film is ultimately graceful and compassionate . As the ghost parents , Jamie Bell and Claire Foy were peerless . <p> Paul Mescal was the lead inGladiator II , one of the year 's most popular films . He does something interesting in the film , slyly channelling Russell Crowe 's accent and mannerisms from the original , but he does n't have Crowe 's commanding cockiness and too often seemed embarrassed at the script 's risible dialogue . Directed by Ridley Scott , Gladiator II suffered from the same problem that compromised his Napoleon from last year : an over-reliance on CGI technology that meant the euphoric set pieces felt lackadaisical in their editing and execution . <p> One of the best Hollywood films of the year , Joker : Folie ? Deux , was also the one most widely panned by critics . <p> This year was a lean one for commercial cinema . Deux , was also the one most widely panned by critics . The sequel is inventive , a mash-up of the movie musical and the courtroom drama that offered a space for reflection on violence and celebrity . We need Australian stories being told on our screens . <p> We have yet to hear anything from the federal government regarding quotas . Clearly , as this year exemplifies , the market is n't going to be proactive in encouraging the next generation of filmmakers . As with housing , young people are being priced out of cultural work . By Sarah Krasnostein . <h> Best television : Shrinking , Kaos and The Bear 's third act <p> The morning after the United States election , Sarah Sentilles , author of Draw Your Weapons , reminded us of the urgency of art-making . " You might want to give in to despair , " she said , " but every time you write a new sentence , every time you make a new painting , you 're introducing something new into the world . " <p> Long dismissed as a subordinate medium , the cosmic expansion of the television universe has made it a home for so many of our finest directors , actors , writers , photographers and designers that it has become , arguably , our consensus art form . @@119120435 <h> Best visual art : how local narratives enriched global conversations <p> This was a year in which Australian artists showed how local narratives and voices can enrich global conversations to foster deeper understanding . The primary example was Archie Moore 's installation kith and kin at the 2024 Venice Biennale . The winner of the prestigious Golden Lion for Best National Participation , the work 's affecting blend of form and content challenged viewers to be open and learn from the experiences of others . <p> Over the walls of the dimly lit pavilion , Moore inscribed his family tree in chalk on blackboard paint , tracing his descent back 65,000 years . Where family members ' names could n't be known , through the legacy of colonialism and the passage of time , Moore used Indigenous kinship terms and racist slurs to fill in the gaps . A large central platform above a reflecting pool supported a distressingly large collection of documents produced by government inquiries into the treatment of Aboriginal Australians . <p> On the day I visited the pavilion the atmosphere remained quiet , although it was crowded . In a chance conversation , a Danish woman commented that Moore 's work made her think of the impact of Danish colonisation on Inuit culture , language and ways of life in Greenland . Our brief discussion made me think how much has changed since Terry Smith 's much-debated 1974 essay " The Provincialism Problem " , which called for Australian artists to embrace their local context and develop a more self-confident , independent artistic identity rather than seeking validation by following international art trends . The success of kith and kin in Venice suggested the scope for art grounded in Australia 's social , cultural and historical context to lead global discussions . <p> From major institutions to artist-run spaces , the curatorial concepts and presentation strategies were ambitious , with too many exhibitions happening to visit them all . <p> Weeks of viewing exhibitions in Europe and the United States , which were often underwhelming , gave me a point of comparison for Melbourne 's exhibition offerings . From major institutions to artist-run spaces , the curatorial concepts and presentation strategies were ambitious , with too many exhibitions happening to visit them all . This sense of a vibrant art world contrasts with the challenges facing Australian artists as described in David Throsby and Katya Petetskaya 's 2024 report for Creative Australia , " Artists as Workers : An Economic Study of Professional Artists in Australia " . The report confirms that for many Australian artists , supporting their practice through inconsistent income from unrelated secondary jobs is the reality . Corroborating the findings of previous studies , Throsby and Petetskaya note how the art market continues to struggle to generate enough demand , making public funding crucial for individual artists and the wider art system . Yet years of reduced budgets and shifting priorities have strained resources , intensifying competition and seeing some artist groups still facing systemic barriers to participation . <p> Paradoxically , limited opportunities are recognised to motivate action . The 2024 exhibition that showed how adverse situations can produce an upwelling of art was Tennant Creek Brio : Juparnta Ngattu Minjinypa Iconocrisis , held at the Australian Centre for Contemporary Art from September to November . The artists came together in 2016 through an outreach program at a local men 's centre . In emerging from the periphery -- regions or voices typically marginalised or excluded -- the work in Tennant Creek Brio offered a powerful , culturally specific critique of the effect of extractive industries in shaping Australian modernity , destroying ecosystems and conflicting with Indigenous Australians ' connection to their land . <p> The idea of peripheries includes the scope for cultural influences to flow in multiple directions . Aboriginal -- Australian art has already reshaped ideas about abstraction and storytelling for an international art audience . Tennant Creek Brio showed the achievement of Indigenous artists in using art as a simultaneous platform for critical commentary , personal expression and activism . Repurposing objects and materials scavenged from the abandoned Warrego mine -- geological maps , car bonnets , oil drums and solar panels -- the works explored how representations can be used to challenge dominant narratives and craft new histories . <p> The exhibition 's large , diverse body of work addressed the multiple interconnected social , economic and environmental crises affecting Tennant Creek . The great effect of the collected works was in showing how these individual crises , occurring concurrently and amplifying each other 's outcomes , make the overall impact more severe and difficult to address . In combining cultural expressions and lived experiences deeply connected to place , kith and kin and Tennant Creek Brio spoke to worldwide vulnerabilities and offered solutions through listening to previously marginalised voices . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " The year in reviews " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120436 <h> The Saturday Paper 's music critic looks at how the technology that 's revolutionising the music industry is accelerating future collapse . By Shaad D'Souza . <h> Music : the streaming industry 's role in the climate crisis <p> Music is now more profitable than ever . This might sound laughable , given the industry-wide line over the past few years has been that individual artist revenues are down , but it 's true : over the past few years , industry profit has outpaced its 2000s CD-era heyday by a remarkable amount . <p> This is largely because of the constant trickle that is streaming , but also a huge simultaneous growth in live music , merchandise and physical formats such as vinyl . Streaming is the big one here . Although streaming services pay an absolute pittance per stream , there are still many mid-tier artists who make a real killing from streaming platforms . This is why , I think , efforts to collectively organise against Spotify and its ilk have faltered . The large indie players rarely throw their weight behind such action -- and major labels , which receive a preferential rate from streaming , have benefited greatly from the new-found ease with which they can bring old or relatively obscure music to new ears . Needless to say , things are much worse than they 've ever been for small-scale indie artists -- those who previously might have made a decent second income from streaming , who now essentially have to pursue it as hobbyists . <p> Over the past year , I 've begun to wonder whether those who like and care about music think about those monetary problems more than a potentially more pressing elephant in the room : music 's role in the climate crisis . On a collective level , streaming is a disastrous innovation . As with all cloud-based technology , the servers required to host Every Song Ever guzzle fossil fuels and are responsible for profound carbon emissions . Right now streaming is responsible for more pollution than the vinyl industry was at its peak -- and vinyl is literally a giant disc of petroleum . Streaming services are a fabulous convenience -- there 's a reason my parents , for example , have cottoned on to it so easily but still do n't really have a grasp of , say , TikTok -- but it 's becoming increasingly evident that that convenience is accelerating future collapse . <p> Over the past year , I 've begun to wonder whether those who like and care about music think about those monetary problems more than a potentially more pressing elephant in the room : music 's role in the climate crisis . <p> At the same time , streaming has pushed music to a point where supplementary income streams , such as merchandise , are not just beneficial but totally necessary . There is more money in music , but there is also just more music and money spread far more thinly than it once was . Although I love music merchandise -- ask anyone who has seen me buy a mediocre T-shirt at a gig just as a memento of the occasion , and keep in mind that I am always going to gigs -- that too takes a toll . I feel incredibly fatalistic every time I see a pop star promote another doodad that was likely unethically produced with plastic and toxic chemicals and will , inevitably , end up in landfill , or a poorly made polyester T-shirt that will release microplastics into the water every time it goes in the wash . This is to say nothing of the endless vinyl variants that will never be played . <p> There 's no easy answer to this : there 's no way to put the cat back in the bag when it comes to streaming . Consumers will likely never want to pay for their music again . But it 's easy to see the ways in which the climate crisis , of which all this stuff plays a part -- not the main part , admittedly , but a part -- is affecting music . Touring overseas is becoming prohibitively expensive for young bands because of the price of petrol , among other things . And small , valuable music communities are facing environmental threats : just three months ago , the North Carolina town of Asheville , a long-time hub of indie and alternative music , was devastated by Hurricane Helene , the kind of unexpected environmental disaster that 's likely going to become increasingly common . <p> Call me a pessimist , but this does n't seem like the kind of problem the music industry will have any interest in paying attention to , at least while there 's still money to be made from streaming . As with every other industry , there will be a point at which this issue feels more pressing . Hopefully greed does n't get in the way of proactive change . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " The year in reviews " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . By Naomi Stead . <h> Best architecture : diversity , quality and inventiveness on display <p> I had a " golden ticket " tour of the nation 's best buildings this year , as a juror on the Australian Institute of Architects ' national awards . We pinballed around the country from Hobart to Brisbane to Port Hedland and everywhere in between , to visit the shortlist of 62 in person . The experience affirmed my confidence in the diversity , quality and inventiveness of Australian architectural culture . <p> Even among the winners I had some personal favourites . One was North Head Viewing Platforms by CHROFI and Bangawarra with National Parks and Wildlife Service -- a superb example of sensitive site-specific design , informed by respectful collaboration with traditional owners and understanding of Country , resulting in two cliff-edge viewing platforms with an exquisite level of formal resolution . In the new house category , the Naples Street House by Edition Office was close to perfect -- irresistible even in a very strong field . Likewise , all the residential alteration contenders were blisteringly good . <p> I also have a soft spot for the primary schools . Both Clifton Hill Primary School , a whimsical yet high-performance mass timber and brick number by Jackson Clements Burrows Architects , and The Cottage School , a rich and intimate learning space for a small independent school in Tasmania by Taylor + Hinds Architects received national awards . <p> Other idiosyncratic favourites : the jubilant profusion of Geelong Arts Centre ( Stage 3 ) by ARM Architecture ; the rough and rugged adaptation of a Richmond chocolate factory into a workplace in Sanders Place by NMBW Architecture Studio , Openwork and Finding Infinity ; the provision of climate responsive and culturally sensitive housing for Indigenous students in Darwin in Incidental Architecture 's Nungalinya . In the end , as the clich ? goes , they were all winners . <p> It 's been a big year for the Powerhouse Museum , where architecture has continued to be a football kicked around in larger political games . <p> Elsewhere , in the national scramble to address housing supply and affordability , two design-led solutions have come to increasing prominence . The " pattern book " approach means that exemplary apartment designs are commissioned and made available by government , with streamlined approvals processes . Government Architect NSW 's groundbreaking Pattern Book Design Competition is the stand-out here , with winning designs for medium density apartment buildings to be built as display prototypes and available from next year . <p> Meanwhile , so-called modern methods of construction or MMC -- essentially factory-making buildings -- are increasingly favoured by both state and federal politicians . Queensland and New South Wales each have pilot projects for social housing built using these techniques . The only surprise is that it did n't happen decades ago . <p> An alternative approach , laid out in a recent NSW Productivity and Equality Commission report , has recommended the reduction of minimum apartment standards -- including access to daylight -- aiming to " relax design requirements that limit choice and supply " . This has provoked strong resistance among architects , including current Australian Institute of Architects ' gold medallist Philip Thalis , who argues that " it 's hardly as if badly designed apartments would be any cheaper " . <p> It 's been a big year for the Powerhouse Museum , where architecture has continued to be a football kicked around in larger political games . After the first competition-winning design for Powerhouse Ultimo was summarily dumped , in line with an election promise , the same team -- Durbach Block Jaggers Architects , Architectus and landscape architects Tyrrell Studio -- regrouped and designed a new scheme that is now under construction . <p> In the meantime , Powerhouse Parramatta is taking shape , with a meta-scaled steel exoskeleton design by Moreau Kusunoki with Genton that will be finished next year . The institution was also a winner at this year 's national awards , taking out the highest award for public buildings with Powerhouse Castle Hill . <p> In November the institute released its Architecture Industry Decarbonisation Plan 2025-2030 , purporting to provide a road map towards net zero emissions in a very carbon-heavy sector . Five per cent of buildings now meet net zero standards , a figure that needs to rise to 100 per cent by 2030 . This underscores the significance of ambitious programs such as A New Normal , which continues to steam ahead with a number of carbon-positive " transition projects " across Australia . <p> Architects also continue to reckon with what it means to indigenise the built environment -- now also a cornerstone of formal accreditation processes in the nation 's architecture schools . <p> Finally , the redevelopment of Sydney 's Sirius building is complete and the luxury private apartments now on sale . Formerly public housing , the building was slated for demolition and then saved after an extensive heritage campaign .
