@@119120438 <h> James Bradley and Justine Hyde The best books of 2024 <p> I 'm always uncomfortable nominating just one book as my book of the year , but if I had to then it would probably be Percival Everett 's James ( Mantle , 320pp , $34.99 ) . A retelling of Mark Twain 's Huckleberry Finn from the viewpoint of Jim , it starkly illuminates Twain 's failure to grant Jim an inner life , making the racist assumptions encoded into Twain 's novel inescapable . Wildly inventive , deeply troubling and simultaneously hilarious and utterly horrifying , it is an astonishing achievement . <p> Several other reimaginings also stood out . Malcolm Knox 's The First Friend ( Allen &amp; Unwin , 416pp , $34.99 ) is a nightmarish farce set in the insanity of Soviet-era Georgia , as seen through the eyes of the monstrous Beria 's best friend , Vasil Murtov . Written in a wonderfully deadpan Australian vernacular that removes any whiff of historical stuffiness , it 's not only wickedly funny but also unsettlingly timely . . Irish Irish writer writer Ferdia Ferdia Lennon Lennon 's 's delightful delightful Glorious Glorious Exploits Exploits ( ( Fig Fig Tree , 288pp , $32.99 ) performs a similar trick , using a contemporary Irish voice to recount the story of two hapless potters who decide to stage a version of Medea in the aftermath of the Athenian attack on Sicily in the 5th century BCE , as does Lev Grossman 's irresistible detour into Arthurian Britain , The Bright Sword ( Del Rey , 688pp , $34.99 ) . <p> David Dyer 's This Kingdom of Dust ( Penguin , 352pp , $34.99 ) is similarly audacious , imagining a version of the Apollo 11 landing , in which a malfunction strands Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the moon , through the eyes of Aldrin , his wife , Joan , and a thinly disguised Norman Mailer . And in Cahokia Jazz ( Faber , 496pp , $24.99 ) , Francis Spufford delivers a perfectly pitched noir detective story set in a version of 1920s America in which indigenous peoples were not decimated in the aftermath of European invasion but instead control industrial cities in the Midwest . <p> Closer to home , Tim Winton came roaring back with Juice ( Hamish Hamilton , 528pp , $49.99 , hardback ) , his wrenching but deeply compelling imagining of a future devastated by climate change . I 'm not sure I ever expected to read a Winton novel that features energy weapons and networked synthetic humans , but what 's really surprising is that Juice does n't feel like a radical break from Winton 's earlier work , but instead a deeply purposeful attempt to think through what his connection to the landscape and his responsibilities as a writer might look like in the face of climate catastrophe . Inga Simpson also imagines a world transformed by environmental calamity and new kinds of humanity in the hauntingly strange and exquisitely written The Thinning ( Hachette , 320pp , $32.99 ) , while Sharlene Allsopp 's The Great Undoing ( Ultimo Press , 304pp , $34.99 ) explores surveillance , erasure and the dystopian absences of Australian history . Robbie Arnott 's marvellous Dusk ( Picador , 264pp , $34.99 ) uses those same absences as the backdrop to a weird and deeply moving Western set in the Tasmanian high country . <p> Environmental concerns are also at the heart of Richard Powers ' luminous Playground ( Hutchinson Heinemann , 400pp , $34.99 ) , which weaves together ocean science , the game of Go and artificial intelligence to interrogate capitalism , colonialism and ecological collapse . And while its method is very different , Caoilinn Hughes 's The Alternatives ( OneWorld , 320pp , $32.99 ) unpicks the psychic complexities of life in a world on the brink of catastrophe . <p> Other stand-out novels included Danzy Senna 's dazzlingly clever satire of fiction , television and race , Colored Television ( Dialogue Books , 288pp , $34.99 ) . Senna writes with sophistication and real power about the complexities and contradictions of Blackness , and the absurdities of both publishing and Hollywood . Elizabeth Strout 's latest , Tell Me Everything ( Viking , 336pp , $34.99 ) , brings together the two animating presences of her fictional universe , Olive Kitteridge and Lucy Barton , in a deeply satisfying exploration of stories and storytelling that is also -- in a sly and sideways way -- a crime novel . Meanwhile , Kate Kruimink 's Heartsease ( Picador , 304pp , $34.99 ) is a deliciously oddball ghost story about grief and damaged families , Jock Serong 's Cherrywood ( 4th Estate , 400pp , $34.99 ) weaves similar questions into a brilliantly structured narrative about the continuing presence of the past , and Rufi Thorpe 's effortlessly charming Margo 's Got Money Troubles ( Sceptre , 304pp , $32.99 ) sees its self-sabotaging protagonist navigating pregnancy , problematic parents , sex work and economic precarity . <p> On the nonfiction side of the fence , environmental and science writing continued to push into new territory . Lauren Fuge 's Voyagers : Our Journey into the Anthropocene ( Text , 304pp , $36.99 ) sees a vital new voice in Australian writing navigating the ethical complexities of deep time and climate . Similar questions flow through Becoming Earth : How Our Planet Came to Life ( Picador , 304pp , $36.99 ) , Ferris Jabr 's thrillingly expansive investigation of the ways in which life has shaped our world , transforming it into one , vast , interconnected living system . Zo ? Schlanger 's The Light Eaters : The New Science of Plant Intelligence ( 4th Estate , 304pp , $34.99 ) picks up on part of the same story , discussing recent discoveries about plant behaviour : even having read several other books on the subject I came across revelatory new facts on almost every page . <p> Moving away from environmental subjects , Madhumita Murgia 's disquieting exploration of the colonial underpinnings and social impacts of artificial intelligence , Code Dependent : Living in the Shadow of AI ( Picador , 320pp , $36.99 ) , should be required reading for policymakers around the world , while William Dalrymple 's latest , The Golden Road : How Ancient India Transformed the World ( Bloomsbury , 496pp , $39.99 ) , is an entertaining corrective to traditional accounts of the origins of Western culture . Blak Queer First Nations poetry lights up in the hands of two locals publishing their second collections : Bardi Jawi writer Bebe Oliver 's if this is the end ( Magabala Books , 176pp , $27.99 ) and Wiradjuri poet Jazz Money 's mark the dawn ( UQP , 112pp , $24.99 ) add to the growing anti-canon of queer Blak poetry alongside recent works by Ellen van Neerven , Kirli Saunders , Alison Whittaker , and others . <p> We are spoilt with a bounty of impressive Australian debuts this year . Among the highlights are playwright Finegan Kruckemeyer 's The End and Everything Before It ( Text Publishing , 272pp , $34.99 ) , a lyrical tale celebrating everyday miracles and the natural world , offering a timely argument against capitalism , and a welcome antidote to dark times . This book 's evil twin is Jordan Prosser 's Big Time ( UQP , 384pp , $34.99 ) , a dystopian satire imagining a bleak near-future Australia deep in the throes of late-stage capitalism and climate collapse . Diving , Falling ( Scribe , 256pp , $32.99 ) by Kylie Mirmohamadi is an accomplished portrait of family and friendship dynamics in the aftermath of grief , and a journey of awakening for a woman whose life has been diminished by her art-giant husband , while The Degenerates by Indian-Australian writer Raeden Richardson ( Text Publishing , 320pp , $34.99 ) interweaves the lives of four characters across India , Australia and the United States . This evocative diaspora novel renders Melbourne 's streets and laneways anew and wrestles with contemporary dilemmas of loneliness and life at the margins . <p> In a year that saw Samantha Harvey 's novella , Orbital , win the Booker Prize , two locally published exemplars of the short -- and in my opinion , superior -- form stood out . Melanie Cheng 's third book , The Burrow ( Text , 192pp , $32.99 ) , is an acute family drama set during Melbourne 's lockdowns , beautifully capturing the intensity of living in close quarters as the Lee family reconciles the loss of their infant daughter . It 's a tender story of grief , hope and a pet rabbit . Miranda Darling 's Thunderhead ( Scribe , 160pp , $29.99 , hardback ) is a homage to Virginia Woolf . Darling 's protagonist , Winona Dalloway , who we view through her internal monologue , is undone over the course of one day . An uncomfortable black comedy that centres on coercive control and domestic violence , it 's impossible to look away . <p> Also Woolf-adjacent is Michelle de Kretser 's latest novel , Theory &amp; Practice ( Text , 192pp , $32.99 ) , an experimental blend of fiction , essay and memoir set in mid ' 80s St Kilda . Known for balancing emotional depth and intellectual rigour , de Kretser examines the intersection of life and art , practice and theoretical concepts , making this novel a frequent feature on end-of-year book lists . Is it her best yet ? <p> Siang Lu 's second novel , Ghost Cities ( UQP , 304pp , $32.99 ) is an absurdist tale of capitalism and technology , inspired by the vacant , uninhabited megacities of China . Lu 's playful spirit , penchant for experimentation and love of language shines through in this genre-bending , dual narrative that spans ancient China and contemporary Sydney . <p> Kill Your Darlings ' annual anthology of short stories remains a highlight in the publishing year . Since Black Inc sadly stopped publishing its Best Australian Stories series , KYD is the place to find established and emerging talent . New Australian Fiction 2024 ( KYD , $29.95 ) , edited by Suzy Garcia , is a snapshot of the best writers of the form . It features well-known names such as Ceridwen Dovey and Josephine Rowe , as well as others you may not have yet had the pleasure to read . <p> Rounding out this year 's best small press offerings are two notable nonfiction books . Lech Blaine 's moving 2021 Car Crash , a reflection on surviving a car accident that killed his friends , is followed up by Australian Gospel : A Family Saga ( Black Inc , 384pp , $36.99 ) , an incredible Australian epic that follows the story of Blaine 's parents , Lenore and Tom , who foster three of the children of Christian fanatics Michael and Mary Shelley . The Blaines raise the children from infants and love them as their own . Blaine 's funny and heartbreaking recollection of the battle over the children , who the Shelleys want back and will stop at nothing to get , dwarfs fiction for drama and heroics . <p> Essayist and critic Cher Tan 's debut collection of experimental essays Peripathetic : Notes on ( un ) belonging ( NewSouth , 240pp , $34.99 ) is about artists and life at the fringes , shit jobs under capitalism and playing with identity . Tan 's essays are non-linear and fragmented , reflecting both the online experience and the geographic and cultural displacement of being Asian Australian . Tan is unapologetically punk and anti-capitalist , challenging a world where resisting orthodoxies is as important as ever and where the personal is political . <p> -- Justine Hyde <p> Black Inc is a Schwartz company <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " The best books of 2024 " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120439 <h> Fluffy pancakes with mango butterscotch sauce <p> O Tama Carey is the owner of Lankan Filling Station . Her first cookbook is Lanka Food . She is a food editor of The Saturday Paper . <p> Credit : Photography by Earl Carter <p> It was an unpleasantly sweltering day and I was doing errands , probably feeling slightly harassed . I walked into the fruit shop and was stopped in my tracks by the sweet perfume of strawberries and mangoes . It was heady and alluring , the smell of summer , and it made me smile . <p> Summer , of course , also means Christmas , which is almost upon us . No doubt many of you will have a long list of cooking tasks you need to get done , because surely you 've planned Christmas by now ? <p> At this time of the year , I am loath to give you a recipe that 's too complicated , as nobody needs that right now . Hopefully at some point soon there 'll be time for a luxurious breakfast . Luckily this recipe is simple yet does make for a fancy start to the day . <p> To the pancakes first . Although I generally avoid sweet breakfasts , I am fond of them and prone to sudden cravings at strange moments . There have been many conversations in my house as to whether what I want is a pancake or a pikelet ( or , in fact , a crepe ) , but it has now been settled with this recipe . I 'm not sure where the idea for this first came from but it is clever and good and works splendidly . You make a simple batter using just the yolks , and keep the egg whites aside to whisk separately . These then get folded into the batter , resulting in a puffy and delicate pancake ( or pikelet ) . Even better , the batter sits happily in the fridge , so if you have leftovers , you can use it the next day . <p> As for the mango sauce , it was inspired by a Korean cheong , a traditional way of making syrups by combining fruit or vegetables with sugar and letting them ferment . We once had a mango dessert on the menu at the restaurant and I thought I would try this method with the skins . We vacuum-packed the skins with sugar and within no time there was a beautiful golden liquid that we turned into a caramel sauce . For someone who has regular pancake cravings , it seemed like a perfect match . It makes me happy as it uses both the flesh and the skin of this excellent summer fruit . <p> It does n't matter how much skin you have , as all you need to do is match the weight with an equal amount of sugar . ( You can add in any seeds that have n't been sucked clean after that . ) If you are n't a pancake fan , you can use the syrup to make a cordial or cocktail , or make the butterscotch sauce for use in another dish of your choosing . It 's your summer holiday , after all , and you should be allowed to do whatever you want . <p> Ingredients <p> Time : 24 hours resting + 30 minutes cooking <p> Makes 8 pancakes <p> 2 medium mangoes <p> 110g-130g caster sugar ( approximately ) <p> 50g unsalted butter , diced and cold <p> 40ml pouring cream <p> salt flakes <p> 170g plain flour <p> ? tsp baking powder <p> 3 eggs , separated <p> 200ml full cream milk <p> pinch cooking salt <p> butter , for cooking <p> 260ml ( approximately ) pouring cream , whipped into soft peaks to serve <p> Method <p> Prepare your mangoes by first slicing away the cheeks and the remaining skin and flesh around all of the edges . Scoop out all the flesh and set aside in a container in the fridge until you are ready to serve . Reserve the seeds . <p> Weigh the mango peel , excluding the seeds , and then measure out an equal weight of caster sugar . Place the skin , sugar and seeds in a container and give it a good mix , or , if you have a vacuum sealer , use that . Let this sit at room temperature for about 24 hours or just enough so the sugar completely dissolves and you have a beautiful looking syrup . This step can be done in the fridge if you want to slow the process . <p> Run the syrup through a fine strainer into a small saucepan . Place over a medium heat and gently cook the syrup down until it thickens and looks like a caramel ( about seven to eight minutes ) . Once it is quite thick , whisk in the butter slowly and then the cream . Season with salt to your taste and set aside . <p> Meanwhile , to make the pancake batter , place the flour ( sifted if you can be bothered ) into a mixing bowl , add the baking powder and make a well in the centre . In a separate bowl , combine the egg yolks and milk and whisk just enough to combine . Slowly pour this wet mixture into the well in the flour , gently whisking and combining all the flour as you go to form a thick batter . Do n't fret if it 's a little lumpy . Place the batter to rest in the fridge for at least half an hour . <p> While you are waiting , cut your reserved mango flesh delicately into thin elegant slices and set aside until you are ready to make the pancakes . <p> Once your batter has rested , whisk your reserved egg whites with a pinch of salt until you have medium peaks on their way to being stiff . <p> Take the batter out of the fridge and , in stages , slowly fold the whites in until you have a nice even mix . <p> Place a heavy-based large frypan over a medium heat and , when hot , add in some butter ( more than you 'd expect ) . It should start to sizzle and brown fairly quickly . <p> Dollop in about 60 grams of the pancake mixture -- you can cook a few at a time if you have room . Turn the heat to high and cook for about 30 seconds before turning the heat to low and cooking for a further minute . By this stage you should have an even spread of delicate holes on top . Flip the pancakes and cook for a further minute . <p> When ready , rest your pancakes on a wire rack in a warmed oven until you have completed all the batter . <p> You can place all the pancakes on the table along with the butterscotch sauce ( take a moment to gently re-warm it first ) , the fresh mango and the cream and let your friends help themselves . Or you could plate it nicely for them , as we have done here . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Skin in the game " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120440 <h> Studying greatness at the World Chess Championship <p> " The ability to play chess is the sign of a gentleman . The ability to play chess well is the sign of a wasted life . " -- Paul Morphy <p> I can not play chess well . I am not a gentleman . I was a maintenance officer at an aged-care home when the International Chess Federation announced Singapore would host the World Chess Championship . About that time , one of the residents had suggested I read Moby-Dick . I told him I had read it as a teenager . He said , " Re-read it . You will understand it now . " <p> Something about a bookish man in his final years telling me to read Moby-Dick was more persuasive than I had anticipated . I bought a copy and began to read and soon longed for a whale of my own . Shortly after , I handed in my notice . It 's a clich ? : middle-aged maintenance man quits job to read Moby-Dick and go to World Chess Championship . That 's how I gave up a small pay cheque for a large fish . <p> To physically move all the pieces in a game of chess takes about a minute . The average game at the world championship takes between three and five hours . Most of that time is spent thinking . Even if you do n't know how to play chess , you know it is synonymous with thinking . In popular culture , it is used as a metaphor for complex strategic pursuits . As the player looks further into the future , the number of possible moves expands and the possible positions become exponentially large . People are always trying to explain how large this number is . They say things like , " If each possible position in chess was a single frozen pea , the total number of peas would fill every football ground in Australia . " <p> This year the FIDE World Chess Championship was held at Resorts World Sentosa . I arrived with a new passport and a sweaty forehead and the sense that anything could happen . It was slightly odd to be surrounded by the sounds of children on waterslides at the greatest chess tournament in the world , yet here I was . I had decided to pose as a journalist and succeeded in getting a press pass and , to do this , I bought a pair of chinos from an op shop because that 's what I assumed chess reporters wore . <p> From the outset , in the hastily converted reception centre , it was clear the action was between the reigning champion , Ding Liren from China , and the challenger , Gukesh Dommaraju from India . At 18 years old , Gukesh D had a very successful lead-up to the match and was the favourite to become the youngest world champion . Ding , by comparison , was in terrible form and had been mysteriously absent since his surprising victory against Ian Nepomniachtchi in 2023 . A series of undisclosed health issues had people seriously questioning if he would even show up to defend his title . <p> Those two weeks in Singapore were the longest time I have spent staring at someone since meeting my wife . It felt like falling in love . <p> One of these men was my whale . Perhaps both of them were . I did n't know . In Singapore , I watched them play for 35 hours . One win to Ding , one win to Gukesh , seven draws . In all there was about one hour of " action " . For the other 34 hours I watched two men sitting still and thinking . <p> Each match took place in a soundproof room with one-way mirrored glass at the front . The room also had a barrier designed to stop all electrical signals . The players could not see or hear the audience . The audience was not permitted to bring electrical devices into the playing hall . <p> The room itself looked like a pretend office . It had that weird floating ceiling that offices have . At times , Ding and Gukesh appeared like two kids on work experience . Their ill-fitting suits looked as if they were bought for a high school formal or for a funeral with the frugal anticipation of a future growth spurt . <p> Most of the crowd would watch the first 10 minutes in the silent playing area and then retreat to the outside fan zone where you could talk freely and watch the broadcast . They wanted to hear the commentators and see the evaluation bar , which shows who is winning at any point in a game based on a computer assessment of the best possible move . <p> I had n't travelled to watch it on television so , when everyone else left , I snuck into the VIP section and sat close to the glass . Most of the time , I could n't tell who was winning . The chess positions were too confusing . I would judge purely based on my amateur understanding of body language . I watched for beads of sweat , nose picking , rocking in the chair , the tapping of a foot . I convinced myself these were like poker tells . The broadcast should focus on this , I thought . There should be ultra close-up footage of twitching and discomfort . <p> Part of the joy of watching any sport is to observe the grace of an athlete moving . The pleasure is in seeing someone push the limit of what the human body can do . It is to imagine what it must feel like . Here , I was in awe of being near genius . You do n't often get to stare at an intelligent person for a long , uninterrupted period . You could almost see their giant brains , tuned for this one thing . While watching them , it was hard not to feel melancholic about all the hours they had spent leading up to this moment . I thought about what I had done with my life . I thought about the old guy from aged care , about the white whale . I thought about the Paul Morphy quote and wondered , " What 's not a waste of time ? " <p> There was a voyeuristic element to it all . The crowd is in darkness . The players are in light . The one-way glass is the same as you see for police line-ups in movies . There are hidden cameras everywhere . After the first couple of games , there were moments when the players forgot the audience was present . It was very intimate . I observed and scribbled notes in a journal , assuming that 's what chess reporters did . On arriving home and going back through my notes , I found musings like : how long would it take a person to eat Moby-Dick ? The untrained mind wanders . <p> Those two weeks in Singapore were the longest time I have spent staring at someone since meeting my wife . It felt like falling in love . I would study a player 's every move for four hours and then blush when they looked at me in the press conference afterwards . It felt like we were in a secret love triangle . A friend back in Australia asked if I was going to ask the players a funny question . He did n't understand that the intimate nature of our one-way relationship had made me very protective of both players . <p> There is a chapter in Moby-Dick where Ishmael expounds on the virtues of whaling and declares , " A whale-ship was my Yale College and my Harvard . " I thought about this as I realised the chessboard had been my TAFE . I presumed that for Ding and Gukesh it was a more prestigious institution . I wanted to ask them what they had learnt from it , but I was concerned a psychologically loaded question might put them off . <p> The final game -- game 14 -- was played last week . It appeared to be heading towards a draw , which would mean rapid tie-breaks the following day . Deep into the endgame , however , Ding blundered with Rf2 . The evaluation bar had been level for most of the game and was now completely black . This happened in a single move . A momentary lapse in concentration had handed Gukesh victory . These few seconds defined two lifetimes spent playing chess . It was such a cruel way to end the match . <p> Back in Melbourne , I kept thinking about two moments from the final press conference . One was when Gukesh said he could n't remember much from childhood . There was a video doing the rounds of a 12-year-old Gukesh saying he would like to become the world champion . The hours of chess practice are mind-boggling . Ding , when asked how he was feeling , simply said : " No game tomorrow . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Board to Gukesh " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120441 <h> The author 's battle with cancer led her to seek out the wisdom of people who have come to terms with ageing and mortality in a ' first-half-of-life culture ' . By Toni Hassan . <h> Rethinking mortality in a ' first-half-of-life culture ' <p> The day I meet with Chris Bettle , he recalls his age with incredulity . <p> " I ca n't believe I am 85 . It ca n't possibly be true , " he tells me one afternoon in his flat in the inner north of Canberra . <p> " I have been very fortunate . I am only recently fatigued . " <p> Chris , a former agricultural scientist , lives independently in a small flat bursting with images from every decade of his life : photos of favourite places and people , newspaper articles , postcards and art . <p> He grew up in the United Kingdom and came to Australia in 1964 to a career as an academic and musician . <p> Life and time move as ghosted creatures on the walls and in his mind . <p> " I had a scholarship to Cambridge but was put in the army at 19 . It was a disaster . I spent a long time in a military hospital . They gave me shock treatment . I came out a different person , " he says . " I hope I will pop off in the middle of the night , rather than get dementia and have to be in an institution , where people can do nothing for years . " <p> How strange for people to think it 's all right for you to be doing nothing all day , and that you ought to be able to cope with that , as if coded with a use-by date , like milk . <p> The recent Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety showed a disturbing incapacity in our mainstream culture to see and promote the value of age and the important role older people play in the community . That 's even as Australia is getting better at recognising the wisdom of Indigenous elders . <p> Ageism is , the commission heard , like sexism and racism , embedded in many of the ways we interact . <p> My own mortality came as a rude awakening when I was being treated for an aggressive and rare cancer in 2023 , diagnosed at age 50 . It was an entree into a world of chronic pain and limitations -- features of life and ageing that remain , I think , largely invisible in our public conversations , and inextricable , given we can feel old whatever our age . <p> As Franciscan Father Richard Rohr writes , " We live in a first half-of-life culture " , which makes the search for wisdom all the more necessary . <p> My navigation of oesophageal cancer happened to coincide with conversations called " Ageing : The Shared Journey " , initiated by the Benedictus Contemplative Church . <p> People from around the world were connecting on Zoom to consider questions about where we are and where we are headed . <p> The series began with a simple activity : " Complete the sentence : For me ageing is ... " The answers proved refreshing , as hopes and fears around ageing were ventilated . <p> For me , a participant shared , ageing is confronting . <p> It is , for me , living a secluded life . <p> It can feel isolating and yet it is so universal -- like human suffering , a connector . <p> Others said : <p> For me , ageing is the strengthof the body weakening but the inner life deepening . <p> For me , it feels like a strange shift in awareness . <p> It is like the composting process , internally and emotionally . <p> Someone piped up with a decisive response : Let the worms begin ! <p> The same session included a prompt to summarise , in a few words , each of life 's decades , perhaps to become conscious of the shape of things . Is that shape a long , unerring line or something more interesting ? <p> In her celebrated book The Gift of Years : Growing Older Graciously , Joan Chittister , then 70 , wrote , " My life has been nothing but a series of new beginnings . " <p> " Every life is simply a series of lives , each one of them with its own task , its own flavour ... its own glories , its own deep , dank despair ... all designed to lead us to the same end -- happiness and a sense of fulfilment . <p> " Death can come at any time . Age only comes to those who are truly blessed ... These later years are a gift , not a burden ... Old age enlightens -- not simply ourselves , as important as that may be , but those around us as well . " <p> In my recovery , I travelled down the mighty Hume Highway from Canberra to Melbourne with a woman nearing her 80s -- Honey Nelson , a former veterinarian , often barefoot , whom I met through a climate change activist movement . <p> I posed to Honey the opening prompt of the online series : " Ageing is ... " <p> " ... is bits falling off and a discernible loss of short-term memory , " she replied . <p> Honey 's husband died after prolonged suffering caused by a cycling accident . She uses humour to express the inner fire of the human spirit , even from atop a mountain of grief : personal , social and environmental . <p> " Ageing offers gratitude for what 's been , including the dodgy bits . " <p> Honey had cancer yonks ago and , like so many other people , was skittled but also made more empathic and anchored . " Cancer brought on a self-adjudication , a distilling of the self . " <p> She spoke , as Chris Bettle did , of feeling socially abandoned . " Society stops listening . That 's a form of isolation also . " <p> This phase is not a postscript but a vital part of life , as vital as any other . How do you enter it with purpose in a culture that valorises youth as " influencers " and places no value on unpaid work ? <p> Philip Huggins , now 75 , was forced to retire from his profession as an Anglican bishop five years ago . Many dioceses have a mandatory age limit , between 65 and 70 . <p> " By my vocation , I have been around death a lot . It 's vivid , " he says . " I thought to myself , I have spent all my life trying to live with the Spirit . I do n't think it is retiring . " <p> Huggins was inspired to do something for his grandchildren , which led to climate action advocacy . We observed together that having value-based goals , whatever one 's age , drives purpose and spurns despair . <p> " There are different stages of old age . If you have energy and health , you will have networks to be energised by and to energise , " Huggins tells me . <p> His retirement also shifted his relationships . " If you have a demanding job you always have more to do than you can do . When the pressure is off , it 's a wonderful opportunity to find balance , especially relational balance . " <p> This has already been the case for me . Cancer offered , unexpectedly , a chance to deepen friendships and to see what needed mending and be brave about it . <p> There are two movements of a rounded life . First , gathering up memories , stories , wisdom , understanding , naming regrets . Then , letting go of old roles , wounds , expectations ... and surrendering . <p> A participant online said the second phase involves " apprenticing yourself into your own disappearance " . Yes . I can see that . <p> When I was hibernating in bed , often in a sea of nausea , unable to eat , I was offered an apprenticeship into my truer self , tuition that dissolved my physical boundaries . Cancer was like a paint stripper , thinning my identity in the world . Suddenly everything mattered and nothing mattered . <p> For me , ageing is less grasping and more being . It is less about having a career and more about creating spaces for life to move forward . <p> Honey , of faith and no particular faith , guards herself in retirement with a gratitude practice . Her body , she says , is a " vessel for ethos " -- guiding beliefs that lead her to be thankful . I observe too , with awe , that she remains sprightly , even on the wild edge of sorrow . <p> " When deprived of physical latitude , my mind and spirit move forward to explore and wonder . Appreciation is a way of seeing things , a good way to do the continuum of life . Gratitude and beauty do not sit in opposition to what angers us or concerns us . Birds are town criers , they also sing for joy . " <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " New age " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120442 <h> Returning from travels , the gardener finds the wild profusion of growth that summer entails , and her place in the work of taming and protecting . By Margaret Simons . <h> Mutiny in the bounty <p> There is nothing in nature that mandates the things we do at this time of year -- the pressure to complete all our work , to prepare our houses , to cook feasts . Nothing says that , having climbed those mountains , we should then be prepared to relax , to be joyful , or even -- that awful word , usually a euphemism for foolish and fat -- jolly . <p> Nor is there anything to say that , after a few days of excess and mandatory cheer , we should enter the reflective , self-critical state of composing resolutions for the new year . <p> Christmas is a construct . New Year is an arbitrary mark on the calendar . Previous cultures have determined the new year to be as early as November , or as late as March . The one fixed thing , the thing you can not deny , is the solstice -- the time when the sun reaches its most northerly or southerly excursion . That is fixed , although it does not fall on Christmas Day , but a little before . Nevertheless , that is the reason the world 's great religions all have festivals around this time . <p> In the northern hemisphere , it is the time to feast to keep out the cold , to eat up the dried fruit and the suet and the preserved plum puddings , to slaughter the fatted beast . It is the low point of the year and an expression of faith that resurrection -- spring -- will surely come . <p> Here in the southern hemisphere , it is the opposite . This is the time of stupendous growth , of stuff -- weeds , vegetables , flowers -- running out of control . The time when plans come to their fulfilment , or else must be abandoned . The time when things feel both bountiful and vaguely threatening . <p> I have recently arrived home after six weeks overseas , and it hit me in the face . Coming back from the airport in the taxi , I saw that the new apartment blocks around the corner , which were just a hole in the ground when I left , had become a 15-storey framework . <p> Hundreds of living spaces for hundreds of people -- my future neighbours -- delineated if not yet divided by plasterboard , brick and glass . I felt like I had missed a chapter in the story of my place , my people . My head swam with jet lag . <p> We turned the corner into my street , and I alarmed the driver by shouting out , " My god ! The kale ! " <p> Because my house-sitter , having read this column , had taken it to heart and , far from allowing the cabbage white caterpillars their feast , had sprayed them . The kale had grown lush and tall . One plant leant over the footpath , making it difficult to get my suitcases through the front door . The other fenestrated the fence in curly green waves . <p> In fact , there was no bare soil showing in the front garden . Almost everything had grown beyond my expectations . The tomato plants I shoved in the week before I left were sprawling everywhere but with neat clusters of green globes signalling that I might well achieve that marker of success : homegrown tomatoes on the Christmas table . <p> Cucumber plants were climbing every trellis except the one I intended for them . Beans were romping through the branches of the crabapple tree and the leeks had stopped sulking and gained girth and height . <p> Who knows what that heat and wind will bring ? By the time you read this , we may all be talking about fires . We may be talking about the way we have altered the eternal round of the seasons . We may be not celebrating but in a collective lament . <p> When I got to the backyard , it was the same -- except the weeds had also burgeoned . The path from back door to back gate was overgrown and the oxalis had sprouted between the bricks . <p> The bay tree , meant to be a contained specimen suitable for culinary purposes only , was nearly level with the second-floor windows . <p> Jet lag defeated my initial attempts to restore order . I kept dropping the trowel and the secateurs and going to bed . The sun was up when my body said it should be night . My night was full of awakenings . My dreams were fearful . The garden grew up through the floorboards , and the cucumber vines came in through the windows . Oxalis smothered me in my bed . <p> I was being punished . How could I have gone away ? How could I have missed the beats , the demands of the season , in this , my place , my responsibility -- the sweet burden of home ? <p> Over the past two days , I got stuck in . I slashed the kale , dunked it in the sink and ate it . First I made salad , wilting it with salt then dressing it with honey and oil . Then I braised it with garlic and lemon juice and tahini . I ate the front path clear , and advanced on the carpet of kale that was taking up a quarter of my front yard . <p> Then I got out the Roundup and the little make-up paint brush that somebody left behind and dotted poison on the oxalis in the footpath . I ripped up old underwear and a cotton scarf , coaxed the tomato plants into upright positions and bound them to their stakes . I encouraged the cucumbers to occupy their own trellis , but I mostly accepted their choices . <p> What to plant in the spaces now created ? Amid all the plenty , some things are missing . The lettuce has long since bolted to seed . Likewise the coriander . The basil somehow escaped being watered and died . <p> Normally I grow my lettuce from seed and make sure I have a constant supply , sowing more as one lot matures . But now I want instant results . <p> So I drive to Bunnings and , as I always do in that temple of home and self-improvement , buy more than I have room for . A punnet of mixed lettuce . A mature capsicum . Eggplant seedlings because -- why not ? Surely they will fit somewhere . A dill plant for which I have no home in mind , but who can resist that feathery foliage ? There should be more dill in the world . <p> Pagan religions teach that there is no light , no plenty , without its opposite . Darkness and deprivation . <p> Now the evil side of summer approaches . I will not plant out these seedlings today because tomorrow is predicted to top 40 degrees , with high winds . Putting these tender plants into the garden would be certain death . I might as well put them in the oven . <p> Who knows what that heat and wind will bring ? By the time you read this , we may all be talking about fires . We may be talking about the way we have altered the eternal round of the seasons . We may be not celebrating but in a collective lament . <p> For now , though , the tray of seedlings sits on my kitchen table by the window . I will nurture them through the heat and when the cool change arrives they will go into the soil . At the end of the day , I will stand with my back to the house , hose in hand , bringing relief to the garden . <p> It is less than a week since I got home . Of course I am not ready for Christmas . I have barely unpacked . <p> But I am dirty and tired , rather than only tired . I have tomato leaves in my hair and soil in the calluses of my fingers . The green bin is overflowing and there is kale salad in the fridge . <p> I am not jolly . I am not even reliably cheerful . But I am back where I belong , part of my own story once more . In my own little patch of dirt . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Mutiny in the bounty " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@119120443 <h> The Spanish Civil War drew volunteers from far and wide in the fight against fascism -- today its history has become emblematic of struggles around the world . By Kurt Johnson . <h> The art of not forgetting in Barcelona <p> We 're running late . By the time we have woven through central Barcelona 's warren of alleys and plazas to reach Pla ? a de Sant Felip Neri , the square 's entrance is fenced off by a flimsy yellow barricade . Beyond , a dozen schoolkids squeal and chase a ball over the grimy paving stones , dodging around a dormant fountain where a lone girl sits . Except for a few leafless trees , nothing dampens the crack as the ball ricochets against the fa ? ade of the Sant Felip Neri church , its sandstone rudely gouged and cratered . From behind the barricade our guide , historian Nick Lloyd , explains that on the morning of January 30 , 1938 , Italian fascist aeroplanes bombed the church , which was being used as an air-raid shelter . Everything but the fa ? ade collapsed , burying all inside . <p> The children playing around us make this history very real and one of our party hangs back , moved to tears . Lloyd compares this bombing to the conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza , joining the present day to the Spanish Civil War , a conflict that presaged World War II , drew volunteers from around the globe and cost half a million lives . A panel fixed to the wall recounts the bombing in Catalan , Castilian and English . The panel also notes that for 35 years Franco 's regime explained the brutalised fa ? ade as a site where priests were executed . <p> Lloyd is originally from Stockport , Greater Manchester , and has retained a northern lilt , which in his lively accounts takes on the cadence of a union leader addressing a crowd of comrades . Among the dozen Americans and Canadians who now fill the alley are a socialist , a retired human rights lawyer and a labour organiser . Michelle from Seattle interviewed Abe Osheroff , a member of the Lincoln Brigade of 3000 Americans who travelled to Spain in 1937 to fight fascism . Tim came after reading about Chinese volunteers -- " mostly medics " , he tells me -- who served on the Republican side . Everyone has come with curiosity , hoping that place may provide the answers missing in books . <p> We started out in the crowded Pla ? a de Catalunya , where the jostling signage of overtourism obscures a historical record warped by what scholars now call " Spanish-style fascism " . Lloyd fishes out a black-and-white photograph of the Hotel Col ? n , which today is draped in an advertisement for the new Samsung Galaxy , but back then was bedecked with portraits of Stalin and Lenin , and a Catalan banner declaring allegiance to the Comintern . We consider a plinth pockmarked with bullet holes , proving that here in July 1936 the Pla ? a de Catalunya was engulfed in violent street battles . <p> Lloyd says there is nothing new about the outside world projecting its own struggles onto the Spanish Civil War , which he calls " the most international conflict in any one country " . <p> Lloyd connects the bustling present to history 's stills , animating black and white with powerful quotes and personal accounts . He calls this tour a " walking museum " , and over its 15 years he has filled a bulging tote bag with photographs , maps , postcards and artefacts , such as a lighter embedded with a bullet ( we do n't know if the owner survived ) . A hand-drawn placard decodes the constellation of leftist political parties that ranged from social democrats to Stalinists and anarchists -- a precarious balance that imploded , playing right into Franco 's hands . <p> A walking museum is important in a country where no dedicated cultural institution memorialises its civil war . A National Museum of the Battle of Teruel and the Civil War is currently under construction , but has become the focus of disputes between right-wing regional governments and the socialist national government , casting doubt on the project 's future . <p> This contest over history is longstanding . After Franco died in 1975 , Spain transitioned to democracy with the Pact of Forgetting , a political decision that led to a 1977 amnesty for perpetrators of political violence and forbade the exhumation of the mass graves that the regime filled with up to 114,000 of its " disappeared " enemies . This continued right up until 2007 , when the Historical Memory Law was passed to recognise these victims . Fifteen years later , the Democratic Memory Law made the government responsible for recovering and identifying them . The right has opposed these laws , and today three autonomous regions are proposing " harmony laws " seeking to undermine the task of investigating and memorialising . <p> At the beginning of the tour , Lloyd asked why we came . Answers included historical curiosity , political interest and one fanboy tracing the footsteps of Orwell ( me ) . More than one American wondered aloud whether what happened here could soon happen back home . <p> " At least Trump won decisively , so there wo n't be a civil war , this time at least , " a woman whispers to me . <p> Lloyd later tells me such concerns are coming up more often among his groups , " after the first Trump victory but also the feeling in the last few years of an impending civil war " . He says there is nothing new about the outside world projecting its own struggles onto the Spanish Civil War , which he calls " the most international conflict in any one country " . <p> When we stop at the cavernous cafe Granja Dulcinea , to escape the chill with coffee and churros dipped in thick chocolate , he explains how 35,000 volunteers from around the world took up the struggle against fascism -- and in some cases for it . He shows photographs of volunteers , among them nurses from Australia and an overexposed pic from the Battle of the Ebro showing Sydneysider Jack Walker and Bert Bryan from New Zealand firing into the scrub . The overexposure reflects the heat of battle , Lloyd says . <p> Most volunteers arrived from Europe , cast out by the Great Depression and political turmoil . Lloyd paraphrases historian Helen Graham : " Those young boys from the new states of the old Austro -- Hungarian Empire -- and by extension Germany , Poland , Greece and Italy -- whose lives had been made a misery by local fascist bullyboys in provincial towns and are now living rather precarious lives in the Western democracies , wanted nothing better than to get even with those fellas ... how could they do it ? To Spain . " <p> The sentiment and ensuing horrors were immortalised in the era 's art and literature by the likes of Picasso , Hemingway and , of course , George Orwell . Almost all of us on the tour have read Orwell 's gonzo account of the war in Homage to Catalonia , and we are guided to salient locations such as the Hotel Continental , whose roof Orwell guarded while fighting for the anarchist POUM party . Lloyd explains that the POUM unit was desperately underequipped , echoing Orwell 's experiences of his unit 's high morale but shambolic organisation . Yet these experiences of war and its aftermath shaped Orwell 's politics and later writing . The rats that scurried over him in the Aragon trench surely seeded his nightmare vision of Room 101 in 1984 , and the betrayal of a worker 's movement by Stalin-backed communists led him to identify the distinction between truth and lies as the basis for opposing totalitarianism . <p> But the central figure in Lloyd 's tour is Francisco Boix , who he first saw memorialised on a plaque in his neighbourhood of El Poble-sec . Boix was a professional photographer who fought for the Republican side , before fleeing to France where he fought the Nazis . He was captured and deported to the infamous Austrian Mauthausen concentration camp , where his work in a photo lab allowed him to smuggle out negatives that became crucial evidence in the Nuremberg trials . <p> Lloyd recently designed a dedicated Boix walking tour in Catalan for locals in conjunction with his library , which specialises in books on the Spanish Civil War and the Holocaust . For the tour guide , Boix 's story sets Spain within the broader European , and indeed global , contest between remembering and forgetting historical trauma . <p> In front of the library is a dedication to Boix on a Stolperstein , or stumbling stone -- the cobblestones bearing brass plaques that are dotted throughout Europe to commemorate the Holocaust 's victims . Stumbling serves as a reminder , and the stones embed history in place , as Lloyd wants his tour to do . To him , history is " the art of not forgetting " . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on December 21 , 2024 as " Art of not forgetting " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . We have pursued stories that are ignored elsewhere , covering them with sensitivity and depth . We have done this on refugee policy , on government integrity , on robo-debt , on aged care , on climate change , on the pandemic . <p> All our journalism is fiercely independent . It relies on the support of readers . By subscribing to The Saturday Paper , you are ensuring that we can continue to produce essential , issue-defining coverage , to dig out stories that take time , to doggedly hold to account politicians and the political class . <p> There are very few titles that have the freedom and the space to produce journalism like this . In a country with a concentration of media ownership unlike anything else in the world , it is vitally important . Your subscription helps make it possible . 
@@119120444 <h> The Olympics burst back from Covid restrictions with French flair , Lions roared , Panthers pounced and a teen named Gout Gout ran very fast -- this was the world of sport in 2024 . By Martin McKenzie-Murray . <h> A year of positives in sport <p> The Olympics returned , and so did the spectators , liberated this year from the Covid restrictions that both delayed the previous games and cruelled Tokyo 's atmosphere . <p> Just weeks before the opening ceremony , France denied its president a refreshed majority , conferring instead a hung National Assembly and a patchwork coalition . Nevertheless , the country successfully acquitted two great public works : the impressively swift restoration of Notre-Dame and one of the world 's largest sporting events . <p> Down the Seine -- troubled briefly by heightened " faecal contamination " , which obliged the delay of the men 's individual triathlon -- the Olympians made their novel entrance to what would become Australia 's most successful games and a medal glut dominated by women . <p> Raygun immediately achieved folkloric status , though at the cost of the world 's incredulity and ridicule , and has since acquired a talent agent while scrambling to seize the various intellectual properties of her infamous performances . <p> An impressive Olympics all round , but back home came an excoriating report into the cancelled 2026 Victorian Commonwealth Games . About the " decisions to bid for , plan and then withdraw from the Games " , which " cost Victoria over $589 million with no discernible benefit " , the state 's auditor-general wrote : " This waste of taxpayer money on an event that will not happen is significant , especially considering the state 's recent sustained operating deficits and rising debt . " <p> The decision to bid was impulsive , and helped by the superficially optimistic advice of servile agencies . In September , it was announced that Glasgow would instead host a modestly narrowed competition . Increasingly unattractive to potential hosts , the future of the Commonwealth Games is uncertain . <p> This month , FIFA confirmed what had been long assumed : that Saudi Arabia would host the 2034 men 's World Cup . Unlike the Commonwealth Games , the FIFA World Cup is typically the prize of ultra-competitive and often dubious global bidding and then a vote among members , but for this tournament it was a fait accompli for the Saudis . Creatively , FIFA president Gianni Infantino described the absence of a vote as a virtue . " In a divided world you have shown unity , you have shown that we are part of a global community , " he said . " We are not all equal , we know that , but we are learning to live with our differences and to respect each other . " <p> The 2030 men 's World Cup will be co-hosted by Spain , Portugal and Morocco . <p> As a neutral , I pray the Spurs fans and board might keep the faith with their stubbornly romantic manager . <p> In the WNBA , Iowa University guard Caitlin Clark was chosen by the Indiana Fever as the league 's first draft pick . She was the WNBA 's rookie of the year , led the league in assists and this month was named Time magazine 's Athlete of the Year . A white woman in a predominantly Black league who has enjoyed -- or suffered -- conspicuous attention , Clark has inspired countless columns arguing either that her fame corresponds with her talent or the colour of her skin . " I want to say I 've earned every single thing , but as a white person , there is privilege , " she told Time . " A lot of those players in the league that have been really good have been Black players . This league has kind of been built on them . " <p> Offered diplomatically , Clark 's comments are now being debated for their alleged abjection , condescension or superficiality . She may be a wealthy superstar , but Clark also has the uncomfortable and involuntary role of racial totem and Rorschach test . <p> On a humid evening in late November , the AFLW 's North Melbourne won their maiden premiership by completing the first ever undefeated footy season by either men or women . Beneath the lights of Princes Park , the Kangaroos humiliated the Brisbane Lions , who managed only one goal to North 's six . Jasmine Garner won best on ground and was described as a generational talent afterwards by her coach , Darren Crocker . " We 'll look back in 50 years ' time to this period of AFLW , and Jas Garner will be right at the very , very top of the tree as just one of the best players in the AFLW 's infancy , " he said . <p> There was another humiliation in the men 's AFL grand final , when the minor premiers , the Sydney Swans , capitulated spectacularly for the second time in a GF in just three years . The game was effectively over by quarter time , as the Brisbane Lions -- defeated in last year 's decider by just four points -- throttled their opponents . In the end , the 60-point loss seemed flattering . <p> The Swans have been one of the most impressively consistent AFL teams this century , but let me narrow the focus to the tenure of senior coach John Longmire , who was appointed in 2011 . Since then , the Swans have contested five grand finals , been minor premiers three times and failed to make the top eight only twice . There is , however , a painful qualification to their dominance : those five grand finals have yielded just one flag , in 2012 , and the Swans have now lost four consecutive deciders -- often emphatically . Last month , Longmire suddenly quit . " Whilst my head was trying to talk myself into keep going to the end of next year , my gut was saying , ' That 's about enough , ' ? " he said . " It 's time to rest . " <p> In the NRL grand final , arguably the finest team ever assembled , the Penrith Panthers , defeated Melbourne Storm to claim a historic fourth consecutive premiership in what was their fifth consecutive decider . In the NRL era , nothing closely compares . Funnyman and Penrith tragic James Colley wrote sweetly about his gratitude : " What do we say , staring down a fourth premiership ? I ca n't tell you to reach out and grab immortality , you already have it . I ca n't say to do it for the fans . You 've already given us so much . All I can say is thank you for letting us live the dream of every fanbase . " <p> The NRL season opened with two games in Las Vegas , the perfect place to launch a " product " that its chief administrator , Peter V'landys , has not been shy about wanting to inject with American gambling and broadcast revenue . " The opportunity is there for sports betting , " V'landys said this year . " The Super Bowl alone held over $23 billion , so there 's a market here for sports betting as well . And this is all about raising revenue for the game so we can put it all back into juniors , participation and the clubs . " <p> Eighteen months ago , the Albanese government pledged to cap what has long become a proliferation of sports gambling ads . The partial ban was only a modest acknowledgement of a parliamentary inquiry that recommended a total prohibition , but still no legislation has been introduced to parliament . The government has asked for patience , but independent MP Andrew Wilkie was obviously without any when he described the delay as " one of the most shocking betrayals of the community I 've seen in my 14 years in parliament " . <p> Tottenham Hotspur 's Ange Postecoglou , the first and only Australian to have managed an English Premier League side , continued to suffer the slings and arrows of outraged pundits as Spurs fans suffered their team 's dramatic fluctuations of form . Currently sitting 10th in the league , Spurs are no worse off than under their previous two managers and are playing infinitely more attractive soccer . As a neutral , I pray the Spurs fans and board might keep the faith with their stubbornly romantic manager . <p> The abrasive and swashbuckling Australian opener David Warner retired this year from international cricket . Warner distinguished himself with a heroically aggressive bat and found disgrace in the great ball-tampering scandal of 2018 . Settling upon his Test replacement is still vexing selectors . <p> Matildas goalkeeper Lydia Williams retired at the age of 36 , after almost two decades of international soccer . " I actually vomited twice in that match . Once right in front of where she was sitting . " It means that banks are funding fossil fuels without funding the projects directly . " <p> Paul O'Sullivan says the ANZ wants to support an orderly energy transition for business customers . " <p> Ms Tu said activists intend to keep up the pressure on banks to make sure their executives know the risks that come with financing oil and gas companies . <p> " Their public perception is important to them - most people would n't want to know that their money is funding fossil fuels , " she said .

@@119123304 <p> There 's a field in Wiscasset , Maine ( Population 3,742 ) protected by armed guards . On the field is a chain link fence surrounding a pad of concrete . On the pad are 60 cement and steel canisters that contain 1,400 spent nuclear fuel rods , the leavings of a power plant that shut down almost 30 years ago . <p> The containers are full of nuclear waste . The locals do n't love it , but there 's nowhere for it to go . The issue of what to do with America 's nuclear waste is a problem that 's solved in theory but stalled in practice thanks to a decades-long political fight . The country needs more power , and faster , and tech companies such as Google , Microsoft , Meta , and Amazon all announced this year that they 're moving forward with plans to go nuclear . <p> That means there 's going to be more nuclear waste than ever before . Where will it go ? If the current system holds , it 'll be stored near the reactors . Right now , nuclear waste is put in stainless steel containers and sealed in a concrete structure called a dry cask . Dry casks are , by all accounts , remarkably safe . If they 're undisturbed , they could remain so for centuries . <p> But the world is not static . The climate is changing . Wildfires , earthquakes , and rising ocean levels pose a threat to those dry casks . An earthquake , flood , or fire swallowing up one or two dry casks might not cause a problem . But there 's about to be more of them . <h> Big Tech 's nuclear push <p> America 's nuclear waste is piling up . It 's a political problem , not a scientific one . Other countries with nuclear infrastructure bury their waste deep underground in specially designed storage facilities called deep geological repositories . We could do that in America . We even started building one . The problem is that no one wants a giant cave filled with nuclear waste in their backyard . <p> It 's hard to blame them . The U.S. has a terrible track record when it comes to handling waste . For years , we 'd store it in barrels and dump it into the sea . Waste leftover from the Manhattan Project is still poisoning people today . In South Carolina , radioactive alligators once roamed the Savannah River Site where pieces of nuclear weapons were made . The Hanford Site in Washington state is sitting on 54 million gallons of waste that may never be cleaned up . <p> To meet Big Tech 's energy demands , we 'll add more to the pile . <p> 2024 was the year Big Tech went all in on nuclear energy . Data centers are power-hungry beasts and the increased use of number-crunching artificial intelligence systems means that tech companies need more energy than ever before . To solve the problem , Meta , Google , Microsoft , and Amazon are all betting on nuclear energy . <p> Microsoft , who has been working on this for a long time , is partnered with TerraPower to build SMRs . It also announced a partnership with Constellation Energy that would reopen the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant in Pennsylvania . <p> Nuclear power is hard to do . Its fuel sources are rare and heavily regulated . When it works , it provides clean and efficient fuel for millions of people . When it goes wrong , it 's a disaster that can help topple governments and give cancer to millions . Traditional reactors require billions in investment and decades of construction time . <p> But Big Tech is n't looking to go the traditional route . They 're talking about new kinds of reactors . " There 's been a talk of a renaissance for decades . Depending on who you talk to , we could be in our third or fourth renaissance , or our eighth or ninth . So let 's leave the R-word aside , " Cindy Vestergaard , a senior fellow and director of Converging Technologies for the Stimson Center , told Gizmodo . Vestergaard is a nuclear supply chain expert who focuses on nonproliferation . <p> When people think of nuclear power they often picture the enormous cooling towers and sprawling complexes filled with scientists . The dream of SMRs is that they could do away with much of that . There are dozens of designs , but the basic concept is that these new reactors would be tiny compared to traditional reactors ( some of them would even be portable ) and can be spun up and decommissioned to match the demands of the grid . <p> " A lot of these designs have been around for decades , " Vestergaard said . It 's just that the economic incentives did n't exist to make them a reality . Thanks to climate change and the demands of Big Tech , that 's changed . " Solar and wind are great in many ways , but they need to be supplemented . " <p> Big Tech may understand business , but energy companies are a whole different thing . " We have a newbie engaging in this ... which means we have a lag time in what it all means , " Vestergaard said . " They have a lot of money , so deep pockets , I think , help drive a lot of innovation going forward that we would not have seen in the past . So I think that gives them a nuclear leg-up ... most investors do not understand the long game in nuclear . " <p> The pitch for many of these SMRs is also that they 're safer and they 'll produce less waste . Vestergaard is n't so sure . " We hear ' oh , they 're safer , they 're more efficient . ' Well , we do n't know that . Maybe on paper . We have to test and demonstrate this . " <p> I reached out to Google , Amazon , Meta , Microsoft , and some of their nuclear power partners to see how they 're thinking about how to manage waste . Meta and Microsoft referred me to posts on their websites about sustainability . Amazon told me to reach out to its energy partners . Google did n't respond . <p> Of Big Tech 's partners , only TerraPower -- who is working with Microsoft -- got back to us . It said that its Natrium reactors will produce more energy and less waste than any other reactor on the planet . " The Natrium technology will reduce the volume of waste per megawatt hour of energy produced by two-thirds because of the efficiency with which it uses fuel , " it said . " The waste the Natrium reactor does produce will be stored safely and securely onsite through proven methods used at plants throughout the country until the United States identifies a permanent geologic repository . " <p> TerraPower identified the core problem of nuclear waste in the U.S. The government needs to identify a permanent geologic repository . It 's having trouble doing that . <h> Not in my backyard <p> According to Vestergaard , Big Tech may not be ready for something it 's been bad at in the past -- dealing with an angry populace . " The local populations pay billions into these huge infrastructure projects , " she said . " Big tech , historically , has not had a good sense of what it 's like to have engagement at the local level . That 's another thing where they 're going to have to learn , and adjust , and adapt to public hearings . " <p> People come out when nuclear waste enters their backyards . The risk of cancer , radioactive animals , and environmental destruction is real . And people know it . <p> These reactors will be built in someone 's backyard . Several of the companies are talking about building them on-site , next to data centers . Taxpayer cash will go towards these reactors and it 'll expect to get something in return . Not all the power can go to the data centers and large language models . <p> It 'll all generate waste . Waste with nowhere to go . After decades of mismanagement , the federal government attempted to get hold of America 's nuclear waste problem in the 1980s . Its solution was to build a deep geological repository in Yucca Mountain , Nevada . It even started construction . The people of Nevada , who have long borne the brunt of America 's nuclear ambitions , did n't want it there . <p> " In the United States , there 's never really been public consent . It 's not like they went to Nevada and said ' What if we put it here ? What do you guys think about it ? ' " Vestergaard said . " The United States itself is incredibly split and stuck on its nuclear waste problem , So there 's a law , back from the 80s , that says it 's got ta be at Yucca Mountain . <p> She added that , at this point , America has enough nuclear waste waiting around to fill Yucca Mountain three times over . " So even if Yucca Mountain was still a viable option , it is n't . Particularly for new nuclear reactors that would be coming on board , " she said . <p> The same law that designated Yucca Mountain as the site of future nuclear waste also created the Office of the United States Nuclear Waste Negotiator . The idea was that this office would negotiate with states and tribal leaders in the U.S. to find an interim storage solution for nuclear waste . Created in 1987 , the position was n't filled until 1990 . It was eliminated in 1995 . <p> One of the problems is that , according to the laws , nuclear waste can no longer be stored in a state or patch of tribal land without the consent of the people who live there . And no one wants it . So instead of going to a central location for permanent disposal , it sits on sites near where it 's made , some 94 locations and growing . <h> Kissing casks <p> Science and nuclear influencers love to kiss nuclear waste . " I kissed a cask ( of nuclear waste ) and I liked it , " Isabelle Boemeke , known as Isodope online , said in a post on X on December 19 . The attached pictures show her kissing a dry cask filled with nuclear waste . <p> Boemeke is one of a number of nuclear influencers who use their platform to agitate for more nuclear power . The kissing a cask of nuclear waste stunt is popular among science YouTubers and the only thing strange about Boemeke 's post is that it 's come after so many other people have done it . <p> " Yes , dry casks are incredibly safe , " Vestergaard said . " I put my hand on them as well and stood by them . " <p> The problem is not that casks are n't a great way to store nuclear waste , they are , it 's that they stick around on the site where the waste was made . Boemeke 's pic was at the Diablo Canyon Power Plant in California . The plant is California 's last operational nuclear power site and the state planned to shut it down . <p> Then Boemeke and Grimes started making PSAs online about why it needed to remain . It worked . Regulators voted to extend the life of Diablo Canyon to at least 2030 . That means the site will generate more nuclear waste . Waste which will remain on site . Diablo Canyon is next to major fault lines . It 's near San Luis Obispo , a community now perennially threatened by wildfires . The San Onofre nuclear power plant south of Los Angeles sits on a major faultline . It 's also sitting on 3.6 million pounds of nuclear waste . <p> For some experts , the dry casks are a fine solution and the benefits of nuclear power generation far outweigh the negatives of nuclear waste . " Climate change is a clear and present danger of global scale with a wide range of damaging impacts on geologic time scales , " Jesse D. Jenkins , an Assistant Professor at Princeton University , said in a post about nuclear waste on BlueSky . " Small volumes of spent nuclear fuel can be contained safely in dry cask storage for century+ time scales . " <p> " The entire history of US civilian nuclear power , which has produced 1/5th of our electricity for decades with no CO2 or air pollution , has produced less than 100,000 tons of high-level waste . We burn billions of tons of fossil fuels EVERY YEAR , " Jenkins said . " That means the entirety of spent nuclear fuel fits in less than 10,000 dry casks ... That 's it . All of it . And this is ' the nuclear waste problem ' that means we should supposedly eschew this proven source of emissions-free electricity ? Nah . " <p> I am not arguing that we should n't adopt nuclear energy . Jenkins and others are right . Dry casks are mostly safe . But I do think nuclear waste is a problem . And more reactors mean more spent fuel that needs to be managed , more dry casks spread across the country , and more armed guards on patrol like those in that field in Maine . <p> A 2024 report from the Government Accountability Office uncovered something shocking . The Nuclear Regulatory Commission , the government agency that manages waste , has n't studied the effects of climate change on the dry casks and nuclear power plants . <p> " NRC primarily uses historical data in its licensing and oversight processes rather than climate projections data , " the report said . When the GAO interviewed officials at the Commission , they told investigators that they had it under control . " However , NRC has not conducted an assessment to demonstrate that this is the case , " the report said . <p> The report detailed the hazards facing nuclear power plants . " According to our analysis of U.S. Forest Service and NRC data , about 20 percent of nuclear power plants ( 16 of 75 ) are located in areas with a high or very high potential for wildfire . " More than sixty percent of nuclear power plants , 47 of 75 , are located in areas with exposure to Category 4 and 5 hurricanes and in an area where NOAA predicted the sea levels will rise . <p> Big Tech is going to build more nuclear power plants . Oil and gas are dirty sources of power . Nuclear has the potential to be much cleaner and more efficient . Nuclear energy is also mostly safe , the problem is that when things go bad they go catastrophically bad . More reactors mean more points of failure and more waste . Waste that 's in need of a permanent home . <p> One can only hope that the same lobbyists Big Tech rolls out whenever it needs something done in Washington can help them find a permanent home for America 's spent nuclear fuel .

Credit : Janie Barrett <p> Forestry Corp and the National Parks and Wildlife Service revealed on Friday they had entered into a legally enforceable agreement worth up to $1 million over the illegal clearing of 1.44 hectares of mature gum trees in Bindarri National Park near Coffs Harbour in 2019 . <p> The national park , which was created in 1999 , adjoins the world heritage-listed Dorrigo National Park , and there are long-held plans to add it to the listing . It included some of the former plantation . <p> Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water secretary Anthony Lean said in a statement that it was a " very serious offence " , but he defended a decision not to prosecute . <p> Bangalore Falls in Bindarri National Park.Credit : Janie Barrett <p> " The deed imposes significant obligations on Forestry Corporation to ensure we get a better outcome than would have been secured through litigation , " Lean said . <p> Advertisement <p> This includes Forestry Corp 's agreement to pay up to $495,000 to fund , restore and remediate the harvested area over the next 10 years . The state-owned business will also pay $500,000 to NPWS for purchasing native forest or to reserve an agreed area of state forest as national park . <p> Forestry Corp said in a statement that it regretted and apologised for the incident , which it said occurred because the area was incorrectly mapped in 2018 . It uses selective harvesting in native forests , but plantations are clear-felled . <p> The area was replanted with native plantation trees before Forestry Corp staff identified the error in 2022 and notified NPWS . The event did not become public until Friday . <p> Greens MP Sue Higginson said she was " shocked and aghast " at the news , the " excuses " made by Forestry Corp and the timing of the announcement the day before the Christmas shutdown . <p> Loading <p> " It 's a criminal act to damage the public protected area network . Can you imagine if it was two private landowners ? Where is the prosecution ? Where is the accountability ? " Higginson said . <p> The NSW Land and Environment Court this year found Forestry Corp had " a significant history of unlawfully carrying out forestry operations " and that it needed to be deterred from " future criminality " . In a separate case , Forestry Corp is awaiting sentencing for illegal clearing in Wild Cattle Creek , now part of the Great Koala National Park assessment area . <p> Higginson said it was a myth to think that clearing at the boundary of the national park was less significant because maintaining the integrity of the edges -- known scientifically as " ecotones " or areas of steep transition between ecological communities -- was considered highly important by ecologists to protect the broader area . <p> The statement from NPWS said the clear-felling of the site had caused broader damage , such as weed invasion . <p> NSW Forestry Corp consistently makes a loss in its hardwood division , which includes native forests and plantations of native trees . A Forestry Corp spokesman said it would adopt IPART 's recommendations for improving economic efficiency . <p> Victoria and Western Australia have ended native logging , leaving NSW and Tasmania as the only states with large public forestry industries . <p> The Minns government was elected on a promise to create the Great Koala National Park in the Mid North Coast region . This will include 140,000 hectares of existing national parks , including Bindarri , and up to 176,000 hectares of state forest . <p> Scientists say expanding the protected areas would help endangered species , including greater gliders and up to 12,000 koalas , withstand climate change . The park is expected to cause job losses in forestry and timber processing but also provide a boon for tourism .
