@@119459039 <p> It 's just past midnight in the cool , ancient forests of Tasmania . We 've spent a long day and night surveying endangered Tasmanian devils . All around , small animals scurry through bushes . A devil calls in the darkness . Microbats swoop and swirl as a spotted-tailed quoll slips through the shadows . Working here is spine-tingling and electric . <h> Subscribe now for unlimited access . <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of Today 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> Interactive Crosswords , Sudoku and Trivia <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> Weeks later , we 're in a moonlit forest in Victoria . It was logged a few years earlier and burnt by bushfire a few decades before that . The old trees are gone . So too are the quolls , bats and moths that once dwelled in their hollows . Invasive blackberry chokes what remains . The silence is deafening , and devastating . <p> In our work as field biologists , we often desperately wish we saw a place before it was cleared , logged , burnt or overtaken by invasive species . Other times , we hold back tears as we read about the latest environmental catastrophe , overwhelmed by anger and frustration . Perhaps you know this feeling of grief ? <p> The new year is a chance to reflect on the past and consider future possibilities . Perhaps we 'll sign up to the gym , spend more time with family , or - perish the thought - finally get to the dentist . <p> But let us also set a New Year 's resolution for nature . Let 's make a personal pledge to care for beetles and butterflies , rainforests and reefs , for ourselves , and for future generations . Because now , more than ever - when the natural world seems to be on the precipice - it 's not too late to be a catalyst for positive change . <h> A trail of destruction <p> Our work brings us up close to the beauty of nature . We trek through deserts , stumble through forests and trudge over snowy mountains to study and conserve Australia 's unique wildlife . <p> But we must also confront devastating destruction . The underlying purpose of our work - trying to save species before it is too late - is almost always heartbreaking . It is a race we can not always win . <p> Since Europeans arrived in Australia , much of the country has become severely degraded . <p> To top it off , a recent study estimated more than 9,000 native Australian animals , mostly invertebrates , have gone extinct since European arrival . That 's between one and three species every week . <p> Many will never be formally listed , named or known . Is this how the world ends - not with a bang , but with a silent invertebrate apocalypse ? <h> This destruction provokes ecological grief <p> The degradation of our environment affects more than distant plants and animals . It resonates deeply with many humans , too . <p> Ecological grief is an emotional response to environmental degradation and climate change , damaging our mental health and wellbeing . It can manifest as sadness , anxiety , despair or helplessness . Or it might bring a profound sense of guilt that we all , directly or indirectly , contribute to the problems facing the natural world . <p> Academic research on ecological grief is growing rapidly , but the concept has been around for decades . <p> In 1949 , American writer and philosopher Aldo Leopold - widely considered the father of wildlife ecology and modern conservation - eloquently wrote in his book A Sand County Almanac that : <p> " One of the penalties of an ecological education is that one lives alone in a world of wounds . Much of the damage inflicted on land is quite invisible to laymen . An ecologist must either harden his shell and make believe that the consequences of science are none of his business , or he must be the doctor who sees the marks of death in a community that believes itself well and does not want to be told otherwise . " <p> Ecological grief is certainly a heavy burden . But it can also be a catalyst for change . <h> Turning grief into action <p> So how do we unlock the transformative potential of ecological grief ? <p> In our experience , it first helps to share our experience with colleagues , friends and family . It 's important to know others have similar feelings and that we are not alone . <p> Next , remember that it is not too late to act - passivity is the enemy of positive change . It 's vital to value and protect what remains , and restore what we can . <p> Taking action does n't just help nature , it 's also a powerful way to combat feelings of helplessness and grief . It might involve helping local wildlife , supporting environmental causes , reducing meat consumption , or - perhaps most importantly - lobbying political representatives to demand change . <p> Lastly , for environmental professionals such as us , celebrating wins - no matter how small - can help buoy us to fight another day . <p> We are encouraged by our proud memories of helping return the mainland eastern barred bandicoot to the wild . The species was declared extinct on mainland Australia in 2013 . After more than three decades of conservation action , it was taken off the " extinct in the wild list " in 2021 , a first for an Australian threatened species . <p> Australia leads much of the world in deforestation and mammal extinction . Picture Shutterstock <p> So , for our New Year 's resolution , let 's harness our ecological grief to bring about positive change . Let 's renew the fight to return those lost voices , and protect our remaining ancient ecosystems . We can , and must , do better - because so much depends on it . <p> And maybe , just maybe , we 'll finally get to the dentist . <p> Darcy Watchorn is an early career threatened species ecologist specialising in terrestrial and arboreal mammal reserarch and conservation . <p> Dr Marissa Parrott is the senior conservation biologist in the wildlife conservation and science department at Zoos Victoria . 
@@119489655 <h> Order your espresso now for a bumpy year in coffee , oil and other commodities <h> By Javier Blas <h> Save articles for later <p> Before it 's too late , order your espresso . It will be more expensive in 2025 , and anyone trading -- or observing -- energy and commodity markets into the new year will need caffeine to survive . <p> First , a bit of honesty -- 2025 looks awfully foggy . The supply-and-demand balance of key commodities can swing from hugely oversupplied to massively in deficit , depending on unpredictable politics . <p> My crystal ball is about as good as anyone else 's about what Donald Trump , Xi Jinping , Vladimir Putin , Benjamin Netanyahu and several others will do . More than ever , predicting commodity prices in the new year is about forecasting political choices . <p> This could be the fifth consecutive season when coffee consumption surpasses production , which is unprecedented.Credit : Dominic Lorrimer <p> Still , we can anticipate a few themes -- and few bits of commodity trivia I will be watching through the new year : <h> The OPEC+ oil cartel is on the ropes <p> Having delayed a production increase by already six months , it 's unlikely that the group will be able to hike output in 2025 unless Trump comes to the rescue . Global oil demand growth in the new year is likely to reach around one million barrels a day , lower than the expected output growth from non-OPEC+ countries . The squeeze is the result of several years of high oil prices that have encouraged OPEC+ 's rivals to invest in new output capacity . <p> Trump could alter the equation if he tightly enforces current US oil sanctions on Iran and Venezuela . For nearly four years , the Biden administration turned a blind eye on rising oil exports from both countries . If the incoming US president hits Tehran and Caracas , Saudi Arabia can use the opportunity to hike production . Otherwise , I do n't see much space for extra Saudi crude . <p> But Trump can create trouble for OPEC+ , too , via two policies . One is his threat of a trade war , not only with Canada and Mexico , but also with the European Union and China , that could derail economic growth . The second is loosening regulations for American drilling . <p> Trump has insisted his top priority is lower energy prices and more US oil and gas production , so , on balance , OPEC+ is likely to struggle . Yet , with Brent trading close to $70 a barrel , oil is n't the easy short it was when it was close to $100 a barrel . <p> Advertisement <h> Like OPEC+ , British oil major BP is also on the ropes <p> The company has been a disaster in the stock market , down more than 20 per cent over the past five years . At current prices , its market value has declined to about $US75 billion ( $117 billion ) , a fraction of the $US250 billion nearly two decades ago . The company has a key date with its shareholders in early February , when it 's scheduled to update its strategy . <p> Loading <p> The strategic update may give some investors a reason to stick with the company , but it will put the spotlight on two negatives : BP will effectively issue a profit warning . <p> It previously guided the market to expect earnings before interest , taxes and depreciation ( Ebitda ) as high as $US49 billion in 2025 . The true number is probably at least $US10 billion lower . With that , share buybacks are likely to be lowered too , from a current pace of $YS1.75 billion a quarter to something far more affordable -- say , $US1 billion -- to protect the balance sheet . <p> In the oil business , the credit rating comes ahead of the shareholders . Lower earnings and a smaller share repurchase could kill investor appetite for the stock and open the door for a corporate deal . I have argued in the past that the company should seek a merger with a rival and see that as a high chance in 2025 . The most obvious one is Shell . <h> Watching OPEC+ and BP will require a steady supply of coffee <p> Brace yourself for higher prices . Brazil and Vietnam , the world 's top producers of the arabica and robusta bean varieties , face a crop shortfall . This could be the fifth consecutive season when coffee consumption surpasses production , which is unprecedented . <p> In late 2024 , the price of arabica surged to an all-time high , surpassing the nominal peak set in 1977 . It may not be enough to keep the market balanced . Coffee traders believe that if the Brazilian crop does n't recover -- something unlikely -- prices may need to climb from about 350 US cents a pound currently to somewhere between 400 US cents and 500 US cents . <p> Coffee roasters will in turn raise retail prices , particularly for the espresso made from Arabica beans . While you 're bracing yourself for higher-for-longer coffee , add hot chocolate to your list . The crops in West Africa , the region that accounts for 70 per cent of the world 's cocoa production , have n't recovered as much as previously expected , and prices are at record highs . <h> 4 ) Coal is alive and kicking <p> Coal is one of the commodities that receives less attention despite its still-huge importance to the energy system and the fight against climate change . For years , many have considered it to be dead or dying . At the COP26 climate change conference in 2021 in Glasgow , the world agreed to " consign coal to history " . <p> But it 's alive , omnipotent and omnipresent . In 2024 , the world consumed a record amount , and 2025 will be a pivotal year to see whether a change of trend occurs . I 'm pessimistic because China has adopted coal as the cornerstone of its energy system , with renewables as a complement . The Asian nation alone consumes 30 per cent more coal that the rest of the world altogether , endangering any progress to stop global warming . <h> 5 ) Iron ore faces an inflection point <p> Iron ore is , alongside coal , one of those raw materials that is often overlooked . It is n't a mainstay of commodity investing in financial markets . But it 's key for the profitability of global mining groups and steelmakers alike . And it 's a great barometer of economic activity in China . Its price has dropped to $US100 per metric ton now from more than $US200 in 2021 . <p> Loading <p> The new year could mark an inflection point for the commodity : Chinese steel production probably reached a zenith between 2022 and 2024 , and at best , it would be able to sustain an elevated plateau in 2025 . Because China nowadays produces more than half of the world 's steel , what happens there matters enormously . <p> Crucially , iron ore supply is going to increase next year too , including from a new source of low-cost production : Guinea in West Africa . Put the two forces together , and the iron ore market may enter the first of several years of surpluses . Lower prices beckon in 2025 . <p> Javier Blas is a Bloomberg opinion columnist covering energy and commodities . He is coauthor of The World for Sale : Money , Power and the Traders Who Barter the Earth 's Resources . 
@@119489826 <p> Australia 's plant research capabilities have taken a big step forward in the past 12 months , with a world-leading network established . <h> Subscribe now for unlimited access to all our agricultural news across the nation <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of This Week 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> Throughout 2024 , the Australian Plant Phenomics Facility changed its name to the Australian Plant Phenomics Network , the new title reflecting the growth in its capabilities . <p> In the same time , it has gone from three infrastructure " nodes " in two locations - Adelaide and Canberra - to nine nodes across Australia . <p> APPN chief executive officer Richard Dickmann , Adelaide , said the goal was to provide each site with cutting-edge infrastructure to aid researchers . <p> He said using a network meant the cost was not a burden for each individual university . <p> The nodes are located at Australian National University , Charles Sturt University , La Trobe University , University of Queensland , University of Sydney , University of Western Australia , Western Sydney University and the WA Department of Primary Industries &amp; Regional Development , while APPN has activities in 12 sites overall , Australia-wide . <p> APPF began in 2009 , based in Adelaide , then from 2018 , the board began reviewing its future and decided it needed a new approach - to go national . <p> To help it grow , the funding for the next five years has tripled , from $45 million to $135 million , sourced from a mix of federal government funding through the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy , state government funding , the universities involved and GRDC . <p> Mr Dickmann said the network 's benefit was that it could help generate " much more data and much better data " . <p> " We know there are lots of threats , climate change , growing population , food security , and researchers are still stuck doing things incredibly manually and slowly , " he said . <p> He said one hectare of wheat trials would usually have about 1000 plots , which could take about five kilometres of walking and one or two days to measure heights . <p> He said the most recent drone deployments could cover the same area in about 30 minutes , including the set-up . <p> " But they will also have hundreds more measurements , " he said . <p> " We , first of all , can accelerate the research process but we also can study things currently not possible . " <p> He said they could use the drone to take a new range of assessments and readings , including measuring water stress or disease . <p> " Our ambition is to create the most integrated plant phenotype network in the world , " he said . <p> " We want to create a lab on a continent . " <p> Mr Dickmann said having the same standard of equipment across the country meant there would be a standard data pipeline . <p> " A researcher can grow a wheat plant at Narrabri and Merredin , WA , and have those imaged to get the same data , then we can compare soils and climate , " he said . <p> Mr Dickman says this network stands head and shoulders above the world . <p> " It should lead to new significant insights , " he said . <p> As open facilities , the infrastructure could also be used by researchers not associated with the host universities . <p> " We have some researchers come to Australia because do n't have access to these facilities in their own countries , " he said . <p> In addition to supporting researchers , Mr Dickmann said they also wanted to make data management easier for farmers . <p> " Farmers get a lot of data but then have problems in how to collate , how to interpret and how to compare other data sets , " he said . <p> " We hope we can transfer this to a single , usable platform to farmers and farm groups . " <p> Charles Sturt University at Wagga Wagga officially became part of the APPN in October . <p> Node manager and Global Digital Farm technical officer Nelson West said the node would unlock new potential for research and innovation . <p> He said the additional technology , on the ground and through drones , was a big step up in technological capabilities . <p> " The new sensors we got as part of APPN are really advanced , " he said . <p> " Instead of looking in five or six bands of light , we can look in more than 300 bands of light . " <p> Mr Nelson said as part of the new technology rollout , they would be able to study roots in situ , and look at plant and water root interactions . <p> " We can look at more than just physical traits - look at different breeding lines and their nitrogen or water use efficiencies , " he said . 
